issues.title: Doc Season 3 Episode 7 Preview: Did Amy Lie for Ben?
issues.summary: Are we finally going to learn the big secret about what Ben and Amy concerning Ben's study on Doc Season 3 Episode 7, "Heroic Measures?" Read on for a preview. The post Doc Season 3 Episode 7 Preview: Did Amy Lie for Ben? first appeared on Tell-Tale TV.
issues.author: Sarah Fields
issues.content_html:
Are we finally going to learn what the big secret Ben is keeping from Amy regarding her involvement in his artificial heart project on Doc Season 3 Episode 7, “Heroic Measures?”

It sure seems that way from the episode promo. The promo shows flashbacks of Ben and Amy while they were romantically involved. That includes Ben asking Amy to lie for him. 

It’s hard to imagine any version of Amy lying about a clinical trial that could have potentially adverse consequences for patients.

That said, on Doc Season 3 Episode 6, “Facade,” Nina Barker (one of the new interns’ stepmother and a major donor) had information about the study that she used to blackmail Amy.

Perhaps just as concerning as whether there is a big bombshell about the past about to drop on Amy is the episode description previewing complications regarding Amy’s brain health. 

Other than the memory seizures that Amy has been having since last season, there hasn’t been much foreshadowing of any kind of major health issue.

People are understandably wary after everything that happened last season, but the seizures have mostly been an annoyance rather than anything to worry about. 

Also, none of the other preview material hints at a health crisis for Amy, so we have little to speculate on.

Whatever it is, hopefully it won’t give Ben any ammunition to undermine her because between Ben and Nina, she sure seems vulnerable to past events being used against her.  

Here’s everything you need to know about this episode, including the air date, cast, promo, and how to watch.

Doc Season 3 Episode 7 Details

  • Title: “Heroic Measures”
  • Air Date: Tuesday, November 10, 2026
  • Time: 9/8c
  • Network: Fox

How to Watch Doc Season 3 Episode 7

  • Streaming: Available next day on Hulu

Doc Season 3 Episode 7 Description

Revelations about Amy’s brain health put her future at Westside in Jeopardy. Gina pushes the limits of medicine to revive a patient who seems beyond saving. Ben begins human trials on his artifical heart implant.

Guest Stars & Returning Characters

  • Main Cast: Amirah Vann, Anya Banerjee, Blair Underwood, Jon-Michael Ecker, Molly Parker, Omar Metwally, and Patrick Walker

issues.title: Todd Howard's game design power is knowing when to make things 'simple and digestible' according to Skyrim's lead designer
issues.summary: Howard is "very good at putting himself in the seat of your typical player" says Bruce Nesmith.
issues.author: Rick Lane
issues.content_html:
//Body

Todd Howard is one of the most recognisable names in game development, yet despite this, the Bethesda director's overarching thoughts on game design remain something of an enigma. Howard has admitted that he doesn't like talking about his games. As such, we rarely get much insight into his broader design philosophy.

Yet according to Bruce Nesmith, lead designer of Skyrim, Howard certainly has a specific set of skills when it comes to game design. In a wide-ranging interview with The Examined Game, Nesmith discussed his time working with Bethesda. During the chat, Nesmith was asked what it was like working with Howard, and he credited Howard with a knack for seeing things from the player's point of view:

"Part of what Todd has, historically for Skyrim and Fallout 3 and everything, been very good at is putting himself in the seat of your typical player," Nesmith explained. "As a developer, I sit in an ivory tower. It's inescapable … I think more deeply about games, definitely, than your typical player. And he's able to cut through that and see 'Oh yeah, they're looking for a little bit of joy here. Don't get in the way with your math and your complex decision here'".

When working up close with code and the day-to-day design of things, Nesmith pointed out that developers can overcomplicate things. "I would try to make things a little more complex, and he was more than willing to say 'No, no, that's not what the players are going to want. They're going to want something simple and more digestible here.'"

Nesmith clarifies that this isn't Howard's only talent and that he "thinks very deeply about games", while Nesmith himself can also "think from the player['s perspective]. But he says that both designers had a "bias" to see things from a particular direction, and in game development, it's often good to "find other people who have a counterbias to bounce your ideas off of so that you can get the well-rounded opinion."

On this subject, Nesmith cites an example of working with an artist who had an issue with the way The Elder Scrolls' 'detect life' spell worked in Oblivion. "He said, 'Look, this spell is cool. It does this really functional thing, but do you realise it ruins all the art? We take all this care in making these creatures and people and whatnot and making them highly detailed and look really great, and all you see is this smudge when you turn on that spell.'

"Well, in Oblivion it just stayed on for long periods of time. Look what we did in Skyrim. We made it a really expensive-to-maintain spell, so the way to use that spell properly was just keep it on for a second … we listened to what the artists were saying because they had a perspective we hadn't considered before."

This approach of seeing things from the player's perspective has certainly worked for Bethesda in the past. While it may not be everyone's favourite game in the series Fallout 3 did an excellent job of making the RPG more approachable for players unfamiliar with the workings of oblique CRPGs. I do wonder, however, whether Bethesda took this design philosophy too far by the time Starfield rolled around, as the sci-fi adventure had such a simple roleplaying core that it lacked much of the dynamism and emergence that made the studios' previous RPGs so appealing.

issues.title: Denzel Washington's Final TV Role Was On An Animated HBO Kids' Show
issues.summary: Denazel Washington got his first big break on "St. Elsewhere," but after he switched to movies he made only two TV appearances, both on this show.
issues.author: James Grebey
issues.content_html:
Photo Works/Shutterstock Add TVLine on Google: Google Discover

Denzel Washington, one of the greatest actors alive, got his start on television. However, the two-time Oscar-winner hasn't graced the small screen for nearly three decades, and it seems unlikely that he'll ever do so again. That means his final TV acting credit is a voice role on a forgotten HBO show from the '90s, "Happily Ever After: Fairy Tales for Every Child."

Premiering on HBO on March 12, 1995, "Happily Ever After" was a cartoon anthology series that retold classic fairy and folk tales in a multicultural setting featuring notable voice actors. Narrated by Robert Guillaume, the roster of guest performers included Harry Belafonte, Rosie Perez, James Earl Jones, Will Smith, Samuel L. Jackon, and New York City mayors Ed Koch and Rudolph Giuliani, to name a few. Washington appeared in two episodes, as King Omar in a season 1 retelling of "Rumpelstiltskin" and as Humpty Dumpty and the Crooked Man in a season 2 episode titled "Mother Goose: A Rappin' and Rhymin' Special."

"Happily Ever After" ran for three seasons, ending in 2000. A New York Times story from when the show premiered said the animation was just passable, but the instinct to reimagine European children's tales in diverse settings was admirable, and the stories were well-told.

Unlike many movie stars, Denzel Washington didn't return to TV in the streaming era

HBO

Denzel Washington's first major role was Dr. Philip Chandler on the acclaimed medical drama "St. Elsewhere," but he essentially left television behind when the NBC series ended in 1988. Since then, he's only narrated three PBS documentaries and directed a 2016 episode of "Grey's Anatomy." Those two voice roles on "Happily Ever After" are his only post-"St. Elsewhere" TV acting credits.

Until fairly recently, this wouldn't have been notable. For most of the medium's history, movie stars rarely appeared on television. Actors like Washington may have gotten their start on the small screen, but once he'd established himself as an A-list film actor, it would've been viewed as a step backward if he appeared in a TV show. Maybe you'd get an actor to pop into a recording booth for a day or two so they could voice a cartoon character, like in "Happily Ever After," but whenever a movie star appeared on TV in the flesh, it was a big deal. 

That started to change with the streaming era, as prestigious limited series with big budgets drew Oscar-winning actors back to TV. Washington, however, never followed in the footsteps of Julia Roberts ("Homecoming"), Mahershala Ali ("True Detective"), or Nicole Kidman and Meryl Streep ("Big Little Lies").

Now it seems as though "Happily Ever After" will officially be Washington's final TV acting role. During an interview with "Today" in 2024, he announced his intent to retire after he wrapped his final projects, and none of them were TV shows.

issues.title: 10 Best Comedy TV Shows Streaming On Prime Video, Ranked
issues.summary: Prime Video is a streaming service with a varied programming lineup spanning multiple genres, but comedy is a place where the platform truly shines.
issues.author: Tyler Pisapia
issues.content_html:
Comedy Central Add TVLine on Google: Google Discover

It's no secret that the streaming app space is pretty crowded these days. There are so many great options with vast libraries of entertaining content to choose from. However, if you're a person who loves a good chuckle, you arguably get good bang for your buck with Prime Video, which has a slew of laugh-out-loud comedies to choose from.

The streamer is chock-full of hilarious, time-tested, award-show-approved comedies. Another feather in Prime Video's cap is that a lot of them have very decent episode counts to keep viewers engaged and binge-watching for longer.

Many of the app's best shows, like "Invincible" or "The Boys," have comedic elements and are often laugh-out-loud funny, but are not technically comedies. To help genre purists who are just looking for some yucks after a stressful day, we've compiled just 10 of the many dedicated comedies worthy of your time that will have you in stitches.

10. Workaholics

Comedy Central

In 2011, Comedy Central and other TV networks were looking to the new frontier of online sketch comedy to identify the next big names in the genre. They struck gold with "Workaholics," starring Blake Anderson, Adam DeVine, and Anders Holm. Based on a series of sketches titled "5thyear" written by and starring the trio and Kyle Newacheck (who went on to direct 41 episodes of "Workaholics") while under the sketch group name Mail Order Comedy, "Workaholics" remains one of the best examples of a comedy that followed the internet-to-TV pipeline.

The premise of "Workaholics," like the original sketches that inspired it, is pretty simple. A group of college friends, who bonded like family in the way that only college roommates can, try to keep the party going into adulthood. While the concept may not seem that creative, it's the chemistry among its stars and the unique humor they painstakingly bring to every single minute of "Workaholics" that make this show a must-watch for comedy fans. 

Even as their individual stars started to rise in Hollywood, the cast poured their all into the show that gave them their start for seven seasons, making America laugh and changing pop culture forever.

9. Upload

Amazon Studios

Whenever Greg Daniels gets a "creator" credit on a show, it's usually worth paying attention to. He's co-created hits like "King of the Hill," "Parks and Recreation," and, of course, "The Office." In 2020, he brought "Upload" to Prime Video as one of its many original series. It stars Robbie Amell as Nathan Brown, a brilliant programmer who dies in the year 2033. In this near-future, human beings are able to upload themselves into a virtual afterlife, assuming they've got the money to do so.

Anything that Daniels touches is usually pretty funny, and when he's at the helm of an entire show, watch out. Not only is "Upload" packed with jokes, some of which are darkly humorous given the subject matter, but the show also isn't afraid to make its audience think. Everything from the writing, directing, and Amell's performance are both hilarious and heartfelt, a definite trademark of Daniels' work. Meanwhile, the show itself has a lot to say about consumerism, relationships, and death while still finding spaces to pack in some clever humor.

"Upload" was a bit of an underrated hit, running a total of four seasons with 29 episodes between 2020 and 2025.

8. Reno 911!

Comedy Central

Those who may have thought that the content found on "Cops" or "Live PD" was so outrageous that you simply can't make the stuff up were wrong. In 2003, series creators Robert Ben Garant, Thomas Lennon, and Kerri Kenney came out with one of the funniest mockumentaries of all time with "Reno 911!" It ended its run on Comedy Central in 2009 after six seasons and a theatrically released movie, before being revived for two more seasons and two more movies on streaming.

The show follows the wildly inept yet heavily armed members of the Reno Sheriff's Department as they patrol around The Biggest Little City in the World. However, the real highlight is seeing the cavalcade of recognizable faces in comedy (some before they were famous, like Jim Rash), each portraying characters you'd typically see on shows like "Cops," exaggerating the outrageousness of their criminal personas just a little bit. Because the officers can encounter literally any odd character in their work, the show proved to be a breeding ground for great sketch comedians and improvisors to thrive and get early attention.

While hilarious, the show often traffics in some pretty raunchy humor, which is perfect for people who want to pull the blinds, close the door, and laugh at some politically incorrect humor.

7. Patriot

Prime Video

An underrated sleeper hit hiding in the Prime Video library, "Patriot" is a dark comedy created by Steve Conrad, who gained a lot of attention with the critically acclaimed miniseries "DTF St. Louis." Like a lot of his work, "Patriot" deals with very complex, interesting, and totally bizarre characters as their lives cross paths in completely unexpected ways. It's a show that isn't afraid to shock you, leave you in an awkward silence, or make you think. In a world where most comedies are lighthearted and kind of broad, "Patriot" stands out as a must watch for any connoisseur of unique comedy.

The show follows John Tavner (Michael Dorman), a spy for the CIA who has recently been through a pretty traumatic experience. He specializes in going undercover with very in-depth secret identities so that the U.S. government can have an agent in strategic yet unexpected places. He also makes his way to open mics at dive bars in the U.S. and Europe, where he can sing about the truth of his life. 

This formula not only provides space for a great, modern dark comedy, but it has some surprisingly good original music that's sure to have viewers tapping their toes and adding songs like "Afternoon Spray" to their playlists.

6. The IT Crowd

Channel 4

"The IT Crowd" is a British series that gained a cult following of sophisticated comedy fans throughout its four seasons and one special. The show is set in the offices of the fictional Reynholm Industries and its headquarters in London. It stars Chris O'Dowd, Richard Ayoade, and Katherine Parkinson as employees of the company's IT department. Also making regular appearances is their boss, Douglas Reynholm, played by "What We Do In The Shadows" alum Matt Berry.

It's a classic workplace comedy, but it's also so much more than that. The series showcases the immense strengths of its cast, with Ayoade playing a socially awkward genius, O'Dowd as an apathetic, roguish screw-up who is somehow still lovable, and Parkinson as a genuine person trying her very best every day and coming up short. Perhaps the most endearing thing about "The IT Crowd" is its relatability despite being completely wacky at times.

Much of the comedy derives from the IT department trying to mingle and be seen as valued members of the company, often going hilariously awry. What's more relatable than failing to fit in?

5. Fleabag

Amazon Studios

For even some of the most critical TV viewers, "Fleabag" is considered by many to be as good as it gets. It's one of the few series to earn a 100% rating on Rotten Tomatoes, for whatever that means to you. Regardless, one thing is clear — something about this very unique comedy captured people's minds.

"Fleabag" is based on creator, writer, and star Phoebe Waller-Bridge's deeply personal, tightly written, and, hysterical one-woman show of the same name that premiered at Edinburgh Festival Fringe in 2013. The series follows a young, sexually liberated woman who calls herself Fleabag, navigating modern life in London. She's snarky, somewhat caustic toward people who try to help her, and has a very cutting wit that she doesn't always use for good.

However, as the series goes on, it becomes clear to the viewer that there is a lot more going on here than just seeing a sometimes abrasive old soul dealing with the modern world. The show deals heavily with grief, adulthood, and all the emotions that go with it. Despite that heavy subject matter, Waller-Bridge finds a way to fill every moment with laugh-out-loud banter.

Although "Fleabag" is only two short seasons consisting of six episodes each, it's worth noting that things really take off in Season 2 with the addition of Andrew Scott's character, The Priest (colloquially referred to by fans as Hot Priest). His banter with Fleabag is unparalleled in TV and well worth any comedy fan's time.

4. The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel

Prime Video

If you came to this list because you like comedy TV shows, how about a comedy TV show about comedy? Taking place in the 1950s and '60s, "The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel" shows all the ways that the comedy business has changed, as well as all of the ways that it's tragically stayed the same.

The series follows Miriam "Midge" Maisel (Rachel Brosnahan) as she discovers a natural talent for stand-up comedy after her marriage to a dismally untalented aspiring stand-up comedian ends. With the help of her intrepid, off-color, and trusty manager, Susie Myerson (Alex Borstein), Midge develops a stand-up career. But what makes the series truly one to watch is that she does so alongside some of the real-life greats brought to life through talented impressions like Lenny Bruce (Luke Kirby), Carol Burnett (Leslie Rodriguez Kritzer), and Moms Mabley (Wanda Sykes). 

Seeing these real-life legends on screen alongside Midge, showcasing the highs and lows of show business at the time, makes the series an enjoyable watch. However, some of the real magic of "The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel" comes from the moments where Midge isn't working on her career, but dealing with her immensely intrusive parents and her family life. When the show isn't highlighting a side of show business people don't usually get to see, it's showing a relatable side of family life that most people get to see. 

3. The Good Place

NBC

What happens when we die? What makes a person good or evil? What do human beings owe each other? These are questions that are tackled at length in the halls of university philosophy departments, as well as the Emmy-nominated NBC sitcom "The Good Place." The show is the brainchild of acclaimed creator and producer Michael Schur, whose other credits include "Brooklyn Nine-Nine" and "Parks and Recreation."

"The Good Place" follows a woman named Eleanor Shellstrop (Kristen Bell), who wakes up in a waiting room and learns from a man named Michael (Ted Danson), who says he's a literal angel, that she has died. Because of the remarkably virtuous and good life she led, Eleanor went to the Good Place, where her every want and need is met, and she'll live in a society made up of other wholly good people. The only problem is they've got the wrong Eleanor Shellstrop.

Due to its literal life-or-death subject matter, handled only in the way a trusted talent like Schur can, there is truly no other comedy tackling the issues that "The Good Place" tackles. In addition to having one of the best twists in television history, the show is wall-to-wall great jokes from an impossibly talented cast including D'Arcy Carden, William Jackson Harper, Jameela Jamil, Manny Jacinto and more. Forget what we owe to each other; you owe it to yourself to check out this once-in-a-lifetime comedy.

2. Freaks and Geeks

NBC

If you're looking for your quintessential teenage high-school series where the love lives of jocks and cheerleaders reign supreme, look elsewhere. "Freaks and Geeks" was created by Paul Feig and stars some big names like Jason Segel, Busy Philipps, Linda Cardellini, Martin Starr, Seth Rogen, and more way before they became household names. In addition, with just one season under its belt before NBC pulled the plug, the show remains a go-to example of a series that was canceled far before its time.

"Freaks and Geeks" is set in a Detroit suburb during the 1980-81 school year, and, for the most part, follows the lives the Weir children — Lindsay (Cardellini) and her little brother Sam (John Francis Daley), as he starts his freshman year at her high school. The show is a uniquely funny exploration of the wrong side of the tracks with some timeless things to say about growing up in America. There have been countless shows about the high-school experience of jocks and cheerleaders. "Freaks and Geeks" takes a much more relatable approach and shows the significantly larger population from every American high school of kids who don't quite fit in trying to find their way. 

With the bonus of seeing a stacked cast act their tails off before they were famous, "Freaks and Geeks" is arguably the foundation for a lot of today's comedy. 

1. Jury Duty

Amazon Studios

Ronald Gladden is an average guy living in California who gets the dreaded call that all adults in America fear. He's got to report for jury duty. He's been told that a documentary crew will be filming the trial as an exploration of the United States judicial system. However, what he doesn't know is that's all a lie.

Ronald is the only person — including the judge, attorneys, victim, defendant, and even his fellow jurors — who isn't an actor. Behind the scenes, producers are carefully crafting one of the most insane and intricately bizarre trials in history, all to see how this regular Joe reacts to everything falling apart around him. The real appeal of the show, though, is the fact that Ronald is such a good-natured guy that he never fails to take an empathetic approach to all the people acting totally insane around him. What could have been a mean prank show ends up being one of the most heartfelt comedies in recent memory.

The premise is wild, and the results are astoundingly hilarious. In fact, the results were so captivating that they somehow managed to do it again to a man named Anthony Norman in Season 2. This time, instead of thinking he's on a jury, Norman thinks he's taken a weekend job to assist a small company on its annual retreat.

issues.title: Keep Me Close: Finding My Home in You, Vol. 1
issues.summary: By Morrinmomo and whimhalooo. Released in Japan as “Watashi ga Kaeritai Basho wa ~Ibasho o Nakushita Reijou ga “Tokenai Hyouzou” to Uwasa Sareru Ryoushu-sama no Moto de Shiawase ni Naru made~” by DRE Novels. Released in North America by J-Novel Club. Translated by Amy Osteraas…
issues.author: Sean Gaffney
issues.content_html:
By Morrinmomo and whimhalooo. Released in Japan as “Watashi ga Kaeritai Basho wa ~Ibasho o Nakushita Reijou ga “Tokenai Hyouzou” to Uwasa Sareru Ryoushu-sama no Moto de Shiawase ni Naru made~” by DRE Novels. Released in North America by J-Novel Club. Translated by Amy Osteraas.

Generally speaking my reviews don’t have continuity, and you should not have to read them day by day to get the gist of what I think. Sometimes, though, timing plays a major role. This week saw the release of two shoujo LNs with, if not similar plots, at least similar framing devices – the evil stepmother and stepsister, and years of horrible abuse. And they came out within two days of each other, so I am reading them one right after the other. Theoretically I could have put Housekeeping Mage in between them, but, well, that also deals with abuse destroying someone’s psyche. So this may be part one of two, as in this review I discuss abuse as a main plot point with romance being secondary, and then in Deja Vute I’ll circle round to the opposite. That said, secondary doesn’t mean minor. It’s just that in the case of Keep Me Close, the abuse drowns out the rest of the book – and that’s on purpose.

The book begins by speed-running the normal “Villainess” beginning. Claudia Innsbruck is whisked out of her home, where she had been doing servant work, and taken to the Crown Prince, who announces her horrible crimes. He wants her executed, but her stepmother and stepsister, who are so so wonderful, convince him to merely exile her to the south, to be a servant to (please read on, I promise it’s a good book) the legendary “Icy Duke”. On her arrival, Julius, who is unsurprisingly merely incredibly bad at dealing with women, and his assistant Anton, discover that not only is the selfish, spoiled daughter who embezzled all that money a broken, quivering wreck of a young woman, but that she’s suspiciously good at some things, such as finances and ledger bookkeeping. Is it possible that this is all another reminder that all stepmothers and stepsisters are evil unless proven otherwise?

Claudia is the highlight of the book, and the story does not skimp in showing what two years of abuse can do to a confident girl. We don’t see much of it, as this takes place after her exile, but we get the staccato refrain of “you will never be allowed to be happy”, which by this time she has taken to heart. Most of the book is not a typical romance as she and Julius, whose words always come out as “angry”, are just completely unable to deal with each other. I also liked the thriller aspect of the second half, as once Claudia recovers somewhat and decides to fight back, it becomes clear that it’s not just a stepmother and stepsister she has to deal with, but a much trickier opponent, who has several backup evil schemes. Fortunately for Claudia, this country has a King, and he’s not dead. Bad news for the Crown Prince. Also, while this book is mostly serious, there were a few laugh out loud moments. The king explaining to a horrified stepmother that money can be exchanged for goods and services just made me imagine him as Homer Simpson.

This is done in one, but there’s a second volume, like so many shoujo light novels. I assume that’s why the stepsister wasn’t completely removed from the story. In any case, if you don’t mind a heroine ground down by trauma, and her journey to recover, this is a very good book.

issues.title: Ridley Scott’s R-Rated Sci-Fi Masterpiece is Officially Being Cut From Netflix
issues.summary: Alien and Aliens are leaving Netflix on Dec. 1, giving subscribers limited time to stream Ridley Scott’s sci-fi classics.
issues.author: Sam Hill
issues.content_html: Ridley Scott has directed some of the most iconic science fiction movies of all time, from Blade Runner to The Martian. However, few have had the same lasting impact as his 1979 sci-fi horror classic Alien. The film helped redefine the genre by combining the terror of a slasher movie with the vast, isolating setting of outer space, introducing audiences to one of cinema's most memorable monsters in the process.

issues.title: 5 Cop Dramas That Were Canceled Too Soon
issues.summary: These short-lived cop dramas deserved better, but timing sometimes isn't right. Whether it was ratings or budget, these shows were canceled before their time.
issues.author: Jonathan Siefer
issues.content_html:
FX Add TVLine on Google: Google Discover

From "NYPD Blues" to "The Wire," many cop shows have enjoyed a long, successful place on television redefining what a cop drama should be, but some of them were short-lived, even though they deserved better. Cop shows have taken audiences by the hand and satisfied their appetite for the procedural and substantive aspects of law enforcement. The intersection of grizzly shootouts, department politics, and the personal lives of police officers makes for a unique, entertaining look at one of society's most dangerous professions.

It goes without saying that several shows fitting this description have aired over the years, but not all of them enjoyed as long a life as "CSI" or "Law and Order." Sprinkled throughout the history of cop shows are the ones that had great ambition, but never got the chance to fully blossom into what they could've been. In honor of those series that got the boot before they could reach their full potential, here is a list of five cop shows that were taken down far too early.

Paris (1979)

CBS/YouTube

A one-season series, "Paris" featured James Earl Jones in his first television starring role as Woodrow Paris, a captain with the LAPD supervising a group of young detectives. Aside from his position as a police officer, the series also showcased his home life with his wife Barbara (Lee Chamberlin) and his second job as a criminology professor at a college.

This CBS series was conceptualized by legendary producer Steven Bochco, who would go on to develop procedural dramas like "L.A. Law" and "Hill Street Blues." Despite good reviews, the show was cancelled after airing only 11 of the pilot season's 13 episodes.

The behind-the-badge look at the main character's life outside the police department was not common for cop shows during this time. This is a structure that Bochco would implement in most of his work. Unfortunately, it was not enough to save the show with a 10:00 pm Saturday time slot. This was one of the worst times of the week to air a show. Most people were either in bed or out with friends at that time.

Prodigal Son (2019-2021)

Fox

Fox's two-season crime/psychological drama "Prodigal Son" featured Thomas Payne from "The Walking Dead" as Malcolm Bright, a former FBI profiler working as a consultant with the NYPD to solve crimes. On the show, Bright regularly consults with his incarcerated serial killer father, Dr. Martin Whitly (Michael Sheen), a former surgeon.

Taking a page from shows like "Hannibal" or like "Criminal Minds," the series utilized the always-intriguing aspect of seeking advice from criminals about the anatomy of crimes. This specific dynamic happening between a father and son is what made the show truly stand out. Sadly, it wasn't enough to keep it going.

Fox cancelled the series after the second season, owing to a drop in viewership from the first season. According to Deadline, the show's status was already on thin ice since it barely got approved for a second season, making the lower ratings the final nail in the coffin. Nevertheless, "Prodigal Son" maintains a loyal fanbase, and audiences could've seen further growth with Bright's professional and familiar relationship with his father. Unfortunately, the series was axed before this could happen.

Crime Story (1986-1988)

NBC

While the 1980s had no shortage of cop shows, show developer Michael Mann took a unique approach to the genre with "Crime Story." Its premise, beginning in the 1960s, centered on the specific feud between Chicago police lieutenant Mike Torello (Dennis Farina) and psychopathic mobster Ray Luca (Anthony Denison). Luca rises through the ranks of organized crime, eventually bringing the feud to Las Vegas when he gets involved with casinos.

Rather than utilizing a "case of the week" format that was standard for most cop shows at the time, "Crime Story" told a continuous story throughout the series. While the structure of the show was intriguing, NBC cancelled the series after only two seasons. It aired Tuesday nights at 9:00 pm, the same time slot as ABC's "Moonlighting." The historical backdrop of the series also incurred high costs that NBC could no longer justify. As a result, they pulled the plug on Michael Mann's series.

The Bridge (2013-2014)

FX

Based on a Scandinavian series of the same name, "The Bridge" centers on the partnership of two detectives pursuing a cross-border serial killer. In this FX crime drama, Sonya Cross (Diane Krueger) is a tight-laced detective with the El Paso Police Department who teams up with Chihuahua police officer Marco Ruiz (Demián Bichir) after someone is found murdered on a bridge connecting Texas with Mexico.

While most cop shows are centralized to one location like Los Angeles or New York City, "The Bridge" was unique for featuring an international setting. Being primarily set around the border, the series explored US/Mexican relations while following Ruiz and Cross' pursuit of the killer.

Unfortunately, the series saw a steep audience drop with its second season, which shifted focus to international issues like cartels and human trafficking after the original showrunner left. FX was also discouraged by the show's lack of accolades and did not renew it for a third season.

Backstrom (2015)

Fox

After playing the beet-loving Dwight Schrute on "The Office," Rainn Wilson went from a Pennsylvania paper salesman to a Portland police officer on Fox's "Backstrom." The series featured Wilson as Lieutenant Everett Backstrom, an offensive and misanthropic detective. Despite his negative tendencies and tumultuous working relationship with his colleagues, he is a brilliant and sharp investigator.

Backstrom was the type of character that audiences were not used to seeing Wilson play. His insufferable attitude provided Wilson the opportunity to show off his acting chops. Viewers compared Backstrom's personality to Hugh Laurie's character on Fox's medical drama "House."

After the first season ended, Fox did not renew it for a second season. Despite very good viewership of the premiere episode, the ratings declined every week following. While Wilson's character was well-portrayed, his brash nature made him unlikable to audiences and critics. If given more time, however, Backstrom could have grown into a likable and respectable character, and personal layers to his complicated self could have been explored more fluently.

issues.title: Xbox is testing a way to use your phone as a controller on smart TVs
issues.summary: Xbox is testing two new ways to play its cloud games, and one of them doesn't require a controller at all. Read more
issues.author: Vikki Blake
issues.content_html:
Xbox is testing two new ways to play its cloud games, and one of them doesn't require a controller at all.

Announced on Xbox Wire on 4th November, the phone controller preview is rolling out on supported TVs wherever Xbox Cloud Gaming is available. The phone option - which works with both Android and iOS devices - lets you use your phone "as a controller when you don't have one nearby". Connect to your TV via QR code, and the controls open in your phone's browser.

The second preview, called cloud connect, is currently limited to the US and lets the new Xbox Nano controller talk to your cloud session over wi- fi instead of pairing directly with your TV to "help reduce input latency, so gameplay feels more responsive".

To try out the phone controls yourself, switch on Preview Features under Settings > Account in the latest version of the Xbox smart TV app.

Xbox has published a setup guide with full instructions, although you should note that both experiences "are still being tested", so the availability and supported games or devices "may be limited while [Xbox] learns from your feedback".

ICYMI, as of yesterday, anyone in the Xbox Insider Program can try Microsoft's updated Xbox PC app. The company claims it now boots up 60% faster, several pages can launch up to 50 percent faster, and in-app windows can open up to 65 percent faster.

issues.title: After furloughing its developers and then hiring some of them back, Star Wars Zero Company developer has laid off an unspecified number of staff
issues.summary: "While it stings, I'm really proud of what we built together."
issues.author: Rick Lane
issues.content_html:
Star Wars Zero Company developer Bit Reactor has laid of an unspecified number of developers, after furloughing its entire team and then hiring some of that staff back.

As reported by the Star Wars website Bespin Bulletin, several designers of the acclaimed tactics game have taken to LinkedIn to announce that they have been let go by the studio. Among those affected are senior environment artist Ryan Lopez, who worked on the game for three and a half years and has been on furlough for the past three and a half months.

"While it stings, I'm really proud of what we built together," Lopez wrote in a LinkedIn post.

Other designers who lost their jobs include UI Engineer Tyler Eichten and senior quality assurance analyst Ryan Mosher, who spent two years at Firaxis and a further two years at 1047 Games before joining Bit Reactor in October 2024.

It's been a tumultuous few months for Bit Reactor. In September, it was reported that the studio had furloughed up to 80% of its staff in the weeks leading up to Zero Company's launch, with the studio having reportedly "run out of most of its money" ahead of the game's launch. At the time, former senior technical artist Zachariah Scott said the project was built with "shocking austerity". Scott also accused Bit Reactor of "concealing the fact that the team was furloughed weeks ago" after the company made the announcement.

Within a month, Zero Company had sold one million copies and Bit Reactor subsequently announced it had hired back some of its staff. In a statement posted on Bluesky, CEO Greg Foertsch stated that the furlough had been a response to "unexpected business developments outside of our control" and "necessary to help us eventually bring as many people back as we can".

Clearly, though, Zero Company's commercial performance hasn't been enough to bring back everybody. Which is a shame, considering that Zero Company is by all accounts a brilliant Star Wars adventure. Resident word Jedi Ted Litchfield called it " one of the best games of 2026 and a new all-timer Star Wars videogame" in his Star Wars Zero Company Review.

Zero Company isn't the only knockout Star Wars game to release this year either, with Star Wars: Galactic Racer providing a similarly scintillating experience in a galaxy far, far away. Indeed, the performance of both games appears to have pleased Star Wars overlords Lucasfilm, and the company is keen to do more creative spins on the universe in the vein of Zero Company and Galactic Racer.

issues.title: 10 Funniest 'Far Side' Comics About Cows
issues.summary: Gary Larson's The Far Side often featured cows in funny situations. Here are the 10 funniest examples
issues.author: Brian VanHooker
issues.content_html: From 1980 until 1995, cartoonist Gary Larson wrote and drew The Far Side. It was a single panel comic strip filled with non-sequitur, surreal jokes mostly aimed at adults instead of children, which was unusual for newspaper comics at the time. Also unusual was the fact that, unlike most daily comic strips, The Far Side had no recurring characters. Peanuts has its gang of kids and Garfield has its cast of humans and animals, but every panel of The Far Side introduces new characters and scenarios all aimed at delivering one single joke.

issues.title: James Earl Jones' First TV Leading Role Was On A Failed Steven Bochco Crime Procedural
issues.summary: James Earl Jones took on a very different kind of role in this Steven Bochco procedural. The show lasted just one season, but it made an impact with critics.
issues.author: Jonathan Siefer
issues.content_html:
Kevin Winter/Getty Images Add TVLine on Google: Google Discover

Producer Steven Bochco was known for procedural dramas, developing shows like "L.A. Law" and "NYPD Blue." But one of his shortest-lived procedurals featured James Earl Jones in his first leading television role.

"Paris" aired on CBS from September 1979 to January 1980, starring Jones as Woodrow Paris, a captain with the LAPD who leads a squad of young detectives. As their supervisor, Paris managed them strictly, while still acting as their mentor. The series also explored Paris' life outside the police department, showing his home life with his wife Barbara (Lee Chamberlin) and his second job teaching criminology at a city college.

Sadly, Jones' first leading TV series was cancelled by CBS less than four months after it premiered. But that certainly did not slow Jones' career. The series also led to his marriage, as he met his future wife Cecilia Hart on set, where she portrayed the role of police sergeant Stacey Erickson. 

Despite low ratings, Paris was a critical hit

Sonia Moskowitz/Getty Images

"Paris" would last just one season, and CBS only broadcast 11 of the 13 filmed episodes. The series aired Saturdays at 10:00 p.m., one of the worst time slots of the week. By that time during the week most people are either asleep or out socializing instead of sitting in front of their televisions. Despite this, the critical reception for Jones' police procedural was excellent.

Praise was directed towards the show's portrayal of Paris' life outside of police work, providing depth to Jones' character beyond the badge. This is an element that Bochco would continue with in other shows, including his next project, "Hill Street Blues."

Aside from his life at home with Barbara, audiences also saw another side to his professional life through academics. The way Paris conducted himself in his classroom was an interesting contrast to how he commanded his officers at the precinct.

issues.title: Mass Effect’s Cruelest Moral Choice Remains Gaming's Most Haunting Mission 19 Years Later
issues.summary: Mass Effect’s Homecoming quest asks you to hand a widower his wife’s body or keep it for research. Neither ending feels clean, but one is better
issues.author: Rebecca Corgan
issues.content_html: So when, years later, an Alliance clerk told Shepard that a fallen marine named Nirali Bhatia “may save more lives in death than she did in life,” Shepard was faced with the decision — the opportunity — to make Nirali’s death count for something. Before the question ended, she was already agreeing. Hand a grieving husband his wife’s body? Or keep her for research that might save more lives down the line? Someone was going to pay for whichever answer I chose. (I knew Shepard would say yes. I also knew, thumbs hovering over the controller, that every part of me wished she wouldn’t.)

issues.title: How A Mistake In Warner Bros. Contracts Helped Eleven Film & Jack Thorne Land ‘Lord Of The Flies’ TV Rights — Thessaloniki
issues.summary: “It’s the only thing I’ve ever done that I’d describe, without feeling embarrassed, as hard work,” Joel Wilson of Eleven Film said when discussing his role as an executive producer on Jack Thorne’s Lord of the Flies adaptation. Wilson was speaking on a panel at the Thessaloniki…
issues.author: Zac Ntim
issues.content_html:
“It’s the only thing I’ve ever done that I’d describe, without feeling embarrassed, as hard work,” Joel Wilson of Eleven Film said when discussing his role as an executive producer on Jack Thorne’s Lord of the Flies adaptation.

Wilson was speaking on a panel at the Thessaloniki Film Festival, where the series is screening this weekend.

Wilson added: “It was genuinely physically tough and psychologically rigorous. But the creative process was the most joyful one I’ve ever been involved in.”

Related Stories

News

Thessaloniki: Walter Thompson-Hernández's 'If I Go Will They Miss Me' Among Titles Set For International Competition

News

Thessaloniki: Adaptation Of Ioanna Karystiani's 'Swell' Among 2026 Agora Works In Progress Titles

The four-part series, based on William Golding’s novel of the same name, launched on the BBC in the UK in February and started streaming on Netflix in the U.S. in May. Adolescence co-creator and Emmy winner Thorne adapted the book for the screen.

Wilson told the audience in Thessaloniki that the process began many years earlier, when he unsuccessfully contacted Golding’s estate to enquire about purchasing the Lord of the Flies TV rights.

Watch on Deadline

“I hadn’t done very much, and they politely told me to come back later,” Wilson joked. “So I did, again and again. Eventually, we made Sex Education, and our reputation had grown since the first time I’d called them.”

Wilson added that he later developed a relationship with the agent who owned the stage rights to the book, whom he called “every six months”, and later tipped him off about a potential quirk in the book’s copyright contracts that could open the door for a TV adaptation.

“Warner Bros. owned the rights and had tried to remake it several times without success,” Wilson explained. “It was unclear in the original contract whether Warner Bros. owned the film and television rights or only the film rights because the idea of making Lord of the Flies for television wouldn’t have been considered at the time.”

Wilson said the Golding family retained the TV rights and, miraculously, around the same time, Thorne, whom he had worked with before, mentioned his interest in adapting the book.

“I’d offered him another project he didn’t want to do, and said, ‘If you don’t want to do that, how am I ever going to get you to work with me again?’” Golding said of the conversation he had with Thorne.

“He responded, ‘If you can get the rights to Lord of the Flies, I’ll do that.’ It’s one of the only moments in my life I’d genuinely describe as serendipitous. I nearly fell off my chair and said, ‘I’m speaking to the family about it now. Can I email them on Monday with Jack Thorne—Lord of the Flies in the subject line? He said, Absolutely.”

Wilson explained that with Thorne attached, the project quickly picked up momentum.

“We then pitched it to the BBC. It was the first time this had happened to me, though it seems to happen to everyone else: We went in and said, ‘Jack wants to make Lord of the Flies. Are you in?’ They said, ‘Yes, please,’” Wilson recalled. “There wasn’t even a script, but the vision was very clear, and they greenlit it.”

Marc Munden (The Mark of Cain, National Treasure) directed the series, with Wilson executive producing alongside his Eleven colleague Jamie Campbell and Thorne. Hans Zimmer provided music for the series, which was nominated for two Emmys.

“I think we managed to do exactly what we set out to do: protect the vision Jack and Mark had, which relates so closely to the original novel,” Wilson said of the series. “I’m glad to say Judy, William Golding’s daughter, was delighted with it. That was one of the most important things, because the book was so precious to her.”

The 2026 Thessaloniki Film Festival runs until November 15.

issues.title: Sydney Sweeney's New Netflix Sci-Fi Epic Is Mandatory Viewing For Transformers Fans
issues.summary: Robots (not) in disguise.
issues.author: Collier Jennings
issues.content_html: Transformers is a franchise that has built-in appeal in more ways than one. Apart from the concept of giant robots transforming into vehicles, there's the fact that two factions of these robots have been engaged in a war that spans millenia. There have been highs (including the grossly underrated Transformers One) and lows (including most of Michael Bay's films), but it's more than likely that we'll be seeing Transformers stories until the heat death of the universe. Netflix is aiming to deliver its own take on another property that features giant robots, and it's tapped Sydney Sweeney to play a leading role in this potential franchise.

issues.title: Nier: Automata developer is 'currently investigating' a bizarre update bug that drastically inflated the game's file size from 50GB to 366GB
issues.summary: Square Enix is 'working to resolve the issue'.
issues.author: Rick Lane
issues.content_html:
Usually, it's a good thing when a patch makes an already excellent game substantially larger. But in the case of Nier: Automata's most recent update, bigger is most certainly not better. On Friday, the beloved action RPG from Square Enix received what should have been a straightforward update to added localisation support for Simplified Chinese, Traditional Chinese and Korean languages. But as reported by Automaton Media, the update also increased the game's file size from 50 gigabytes to a staggering 366 (and a half) gigabytes.

"We have identified an issue following the latest update for Nier: Automata … where installation requires significantly more storage space than intended," wrote Square Enix in a Steam post. "We are currently investigating the cause and working to resolve the issue. We apologise for the inconvenience."

It isn't clear how this issue has occurred, but it may be related to Nier: Automata's DLC. When selected for download on Steam, each DLC appears to have the same file size as the base game. Weirdly though, this is only true for the initial download and installation. Once the game is installed, the file reportedly reverts to a more appropriate size of roughly 50 gigs.

Indeed, as a temporary solution, Square Enix suggests that anyone who needs to download Nier: Automata deselects all eight DLC when they do so. "As a temporary workaround, you can download the base game using the intended amount of storage space by going to "Properties" à "DLC" in Steam and unchecking each DLC item."

While 366 gigabytes is obviously a ridiculous size for a game, what's frightening to me is that games are on track to become that massive in the coming years. Big budget games regularly exceed the 100 gigabytes in file size these days, while several major titles like Call of Duty: Modern Warfare and Call of Duty: Black Ops Cold War, have surpassed 200GB.

One of the largest reported installations to date is for the combat simulator DCS World, which had a maximum file size of 250GB back in 2021. So although Nier: Automata's SSD-choking file-size is an accidental anomaly, it might also be an ominous glimpse into the future of PC gaming.

issues.title: PÖFF Stands With Ukraine: A Look at Films Featured at Tallinn Made Despite, and Because of, the War
issues.summary: The Estonian fest has been showing solidarity with Ukraine across its film, industry and other programs since the 2022 full-scale invasion of the country by Russia, and its 30th edition is no different.
issues.author: Georg Szalai
issues.content_html:
The Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival (PÖFF) has been standing with Ukraine and showing solidarity since the 2022 full-scale invasion of the country by Russia, featuring Ukrainian films, showcasing works-in-progress and organizing Ukraine-themed panels in its industry strand Industry@Tallinn & Baltic Event.

“We are obliged to do everything possible to help and support the Ukrainian film industry at this difficult time, but even more so the Ukrainian people,” PÖFF founder and CEO Tiina Lokk said in 2022. This year, for the 30th anniversary edition of the festival, its PÖFF Standing With Ukraine film showcase is back.

“Ukraine is fighting not only for Ukraine, but also for Europe and the democratic world,” Lokk tells THR. ”And so we are going to support Ukraine and stand with Ukraine as long as needed. It is important for Ukraine to remain very visible and to keep its culture. And it is very important for every country.”

Related Stories

Oscars 2027: Int'l Films in Focus

'Hold Onto Me,' Cyprus' First Oscar Hopeful, Stars a Newcomer and a 'Dogtooth' Actor in a Very Personal Father-Daughter Drama

TV

'The Remarried Empress' Sets Disney+ and Hulu Record With Biggest Local Original Launch Ever

Marge Liiske, head of the Industry@Tallinn & Baltic Event, emphasizes that the industry strand of the Estonian festival also continues to put a spotlight on the war. “We have since the 2022 [full-scale invasion by Russia] very supportive of Ukraine and have always reflected that in our program, both for the festival and the industry events,” she tells THR.

She and Triin Tramberg, PÖFF’s new artistic director, highlight that they will always put a spotlight on Ukraine and other countries standing up for important democratic values. “Throughout our program, we’re supporting countries that are fighting for their rights and for their democracy,” Tramberg tells THR. “We also have to understand where we are located. Standing With Ukraine is really important for us as a region, and it speaks to our audiences and our communities, including Ukrainians who live here. It is important to have this moment where they see their own cinema.”

PÖFF’s Standing With Ukraine strand this year showcases nine features that are diverse and different. And many also screen in other Tallinn strands, as you can see below. Take a closer look at the films right here.

Slava: Shooting With Music
Director: Jacqui Morris, David Morris
Festival section: Special Screenings

Silence the guns and let the music play! This world premiere is about the power of music and culture more broadly.

“Sviatoslav Vakarchuk is the lead singer of Okean Elzy, Ukraine’s most successful rock band. He is a former politician and activist who has a PhD in theoretical physics,” reads a synopsis of the film. “Slava has been compared to Bruce Springsteen and Paul McCartney, and his songs are an important part of Ukrainian identity, part of the country’s cultural DNA. He is now channeling his talents to liberate his country.”

After playing more than 200 concerts for the troops, he decided to take his band on a worldwide tour to bolster the morale of Ukrainian refugees living abroad. And an international coalition of artists, including Coldplay, stepped up to support the band. Highlights the Synopsis: “Another reason for the tour was to leave a lasting legacy in the minds of the rest of the world of Ukrainian culture – a unique culture Russia has been trying to eradicate for centuries.”

Vesna
Director: Rostislav Kirpicenko
Festival section: Baltic Film Competition

Honoring the dead becomes dangerous in times of war, as this film shows. In a town in southeastern Ukraine that is occupied by Russian forces, burying the dead has actually been forbidden. The church of a young priest has even been turned into a morgue for executed civilians. But the priest begins to quietly resist, secretly returning the bodies to their families at great personal risk. And in the process, he forms an unlikely bond with an 11-year-old boy who becomes a silent witness to his rebellion.

The drama adds a focus on the psychological and emotional warfare beyond the physical battles. “Lithuanian-born Ukrainian director Rostislav Kirpicenko uncovers cynicism, blackmail, and the brutal cruelty of the merciless attackers,” the PÖFF website says about the film.

What would you do if you were in the shoes of the locals who face horrible choices – fight back, obey and adapt to the brutal new reality, or even betray? Emphasizes the festival website: “The mightiest impact here is heartbreaking authenticity, showing how Ukrainians are surviving the ongoing occupation.”

I Rarely Wake up Dreaming
Director: Isabelle Stever
Section: Standing With Ukraine

War surely can affect love. But how does the transition from peace to warfare – yes, Russia’s full-scale invasion! – affect a queer couple in Ukraine, especially when the geopolitical change comes in parallel with a gender transition?

I Rarely Wake Up Dreaming made an impact when it world-premiered at Locarno, leading to conversations between viewers and beyond. You can read our chat with the creators right here.

But you really have to watch the film to see how the relationship between Olya and Oleh is put to the test when the gender transition allows the couple to get married, but also stirs up all sorts of personal and national identity struggles.

To Die to Live
Director: Yuliia Hontaruk
Festival section: Doc@PÖFF Baltic Competition

Yuliia Hontaruk’s doc introduces us to three men who have experienced huge change over the course of their lives.

In 2014, they had no military experience but volunteered to go to the front line. When they returned home after two years, they tried to find an ordinary life rhythm again. But they just can’t seem to succeed. After all, the war has left its mark on their bodies and minds, which affects their family lives.

“It is a brutal truth that is not always easy to capture on film,” the PÖFF summary of the film notes. “And then the men have to go back to war. Their previous experience was merely a preparation for what would happen in February 2022, when Russia launched a full-scale invasion. They are back on the front line, now fully aware of what this does to them.” The filmmaker followed the three men for 12 years, leading to a film whose fragmented feel mirrors the fragmented lives and trauma.

Wings
Director: Ana Rocha de Sousa
Section: Standing With Ukraine

You can take people out of a war zone. But can you ever really take the war trauma out of their lives? Or in other words: Is living in peace the same as enjoying peace of mind?

Wings is a drama, shot in Ukraine and Portugal with creatives from both countries, but it was inspired by the real-life story of a Ukrainian family who fled the war and found refuge in Portugal.

If you are interested in a deep dive into the lasting impact and trauma of experiencing war and displacement, plus how there may be a path to finding hope, this one is for you.

Living On
Director: Nerijus Milerius
Festival section: Doc@PÖFF Baltic Competition

Art therapy at a veterans’ theater, yoga sessions, hair salons, para-archery and mountain peaks and much more feature in another Ukraine-focused world premiere coming to PÖFF.

Standing with Ukraine is exactly what Lithuanian philosopher and director Nerijus Milerius did when he volunteered to drive cars with medical aid to Ukraine’s front lines. Between August 2024 and June 2026, he documented his experiences on 15 dangerous missions and used the filmed material for his fourth feature.

“He records daily life under attack and hears dark humor in Kyiv, Kharkiv, Odesa, Kherson and other bombed areas where he needed a fixer even to gain access,” reads a Tallinn festival tease for the film. And it highlights: “Milerius captures Ukrainians’ resilience and spirit.”

Slava
Director: Denis Sobolev
Section: Standing With Ukraine

No, this one is not about the rock star Slava we met earlier but a woman. And the story is much more complex. The political thriller is based on a real-life story and shows Slava and Yaroslav Stetsko launching an information campaign, via media and protests, in the U.S. and Europe in the 1960s. Their message: the KGB and the USSR are the architects of political murder beyond Soviet borders.

That makes a trial in Karlsruhe, West Germany, take on a political dimension. Bohdan Stashynsky, a KGB agent, has confessed to killing Stepan Bandera, a controversial far-right Ukrainian politician. But while the case is being framed as a “routine” crime, the activists want to highlight that Moscow is exporting political violence via assassinations abroad.

The Kremlin responds with threats. And the activists’ friends become concerned, urging them to soften the rhetoric. To see how it all plays out, you’ll have to watch Slava.

Camouflage
Director: Mykyta Gibalenko
Section: Standing With Ukraine

A clash of identity and war already played a key role in one of the films we discussed earlier. They are also in focus in this movie, which premiered at Venice, but in a different way.

Vitaly, 22, studies German and moves from Ukraine to Germany, leaving behind his mother, a teacher shaped by the Soviet era, and his sister. And once in Munich, Vitaly finally feels free to be himself and live the life he wants to lead.

But a year later, Russia invades Ukraine. And, as you may have expected, due to the war, his mother and sister have to flee their home and seek refuge with Vitaly in Munich. That’s where they learn about his new identity…

Traces
Directors: Alisa Kovalenko, Marysia Nikitiuk
Section: Best of Docs

Last, but certainly not least, PÖFF Standing With Ukraine will screen a Ukrainian awards season contender. Silence isn’t always golden. Just listen to the six Ukrainian women who survived sexual violence and torture during the Russian war against Ukraine and speak out in Traces.

Iryna Dovhan, a former captive-turned-activist, documents testimonies of women affected by the trauma of war-related violence. And following her work, the film weaves together a portrait of collective trauma while opening space for hope.

The film premiered in the Panorama section of the Berlin International Film Festival, winning the program’s best documentary award, and became Ukraine’s submission for the best international feature film Oscar.

issues.title: ‘3 Body Problem’ Director Derek Tsang Boards DEA True-Crime Series ‘Group 41’ From Zhang Yimou’s ‘Shadow’ Producer Jonah Greenberg (EXCLUSIVE)
issues.summary: “3 Body Problem” and “Better Days” filmmaker Derek Tsang is attached to direct and executive produce “Group 41,” a true-crime drama series about the first Asian-American squad at the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA). The project, from Jonah Greenberg’s Salty Pictures…
issues.author: Naman Ramachandran
issues.content_html:
“3 Body Problem” and “Better Days” filmmaker Derek Tsang is attached to direct and executive produce “Group 41,” a true-crime drama series about the first Asian-American squad at the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA).

The project, from Jonah Greenberg’s Salty Pictures, is at the Taiwan Creative Content Fest (TCCF) in Taipei.

The 10-episode series, with 45-minute episodes, opens in New York in 1986. While the DEA has its sights set on Colombian cocaine cartels and the city’s “Five Families” of the Mafia, a scrappy crew of Asian-American agents teams up with a hard-charging Irish prosecutor nicknamed “The Dragon Lady.” Together they form DEA Group 41, which becomes the first squad to chase the No. 4 heroin pouring into the U.S. through a network few had noticed.

Related Stories

Liev Schreiber and Stephen Graham Lead Apple TV's Gripping Serial Killer Thriller 'Nocturne': TV Review

Over the next decade, the underfunded unit grows into an elite international task force. Its targets include Johnny Kon, a Hong Kong boss whose billion-dollar triad spans five continents; Johnny “Onionhead” Eng, a brutal Chinatown gangster; and Khun Sa, a warlord in the Golden Triangle with a 20,000-strong narco-army. The show explores immigration, prejudice and what the American Dream costs, with stories from both sides of the law.

Greenberg, a former managing director of CAA’s China office whose producing credits include Zhang Yimou’s “Shadow,” wrote the source book with Marc Iserlis and Aidan Swift, who are also producers and writers on the series. Greenberg says shows about present-day law enforcement can be great, but surveillance technology now gives cops the upper hand.

“Back in the 1980s when you went undercover, you went deep. And all the bad guys carry guns, and the danger to cops and informants is real,” Greenberg says.

The crimes, and the agents who solved them, were largely overlooked at the time, he adds.

“It simply wasn’t considered as sexy to work Chinese cases in the 1980s. People were busy watching ‘Miami Vice’ (myself chief among them!) and watching Rudy Giuliani convict the Italian mobsters,” Greenberg says.

Neither the media nor even the DEA made Asian cases a priority, according to Greenberg. “So it’s an underdog story. It’s literally the war on drugs we actually won but which no one knows about.”

He also sees room for several seasons across the 10-year saga, with Khun Sa looming over the whole show as a Colonel Kurtz-like final target, giving the series what Greenberg calls a “save the best for last” advantage.

The source material, a 180-page nonfiction book titled “The Incredible Story of D.E.A. Group 41 & The Rise and Fall of the Asian Heroin Trade,” will be published next year. Greenberg says the team has the trust and cooperation of the real people involved. Taiwan’s Each Other Films, co-founded by co-producer Tiffany Yu-chia Chen, is on board as co-production partner, and former CAA TV co-head Adam Berkowitz of Lenore Entertainment Group serves as executive producer.

After seven years of development, the next steps are to find a writer-showrunner and possibly attach cast before pitching to platforms next year.

Greenberg says what has kept him with the project is a wish to tell stories about people driven by purpose, pointing to Cathy Palmer and the agents of Group 41, who took apart a heroin pipeline running from Southeast Asia to the U.S.

“‘Serpico’ was always a foundational film for me and well, maybe nobody liked the guy, but he lived by a certain code. And that’s what interests me,” he says.

At TCCF, the team wants to learn how incentives in Taiwan and elsewhere in the region could offset the budget, and to explore distribution in Asia, so that production, financing and perhaps even distribution are lined up efficiently before pitching to U.S. platforms.

The Taiwan Creative Content Fest, organized by the Taiwan Creative Content Agency (TAICCA), runs Nov. 6–9 at the Taipei Nangang Exhibition Center.

issues.title: Davika Hoorne Returning for ‘Inherit’ Sequel, Director Banjong Pisanthanakun Confirms (EXCLUSIVE)
issues.summary: Banjong Pisanthanakun, the Thai director of horror hits “Shutter” and “Pee Mak,” tells Variety his new psychological horror film “Inherit” will get a sequel, with star Davika Hoorne set to return. “Inherit,” a Centrepiece selection at the Toronto Film Festival, where it world…
issues.author: Naman Ramachandran
issues.content_html:
Banjong Pisanthanakun, the Thai director of horror hits “Shutter” and “Pee Mak,” tells Variety his new psychological horror film “Inherit” will get a sequel, with star Davika Hoorne set to return.

“Inherit,” a Centrepiece selection at the Toronto Film Festival, where it world premiered in September, is closing the Jakarta World Cinema festival.

Pisanthanakun and Hoorne first worked together on 2013 horror-comedy “Pee Mak,” Thailand’s biggest local box office hit of all time.

Related Stories

Taylor Swift, Inducted Into Nashville Songwriters Hall of Fame, Says 'There Is No Music Community Like This Music Community. I Know, I Checked All the Communities'

Hoorne plays Woranart, a youthful-looking grandmother who moves in with her granddaughter’s wealthy family. The family soon discovers she harbors a centuries-old centipede spirit with sinister designs on the youngest in the household, Oui (Baipor Thitiya Jirapornsilp).

Hoorne was Pisanthanakun’s first choice for the immortal grandmother.

“The character has to be sexy, beautiful, and funny at the same time. I think of her as a fashion icon, too,” Pisanthanakun tells Variety. “The first image that I have was her wearing a bikini and sunbathing beside the pool, which is very modern. She talks like this [era’s] woman, talking to ChatGPT. She’s a very adaptable girl.”

On set, Pisanthanakun advised Hoorne to study Catherine Tramell, Sharon Stone’s character in “Basic Instinct,” and Anthony Hopkins’ Hannibal Lecter in “The Silence of the Lambs.”

Hoorne also starred in “A Useful Ghost,” the satirical Thai comedy-thriller that took Cannes’ Critics’ Week Grand Prix in 2025. She regards that film and “Inherit” as her return to cinema.

“For movie, I carefully choose the project that I want to do,” Hoorne says. “One project takes around one year of working, so I really have to choose the one I’m gonna live with for such a long time to bring up my soul as an actress. So, trust me, watch it, I pick for you guys already.”

Pisanthanakun says that 20 years ago, horror was all about the concept – ghosts in photos or on videotapes – with filmmakers competing over where to make the ghost appear.

“Actually, after ‘Shutter’ and ‘Alone,’ there came a time when I really got bored of making horror films; even going to the cinema to watch horror films made me fall asleep right away,” the director says. “After films like ‘Hereditary’ and ‘It Follows’ came out, I felt like there were still other new, refreshing ways to make horror films. The modern horror, especially from the Hollywood side, is now very creative. I think it’s the only genre that still has something creative coming up.”

His film “The Medium” was produced by Korean director Na Hong-Jin.

“When I made this project with him, he shared his opinion on how the international market would react all the time. I just made this film [the way I normally do]. But he’s gonna give his opinion on how the international audience would perceive it,” Pisanthanakun says.

“I want the concepts and the story to be as solid as possible, and I want the atmosphere to be everything. It has to be very unique, and everything has to be like authentic,” he adds.

On AI, he says: “I think it’s inevitable in the system, but I think people can use it as long as it’s not violating other people’s rights.”

“The Thai film industry right now is not so good – that’s the real pressure because I want this movie to bring Thai audiences back to the cinema,” Pisanthanakun says. “Inherit” opens across Thailand Nov. 19.

He adds that public funding for Thai film production is neither robust nor consistent, and only goes to horror.

Hoorne has moved into producing girls’ love (GL) titles, a genre of romance stories between women that is popular in Thailand.

“It’s gonna be better if we have funding from the other help of the government; that help is the independent themes that can go internationally,” Hoorne says. “When I’m producing a movie or series, it is very hard to find the funding, and it is really hard for Thai films to recruit people for different genres. Because you have to draw people into the cinema, drama or comedy, something that looks small, people tend to wait.”

Hoorne has also directed a family short film, “Soap Opera,” which recently wrapped, and will focus on TV series in 2027. Pisanthanakun is leading a Thai-Korean horror co-production.

issues.title: 'There Was a Cute Girl in the Hero's Party, So I Tried Confessing to Her' Anime Gets 2nd Season

The story centers on Yōki, a man reincarnated into a fantasy world. Yōki did not reincarnate as a hero or the demon lord, however, but as the demon lord's underling. issues.title: AI Filmmaking Platform Core Studio Launches at Taiwan Creative Content Fest With 24 Specialized Agents
issues.summary: Taiwanese technology company imCore Corp. launched Core Studio, an AI filmmaking platform that aims to cover the full production process, from script development and storyboarding to image generation, editing and color grading, at the Taiwan Creative Content Fest (TCCF) in…
issues.author: Naman Ramachandran
issues.content_html:
Taiwanese technology company imCore Corp. launched Core Studio, an AI filmmaking platform that aims to cover the full production process, from script development and storyboarding to image generation, editing and color grading, at the Taiwan Creative Content Fest (TCCF) in Taipei on Saturday.

Built by a Taiwanese team with roots in animation and visual effects, the platform runs on its own in-house image-generation model and also works with outside generative AI models. It follows standard filmmaking workflows, so creators can handle several stages of production in one place instead of switching between tools.

Related Stories

Taylor Swift, Inducted Into Nashville Songwriters Hall of Fame, Says 'There Is No Music Community Like This Music Community. I Know, I Checked All the Communities'

Guests at the launch included Erica Wang, CEO of TCCF organizer the Taiwan Creative Content Agency (TAICCA), along with representatives from the Taipei Film Commission and imCore’s strategic partners, filmmakers and AI industry professionals.

“Our team understands that professional creators need more than just image-generation tools. They need a comprehensive solution that can genuinely integrate into their production workflows,” said Charles Lee, founder and CEO of imCore Corp. and founder of TWR Entertainment. “Core Studio was developed around the needs of frontline film professionals, transforming years of production expertise into an AI-powered platform that provides more comprehensive creative support for filmmakers.”

The platform’s main draw is a set of more than 24 specialized AI agents that act as a virtual production crew, handling story development, asset generation, visual effects, editing and color grading. imCore pitches them as a way to lower the technical hurdles of AI-assisted filmmaking.

For pre-production, Core Studio’s Story Atlas tool breaks an imported script into scenes, shots and storyboards. It also sets up character designs, costumes, props and voice profiles so they stay consistent from one sequence to the next.

Every AI-generated output comes with a record of the models, prompts, parameters, costs and human review results behind it. Production teams can use it to track creative decisions and keep an eye on budgets.

The platform also includes Real Engine, which combines three image-processing tools: Real Video, Real HDR and Real Revive. They sharpen image detail, raise color depth from 8-bit to 16-bit and fix blown-out highlights in AI-generated footage.

A cloud workspace with real-time communication, version control and access management lets teams in different countries work on the same project.

Creators of four AI-assisted projects presented their work at the launch, among them Jerry Zhou, the creator of “God Being.”

“There are many agents on the editing page that can help with sound effects. I can separate the sound effects and dialogue from AI-generated footage and make detailed adjustments,” Zhou said. “This gives me more flexibility and creative space, allowing me to work more comfortably as a creator.”
