issues.title: Toei CEO Fumio Yoshimura Talks Global Expansion, GenAI Adoption & Entry Into Games
issues.summary: Fumio Yoshimura, CEO of Japan’s Toei Co, explained how the studio is working with local partners to globalize its long-established IP, as well as innovating in areas including GenAI and gaming, in a keynote Forum session at Taiwan Creative Content Fest (TCCF). In 2023, the…
issues.author: Liz Shackleton
issues.content_html:
Fumio Yoshimura, CEO of Japan’s Toei Co, explained how the studio is working with local partners to globalize its long-established IP, as well as innovating in areas including GenAI and gaming, in a keynote Forum session at Taiwan Creative Content Fest (TCCF).

In 2023, the 75-year-old studio launched an ambitious $2BN ‘Toei New Wave’ plan to boost its international revenue’s share of total income from 30% to 50% by 2033, which included upgrades to its studio facilities in Tokyo and Kyoto. Since then the company has embarked on several international co-productions and partnerships, started exploring GenAI technology and moved into production of games.

Related Stories

News

'Dune' Star Chang Chen Introduces Six Rising Taiwanese Actors In Golden Horse & TCCF Showcase

News

Weta FX CEO Daniel Seah Unpacks TAICCA Partnership: "Taiwan Has Creative Talent, Technology & Government Support"

Yoshimura started the session by explaining how the company has been introducing its popular IP to international markets. The latest series in one of its oldest franchises, Kamen Rider Zetz, is currently streaming in Taiwan and other international markets, with India a particular focus.

Watch on Deadline

“In 2025, we held an event to introduce Kamen Rider to India consumers. We got a very good response and signed a contract with a Disney affiliate to distribute the content. Due to its population size and the growth of its middle-class, we see India as a promising market,” Yoshimura said.

Kamen Rider was one of the first franchises that Toei globalized, working with U.S. partners to produce an English-language verskon, Mighty Morphin Power Rangers, more than 30 years ago, with the franchise now handled by toymaker Hasbro. Both the Kamen Rider and Power Rangers franchises have been extended to toys, merchandising and live events.

In other IP extensions, Toei recently teamed with Sony’s Anyplex Inc and Godzilla VFX house Shriogumi Inc to launch a Kamen Rider anime label.

Other recent localization efforts include the Voltes 5 franchise, which was first launched as an anime in Japan in 1977 and became a cultural phenomenon in the Philippines where its themes of resistance against a repressive empire got it banned by the Marcos regime. In 2023, Philippines broadcaster GMA produced a live-action remake, Voltes V: Legacy, which became a ratings hit in the Philippines and also aired in Japan.

“Simply exporting content limits its reach, so in order to break through constraints, we are producing remakes and localisations,” Yoshimura explained.

After getting started with remakes, Yoshimura said the studio is now also working on local productions based on original stories: “We’re developing local content from scratch, working with local talent to release locally and then sell globally. We believe this local first model will generate more sustainable long-term revenue than the traditional export model.”

Among recent productions, Toei worked with Taiwan’s Lou Lou Film Studio on Dear Stranger, directed by Tetsuya Mariko and starring Hidetoshi Nishijima and Gwei Lun-mei, which screened on the festival circuit last year. More recently, the company worked with Taiwan’s Wowing Entertainment Group on horror film The Rope Curse 4: Kuntilanak, directed by Liao Shih-Han and starring Lee Kang-sheng.

Yoshimura identified Taiwan as another key market for Toei’s global expansion, due to cultural similarities and the popularity of Japanese IP in Taiwan. “Data shows that Japanese films had a 26% share of Taiwan’s box office last year, the second highest share after Hollywood with 41%,” Yoshimura said. “Taiwanese audiences have a strong interest in Japanese content.”

Toei has also partnered with Thailand’s M Studio on a slate of Thai-language remakes and local features, and is currently working with both M Studio and Korea’s Showbox on a horror feature based on Japanese manga The Long Hair In The Attic, by artist Junji Ito.

The studio has also stepped into assisting the growing number of international productions now shooting in Japan, encouraged by Japan’s incentives scheme, including U.S. indie action thriller Iris, created by and starring Dani Swan (The Matrix Resurrections). In addition to providing facilities, Toei helped with casting for the film and assisted on the incentives application.

On the tech front, Yoshimura explained that the company is expanding the Virtual Production and motion capture facilities at its studios in Tokyo and Kyoto and also starting to use AI in workflows.

“We’re also experimenting with GenAI image generation,” Yoshimura said. “The Toei team is performing tests on practical AI applications daily; building tools to assist junior producers in estimating production budgets, and using AI in background artwork. However we believe human creativity remains the core of everything we do.”

Microdrama is another area that Toei has stepped into – producing Everyday Host Club, a 24×3-minute anime series, and a 30-episode short-form vertical drama, Meshimori Onna, made for smartphone screens.

Gaming is another new area for Toei as it explores how to expand its IP across borders and formats. “Gaming is a global entertainment medium and delivering games to users worldwide aligns perfectly with our global expansion strategy,” Yoshimura said.

Toei plans to launch its first game, Hino, developed by UnGloom Studio, in spring 2027, followed by Debug – Nephemee and Killa later next year. All the games will be distributed across platforms and consoles including Steam, Nintendo and Xbox.

The session entitled ‘Survival Strategies for Global Enterprises: Japan’s Toei on IP, Globalization, and Business Mindset’ took place as part of TCCF’s Forum section, which also includes sessions on Japan’s K2P Film Fund, Indonesian studio MD Entertainment’s scaling strategy, as well as panel discussions on co-production, mircodrama, AI adoption and IP exploitation.

TCCF is taking place November 6-9 at the Nangang Exhibition Center in Taipei.

issues.title: Tesla is pulling the plug on the Cybertruck
issues.summary: The company will halt production of the head-turning pickup truck to make way for Cybercabs.
issues.author: Sam Klebanov
issues.content_html:
The most common reason for someone to start posting pictures from the highway will soon be no more. Tesla will stop producing the Cybertruck at its Texas Gigafactory by mid-2027, Elon Musk said yesterday.

Musk said the move is meant to make room for the company’s autonomous Cybercab. The decision to nix what was once Tesla’s most hyped vehicle comes after the Cybertruck became a commercial flop, hitting just 10% of its sales goal.

Shattered window dreams

At the Cybertruck’s 2019 unveiling—when Tesla’s design chief broke its supposedly bulletproof window—Musk billed the futuristic pickup truck as Tesla’s “best product ever.”

Tesla bet the Blade Runner-inspired stainless steel design, planned $40,000 price tag, and a version with a 500-mile charging range would make it the first EV to dominate the lucrative pickup market. But like a brutalist municipal building, the head-turning creation looked more promising in the blueprint:

  • After Covid delayed its initial release, the pickup’s late-2023 arrival in showrooms was met with lukewarm demand.
  • It didn’t help that the Cybertruck was plagued by tech issues that led to several recalls, ended up costing $60,000, and never had a range that surpassed 325 miles.

Few takers: While Musk predicted yearly sales would reach 250,000 vehicles, just under 73,000 have been sold in total so far, per data from Motor Intelligence. The vehicle continues to have a cult following among Musk fans. But sales dropped sharply after he vocally backed President Trump, and it turned into a polarizing symbol amid the Tesla CEO’s controversial effort to downsize the government. US sales dropped to 20,237 in 2025 from 38,965 in 2024—and are down a further 28% this year.

Looking ahead: After the Cybertruck rides into the sunset, Tesla will have just two human-driven models in production, the Model 3 and the Model Y (its Roadster airborne sports car isn’t scheduled to start production until 2028). The company is going full throttle with plans for a nationwide rollout of its two-seater autonomous Cybercabs, which are already ferrying passengers in Austin.—SK

issues.title: Italian chef fired for refusing to put pineapple on ’za
issues.summary: The pizza maker said it was an “insult to his culture.”
issues.author: Dave Lozo
issues.content_html:
An Italian chef working in Australia claimed he was wrongly fired from his job for refusing to put pineapple on pizza, telling the country’s Fair Work Commission the dish is an “insult to his culture.”

The commission dismissed Davide Tamburella’s claim on the grounds that he filed it too late, not that he was wrong. The La Costa restaurant, located in Queensland, has since closed. The state produces 100% of the country’s commercial pineapples and is home to a 52-foot-tall pineapple called The Big Pineapple (makes sense).

But, just like a Chicago pizza, this goes deeper:

  • Tamburella’s bosses cited his foul language and communication style as reasons for his firing in the ruling, which also included a claim that he broke his hand punching a metal railing.
  • This was allegedly the third time in four years that he refused to put pineapple on pizza.

Most surveys show that Americans are split on the tropical fruit topping, but one poll in 2023 found that 72% of Australians love it.

In the end, Tamburella got a new job at another Italian restaurant in Brisbane that does not have pineapple pizza on the menu.—DL

issues.title: ‘Hold Onto Me,’ Cyprus’ First Oscar Hopeful, Stars a Newcomer and a ‘Dogtooth’ Actor in a Very Personal Father-Daughter Drama
issues.summary: Writer-director Myrsini Aristidou's feature debut, starring Maria Petrova and Christos Passalis ('Dogtooth'), tells the story of an 11-year-old girl whose father she has never known comes to town.
issues.author: Georg Szalai
issues.content_html:
It’s summertime in Cyprus. Iris, 11, spends her days with her older best friend, Danae. But then she hears that her grandfather has died. Visiting town for his funeral is Iris’ father, Aris, whom she has never known.

That is the starting point for Hold Onto Me, the feature debut of writer-director Myrsini Aristidou. Can Iris and Aris find a way to connect, even though he is a petty criminal and doesn’t want to take responsibility? Iris doesn’t give up and gets involved in his various schemes, despite warnings from her mother and her older brother. What begins as a stubborn attempt to reconnect slowly unfolds into a fragile bond. But then, Aris’ dark past gets them into trouble.

Related Stories

TV

'The Remarried Empress' Sets Disney+ and Hulu Record With Biggest Local Original Launch Ever

Movies

AFM Hot Project: Rosamund Pike to Star in Body Horror 'Feed'

Hold Onto Me, starring newcomer Maria Petrova and Christos Passalis (Dogtooth), premiered at Sundance, where it won the World Cinema Dramatic Audience Award. It then became Cyprus’ first-ever international feature film Oscar submission.

Now, the film screens in the Just Film youth and children’s event of the 30th edition of the Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival (PÖFF) in Estonia. Cercamon is handling sales.

Lasse Ulvedal Tolbøll was the cinematographer on the Cyprus-Denmark-Greece co-production. The editors were Jenna Mangulad and Aristidou. Aristidou and Monica Nicolaidou produced the film, with Thomas J. Mangan IV and Mark Hollinger as the executive producers and Anders N.U. Berg, Konstantina Stavrianou and Rena Vougioukalou as co-producers.

Watch a trailer for the film right here.

Aristidou talked to THR about her bittersweet first feature, pairing an unknown as the young girl at the heart of it with the man who played the son in Dogtooth, her desire to make Hold Onto Me feel different and that first-ever Cypriot Oscar submission.

The father-daughter theme is one that the filmmaker has also explored in two shorts. “I feel like this is like a triptych,” Aristidou tells THR. “My first short film called Semele in 2015 is also a father and daughter story and was the first time that I began exploring this theme. Then I did my second short film, Aria, which has a father daughter dynamic again, but with an older daughter – she’s a teenager. They were short, and I wanted to go deeper in this subject matter.”

Hold Onto Me allowed her to do so in feature form, but she wanted it to be surprising and different from other films about similar familial relationships. “I wanted to use the archetypical relationship of father and daughter within a love story,” she explains. “It’s kind of a love story. It’s about two people who don’t know how to be together. They are sort of strangers in the beginning. They meet, then slowly come together, and they end up accepting each other or even loving each other in their own way. And when you set this up within the framework of a father, daughter and their family, it creates a different energy.”

That is driven by societal expectations we have for family members. “When someone is your family, you are expected to love them, or you have more expectations than from just any stranger,” Aristidou highlights. “However, they are strangers. They have never really met or had any shared experiences. So this is the first time they are reconnecting, and I wanted to explore this.”

The characters and story of Hold Onto Me keep developing as the movie unfolds, and that is by design. “On a first feature, it’s very easy to get very obsessed with what you want to do, so I was very tough on myself,” Aristidou tells THR. “When it comes to narrative structure and characters, I like to move the story forward in every scene. When I was writing, I was really thinking about that.”

One key reason that the filmmaker has returned to father-daughter stories lies in her own life experience. “It’s very personal in many ways,” she shares. “My parents divorced when I was very young, and I was not really growing up with my dad. He wasn’t entirely gone like this character, but he was not that present. And he’s not a criminal but a writer. It was only when I turned 12 or 13 that we started having more of a relationship. And when I was 15, 16, we really bonded. We reached a point where we started talking about everything and we really forgave each other. We reconnected, and there was really an understanding and acceptance.”

The film’s setting is also personal. Hold Onto Me was shot in Cyprus, and for the writer-director, it was particularly important to film near the sea. “I grew up near the sea, so there are references that are very personal,” Aristidou tells THR. “My dad used to have a small boat when I was a kid. I also always used to hang out with older kids because I had an older friend who was my best friend. There is a lot of truth in the film.”

The chemistry between Iris and Aris in the film is palpable To ensure the right fit, casting took a lot of time. “We were shooting in July. Around April, I decided I was going to work with Christos,” the director recalls. She wanted to see him interact with different kids, most of them in Athens. The actor then went to Cyprus to meet the girl who ended up making the cut. “I saw Christos with Maria, and they felt family in a strange way,” Aristidou tells THR. “They phsically have things in common and look a bit like family. But Maria had zero experience. She had never done anything [in acting]. But I felt that there was something with them.”

With the big casting decisions made, she was hoping to rehearse with the two leads, but that didn’t work out. “Christos was shooting something. And then, he got COVID, so he only arrived a day before the shoot,” she recalls. “We only read the script once, and then I just started shooting with both of them. So I just threw Maria into the wild with him. But I think it worked out perfectly because they didn’t know each other really – just like their characters.”

The Oscar submission was, of course, special for the writer-director feel, especially since it’s the first for Cyprus. “It’s a big honor,” Aristidou shares. “I suddenly felt very responsible for my whole country. But in many ways, this film and I are carving this path for Cyprus. There was no film from Cyprus in Sundance before, and then we won an audience award. And then the Oscars. I guess it’s a new thing for everyone here and for me. So I’m learning a lot in the process. I know we’re a bit of the underdogs, but I’m trying to enjoy the ride.”

So, what’s next for the filmmaker? “I really love this dynamic of strangers coming together and realizing how similar they are or bonding,” Aristidou says. “I don’t think I would do a father-daughter film again. But there’s something about this narrative arc that I really love. Actually, I’m trying to work on a TV show, which is a crime, spy thriller. But, let’s see. I’m working on a couple of things, and I’m reading a lot of scripts because my agents in the U.S. are sending a lot of scripts to read. So I’m also open to directing something I haven’t written.”

issues.title: After 2026 Midterms, Bill Maher Asks Trump, “Donnie, Are You OK?”
issues.summary: “Here’s something I could not have predicted, which was Trump’s reaction to the election. He said, ‘Congratulations to the Democrats, they did a good job,'" Maher said on Friday's 'Real Time' episode.
issues.author: McKinley Franklin
issues.content_html:
Bill Maher reacted to the 2026 midterm results during the Friday episode of Real Time, moreso reacting to President Donald Trump‘s response to the election.

During the host’s monologue, he said he predicted the midterms would be positive for Democrats. “Well, look, I hate to gloat, but sorry, I have to do a little bit because everybody was hedging about this election,” he said, as a montage of clips of him predicting the results was played.

One thing Maher said he couldn’t have anticipated? Trump’s response to the results, he said.

Related Stories

TV

The Other Midterms Flip: Broadcast Networks, Led by NBC, Dominated Election Night Coverage

News

Jimmy Kimmel, Seth Meyers Call Out Trump's "I Wasn't on the Ballot" Excuse for Midterm Losses: "Shut Up"

“Here’s something I could not have predicted, which was Trump’s reaction to the election. He said, ‘Congratulations to the Democrats, they did a good job,'” Maher said wide-eyed, looking around at his Real Time audience. “Donnie, are you OK? I know we’ve been feuding. You sound unwell. You’re not even going to fake it was rigged?”

He continued, “And let me tell you something, even with the attempted rigging — and they did try to rig it in every different kind of way; mail-in balloting, intimidating the voters, all that shit — democracy, man. Kind of fucking awesome.”

During an interview with The New York Times shortly before 10:30 p.m. on Tuesday, the president said he was “absolutely willing” to accept the results. Trump added, “We’ll work with the Democrats, and we’ll, you know, look forward to working with them. We’ll probably work something out.”

However, he also ranted about the midterms, writing on Truth Social that if he was on the ballot, “we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!”

Maher’s comment about “feuding” with the president was likely a reference to their recent back-and-forth that was heightened after Trump penned a lengthy social media post where he slammed the comedian as a “complete and total loser,” and shared more details about their recent dinner at the White House.

Maher responded to the rant during last week’s Oct. 30 episode of Real Time, joking that the president “went off on me like Kelly Clarkson in a toy store.”

Elsewhere in the episode, the comedian said he thinks the president has been “amazingly humble” amid the results. “I thought by this time, he’d be suing the voters by name, individually, and arresting the poll workers. Instead, even he was like, ‘You know, even I’m sick of me a little bit.’”

He joked that Trump saying he has “a lot of friends in the Democratic party” might open the door for him to visit the White House for a third time. “Wow, I might get to go again. Look at that,” he joked.

issues.title: Robert Pattinson & Nicholas Hoult Round Out James Bond Screen Tests
issues.summary: After weeks of wondering who could be up for the mystery James Bond screen test, Deadline has not only found out who the actor is, another suitor was also added to the mix. While not confirmed, insiders tell Deadline that Robert Pattinson and Nicholas Hoult joined Jack Lowden…
issues.author: Justin Kroll
issues.content_html:
After weeks of wondering who could be up for the mystery James Bond screen test, Deadline has not only found out who the actor is, another suitor was also added to the mix.

While not confirmed, insiders tell Deadline that Robert Pattinson and Nicholas Hoult joined Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor and Callum Turner in recent screen tests to play the next 007. While it was recently reported that four actors tested, insiders say a fifth test was added at the 11th hour (though it is unknown which actor was that last addition).

Amazon could not be reached for comment.

Related Stories

News

'Primetime' Star Skyler Gisondo On Pushing Beyond His Comfort Zone & Teasing What's Next For Jimmy Olsen

News

Robert Pattinson To Receive 40th Annual American Cinematheque Award

Deadline hinted at who the potential suitors were earlier this afternoon with confirmations coming tonight:

Watch on Deadline

The process to find the next 007 goes back to the spring, when the studio announced casting director Nina Gold was joining the project and that the search was underway. Following two months of meetings, Deadline reported the first round of auditions would take place in August; since then, the studio, producers Amy Pascal and David Heyman and director Denis Villeneuve cut the list to its final group and worked out test offers in September.

The final tests were originally planned for earlier in October, but due to scheduling conflicts with the finalists, were pushed to the end of the month so they could happen around the same time. While not confirmed, sources say the group was no bigger than five actors, with Turner and O’Connor among the others who would end up testing.

It is unknown when the decision will be made, though most believe it will come by the end of the month and potentially before Thanksgiving. Stay Tuned.

issues.title: 9-1-1: Nashville Season 2 Episode 4 Review: A Cold-Blooded Snake in the Grass
issues.summary: 9-1-1: Nashville Season 2 Episode 4 is a wild ride with snakes on a plane and a shake-up to the call center. Read on for our review! The post 9-1-1: Nashville Season 2 Episode 4 Review: A Cold-Blooded Snake in the Grass first appeared on Tell-Tale TV.
issues.author: Alice Ekong
issues.content_html:
9-1-1: Nashville Season 2 Episode 4, “In Cold Blood,” delivers a zany and entertaining ride.

The biblical arc continues as the Pharaoh unleashes his next plague — snakes aboard Flight 729.

As we inch closer to the Pharaoh’s reveal, we must address the elephant in the room: Blythe and Dixie’s rivalry. This outing confirms that the war is far from over after Dixie makes a bold statement during a concert.

On “In Cold Blood,” Dixie announces that her diss track “Hey Lady B” is about Blythe.

This petty move drives the final nail in the coffin between her and Blythe as Dixie reclaims her power. Blythe’s control over Dixie’s music releases doesn’t prevent Dixie from using the situation to her advantage.

While Dixie’s indebtedness to Blythe still lingers in her mind, the announcement lets Blythe know she isn’t afraid to go toe-to-toe. Dixie’s tour not selling is one of the many forces that bruise her ego, but it doesn’t stop her from pursuing her music career.

In Dixie fashion, she does whatever it takes to get what she wants.

What makes Blythe different from Dixie is that she can admit her mistakes and put her family first before making tough decisions. Blythe has self-control and fights back when provoked, whereas Dixie only cares about herself and won’t back down without a fight.

Nevertheless, this episode is a major leap for Dixie and Blue’s relationship.

Dixie wears her heart on her sleeve and asks Cammie to tell Blue she’s proud of him — a small token of Dixie’s love for her son.

Dixie and Blue’s relationship has come a long way from the days of degrading and gaslighting him. That said, the character development is only temporary.

9-1-1: Nashville could have made us believe that Dixie has grown from her past mistakes, but her reversion to her old self after trying to be a good person is more realistic.

Dixie reigniting the feud with Blythe puts Blue back in the middle. Hopefully, Blue recognizes that she hasn’t changed.

She has broken his trust before, so it’s reasonable to assume she’ll do it again. This will be the ultimate test for Blue of whether he wants to be on the side of good or evil.

“In Cold Blood” begins with Dixie ready to give up on her dreams and throw it all away. However, during a chance encounter on her flight to Wisconsin, she discovers her life isn’t completely over. 

9-1-1: Nashville makes Dixie a lot more bearable when she’s away from Don and Blythe. Dixie is ready to give up on her music career, but meeting Danny changes her perspective.

She never leaves Danny’s side, especially after he tries to retrieve her fake cigarette from the ground. After Danny gets bitten, she never gives up on saving his life. For once, Dixie prioritizes someone else’s life before her own.

Danny enjoying her music is a small part of this newfound bond, but what stands out most is that she isn’t seen as a villain. He treats her like a real person and shows a genuine interest in her music career.

Dixie saving Danny puts her in a more favorable light. However, after discovering Russell Dickerson’s son is Danny, the episode reintroduces the Dixie who seizes any opportunity to her benefit.

This is what makes Dixie’s characterization so complex because you never really know what to expect from her.

9-1-1: Nashville continues to portray how Cammie is an exceptional dispatcher due to her caring spirit and assumed leadership role.

However, with the arrival of the new 9-1-1 operator supervisor, Dr. Marcia Zellner, she doesn’t believe Cammie’s technique is appropriate.

“In Cold Blood” is a prime example of the harrowing realities of coercive power in the workplace. Marcia’s scathing assessment of the team’s performance instills fear in the 9-1-1 dispatchers and puts everyone’s jobs at risk.

From Marcia’s perspective, you can understand wanting dispatchers’ heads to be clear on calls. Marcia doesn’t want these intense calls to affect their ability to do the job because lives are always on the line.

This approach may seem like the most reasonable route for 9-1-1 dispatchers in the long run, but how can they eliminate what they do best — showing empathy?

Across the 9-1-1 universe, we have dispatchers like Maddie Buckley-Han, Grace Ryder, and Cammie Raleigh.

What makes each of them impressive is their ability to connect with callers and remember they’re real people. Their efforts leave a lasting impression on callers, and most rescues can’t be done without dispatchers.

Marcia will do everything in her power to terminate anyone whom she deems unworthy of being a 9-1-1 dispatcher.

Stray Thoughts

  • Rogue shattering Ryan’s spirit by saying he’s living a “cop fantasy” is painful to watch. Rogue sees him as a liability and doesn’t think he’s worthy of being a police officer, yet he couldn’t have gotten this far without Ryan’s help.
  • Don has come around to Rogue; the old Don surely would’ve resisted Ryan tagging along with Rogue.
  • The Staten Island Strangler’s role in killing Rogue’s wife is surprising, but it explains his deep investment in the Pharaoh.
  • The inclusion of Keystar Airlines is another great way to tie the 9-1-1 universes together. For any future characters, avoid this airline at all costs.
  • It’s always a delight to see Blue, Taylor, and Roxie together; we need more scenes of them outside the firehouse.

What did you think of this episode of 9-1-1: Nashville? Share your thoughts in the comments below, and don’t forget to leave your own rating!

issues.title: James Bond Surprise: Robert Pattinson Screen Tested to Play 007
issues.summary: The A-list star, already juggling the Batman franchise, teamed with Bond director Denis Villeneuve on the upcoming third 'Dune' movie.
issues.author: Aaron Couch
issues.content_html:
In a surprise few saw coming, Robert Pattinson has emerged as a contender for 007. The actor, 40, is among those who have screen tested for the role of James Bond, multiple sources tell The Hollywood Reporter, joining hopefuls Callum Turner, Jack Lowden and Josh O’Connor.

Conventional wisdom has been that the next man to get the license to kill would not be a globally recognized star like Pattinson, one of the biggest actors of his age cohort, and already the face of DC Studios’ Batman franchise. The screen tests are said to have occurred the weekend of Oct. 24. THR previously reported that four, possibly five actors were in the mix but only three names surfaced at the time.

Related Stories

Movies

Robert Pattinson to Be Honored With American Cinematheque Award

Movies

Scarlett Johansson Breaks Silence on 'The Batman Part II' Role: "It Was Very Hard to Figure Out"

Another name now surfacing as one of the Bond mystery men is Nicholas Hoult, a runnerup to Pattinson for Batman years ago.

Pattinson is a favorite of auteurs from Robert Eggers and the Safdie brothers to Christopher Nolan, whose 2020 spy movie Tenet might feel like a Bond audition in hindsight. And more importantly, he worked with Bond director Denis Villeneuve on the upcoming Dune: Part 3, which bows Dec. 18 and is said to have gone well for the two men.

The actor is in the midst of the biggest year of his career, with a key role in Nolan’s The Odyssey and as the co-lead of A24 hit The Drama and anchoring the well-reguarded movie Primetime, also from A24. He’s currently filming The Batman Part II in London, where screen tests have been taking place.

Amazon had no comment on the testing.

While conventional wisdom goes against a world famous Bond, these are unprecedented times in the franchise. It is the first Bond movie made under the control of Amazon, which bought out the creative rights from the Broccoli family in February 2025. And producing are Spider-Man‘s Amy Pascal and David Heyman, producer of the Harry Potter movies. A young Pattinson broke out with a tragic role in 2005’s Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire, before gaining global fame a few years later in Twilight.

The Bond casting search comes 21 years after Daniel Craig was set as the next James Bond back in October 2005. He retired from the role after five films with 2021’s No Time to Die, his tenure including the franchise’s first and only $1 billion hit, the 2012 feature Skyfall.

issues.title: Eric Bauza’s Final ‘Looney Tunes’ Performance Is ‘Daffy Season,’ Now in Theaters Ahead of ‘The Cat in the Hat’
issues.summary: The new film from Warner Bros. Animation is the first theatrically released "Looney Tunes" short in over a decade.
issues.author: J. Kim Murphy
issues.content_html:
The death of Eric Bauza in October shocked the entertainment industry. An impressively prolific voice actor, it would’ve been nearly impossible for anybody engaging with animation over the past 15 years to never come across his work. Bauza’s death came just two months after the delayed release of “Coyote vs. Acme,” the “Looney Tunes” feature once deemed unreleasable by Warner Bros. Discovery and later sold off to Ketchup Entertainment. The film, which grossed $101 million worldwide, is a true showcase for Bauza, who lends his voice to a plethora of iconic characters, including Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck, Elmer Fudd, Foghorn Leghorn, Tweety, and Porky Pig. Related Stories

Box Office: ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Roars with $6.7 Million in Previews, ‘Ramayana: Rise of a Legend’ Earns $3.5 Million David Ellison’s Big Bet: Why the Mogul Thinks Skydance Film Chiefs Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein Can Deliver 30 Movies a Year

Bauza became something of the defining voice of modern “Looney Tunes” in his final years. Fans can see him give one final performance with the property in “Daffy Season,” a 7-minute animated short that plays before screenings of “The Cat in the Hat,” opening Friday from Skydance’s Warner Bros. Pictures. A representative for the studio confirmed to IndieWire that the short is Bauza’s final “Looney Tunes” movie. Bauza is also credited as providing additional voices for “The Cat in the Hat.”

“Daffy Season” centers on Daffy Duck, voiced by Bauza. He’s joined by Jeff Bergman as Bugs Bunny, Gabriel Iglesias as Speedy Gonzales, and Jeannie Tirado as Lola Bunny. The plot follows Daffy, turning his beak up at his fellow Tunes as they mindlessly obsess over the game of soccer. Todd Wilderman and Hamish Grieve are co-directors. “Daffy Season” is the first theatrically released “Looney Tunes” short since “Daffy’s Rhapsody” played before “Journey 2: The Mysterious Island” back in 2012.

Before “Daffy Season,” Bauza had already provided some voice work for a “Tunes” musical feature titled “Bye Bye Bunny,” which was canceled after some years of development and production. Other “Looney Tunes” credits from Bauza include the HBO Max series “Looney Tunes Cartoons” and the features “The Day the Earth Blew Up: A Looney Tunes Movie” and “Space Jam: A New Legacy.”

Bauza died at his home in Los Angeles on October 25 as a result of hypertensive cardiovascular disease. In a tribute in The Hollywood Reporter, Warner Bros. Pictures Animation producer Susan Rogers credited Bauza with playing a huge role in reviving the “Looney Tunes.”

“There wasn’t a single short he couldn’t quote or couldn’t reference,” she said. “I don’t think you replace Eric Bauza … The hole he leaves is huge. There are many talented people out there, and the franchise will move on. But there’s only one Eric Bauza.”

issues.title: Elijah Wood and Natalia Dyer to star in unexpected, unrequested 1408 sequel
issues.summary: Elijah Wood and Natalia Dyer to star in unexpected 1408 sequel
issues.author: William Hughes
issues.content_html:
Today, in “Why does Elijah Wood keep co-starring in extremely unnecessary sequels to decent horror movies?” news: Elijah Wood and Stranger Things veteran Natalia Dyer have both signed on to star in a follow-up to 2007 Stephen King adaptation 1408. Specifically, Dyer will (per Variety) take on the starring role in the unexpected sequel, while Wood will land in a supporting one, with both appearing alongside original stars John Cusack and Samuel L. Jackson.

Details about the sequel movie, which is being directed by original 1408 director Mikael Håfström, from a script he co-wrote with Mark Verheiden, are being kept quiet. (It feels worth noting that King never wrote a sequel to the original short story, which Håfström already had to stretch out pretty extensively to get to feature length two decades ago.) The fact that Cusack’s character will appear, alongside Jackson’s, in a supporting role, suggests that, of the original film’s various endings, ones where horror writer Mike Enslin survived are likely canon; on the other hand, this is a story centered on a haunted hotel room, so…

Reports that a 1408 sequel was in early development began circulating last week. (Building on comments Cusack made last year about how it was one of his only films he thinks deserves a continuation.) Dyer is, of course, still fresh off of Stranger Things, which she starred in for its entire run; Wood most recently popped up on the animated Among Us TV series, and before that, the previously alluded-to Ready Or Not 2.

issues.title: The Traitors: New Blood Season 1 Episode 9 Review: Playing Chess
issues.summary: The Traitors: New Blood Season 1 Episode 9 is a nicely balanced episode with a cliffhanger worthy to return for. Read our review. The post The Traitors: New Blood Season 1 Episode 9 Review: Playing Chess first appeared on Tell-Tale TV.
issues.author: Jerrica Tisdale
issues.content_html:
We finally had an exciting episode after a few weeks of duds. The Traitors: New Blood Season 1 Episode 9,” Playing Chess,” gives us some of the things we have been begging for.

“Playing Chess” starts with a dinner party where someone gets murdered. This is unlike how many previous episodes begin, so that automatically adds some excitement. That continues with us trying to figure out, along with the Faithfuls, who the Traitors murdered.

R.I.P. Morgan.

After this major event, expect the same Fruitgate rehashing, but it’s a bit more intriguing. Despite Victor successfully eliminating Traitor Tomica, the Faithfuls still don’t completely trust him.  It also just seems like people aren’t willing to say goodbye to their friend Joe.

They’re looking for any excuse to banish anyone but Joe.

Some clever editing could be at play here, but Joe doesn’t seem dead yet.  However, the editors’ love of cliffhangers continues. The editors leave us in the dark about whether Joe leaves or if the target has successfully shifted to someone else, likely Wyatt.

This cliffhanger has us intrigued again because it seemed like Joe wouldn’t make it to the next episode, and he might not, but now we’re uncertain.

That’s enough to keep us glued to The Traitors: New Blood for at least one more week. Additionally, “Playing Chess” hints at a romance between Katie and Victor. We hadn’t really seen this discussed in previous episodes.

This may be why his suspicions haven’t gone her way, and that may be something to watch for in the final few episodes. Katie may become Victor’s blind spot. This could lead to an epic finale if they’re both in it. 

The missions are always one of the weaker parts of The Traitors episodes, especially the US version. However, this Traitors classic is one of the more entertaining ones. “Playing Chess” works on multiple levels this week.

We learn more about everyone else, we have an entertaining challenge, and the cliffhanger works this time.

Maybe the producers and editors have been having a slow mid-half because they’re planning to go full force with the final episodes by really highlighting the other players, giving us some intrigue, and maybe an exciting finale.

We were starting to lose hope with The Traitors: New Blood. However, this episode feels like a major step back in the right direction. It isn’t perfect but a vast improvement from the last few weeks.

We can now see a path of an entertaining and enthralling finale.

“Playing Chess” allows other characters beyond Victor and Joe to shine, while not making Fruitgate disappear, but not preoccupying the episode so much. It’s nicely balanced with a fun classic Traitors challenge and a cliffhanger worth waiting for.

Let’s hope New Blood keeps up the momentum set from this episode.

issues.title: Skydance realizes this must be the moment for Larry The Cable Guy's triumphant return
issues.summary: Skydance realizes this must be the moment for Larry The Cable Guy's triumphant return
issues.author: William Hughes
issues.content_html:
It’s strange, optimistic days in America; a sense that things might finally be on the upturn, after years of feeling like the ghouls and demons infesting the national spirit might have installed themselves, permanently, at the helm. Is it any wonder, then, that minds like those at the Skydance-owned Paramount Network might be a little giddy at the potential of it all, or believe that this might just be the right time to bring an old, semi-forgotten friend back into the forefront of the public consciousness? After all, in the aftermath of “Holy crap, they did it,” what could be more appropriate than a boisterous “Git-r-done!”?

That’s right: Somehow, Larry The Cable Guy returned. This is per Variety, which reports that comedian Dan Whitney, whose recent credits have basically amounted to a single 2025 Prime Video stand-up special, and whatever Mater work Disney still occasionally requires, has lined up a new gig: A cable version of American Mayhem, a syndicated show he apparently launched last month without having the courtesy to tell the rest of us. Per Variety, this new version of the series will feature 13 brand new episodes, distinct from the 52 that Whitney already banked for a robust syndication package.

From a brief perusal, it would be easy to dismiss American Mayhem as “backwoods Ridiculousness.” Which, to be fair, is because it basically is: A bunch of clips culled from the internet, with Whitney providing commentary, catchphrases, and wide-eyed gaping at the camera. Whitney was not shy about his own reasons for taking the job, either, noting in interviews that it makes for a very nice contrast to working as a touring stand-up: “I can do it a mile from my house with greenscreen and I don’t have to go anywhere.” (Honestly: Fair enough.) 

The big question here, obviously, is why Paramount Network decided it needed its own version of the series, launching in a primetime Friday night slot next week; we know the network misses Yellowstone and all, but we’re not sure an America’s Funniest Home Videos knock-off from a guy who did a single-episode cameo on that series is going to scratch the exact same itch.

issues.title: Here's what's in Path of Exile 2’s huge 1.0 release, coming in December
issues.summary: The full release will feature new classes, finished campaign, a new league, and more.
issues.author: Russell Adderson
issues.content_html:
Path of Exile 2's full release is out on December 11, and coming with it are two new classes, two new acts, a new league, tons of new monsters, bosses, battles, endgame changes, gem updates, atlas and skill tree updates, a new pinnacle boss, base types, uniques, and, I don't know, probably a kitchen sink or something. Let's go over it.

First of all, we'll have two new classes: the Shadow and the Duelist. With them, we'll get all new skill gems for daggers and swords, with tons of new builds available. Daggers introduce new mechanics around stealth, traps, shadow skills with clones that attack with you, and classic skills like blade vortex and fire trap.

The Duelist will introduce swords, and with it fan favorite skills like cyclone and hemorrhage. With swords we'll be able to use stances like blood and sand or ready stance. Add to this being able to two-hand, dual wield, or sword and board and swords look to add a huge amount of mechanical complexity.

After two years of early access, the campaign will finally be fully finished. Acts five and six will complete our story of chasing the Beast through the world, with a return to Oriath and beyond. The campaign will also feature new bespoke rare monsters with their own abilities, appearances, and even mods. In addition, the campaign will feature an introduction to the league mechanic for 1.0, Conquerors of Wraeclast.

The league will feature a base building mechanic, where you recruit armies and build up a castle. As you progress through the campaign, you'll recruit armies to battle against enemy armies. There are over 70 points of interest throughout the campaign that let you recruit new types of soldiers for your army, and battle through to kill the boss and get loot.

As you progress your base, you can recruit commanders that will be able to take your recruits and fight battles for you. Like Kingsmarch in Path of Exile 1, these commanders can run maps for you, letting you convert your gold into progress through the atlas and lots of loot. Your castle gets upgraded just like Heroes of Might and Magic, with a beautiful base that you can spend gold to upgrade.

After all the pinnacle bosses and campaign, you can use your armies to battle against other players. Depending on which of the three factions you choose to join (Karui, Ezomyte, or Marraketh), you can battle to take control of various castles around the atlas. As long as your faction controls a castle, you can travel to it on the Atlas to skip around and get to sweet new maps, and you'll receive additional item rarity. It also unlocks hunting grounds nearby that feature rare monsters with increased loot. You'll be able to use currency you find in battle to craft gear, a system which lets you pick mods to remove and reroll into new fractured mods.

All of the new campaign areas feature new bosses, which you'll also face in the endgame in over 25 new maps.

The endgame has been updated as well—in addition to being able to use castles to jump around the atlas, the atlas skill tree has been substantially changed. Instead of 300+ nodes, it's been trimmed way down to about 70. If you beeline the skills, you should end up with about 50 of 70 by the time you battle against the Arbiter of Divinity.

Tons of gems have been updated. Not only are we getting new gems for daggers and swords, but they've added new skills for existing weapons as well. Support gems have been overhauled so that they're more useful as well, like all of the different elemental penetration gems being rolled into one called elemental penetration. Support gems like brutality are also better, with less of a penalty for chaos damage. Chain support becomes just an upgrade, without the penalty to damage on the initial hit.

The passive tree has had huge changes. In addition to a bunch of new nodes, they've changed how jewels work. Instead of always being located on the travel nodes on the outside of the tree, they'll be located in actual skill clusters. Hopefully this will prevent all of our endgame skill trees looking the same, with a big circle maximizing jewel slots and nothing else.

With tons of new items including base types and uniques, there will be lots of new loot to find. Some of the base types look insanely powerful, like an armor that makes you immune to curses. They've overhauled over 70 uniques and added about 40 more, which should make finding uniques way more exciting, especially in the campaign.

Taken all together, 1.0 looks like it will be an incredible moment for Path of Exile 2, both for players who've been waiting to play it, and for those of us who already have hundreds or thousands of hours in the ARPG. The full release of Path of Exile 2 will be available on December 11.

issues.title: Law & Order: Special Victims Unit Season 28 Episode 5 Review: Jalen Brunson and the Ties that Bind
issues.summary: Law & Order: Special Victims Unit Season 28 Episode 5, "Forsaken," features the New York Knicks' Jalen Brunson's acting debut as Detective Jay Madison, Olivia Benson's mentee. The episode also focuses on misogynistic double standards between sons and daughters. Read our review!…
issues.author: Sarah Novack
issues.content_html:
Law & Order: Special Victims Unit Season 28 Episode 5, “Forsaken,” features heavy themes surrounding family and the lengths people go to protect someone, even if it tears the family apart.

It is a highly compelling episode that tugs at the heartstrings, but it still delivers a satisfying narrative.

Despite the emotional aspect, there are still exciting moments, especially with the New York Knicks’ Jalen Brunson guest starring as Detective Jay Madison.

Even though Brunson appears only for a short scene, it is still extremely worthwhile.

One short conversation establishes Benson as Madison’s former mentor. He also provides critical information that sets a plot twist in motion, redirecting the narrative to the victim’s stepbrother, Tyler Davis. 

Olivia Benson: Rape is about power.

Jalen Brunson’s scene comes in the middle of the episode, providing much-needed relief from a difficult case before diving deeper into the narrative.

Hopefully, this is just the first of many appearances featuring Detective Jay Madison. It would be fascinating to learn more about how he and Benson met.

Detective Bruno also returns after a well-deserved break, and he seems to be back on track.

It is a relief after the events on Law & Order: Special Victims Unit Season 28 Episode 3, “Anonymous,” when he takes on more than he should.

Bruno returns for a particularly difficult case, so it is nerve-wracking to see whether or not he can compartmentalize the job. Thankfully, he does.

It is a tough feat to accomplish, especially considering how Tyler sexually assaulting his stepsister, Chloe, tears their family apart.

However, it only does so because of how their parents approach the situation. Instead of disowning Tyler, a grown adult, Rick and Monica Davis choose not to take sides.

Tyler and Chloe do not fall out over a complex argument. Tyler rapes Chloe after years of physically assaulting her, and the parents still choose to treat the incident as if it is a fight where parents cannot pick sides.

Of course, Rick has no problem throwing Chloe under the bus if it means protecting Tyler. He claims he works hard for their blended family, but saves Tyler every time he is violent, whether it involves breaking Monica’s fingers or hurting Chloe.

Law & Order: Special Victims Unit illustrates the cruel lengths some parents will go to protect their sons, even if it destroys their family. 

The show also highlights the double standards sons and daughters often face at the hands of their own parents. Rick and Monica want justice for Chloe as long as she does not hold the real perpetrator accountable because it is her stepbrother.

Of course, this case is an extreme example, but it is still important to emphasize that many families often contain these misogynistic double standards, regardless of the situation. 

Law & Order: Special Victims Unit might depict the most extreme scenario, but it is still a necessary theme to include.

Amanda Rollins: You don’t need to keep this in. You don’t need to protect Tyler. And you don’t—you don’t need to feel like you have to preserve your mom’s relationship at your own expense.

While “Forsaken” does not focus on any of the series regulars, the case is strong enough to stand on its own and let the main cast serve Chloe and her family instead.

This decision allows the final plot twist to impact the narrative profoundly once the squad realizes Evan, the youngest son, witnesses Tyler’s assault of Chloe.

Evan is in a unique position because he is both Rick and Monica’s son. This shows that Rick choosing Tyler over Chloe is not about Tyler being his biological child because Evan is too. In fact, Rick even allows Tyler to get away with hurting Evan.

Evan’s last-minute witness testimony is an excellent way to end the episode.

After Rick decides to protect Tyler at any cost, it is difficult to determine what comes next for this broken family. Rick worked hard to maintain an illusion, but it can never be real because of how he protects Tyler.

The Davis family could have a chance if Rick let Tyler take responsibility for his actions, but he does not. Rick only cares about the superficial fantasy in his head, so when it falls apart, his family does too.

Ending “Forsaken” without clear direction is the right choice for this narrative because it heightens the impact of this episode’s themes.

issues.title: John Wick animated prequel movie to finally spare poor Keanu's knees
issues.summary: John Wick animated prequel movie to finally spare poor Keanu's knees
issues.author: William Hughes
issues.content_html:
The John Wick franchise ran up pretty hard against the physical limits of star Keanu Reeves a few years back, as the action star revealed that one of the main things stopping a John Wick: Chapter 5 from happening—besides, y’know, the climactic events of John Wick: Chapter 4—was his 62-year-old body and its 62-year-old knees. Sure, Lionsgate keeps making noises about a fifth mainline Wick movie being in active development, bringing both Reeves and director Chad Stahelski (fresh off his sojourn in Highlander land) back together. But we haven’t heard much about anything concrete on that front in several months. Now, though, The Wrap reports that at least one of the various side projects and spinoffs surrounding the franchise is moving forward, as Lionsgate gives the green light to an animated film prequel to the original John Wick.

Although currently untitled, the film reportedly centers on the biggest question mark in the Baba Yaga’s personal backstory, i.e., the “impossible task” he completed in order to earn his way out of the hitman game for a shot at what turned out to be some extremely short-lived marital bliss. (Darn it, narratively convenient terminal diseases!) And while we’re a bit hesitant at the idea of animated Wick—since the series derives such huge amounts of its joys from the extremely grounded and realistic kinesthetics created by Stahelski’s direction, an incredible fight choreography team, and Reeves’ full-body commitment to the bit—we will admit that this is probably the only way to tell this particular story without committing the genuinely unthinkable sin of recasting Reeves with a younger performer. 

Per The Wrap, the film is being directed by Shannon Tindle, a veteran animator whose credits include Samurai Jack, Kubo And The Two Strings, and 2024 Netflix film Ultraman: Rising, and written by Eternals writers Ryan and Kaz Firpo. Stahelski and Reeves are both expected to produce. The project is one of several Wick spinoffs in the works, including Donnie Yen’s Caine, and another potential TV series titled Under The High Table.

issues.title: In the trailer for Drag, Lizzy Caplan's bad back bungles break-in
issues.summary: The upcoming comedic thriller, Drag, stars Caplan and Lucy DeVito as they invade John Stamos' luxurious house and find something sinister.
issues.author: Matt Schimkowitz
issues.content_html:
What a drag it is robbing homes. Lizzy Caplan learns the importance of stretching and the dangers of bathtubs in the trailer for the upcoming home-invasion comedy Drag. The film follows two sisters, played by Caplan and Lucy DeVito, who break into a luxurious home in rural upstate New York. It’s an easy job until Caplan throws her back out and the homeowner (John Stamos) unexpectedly returns. The trailer teases a home-heist thriller where, as the title implies, DeVito must drag Caplan out of the house without alerting the mysterious owner or his date (Christine Ko).

Written and directed by Raviv Ullman and Greg Yagolnitzer, Drag is both filmmakers’ first feature. Ullman is an actor from R.J. Decker, Broad City, and Criminal Minds; Yagolnitzer is a music video director best known for work with Green Day and Weezer. Since premiering at SXSW this year, the film has received solid reviews. 

“I think the only option is to drag you out of here,” DeVito says. Trailer editors dream of a line like that. The premise is juicy, but who the sisters are hiding from remains a mystery. Is Stamos a killer? Is his date a stalker? Will DeVito drag Caplan to safety? All will be revealed when the film opens on January 29, 2027.

issues.title: Zach Cregger Doesn't Outline. Here's How He Writes Instead
issues.summary: Twenty years ago, Zach Cregger was making sketch videos with The Whitest Kids U'Know, and after that, he was a working sitcom actor. Then he wrote and directed three hits in a row. He made Barbarian for $4.5 million in Bulgaria, which is a miracle given that he had "no clout…
issues.author: Jo Light
issues.content_html:
Twenty years ago, Zach Cregger was making sketch videos with The Whitest Kids U'Know, and after that, he was a working sitcom actor. Then he wrote and directed three hits in a row.

He made Barbarian for $4.5 million in Bulgaria, which is a miracle given that he had "no clout whatsoever," according to him. Then Weapons grossed about $270 million worldwide and earned Amy Madigan an Oscar. This year, Resident Evil opened to a franchise-record $60 million domestically, according to Variety.

Next up is The Flood, an original sci-fi thriller starring Jennifer Lawrence, which New Line will release in August 2028, per The Wrap.

Cregger is now in a position few writer/directors reach, where studios come to him with offers. He sat down with Matt Belloni of The Ringer and Puck for The Town in front of students at Loyola Marymount. He spoke candidly about how he writes, why he's wary of IP, and why he'd rather work with a smaller budget than a bigger one. We pulled his best advice for screenwriters and directors. Check it out below.

- YouTube www.youtube.com

Comedy Is the Gym for Horror

Cregger has famously relied on his comedy background for his writing. Belloni asks whether a comedy background is a random path into genre filmmaking.

"It's not random," Cregger says. "It's a very, very similar muscle set that you need to be effective with comedy and with horror. You know, what you're doing is you're essentially trying to elicit a physiological response through timing and tone. And so that's what you're doing when you're trying to get a joke, and that's what you're doing when you're trying to get a scare. They both live or die by frames. They're both all about the buildup versus the payoff. And so I think that all of my time spent in the comedy trenches was me going to the gym for horror."

He paraphrases a Jordan Peele line about the difference between comedy and horror being just the soundtrack. He doesn't know if he would go that far, but music does play a big part, too.

Timing, buildup, and payoff are skills writers can practice in any genre. Comedy is also a great pathway into multiple genres, including horror (obviously), romance, and drama.

Write for Yourself First

Cregger almost fell into horror filmmaking. The genre was never a career strategy.

"For me, writing is just something that is cathartic. It's joyful. I would do it whether I could make a movie or not. You know, I think that's the secret sauce is when you're doing it because it's inside of you and you want to get it out. And if you're doing any art for yourself as the audience member first and foremost, then I think you are on the righteous path."

He was a working actor, but the work wasn't fulfilling him, so he wrote in his downtime and followed his taste for dark material.

When Belloni pushes back that horror is simply the genre that sells, Cregger concedes the point but says it wasn't part of his thinking.

For you, it can be, but if your heart isn't in it, it's likely to feel obvious. You should be excited about the stuff you're writing. It should hopefully feel cathartic, like it does for Cregger, where you're exploring something that invigorates you or helps you work through something.

'Resident Evil' Credit: Sony Picture

Write the Messy Draft, Then Do the Hard Part

Cregger talks about Resident Evil being extremely easy to write, joking it felt like it took 15 hours. Which makes sense because it's a story about a character going from one point to another and facing obstacles along the way, told in almost real-time over one night. It's the easiest story ever.

In contrast, Weapons is nonlinear and switches points of view and overlaps in weird ways before revealing what's really going on. The writing of that was also almost exploratory, the way the story is structured, where he just started following different characters to see what they'd do. It was messy.

"I just started to see the shape," he said, "but I didn't outline. I just wrote from beginning to end, and it didn't work. It was a mess, but then I go back, and I put my thinking cap on, and I try and make it connect and make sense and not just be chaos. And that's where it's hard. But that first draft was easy. That first vomit draft is a really beautiful, fun thing. It should be fun."

I feel like we've talked about vomit drafts quite a few times around here lately, but it's because it's so important. If you feel like your writing has to be perfect on your first try, you might never start your script.

To be clear, Cregger is not against structure books. He says he loves Save the Cat and Robert McKee and calls them "truth in a book."

"But for me, I need to just sit down and just play. And so I just play by just, I have this idea for a scene. Let's go. And I just start, let my fingers lead before my brain can get in the way. And then I just try and entertain myself. See if that blooms into something cool. You don't know how many scripts I have that are like 30 pages, and then I hit a dead end, and then I'm dead."

(For what it's worth, that's the place where a lot of scripts die if you haven't thought through a plot fully.)

Barbarian itself started as a writing exercise inspired by a self-help book, he told Rotten Tomatoes. He also does two drafts before anyone else reads a script.

Define Success, and Let Collaborators In

Cregger says he's frustrated that so much of the conversation around Resident Evil was about how faithful it was to the games rather than about the movie itself. He's proud of the film, but he's wary of taking on IP again.

"When I watch Weapons and Barbarian and when I watch Resident Evil, my biggest win is that I'm seeing the movie that was in my head when I was writing the movie."

That doesn't mean shutting other people out. He took notes from Sony executive Nicole Brown that made Resident Evil better, because she acted as a collaborator and supporter. On set, he wants to hear others' ideas.

"Otherwise, your movie is only as good as you're capable of doing. I don't want to be the limit to my movie. I want everyone working on the movie to improve, to raise the roof, you know?"

issues.title: Letterboxd’s Sale to the New York Times: 9 Pros, Cons, and Big Questions from the $330 Million Deal
issues.summary: As the social media platform at the center of film culture gets new ownership, some changes are likely in store.
issues.author: J. Kim Murphy
issues.content_html:
After several months of business talks and speculation, Letterboxd is about to have new owners. The New York Times is closing in on deal to acquire the film-logging social media platform, which values the company at $330 million. It’s an eye-popping increase from 2023, when the Canadian holding company Tiny bought a majority stake at a $50 million valuation.

Far beyond the film industry, there is a dismal track record and daunting uncertainty when it comes to companies’ ability to maintain their identities after being acquired. Social media reception to the pending New York Times deal generally peaked at resigned relief (“the best case scenario” was a common refrain) while also drawing more cynical, even existential responses about the future of Letterboxd. As the website’s user base holds its breath over the future, these are some pros, cons, and big unknowns to consider about where Letterboxd is going. Related Stories

Letterboxd Finalizing $330 Million Sale to The New York Times ‘The Weed Eaters’ Lands Expanded Release from Yellow Veil Pictures: New Zealand Cannibal Movie Sets Winter Rollout

PRO: Hey, at Least a Studio Didn’t Buy It

There’s understandably a lot of negative social chatter about the news of Letterboxd’s looming acquisition, but let’s rest assured that it’s at least not a studio taking ownership of the wildly popular cinephile engagement platform. A24, Sony, Netflix, and Skydance were all reported to have registered talks about an acquisition. Whether or not this new iteration of Letterboxd will exist behind a paywall is one matter, but that’s not the worst thing compared to the potential studio-ification (i.e. A24-ification, as they were in talks for the sale) of the brand. Compare it to studios running an exhibition chain — not just Sony purchasing Alamo Drafthouse, but all the way back to the days before the Paramount Decrees, which legislatively blocked studios from having a monopoly on theaters. (Decrees that are no longer in effect.) In that situation, there’s more potential for marketing nepotism and favoritism to titles and properties in-house. A media company taking over Letterboxd should, in theory, prevent the kind of self-interest that threatens independence. —Ryan Lattanzio

CON: Letterboxd Users May Not Trust the Times With Their Community

A deal would bring two unusually loaded cultural conversations under one roof. The movie-logging platform has helped reshape the world’s repertory film scene — effectively gamifying the enjoyment of archival art — while debates about the Times often wind their way back to the paper’s coverage of Palestine and trans rights. For Letterboxd users who see that coverage as having real consequences for whose lives and experiences are taken seriously by mainstream journalistic institutions, the prospect of the Times owning a community they helped build raises questions of trust. A bigger audience would be a genuine upside, but for some users, who owns the room is an existential issue. —Alison Foreman

UNKNOWN: The Fate of Letterboxd Journal and Changes to the New York Times Culture Desk

While some users might not even know about Letterboxd’s digital magazine, the Journal has been a growing presence on the platform, with a staffed editorial team regularly publishing interviews, retrospective considerations, film festival coverage, and other longform articles. The question remains on how, or if, those writers and editors will be integrated into the New York Times newsroom. A shuttering of the Journal would wreck yet another publication for professional film coverage and freelance opportunities, of which there are fewer and fewer. On the other hand, when the New York Times bought The Athletic in 2022 for a whopping $550 million, the banner initially continued as a semi-independent banner. But a year later, the Times dissolved its existing sports department, laying off or reassigning staff, and positioned The Athletic as a replacement. The New York Times’ culture desk has not been immune to shake-ups over recent years; the potential addition of Letterboxd begs the question of whether further changes are in store. —J. Kim Murphy

PRO: Fewer Gremlins in the Server Room

As the number of Letterboxd accounts has skyrocketed over the past few years, navigating the platform has become a bumpier experience for users. Pop-up Cloudflare turnstiles reading “Verifying you are human. This may take a few seconds” make frequent interruptions clicking from page to page, while Gremlins-centric error messages signaling server crashes are semi-regular occurrences. The New York Times draws much more web traffic than Letterboxd and such technical hiccups are essentially anomalous. The company certainly has the resources to bolster the strength of Letterboxd’s servers. —JKM

CON: Potential Interface Changes for a Userbase Sensitive to Them

Letterboxd users have historically been an extremely discerning audience, sensitive to changes that might be seen as minute or inconsequential for other websites. A memorable hiccup from recent years came when the platform abruptly removed an option to list out all star-ratings given by the accounts one follows on a single web page. After some backlash from users (like myself) who noticed the feature’s disappearance, Letterboxd was swift in reintegrating the tool. It was a small crisis with a happy ending, but it speaks to how quickly UI changes can dishearten the platform’s users. If the New York Times wants to make even small tweaks to the platform, or heavily integrate it into its digital ecosystem, it will face an audience that’s quick to rally against such changes. —JKM

UNKNOWN: What Does the New York Times Want Letterboxd to Be?

The New York Times Company is the poster child for brand elasticity in the digital media age. America’s newspaper of record didn’t just adapt to the Internet; it built an empire of games, recipes, and sports that a sizable chunk of the world needs to engage with in a daily basis. But it’s less apparent how Letterboxd fits into the strategy. The social network exists somewhere between an editorial product and a game and doesn’t have a clear comp within the NYT organization. Is the plan to simply move the entire Letterboxd infrastructure behind the NYT paywall, making the $30 monthly subscription tier even more unavoidable for cinephiles? Draw on users’ data to bolster revenue opportunities for streaming promotions and the Times’ product recommendation banner Wirecutter? The answer might be some combination of the above, but the Times is entering uncharted territory. —Christian Zilko

PRO: A Steward That’s Survived Nearly 200 Years

The New York Times was first established in 1851. It has weathered the shift to digital media better than just about any other paper. It is one of the few publications that is growing its readership, with paid subscribers last reported at 13.8 million. While Letterboxd has grown its user base significantly, the company has never disclosed the number of accounts that pay for its two subscription tiers. The Times places Letterboxd in a more established ecosystem. The paper’s history of supporting cultural frameworks suggests that it can make the platform, which was only founded in 2011, into an enduring institution. —JKM

CON: Social Media Hot Takes and Longform Criticism Under the Same Roof

Plenty of filmmakers IndieWire has spoken to are concerned about the widening gap between what defines film criticism and what defines a hot-take social media sound-off, i.e., the “instant reaction.” Reviews on Letterboxd can range from the thoughtful and long-form to the pithy and snarky. As film critic jobs evaporate globally, what happens when you merge Letterboxd closer to the purview of established, institutional film writing, the kind that’s hard, that demands a chunk of your soul? Letterboxd has further democratized criticism, no question, and while many of us argue that we need an elevated discourse, what happens if more people start to think… we don’t? Will the fusion of the Times and Letterboxd stoke that debate, or create harmony? Will this only fuel the growing primacy of influencers over critics and journalists as an authority on a film’s quality? Either way, cantankerous conversation will abound. —RL

UNKNOWN: What If Everyone Takes Their Watchlist and Just… Goes Home?

It follows then that if enough Letterboxd users distrust the Times, they might log fewer movies, post fewer reviews, or exit the app altogether. From a web-development perspective, the basic mechanics of a movie diary are incredibly easy to replicate. (Hell, AI just cloned Adobe Photoshop.) The hard part is getting the consumers whose aggregate taste is a cultural bellwether to once again show up in the same place. It wouldn’t take a mass exodus for Letterboxd to feel fundamentally different, and if the core group of people who reliably made consumers laugh or put weird repertory picks on your radar stop contributing, there will be fewer reasons to engage. The community could splinter across new competitor sites — which, yes, opens up potential opportunities for aspiring critics to gain exposure and find their followings. But we can’t know if any of that would be as big as the OG Letterboxd. —AF

issues.title: How ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Used Real-World Sound to Make Its Monsters More Terrifying
issues.summary: Sound designer Natsuko Inoue and sound mixer Hisafumi Takeuchi tell IndieWire how they breathed life into the warring monster kings of "Godzilla Minus Zero."
issues.author: Sarah Shachat
issues.content_html:
No one is doing monster movies quite like director Takashi Yamazaki and his team — who not once but twice now, with “Godzilla Minus One” and “Godzilla Minus Zero,” have made Godzilla feel both bigger than Tokyo Bay and extremely emotional and personal, even handcrafted. Much of that comes down to the narrative balance between our human heroes and the King of the Monsters, of course. But it’s also about the grounded, physical ways the monsters are brought to life.

Much has already been made of the fact that both Godzilla’s and King Ghidorah’s roars were recorded by blasting the sound effects against real physical spaces (and probably scaring some hikers in the process) so we wouldn’t just hear something otherworldly. We’d hear the texture of the loudspeakers, the reverberation of the sound on the concrete of a dam (for Ghidorah) or a dome (for Godzilla) — the unreal brought into a real, physical space. Related Stories

‘Zi’ Review: Kogonada Rediscovers His Voice with a Microbudget Hong Kong Experiment Starring Michelle Mao and Haley Lu Richardson ‘To Hold a Mountain’ Took on the Government — Now It’s Montenegro’s Oscar Submission

But that is only the light-up blue tip of the kaiju for the work done by the “Godzilla Minus Zero” sound design team. Sound designer Natsuko Inoue and production and post-production sound mixer Hisafumi Takeuchi constantly found ways to tie the most fantastical moments back to Earth, because that sonic believability keeps the audience invested in the action.

“ When audiences hear sounds that they’ve never heard before too frequently, I think it removes you from the world because it’s too foreign and it’ll stand out,” Inoue told IndieWire. “Once a fantasy-like or fictitious sound goes through the sort of real-world echo, then it becomes a lot more palatable, or we become more receptive to how it sounds because it’s echoing in a way that we recognize. So that was a way that we really tied the visuals to the sound and made it feel more grounded.”

issues.title: Stream It Or Skip It: ‘Under Seige’ On Netflix, A Dramatic Retelling Of The 1985 Seige At Colombia’s Palace Of Justice
issues.summary: The series is based on the real-life taking of the Palace of Justice by the M-19 guerilla group in 1985.
issues.author: Joel Keller
issues.content_html:
In November, 1985, the Colombian guerilla group M-19 took the Palace of Justice in Bogotá. The two-day siege ended with a military raid that killed over 100 people, including a number of Supreme Court justices. The siege and the aftermath is examined in a new scripted series on Netflix.

UNDER SEIGE: STREAM IT OR SKIP IT?

Opening Shot: A woman with a stunned look on her face walks through the charred remains of an office in the Palace of Justice in Bogotá, Colombia.

The Gist: Two months before the November 6-7, 1985 siege of the Palace of Justice by the guerrilla group M-19, a couple meet at the Palace. Memo (Santiago Londoño) tells Mona (Mariana Gómez) that he wants to take her to the cafe there for a date, but he’s really there to scout out the fourth floor, where the Supreme Court justices have offices. He’s a part of M-19, and his group is seeking to take over the sprawling complex and make demands of the government.

The tensions between M-19 and the government have been at the breaking point for some time, to the point where Alfonso Reyes Echandía (Santiago Alarcón) requests protection for the Palace of Justice. The military generals think that the guerillas wouldn’t dare take such a massive building. But as we see, the group is planning just that.

In the meantime, TV journalist Olga Behar (Luna Baxter) digs for information on just how the government is responding to M-19’s threats. Jimmy Beltrán (Camilo Amores), a waiter at the cafe, is just trying to sock away enough money so he and his wife Pilar Navarrete (Natalia Reyes) can move their family to a larger home.

What Shows Will It Remind You Of? Created by Natalia Santa and Mariana Berenguer, and based on the real-life 1985 siege of the Palace of Justice, Under Seige (Original title: Palacio) reminded us of two recent dramas about the October 7 attacks in Israel: Red Alert and One Day In October.

Our Take: While Under Seige is a fictional retelling of the Palace of Justice siege — disclaimers make pains to say that some of the characters are fictional — it is based on research and interviews about the incident, including those who survived the military raid that killed over 100 people and ended the siege. What the show is trying to do is examine the siege and the decades of aftermath from multiple perspectives and not assign blame to any one party.

It’s ambitious to say the least, and in later episodes the timeline ping-pongs between the siege and the aftermath, which stretched out over 20 years. There’s a lot of complexity and nuance that will probably resonate with people in Colombia who studied the political environment that created M-19 and led them to try to take the Palace of Justice, and it will be especially trenchant to those who lived through it or watched it unfold on TV.

We’re just not sure how it will resonate with viewers who are not as familiar with Colombia’s political history from that time period. Sure, the writers have set up a structure that helps you follow certain characters, like Jimmy and Pilar, who are more innocent bystanders than anything else. But viewing the show as just an action series without much of the context behind the story makes the bevy of characters and situations introduced more confusing than anything else.

Performance Worth Watching: We like the fact that the show’s story is structured around the three female protagonists — Natalia Reyes as Pilar, Luna Baxter as Olga and Mariana Gómez as Mona.

Parting Shot: The siege begins, with one of the M-19 guerillas screaming out, “We’re the M-19! Long live Colombia!”

Our Call: STREAM IT. If you’re not familiar with Colombian’s political history, you should look up the Palace of Justice siege before watching Under Siege. It will definitely make the viewing experience of this historical drama a whole lot better.

Joel Keller (@joelkeller) writes about food, entertainment, parenting and tech, but he doesn’t kid himself: he’s a TV junkie. His writing has appeared in the New York Times, Slate, Salon, RollingStone.com, VanityFair.com, Fast Company and elsewhere.

issues.title: Is The New York Times Buying Letterboxd?
issues.summary: According to The New York Times, they have entered into exclusive discussions to purchase Letterboxd. If it goes through, the transaction would give The New York Times another feather in its cap for apps people use daily and bring tech and cinema together in new ways. There has…
issues.author: Jason Hellerman
issues.content_html:
According to The New York Times, they have entered into exclusive discussions to purchase Letterboxd.

If it goes through, the transaction would give The New York Times another feather in its cap for apps people use daily and bring tech and cinema together in new ways.

There has been a lot of interest in Letterboxd and its growing subscriber base. Will the New York Times improve the app or make it worse?

Let's dive in.

Why Studios Lost to the Times

The big fear around Letterboxd being sold was that a movie studio would buy it and use it to shill its own titles or manipulate ratings.

We heard places like Sony and A24 might be in the mix, but The New York Times seems willing to offer much more money for access to Letterboxd’s user base, around 30 million people.

So, what does this mean?

What Changes for Letterboxd Users?

It seems like nothing for now. I would assume there will be some sort of integration with New York Times reviews or maybe critics you can follow on the platform.
