But right away, this just slides into other apps the NYT owns, like Wordle, that diversify their holdings. They also own the sports news site, The Athletic.

Again, this could just be an expansion of those endeavors. I could see Letterboxd hiring more film journalists for more interviews or how-to articles to capture the imagination of the broader filmmaking community.

Expansion has to be on their minds, but nothing has leaked.

Now, I am not sure how they think they will recoup the money they paid for the app; the $330 million is definitely more than paid users, and rentals will make up the difference, so maybe there will be more ads or another thing moving forward.

But right now, nothing.

Based on the reports I've read, Letterboxd will continue to operate as a stand-alone site and won't face much interference.

And the Times umbrella directly supports the publisher’s goal of expanding its 13.8 million subscriber base to 15 million by the end of 2027.

What’s Next?

Neither The New York Times Company nor Letterboxd co-founder Matthew Buchanan has formally commented on the pending sale.

We'll keep you updated if anything changes, but this is probably the best outcome I could have predicted.

You get the platform you want, with an owner who's just trying to get more people on it, as it is for now.

If anything changes, we'll let you know.

issues.title: Stream It Or Skip It: ‘Motor City’ on AMC+, an Alan Ritchson Dialogue-Free Action Stylegasm
issues.summary: The soundtrack functions as narrator in this retro revenge story set in scare-quotes-necessary “Detroit.”
issues.author: John Serba
issues.content_html:
Uberviolent Alan Ritchson action vehicle Motor City (now on AMC+) opens with a very Quentin Tarantinoesque font on the title card, then proceeds to be very UN-Tarantinoesque as it plays out with almost no dialogue. What Motor City director Potsy Ponciroli aims for is the classic Tarantino regurgitated pulp, funneled through the working-class dinge of 1970s Detroit and a thematically curated selection of era-specific songs on the soundtrack. And the result is an entertaining, somewhat experimental riff on revenge-story tropes.

MOTOR CITY: STREAM IT OR SKIP IT? 

The Gist: This is a revenge story within a revenge story, as one man seeks revenge on another man for stealing his girl, then the second man seeks revenge on the first man after he steals her back. The girl doesn’t seem to have much agency here, but that’s kinda the way movies in the ’70s worked, and this movie wants to be one of those movies, so it’s up to you if you want to accept that excuse. Anyway. You’ve already notched that there’s almost no dialogue here, which means character names are a challenge to glean. The credits reveal them but I’d already dubbed them like so: the Put-Upon Man (Ritchson of Reacher fame), the Girl (Shailene Woodley), the Sleazemeister General (Ben Foster), the Good Cop (Ben McKenzie), and the Bad Cop (Pablo Schreiber). Stereotypes of the genre, for sure.

The other character is a narrator who doesn’t speak, but feeds dimes into the jukebox, shaping the story with Bowie, Fleetwood Mac, the Moody Blues and real cool shit like Bill Withers and Foxy. Drop into the lyrics and you may find some nuance to the story, which otherwise plays out in broad strokes in 1970s Detroit as the Put-Upon Man is framed by the Bad Cop, who’s on the Sleazemeister General’s payroll. Why frame the guy? The Put-Upon Man ended up with the Girl, who used to be the Sleazemeister General’s abusee. Meanwhile, the Good Cop noses around, suspicious of the Bad Cop’s actions. And everything is authentically cigarettes. Everything! CIGARETTES!

The fact that the Put-Upon Man is built like the proverbial shick brithouse doesn’t scare the Sleazemeister General, who’s a rich-as-hell Dee-troit drug lord. But the Sleazemeister doesn’t realize his new enemy is a former Army Ranger — it’s always OPS guys in these movies, black OPS, special OPS, classified OPS, all the OPS OPS OPS — who apparently learned how to endure enormous amounts of pain and shrug off the psychological trauma inherent in murdering people. Car chases, gunfights, fistfights, knife fights, prison breaks, etc., ensue as the righteous face off against the wicked, as the movie gods intended.

What Movies Will It Remind You Of? This is Martin Scorsese’s Rambo funneled through some modern Wick-core aesthetics.

Performance Worth Watching: Well, nobody can eat scenery without dialogue. So the movie inherently sides with Ritchson’s strong, silent type while making Foster’s wordless emoting — even his sweat seems to be sweating — look extra pathetic. The latter is fun to watch.

Sex And Skin: Topless Woodley.

Our Take: Motor City’s emphasis on style over all else means it isn’t the most emotionally engaging story. But it is enjoyable, less experimental than it is a dalliance, Ponciroli toying with form for his and our entertainment, less so as artistic exploration. The amalgamation of needle drops and pantomime is fun and clever, although all creatives involved clearly understand that, even in movies with dialogue, violence is always the loudest language that’s “spoken.” Action speaks louder, and all that.

issues.title: ‘Zi’ Review: Kogonada Rediscovers His Voice with a Microbudget Hong Kong Experiment Starring Michelle Mao and Haley Lu Richardson
issues.summary: Smarting from an ill-received foray into studio filmmaking, the "Columbus" director rebounds with a DIY curio about a wayward artist's journey back to herself.
issues.author: David Ehrlich
issues.content_html:
Since arriving in Hong Kong, she’s made a habit of collecting sounds in much the same way as Kogonada has come there on the hunt for images. They both find a dissonance around Victoria Harbor that reflects their internal feelings of otherness and self-alienation. It’s China, but not. It’s a single city, but one split across two main areas by a stretch of the sea that some people never cross. It’s among the world’s most densely populated metropolises, but the vertical terrain seems fundamentally inhospitable to human civilization, and nature continues to assert itself between every skyscraper, shopping mansion, and crack in the sidewalk. Zi is the only native character in the film, but the history and design of Hong Kong reflects her disassociation as well — like her, the former British colony’s experience of the present is delayed. 

That’s the closest thing to a diagnosis we get for what ails her, though it’s clear that Kogonada is leaning more towards soft science-fiction than the stuff of hard medicine. “Temoral relativism” is how L’s ex-fiancé Min (Jin Ha) describes it, though he’s slow to reveal how much he knows about Zi’s condition. Everything she perceives is already in the past. I suppose that’s true for all of us to some degree, if you factor in the nanoseconds that elapse between stimuli and our ability to perceive it, but the situation is more pronounced for Zi (who Mao plays with the effervescent helplessness of a paper airplane). Of course, that doesn’t explain why she believes she’s bearing witness to visions of her future self, but that confusion only exacerbates her feelings of distance from the present. 

Even in its more platonic dimensions, the threadbare story that gradually allows Zi to close that gap is awash with the romance of loss, reconciliation, and belonging. Kogonada is falling back in love with the movies right before our eyes, and yet,  in characteristic fashion, that process isn’t garish or forced. His is a vision that is revealed through careful subtraction — by clearing away all of the dust and smudges that came to obscure it.

While Kogonada indulges in a few legible winks to his cinematic forebears (the most obvious of those being a step-printed homage to Wong Kar Wai, and my most far-fetched being a disoriented nod to José Luis Guerín’s “In the City of Sylvia”), he and cinematographer Benjamin Loeb almost completely eschew the neon exoticism that foreigners tend to look for in Hong Kong, with the vast majority of the film being captured in unfussy handheld shots that accentuate its here-and-now anxiety and delegate the emotional heavy lifting to an impeccably curated soundtrack of Ryuichi Sakamoto remixes and originals. 

By the end, “Zi” engenders a certain emotional attachment toward and between its characters, all of it building to a gently unexpected gutpunch of a final minute. But even that last-minute reveal — not a plot twist so much as a sudden change in perspective — is rooted more in the movie’s form than its plot, as Kogonada’s characters remain largely symbolic of their function in the writer-director’s journey back to himself.

It’s a testament to Mao, Ha, and especially Richardson — who continues to be so good at grounding Kogonada’s most abstract ideas in a tender human place — that “Zi” retains even a soft dramatic pull as it searches for the present, though its recursive nature certainly wasn’t conceived with a casual audience in mind. If you’re hooked, which I wasn’t, or haunted by it, which I was, that will likely have less to do with an acute emotional connection to these characters than with the overflowing rewards of watching someone rediscover the sound of their own voice, and hear a way forward into the future in its echoes. 

Grade: B

“Zi” premiered at the 2026 Sundance Film Festival. Grasshopper Film releases it in select theaters starting Friday, November 6.

issues.title: Vincent Price’s 5 Best Roles, Ranked
issues.summary: Vincent Price was synonymous with horror. His indelible voice and a piercing stare could topple the characters around him when he played campy and aristocratic villains who, many times, we didn’t want to see get defeated. Price’s first collaboration with producer and director…
issues.author: Chris Sasaguay
issues.content_html:
Vincent Price was synonymous with horror. His indelible voice and a piercing stare could topple the characters around him when he played campy and aristocratic villains who, many times, we didn’t want to see get defeated.

Price’s first collaboration with producer and director Roger Corman in adapting the literature of Edgar Allan Poe was House of Usher (1960), but was that his best role in their partnership? I think that honor should go to another Poe adaptation.

This is my ranking of the five best roles of Vincent Price.

5. Witchfinder General (1968)

‘Witchfinder General’Credit: Tigon Pictures

Set during the English Civil War of the mid-1600s, men and women are accused of witchcraft by the self-appointed “Witchfinder General,” Matthew Hopkins (Price), who uses religious fanaticism to fuel his reign of terror.

Directed by Michael Reeves, Witchfinder General is loosely based on the real-life Matthew Hopkins, and in the role, Price never brings out the flamboyant wickedness that he could do so well. His depiction of Hopkins is unsettling as we watch a man order the torture and execution of innocent people with cruel indifference.

It’s one of the actor’s best roles, but this bleak movie just isn’t as fun to rewatch as his others.

4. The Great Mouse Detective (1986)

‘The Great Mouse Detective’Credit: Buena Vista Distribution

Price gets to be a Disney villain in this rodent-themed take on Sherlock Holmes, The Great Mouse Detective, adapting the children’s book series, Basil of Baker Street.

As humans go about their day in Victorian London, they are unaware of the animal society that lives by their feet, where a mouse detective goes looking for a toymaker who has been kidnapped by the criminal mastermind Professor Ratigan (Price).

The actor’s iconic voice is a hallmark of his live-action roles, so it’s no shock that it is a perfect fit for animation. He goes big, which is exactly what the arrogant and evil Ratigan needs as he towers over the mice characters, while singing a villain song and plotting to overthrow the Mouse Queen.

3. Dragonwyck (1946)

‘Dragonwyck’Credit: 20th Century-Fox

Farm girl Miranda (Gene Tierney) accepts the invitation from her distant cousin Nicholas Van Ryn (Price) to come to his estate, Dragonwyck, along the Hudson River. Soon, Miranda realizes the life of luxury demands a deadly cost.

In the directorial debut of Joseph L. Mankiewicz, this Gothic drama was an early villainous turn by Price for a subdued performance compared to his later bad men. The charisma of Nicholas is seductive. In one scene, a visiting doctor admits to being nervous around Nicolas: “He watches me all the time too with those icy eyes of his. Sometimes, I think he’s mesmerizing.” The doc could be talking about our reaction to Price.

There is something wrong with Nicolas, but Price bottles the malice until it slips when his authority is challenged, and then completely spills out during the last twenty minutes.

2. The Masque of the Red Death (1964)

‘The Masque of the Red Death’Credit: American International Pictures

After a plague infects a village, Prince Prospero (Price) confines himself to his castle, inviting his wealthy friends to seek shelter as well. Debauchery and hedonism ensue, but the castle may not be the stronghold the prince believes it to be.

The Masque of the Red Death has a deliciously corrupt performance by Price in one of the final Corman-Price collaborations that adapted Poe. Everything is extravagant on-screen, from the lavish, colorful sets to the darkness of the Devil-worshipping Prospero.

But Price’s best role brings what he did throughout his career into one homicidal, over-the-top character.

1. Theater of Blood (1973)

‘Theater of Blood’Credit: United Artists

After faking his death, stage actor Edward Lionheart (Price) plans to have the final word on the critics who wrote negative reviews of him in a series of murders inspired by the plays of Shakespeare.

Price mastered how to play camp villainy, and what he does as the vengeful thespian in Theatre of Blood might just be the showcase of his career. He delivers famous soliloquies on a dilapidated stage in one scene; he orchestrates stylized, ghastly kills in the next.

It’s a horror-comedy where Price is having the time of his life as he turns Lionheart into a tragic monster who is consumed by his rancor.

What do you think is Vincent Price’s best role?

issues.title: Stream It Or Skip It: ‘Possible Love’ on Netflix, A Patient, Powerful South Korean Drama About Class Differences, Discontent, And Ethically Dubious Documentary Filmmaking
issues.summary: Jeon Do-yeon, Sul Kyung-gu, Cho Yeo-jeong, and Zo In-sung star in this must-see film from acclaimed director Lee Chang-dong.
issues.author: Maddy Casale
issues.content_html:
From acclaimed South Korean filmmaker Lee Chang-dong, Possible Love is a must-see drama film now streaming on Netflix. After winning the Grand Jury Prize at the 83rd Venice International Film Festival, Possible Love looks to impress viewers worldwide as it tells the story of two married couples whose very different lives grow intertwined while filming a documentary. Jeon Do-yeon, Sul Kyung-gu, and Parasite‘s Cho Yeo-jeong lead the way in this patient, exceptionally crafted movie exploring class differences and hidden desires.

POSSIBLE LOVE: STREAM IT OR SKIP IT?

The Gist: Choi Ho-seok (Sul Kyung-gu) was once an experienced welder at automaker SP Heavy Industries, proudly considering his coworkers brothers and finding community in the company, until mass layoffs cut 40% of the labor force. Although the wrongfully terminated metalworkers attempt to strike and stand strong as a union with the support of their families, their efforts are violently suppressed by police intervention, leaving Ho-seok bitter, hurt, and coping with alcohol. Two years after the layoffs, he joins his wife, Mi-ok (Jeon Do-yeon), and their 10-year-old son, Cheol (Jung Seol), at the funeral of a coworker who took his own life. There, Mi-ok tries to stop Ho-seok from drinking, inadvertently making a scene that catches the eye of documentary filmmaker Lee Ye-ji (Cho Yeo-jeong).

Ye-ji wants to make a film about labor shrinking due to corporate restructuring, and she thinks she’s found her main “characters” in the Choi family. Mi-ok is immediately impressed by Ye-ji’s expensive lifestyle, effortlessly cool demeanor, and openly affectionate relationship with her handsome, rich husband Sang-woo (Zo In-sung), and she’s soon swept away by the chance to be seen, heard, and feel interesting outside of her working-class life and mundane job at a small factory. Ho-seok, however, is much less cooperative, repeatedly denying interview requests and refusing to participate in the group counseling sessions for those affected by what transpired with SP Heavy Industries.

As the two couples spend more time together, their economic disparity and different ways of life grow starker in contrast, leading to friction, jealousy, and revelations. Through it all, Cheol bears silent witness to grief, conversations, and scenes he’s likely too young to be confronted with, acting as the true documentarian unobtrusively watching the difficult realities unfold around him.

What Movies Will It Remind You Of? The artful, unflinching focus on the dynamics between the wealthy and working class certainly evokes Bong Joon-ho‘s Academy Award-winning film Parasite. You may also be reminded of historical drama films like Roma and Matewan. Strangely, I also couldn’t help but think of You Can See Everything.

Performance Worth Watching: Both Jeon Do-yeon and Sul Kyung-gu are incredible as Mi-ok and Ho-seok Choi. They deliver layered, evocative, and lived-in performances that immediately engage the viewer, only growing more arresting and vulnerable as the film goes on. Jung Seol is also impressive as the child actor playing their stoic son, Cheol.

Sex And Skin: There’s an instance of skinny-dipping where you see bare breasts and butts, and then later on, a short sex scene. Somehow it’s the former that feels more intimate, but both moments help cement this film’s “R” rating.

Our Take: Possible Love begins with the quote “Thou shalt not covet,” and this Commandment remains at the core of this movie as every main adult character seems to lose parts of themselves in desire for things they lack. While Mi-ok and Ho-seok’s desires seem to come from genuine places of familial love, pain, and wanting to belong, Sang-woo and Ye-ji’s desires feel more shallow. Ye-ji wants to feel like an altruistic everywoman and serious filmmaker, and believes she can achieve that by “helping” the Chois. Sang-woo seems content with his affluent lifestyle yet still appears to wish for “simple” things like children or easy gratification or amusement. All of this makes the four characters extremely intriguing in their messy realism, and all the more fascinating when brought to life by talented, dedicated actors.

Possible Love‘s beautiful shots are bolstered by Lee Chang-dong’s bold directorial choices that draw the eye and embrace the uncomfortable. Long silences or moments acting as painful reminders of the characters’ class differences make everyday subject matter feel bold and exceptional. The film shows more than tells, making it consistently affecting and relatable across language or cultural barriers. Cheol’s role is particularly fascinating to me, as a character whose constant presence and quiet judgment feel more moving and honest than anything documentarian Ye-ji could portray with her own narrow vision of the world. Overall, the film is full of sharp social commentary, thought-provoking interactions, and powerful performances that stick with you well after the credits roll.

Our Call: Possible Love is a compelling, beautifully made, and wonderfully acted South Korean film that’s sure to leave a mark on anyone willing to let the action unfold at its own pace. I can only hope this receives the Oscar noms it deserves. STREAM IT!

Maddy Casale is a Chicago-based writer and comedian who covers everything from animated series to Hallmark movies. Follow her on Duolingo @MCasale.

issues.title: The Iconic Roles That Jack Nicholson Turned Down
issues.summary: When you look back on the career of Jack Nicholson, it’s hard to not immediately jump to the conclusion of him just being the greatest film actor of all time. I mean, One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest, Chinatown, The Shining, The Departed, his record is undeniable. And it somehow…
issues.author: Eric Hardman
issues.content_html:
When you look back on the career of Jack Nicholson, it’s hard to not immediately jump to the conclusion of him just being the greatest film actor of all time. I mean, One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest, Chinatown, The Shining, The Departed, his record is undeniable. And it somehow was almost a lot longer.

Nicholson has rejected a lot of big roles in his tenure, so let’s look back on some of the biggest ones.

Roy Neary in Close Encounters of the Third Kind

'Close Encounters of the Third Kind'Credit: Columbia Pictures

What’s perhaps most strange about this near casting is not that Nicholson almost had Dreyfuss’ part, but that Spielberg’s follow-up film to Jaws struggled to find someone to play the part at all. In addition to Nicholson, the part was offered to actors including Gene Hackman, Al Pacino, Steve McQueen, and Dustin Hoffman, who all turned it down due to various conflicts.

Dreyfuss had been loudly campaigning to Spielberg since their time on Jaws for the part, since he felt that he was perfect for the role. Spielberg initially disagreed, citing that he thought Dreyfuss was too young, but then when push came to shove, he ultimately changed his mind. The right decision, in my opinion, as seeing Nicholson in this role is a bit of a weird image to picture.

Raymond Babbitt in Rain Man

‘Rain Man’Credit: United Artists

Another entry involving Dustin Hoffman and Steven Spielberg, the latter was originally slated to direct the film, which would have starred the real-life Quaid brothers in the respective roles. This fell through when Spielberg had scheduling conflicts surrounding Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade, so the role of Raymond Babbitt got shopped around town a lot with actors like Nicholson, Mel Gibson, Bill Murray, and Mickey Rourke all turning it down, before finally landing on Dustin Hoffman. Once again, absolutely the right call there.

Benjamin L. Willard in Apocalypse Now

‘Apocalypse Now’ Credit: United Artists

No disrespect is meant to Martin Sheen, but this is definitely a pairing that I would love to have seen happen. That also doesn’t mean that Nicholson still may have made the right choice passing on the role. Even though Apocalypse Now has endured the test of time as one of the greatest films ever made, I’m not sure I could have survived fifteen months in the Philippines with Francis Coppola. And Martin Sheen almost didn’t, famously suffering a stress-induced heart attack in the middle of production.

The laundry list of other actors besides Nicholson that passed on the role included Steve McQueen, Clint Eastwood, Al Pacino, Nick Nolte, Robert Redford, James Caan, and Tommy Lee Jones.

Michael Corleone in The Godfather

‘The Godfather’Credit: Paramount Pictures

Another Coppola film on the docket, Nicholson actually had a very noble reason for rejecting this offer. Coppola was fighting tooth and nail for Al Pacino for the role, but the studio’s lack of faith in both Coppola and Pacino made them pivot over to Nicholson, who was a much more reliable of a performer at the time, having just had his breakout turn in Easy Rider.

Nicholson wound up turning down the part because he felt strongly that the part should be played by an Italian American actor. After some more internal conflicts, the studio lamented and finally allowed Al Pacino to take the role.

Gordon Gekko in Wall Street

'Wall Street' Credit: 20th Century Fox

This is one of the funniest and most cyclical rejection stories we’ve had yet. Nicholson was initially offered the role in Wall Street, but had to turn it down in order to fulfill his commitment to the films The Witches of Eastwick and Ironweed. The part eventually wound up going to Michael Douglas, who wound up winning a Best Actor Oscar for his work. But not without a tight race with, you guessed it…Jack Nicholson in Ironweed. It’s funny how all of this works out, sometimes.

Sy Parrish in One Hour Photo

‘One Hour Photo’Credit: Searchlight Pictures

Although Robin Williams’ performance in One Hour Photo is one of the best dramatic turns of his career, he’s probably the last person you would have thought to cast at the time. Ironically, the first would probably be Jack Nicholson.

Director Mark Romanek seemed to have felt the same, since he initially approached Nicholson for the part. Nicholson turned the part down because he felt that it was a little too similar to the role he played in The Shining, and felt that someone else would be better suited for it.

issues.title: ‘Elf Unwrapped’ Co-Authors Andy Richter and Aaron Karo On “How Close” ‘Elf’ Was To “Not Being Made”: “Nobody Was A Sure Bet”
issues.summary: The co-authors of the new Elf oral history took DECIDER through the candy cane forest and down memory lane to discuss the making of the beloved 2003 Christmas movie.
issues.author: Alex Vena
issues.content_html:
Elf has cemented itself as a holiday movie staple, but Andy Richter and Aaron Karo‘s new oral history unwraps (quite literally) the ways in which the 2003 Christmas comedy nearly didn’t make its way down the chimney and come to fruition.

Elf Unwrapped, which hit shelves on Tuesday (Nov. 3), features insights from a slew of those involved with the fan-favorite film, including stars Will Ferrell and Zooey Deschanel, director Jon Favreau, and of course, Richter himself, who played Morris, a colleague of Walter Hobbs (the late James Caan).

While Richter’s role may have been small—as he teases in the new book, his character doesn’t even have a last name—Karo pointed out during a recent visit to DECIDER’s Manhattan studio with Richter that his co-author was the “secret weapon” in securing time with the power players behind Elf. Richter, who booked the interviews and credited his experience with his interview podcast The Three Questions with Andy Richter for feeling so “natural” during the process, was grateful for how many people were willing to open up.

“People were incredibly generous with their time. A couple people said, ‘I don’t do this, but it’s you, so I’ll do it.’ So that’s nice. I guess it pays to have dirt on people,” he quipped. “And it was really a fun process. It was fun to get to talk to people.”

As for Karo, he was unaware that Elf had “such a fandom” before being approached to co-write Elf Unwrapped, joking, “When our agent said to me, ‘We have a book project, it’s about a Christmas classic,’ I thought it was going to be Die Hard.”

“Then I, of course, realized that people go nuts for it. When I tell people I co-wrote a book about Elf, they go nuts like Buddy does when he finds out Santa is coming,” he shared. “So now I just drop the fact that I am writing a book about Elf even when no one’s asked.”

Just before we had Richter and Karo indulge us in taste-testing their own take on Buddy the Elf’s signature, syrupy spaghetti, we sat down with the co-authors for a conversation filled with laughs and Elf revelations. Keep reading for more of our sit-down with Richter and Karo.

DECIDER: It’s crazy to think that this movie is turning 23 years old this year. I was just doing a rewatch on HBO Max and they put it in a category titled, “Yes, These Movies Are 20 Years Old.”

ANDY RICHTER: Yes.

And so why was now the right time to revisit the making of this movie?

AR: You know, I didn’t make that decision. Carrie Thornton, who is the editor of Dey Street, she said,”Hey, I want to do book about the making of Elf, and I think Andy Richter would be a good person to write it.” And she was telling that to our agent, and he said, “Well, I think we can make that happen.” So it was kind of her call. I wouldn’t have had the nerve to say, “I’m going to chronicle Elf,” you know? So she brought it to us and we said “Okay.” And it is good— maybe five years earlier would have been better because people’s memories would be better. Because there was a lot, and I mean for me personally, I wrung out my memory banks for everything that I could remember from that, and it was the same for everybody we talked to. We’re like, “Any more particular anecdotes?” And they’re like, “Look, this is all I got. It’s 22 years ago.”

Yeah, there was a quote from Judd Apatow that was like, I have no recollection of [helping make] this movie.

AR: Yes, yes… There’s no way to verify […] Because different people came in, and this is a common thing, especially with comedies. They bring in a group of comedy writers to just do a quick pass and have suggestions, add jokes. And one of the producer said, “Judd Apatow came in and worked on it.” And I reached out to Judd. He’s like, “I have no recollection of working on that.” So he says he didn’t, but he might have and just doesn’t remember.

AK: I mean, I wasn’t even born when the movie came out, so this is all news to me.

And Aaron, coming into this project, were you an Elf fan? How familiar were you with the making of the movie?

AK: When our agent said to me, “We have a book project, it’s about a Christmas classic,” I thought it was going to be Die Hard. I was a very casual fan of Elf. I did not actually realize it had such a fandom. Then I, of course, realized that people go nuts for it. When I tell people I co-wrote a book about Elf, they go nuts like Buddy does when he finds out Santa is coming. So now I just drop the fact that I am writing a book about Elf even when no one’s asked.

AR: When Will Ferrell showed up for the interview, he was pissed that it wasn’t Bruce Willis.

AK: Yeah.

AR: It was weird.

AK: It was strange.

AR: Awkward.

AK: It was awkward, yeah.

The interview access you both got for this book was pretty incredible. The quotes span from Will Ferrell—who also wrote the foreword—to Jon Favreau, and even the actor who plays the iconic “Mailroom Guy” [Mark Acheson]. I loved getting to see those quotes. Take me through your process of reaching out to these interview subjects. How hard was it to get in touch with everyone?

AR: *Points to himself*

AK: Andy’s the secret weapon.

AR: I booked the interviews, too… Because I had access to everybody—some people I had to talk to their manager and see if I could get their email. There were other people where they’re just a matter of [reaching out]: Will and a couple of the producers I was friends with prior and continue to be friends with. But yeah, no, I just set up the interviews and kind of conducted them, because I have an interview podcast. I’ve been doing it for a while. It was kind of natural for me to do that. And Aaron was with me and helped me remember the things, like there are particular things that…

AK: I had to bring him his pills every morning.

AR: Yeah, yeah, yeah. So yeah, I just set them up and it was really great. People were incredibly generous with their time. A couple people said, “I don’t do this, but it’s you, so I’ll do it.” So that’s nice. I guess it pays to have dirt on people. And it was really a fun process. It was fun to get to talk to people.

Well, it was so fun to read.

AR: Thank you!

I could imagine there was a surplus of interview footage and information that you guys got to parse through for this book. Was there anything that you couldn’t include in the book, or that you had to cut out throughout this process?

AK: Oh, that’s a good question.

AR: Nothing that we’re going to tell you! I mean, c’mon! I don’t want to pay lawyers.

AK: I think more discussion of sequels, probably. There were two sequel scripts written. One was by Scot Armstrong, who did rewrites, who’s a buddy of Andy’s. New Line [Cinema] hired him, he got paid a bunch of money, and then the project just died. And then The Edge from U2 wrote a sequel of Elf on his own, and called one of the producers and said, “I want to meet with you.” And they never met, and we’ve never seen the script. No one knows what happened, and we need to find out what happened with The Edge’s [script].

AR: Yeah, Shauna Robertson said out of the blue, hey, The Edge wrote an Elf 2. Want to meet with him? And she was like, “Absolutely.” And then it just never happened.

AK: Do you think The Edge watches the Decider?

I hope so. We’re going to have to tag him and get this out to him.

AR: Come on, Edge.

AK: We need The Edge to release [the script].

AT: Cough it up.

Well, I saw an interview of you two and you both were divided on whether there should be an Elf sequel.

AR: An Elf 2, yeah, yeah.

But would you be open to collaborating on a book about the tribe of asparagus who hate the smell of their pee?

AR: [Laughs] I’m not sure that that really has legs.

AK: He doesn’t need me if the book’s only 25 pages.

AR: Yeah, I can do that on my own. I don’t need to cut him in on it. I think we’re done.Unless we do a book about the making of the Elf Broadway show, the making of the Elf animated special, the making of the Elf mannequin that Home Depot was selling that was frightening children. We could do those making-of’s.

Honestly on the costuming section alone. I loved all the quotes from [costume designer] Laura Jean Shannon, and learning about the [near legal action taken] with [regard to] Rankin/Bass and the likeness. That was super interesting.

AR: And there’s some original sketches. I mean, she did some amazing work. She’s gone on to work with Favreau, they’ve been together their whole career. The costume stuff is great. There was a definite tip of the elf hat to the styling of Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer, and lawyers were afraid that the costumes were a little too close. So in the middle of filming, they were like, “We have to change all the costumes.” They ended up figuring it out, which is one of the real juicy details you gotta buy the book for. [Laughs] How did they resolve the wardrobe?

Exactly! […] There are so many “what-ifs” with respect to the making of this movie, especially when it came to its casting; how Chris Farley was originally up for the role of Buddy the Elf, Gary Shandling was being considered for Walter Hobbs, and Katie Holmes and Selma Blair were contenders for Jovie. What was the “what-if” that surprised you the most while writing this book and looking back?

AR: I guess none of those really did. I’m happy that it all turned out the way it was. And Chris Farley was just—you know, the script was passed around for eight years before it settled at New Line, and he was just attached to it for a moment, and we don’t have any way of knowing exactly what that meant. It meant a few meetings, phone calls, but whoever had the option at that point, it passed to them. I think the thing that just surprised me the most was how close this movie came to not being made. And a good amount of the book is about that, it’s about how close it came to Bob Shaye at New Line not writing a check to start the movie. So it might have happened, because nobody was a sure bet. Everybody was fairly fresh and untested in terms of feature films. And that was the days when there was a big difference. There was TV and there was movies. Now it’s all together.

AK: To me, what was interesting is not just that Selma Blair was considered for Jovie, but it was because she skateboards.

AR: Jon wanted to have a skill of the actor’s be a skill of Jovie’s, which is why Zooey and Jovie sing. Zooey sings, so Jovie sings. And Selma—

AK: Skateboards, so they were going to have her skateboard.

AR: A skateboarding Jovie.

AK: And what was your special talent?

AR: Umm… showing up on time?

You know what? A very essential skill.

AR: It is. It’s rare these days.

And how many times did you both rewatch Elf in the process of writing this book?

AR: I think about three, for me.

AK: I mean, it’s so different because he’s in the movie! He was literally there. I think I pretty much have it memorized. It’s also a very short movie. It’s like 85 minutes long. I also watched all the director’s [cuts]. There’s a Will Ferrell commentary, and a Jon Favreau commentary, which they don’t really do that anymore…

There was a moment you wrote about in the book from the Elf premiere after party, where Toby Emmerich, a New Line executive and one of the executive producers of the movie sees the Time Warner CEO who hands him a pirated Elf DVD…

AR: Yeah.

Which is so crazy. How do you think this would have been handled now? Because with so many things being able to be leaked now on social media, it’s just so interesting what was happening then and how they were able to kind of put a stop to it, as opposed to now it’d probably just be out in the world.

AR: Yeah, I have no idea because that’s such a grown-up problem that I don’t want to know [laughs]. I mean, even as we were retelling it in the book, I just kind of felt like, well, what are you going to do? Because it was one of those classic, somebody holding a camcorder the entire time watching the movie. And all the movies that came out, there would be those versions of them on the street in New York. So, you know, Toby was very alarmed by it. I kind of would have been [like], “Eh, what are you gonna do?”

AK: I think they also took a picture of the poster and then Xeroxed it, and slid it in. Quaint. Very quaint.

AR: Apparently they put a stop to that somehow. I don’t know what that means. You know, kneecaps being broken.

AK: He still has the DVD.

Well, that’s a relic now.

AR: Uh-huh, it is.

Outside of Elf, what are your go-to Christmas movies to watch during the holiday season?

AK: Well, Die Hard is my favorite movie. So I would say Die Hard is 1 and 2 for me. What about you?

AR: Wait, you mean. Die Hard 1 and Die Hard 2? Or just watching Die Hard again?

AK: Both. I do like Die Hard 2. And I know Andy’s going to say, “The 1942 classic…”

AR: No! 1951 version of A Christmas Carol starring Alastair Sim. […] There is a version of A Christmas Carol that’s fantastic. There’s also this movie It’s A Wonderful Life. It’s pretty good. Christmas-themed, vaguely. That’s a good one.

At DECIDER, we’re a website that celebrates all things streaming, so outside of these holiday movies, what TV shows and movies are you watching right now?

AR: Oh boy. Right now, well, there’s The [Great] British Bake Off. Always invested in that every year. I’m mad that there’s not a thousand episodes of Slow Horses.

AK: Oh, you stole mine!

AR: Really? That’s so, so good. And I’ve only, over the seasons, grown to love it more and be more obsessive about it. That’s a good one.

AK: Widow’s Bay.

AR: Yeah, Widow’s Bay was pretty fantastic. I don’t have any, like, real sort of hidden gems. There is one that I have which is a French show called The Bureau. It’s a spy show. And The Agency with Michael Fassbender is based on it. It basically is just the English-language version of that, and it’s fantastic. I’d say it’s Sopranos-level, The Bureau.

AK: Have you ever seen Colin From Accounts?

AR: Yes! That’s a very, very funny show.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

issues.title: Let’s Turn A DualSense Edge Inside Out
issues.summary: If you're lucky enough to win the ewaste lottery, a 'for parts' controller can be a great opportunity for fun
issues.author: Chris Person
issues.content_html:
Once you get halfway good at electronics repair, you start to value the words “for parts” while looking at listings. The definition of this is more elastic than it appears, and varies depending on the device and context. Many times the object is quite literally just junk or unsalvageable garbage. Sometimes the tweaks it needs are minor, like a bad solder joint that would take 20 minutes to fix. In other situations the issue is simply cosmetic and easily fixed with a combination of aftermarket parts from Aliexpress or some 3D printed bullshit that some hero in your exact situation once put online. 

But the funniest scenario is when the device is functionally like new. This can happen for a lot of reasons, but a primary one is that we produce a lot of complex bullshit and most people would rather return something than try to repair it. This is understandable; products are often not made to last and we have not fostered the skill of caring for your goods as a culture since Radio Shack existed. Returned electronics that are not that broken often end up in the hands of bulk electronics sellers, electronics recycling warehouses, and on the secondary market. Though much of what you’ll find is often legitimately broken beyond repair, you can find gems. If you’re smart and a little lucky, you can clean up.

This is the exact situation I ended up in when I bought a DualSense Edge recently on eBay for 65 bucks with the intent of turning it into a project. After ripping off the rubber grip that the previous owner had swathed the controller in and thoroughly wiping it down with isopropyl alcohol, I turned it on, paired it with my PS5, and it worked perfectly fine. There was maybe a tiny bit of an audible click on the thumb sticks, and the amount of drift on the sticks according to software from Gamepadla was enough that it would only bother you if you professionally played Call of Duty. (Unsurprisingly, the profiles on the device were named “MW2 Test” or “WWE Copy”) But just because the controller was basically fine did not mean I wasn’t going to turn it inside out.

Shell swap

One of the most annoying yet rewarding mods you can do to a controller or handheld is a shell swap, where you replace the external plastic with a cool new color or texture. Sometimes this is done because the original device got dirty, yellowed with age, or suffered cosmetic damage, but most of the time it’s because you want to make your controller semi-transparent. Though the complexity of each mod varies from device to device, it’s rarely as simple as just removing the shell and putting a new one on. You usually have to completely disassemble the thing module by module, and every piece of hardware is slightly annoying in its own unique way. The part that sucks on a Steam Deck shell swap, for example, is removing the display, which is why mine remains stock minus the SSD.

Normally, I would probably not do this to a controller that cost 200 dollars, but the math shifts slightly if you win the For Parts lottery like I did, or if you didn’t and need to go in there to repair it anyway. In terms of aftermarket controller shell swaps,  ExtremeRate is a go-to brand and they’re the same people I went with when I added rear bumpers to my regular DualSense so many years ago. The kit that ExtremeRate sends you comes with a cheap prying tool for removing the shell (if you need a better prying tool my aforementioned friend recommends RELIFE on Aliexpress), a screwdriver, replacement screws in case you mess up, and several tiny replacement parts like springs. They also have a YouTube tutorial with a robotically machine translated voiceover, but it’s pretty thorough in its steps.

The inside of the DualSense Edge is complicated, but it’s laid out far more logically than the base DualSense. There’s a clear order inside of it, fewer opportunities to fuck up, and while Sony didn’t make a truly user-serviceable piece of hardware, they made one that is generally pleasant to work inside of. Ribbon cables can still be torn if you aren’t careful, but you’re less likely to do so because only one of them is in an annoying place. There are a few springs that can get lost easily if you aren’t careful, like the ones near the PlayStation logo button, the one that connects the latching mechanism latch, or the little tension levers that provide force against L2 and R2. The battery requires some effort to get to but connects and disconnects by simple pressure, although you have to be careful to pull the battery connector in the proper direction, namely up away from the controller. 

If you follow the instructions, there are really only three parts of a DualSense Edge shell swap that suck and two of them are optional. The first is the touchpad, which is the last thing you remove from the controller and thus the first thing you place in the new shell. If you want to replace the touchpad with the included transparent one, you’re going to need a heat gun or hair dryer to loosen the adhesive, pull it off, then reapply the board to the new pad. If you like the back pad or know you’re too OCD to handle possibly seeing imperfections on the adhesive you can skip that. 

The second and by far the worst is replacing the triggers with the included clear ones. This requires you to remove the individual trigger modules, disassemble them without losing the tension levers, remove the trigger, wrench out the internal base of one of the triggers with immense force, snap them into the new triggers, then reassemble the entire thing. I liked the old triggers and buttons anyway and thought they contrasted nicely with the smoked clear plastic, although I did try and can confirm that it’s not worth doing if you can avoid it. 

The third annoying part, which is mandatory, involves carefully sandwiching slivers of PET film that cover two trigger depth levers. I dislike doing this, but it’s not the end of the world. Whatever you do, make sure you put a couple of thumb sticks in and test the controller halfway through assembly to make sure you didn't miss a ribbon cable and have to completely disassemble it again. I did when I tried a trigger swap, and having to go back in sucks. 

A few hours worth of work here and there and I had a smoked translucent controller of the exact same quality as when I started. The grips lack the rubber of the original Edge, but that and the strange but beautiful microtexture of the original controller can be dirt magnets so it’s not all bad. With that done, it was time to upgrade the modules.

TMR time

Despite me writing, publicly and on this site, that the DualSense Edge is far too expensive a controller for what you get, I do think it’s a good controller in terms of how it feels in the hand. Sony remains correct that symmetrical thumbsticks should be the default layout, and the DualSense Edge having replaceable stick modules should be standard even if I think the modules are far too expensive and need to be replaced with TMR modules instead. The adjustable trigger throws are good, and I quite like the dome buttons that Sony uses for its back paddles, another feature which should just be standardized at this point. I still dislike how proprietary much of the PlayStation ecosystem is for controllers, but I won’t deny that their product designers are talented.

TMR modules are low-powered stick modules that are far less prone to drift. When stick drift became a huge issue years ago, the successor in DIY spaces was initially Hall Effect sticks, which use magnets, but TMR sticks have more or less eclipsed those in every new controller in the last few years. The Steam Controller comes with TMR modules stock, and that’s one reason I respect it so much and it’s become my default controller for most of my gaming. Countless Chinese controller companies have popped up, like Gullikit, GameSir and 8-Bit Do or ZD-0, and so the price of a feature-rich controller has gone down immensely. You can actually just buy those modules yourself and solder them in, and some of those controller companies just straight up sell those too.

The solution that Sony came up with for the DualSense Edge was user-replaceable modules. In the abstract this is a good idea, and more companies should aim for their products to be user-serviceable with the least amount of futzing possible, something Valve has been quite good at by partnering with iFixit and generally being transparent with its documentation. The Edge modules cost about 20 bucks each, but the issue is that you are replacing them with the exact same modules either way, so there’s a nonzero chance you may run into the same problem for a controller you’ve already dropped 200 bucks on plus the cost of those replacement modules. Product timelines are long, particularly at scale, and the controller came out in 2023, but there needs to be a better solution for whatever replaces the Edge when the PS6 drops.

If you spend 200 dollars on a controller you’re probably anal enough that you want it to function perfectly. But despite the modules themselves being easy to remove, replacing the existing sticks with TMR sticks is surprisingly tricky. The most direct way to go about this is to crack open Sony’s modules, desolder the existing sticks, and replace them with modules like the K-Silver JS13 Pro+. K-Silver modules are becoming standard in the DIY space, and a modified version of those modules appear in the Steam Controller. There’s actually dedicated solder tips just for removing the sticks of these controllers if you do enough to require that. But the complication is that there’s a crucial chip on the bottom of the module that’s very easy to damage with heat. If you go this route, heat-resistant Kapton tape on crucial components is your friend. The other issue is that calibration is typically done at the factory, and so if you want to calibrate the new modules you need to disable or desolder a handful of 0201 SMD components. 

This entire procedure sucks so much that there is a market for people who will modify Sony’s stick modules for you. However, in the last six months, aftermarket clone TMR modules for the Edge appeared online. In the interest of journalism I decided to try some out and went with a company called Besavior. The modules themselves contain K-Silvers. The most expensive Besavior module specifically does adjustable by rotating the sticks, and I believe they are using the JT13s from K-Silver. Adjustable tension is conceptually neat and appears in competing modules like the NS-55 stick from Gulikit, but if you don’t need that feature it isn’t worth the extra money. What’s more, the tension twist removes the ability to quickly swap endcaps, and the modules themselves have a slightly longer throw than stock. As a part of this build, I also have some high grade polyurethane stick caps coming from a guy on Etsy called LiveZone, so I’m probably going to return these TMR modules in favor of the lower cost model. 

The Besaviors feel quite nice, have decent circularity, and the endcaps feel solid, although their base is shiny instead of matte. Besavior also includes a USB dongle for updating the firmware on the sticks themselves, which I believe is there in the event that Sony pushes an update that bricks them. Having to include a PCB dongle for your aftermarket controller thumbsticks as a contingency because Sony itself does not sell a sufficiently durable stick module is the height of absurdity, and one that could simply be solved by Sony selling Edge modules that don’t suck.

No matter which way you go, either the onerous soldering job, outsourcing it to a random guy, or buying an aftermarket clone module, you will need calibration. Dualshock Tools on Github is used to fine-tune calibration on either modded or aftermarket modules. In terms of testing gamepads, the open source software suite at Gamepadla remains the most reliable. The reassembled Edge with its new sticks and shell worked perfectly. 

I didn’t really have to tear this Edge controller apart. I did it because I like a project, I enjoy writing about strange corners of the hardware universe, I need a good PlayStation controller for when GTA comes out, and I took a gamble on a deal and won. All told I still spent a decent chunk of money to get it into shape, although it was far less than the cost of an Edge controller retail. 

Despite my criticisms, the Edge is still a beautiful if extravagant controller and laid out better than the normal DualSense. If you have to stay in Sony’s closed garden, it can be transformed into an endgame controller with a bunch of work. But technology has lapped it; it is far too expensive for its feature set, and it exists frozen in a strange in-between area by leaner companies. By virtue of mainly gaming on the PC, I find that I use my Steam Controller far more. It’s half the price of the Edge, also has symmetrical sticks, the battery lasts for ages, and I didn’t have to torture it to get driftless TMR sticks. I wonder what will happen when Sony finally decides to update the Edge. I just hope that I won’t have to hunt through ewaste listings for it and turn it inside out for it to make sense in my life.

issues.title: The Comics Beat STAR TREK crew remembers SIR PATRICK STEWART
issues.summary: Comics Beat's Star Trek team gathers in Ten Forward to fondly remember Sir Patrick Stewart, Jean-Luc Picard on Star Trek: The Next Generation.
issues.author: Avery Kaplan
issues.content_html:
DEAN: During the peak of Covid, I remember enjoying his daily reading/renditions of the Sonnets of Shakespeare. Sharing his passion for the bard during such a bleak, scary (and at times dull) time.

CHRISTOPHER: Besides Professor X (who, for what it’s worth, I feel he gave his best performance as in Days of Future Past), there are just so many. I really enjoyed the version of A Christmas Carol he did as a kid, and he lent his wonderful voice to The Simpsons, The Pagemaster, The Prince of Egypt, Jimmy Neutron, and many more childhood favorites. More recently, he was a lot of fun as the older Merlin in The Kid Who Would Be King, although the younger version (Angus Imrie) has much more screentime.

I think Stewart had the most fun playing himself in recent years, subverting the stoic expectations he set in so many of his roles, by just being really goofy on late-night shows like Kimmel and Colbert, or that Paramount+ commercial with Arnold from Hey Arnold!, as well as being Ian McKellen’s partner-in-crime. On that note, I’ve never seen the film, but the scene in Safe House where he screams, “You motherf***ers are gonna kill all my lillies!” is absolute comedy gold. And who could forget the way he introduced Salt-N-Pepa on Saturday Night Live with such gusto!?

AVERY: It’s really hard to beat Professor X. And while he wasn’t directly involved, I really adore the moment in Planet X, previously mentioned by my husband Ollie, where Picard meets Charles (via the holodeck). 

But aside from many of the roles already mentioned by my friends Dean and Christopher, I want to mention his guest starring role on Futurama, in the episode “31st Century Fox.” At the end, it is revealed Stewart’s character, the Master of the Hunt, is actually a robot rather than a human. While the episode was released in 2012, this now feels like a reference to Picard Season 1 to me, which makes it extra hilarious.

Z.: Shocking to no one, Professor X, but especially in Logan. No one else (except perhaps Stewart’s bestie McKellan) could better play this all-powerful X-Man turned vulnerable invalid, losing control of his powers and his mind. But still badass as hell. —Z. Rice

OLLIE: Not to be cheesy, but my favorite “other” role from Sir P. Stew is all of his activism. The man really earned that knighthood, with all the work he did for others. Domestic violence activism. Check. LGBTQIA+ activism. Check. COVID-19 safety activism. Check. Animal rights activism. Check. And in his final hour, he even requested that fans donate “memorial contributions may be made to Johns Hopkins Alzheimer’s Disease Research Center Fund and Alzheimer’s Foundation of America Caregiver Resources,” according to an Instagram post reported on by Trash Kitty Comics.

GEORGE: Besides the franchise work with Star Trek and the X-Men, Sir Patrick is also known for his Shakespearean work, but he quietly built a reputation for being funny. And for me, his run as Walter Blunt in the Starz channel sitcom Blunt Talk. Sir Patrick plays an overbearing cable news personality with major issues, like being unable to go in a public bathroom with other people around, and watching Captain Picard struggle with a toilet seat cover, priceless.

TAIMUR: Numerous that’s it’s hard to choose. In terms of animation, I have a soft spot for his role as CIA Deputy Director Avery Bullock in American Dad. Besides a great showcase of his comedic skills, I also find it really endearing that self-professed Trekkie Seth MacFarlane developed a deep professional and personal relationship throughout the years.

But I’m sure the most obvious is Professor Xavier in the X-Men film franchise. It’s one of those no-brainer casting decisions fans knew would be perfect from the get-go. And sure enough. There is certainly some overlap not just between Picard and Xavier as characters but also Star Trek and X-Men as franchises.

Stewart never phoned it in or looked down upon the material in any way. In fact, his involvement elevated the material. I know it’s easy to joke about how often he’s been killed off playing Professor X. I think it’s safe to assume that’s the case for Avengers: Doomsday, so I’m hoping it will be a fitting and touching swan song.

Do you have any other reflections on Stewart to share on the occasion of his passing?

DEAN: I loved how he was able to evoke a sense of calm in his many more well-known roles. And his deep sense of empathy he displayed in his public life.

TAIMUR: Even being highly educated and classically educated, I love that Stewart was never elitist or looked down upon popular entertainment. In fact, he wasn’t shy about enjoying it for himself. I vaguely recall years back that Stewart was a fan of Beavis & Butt-Head. I wasn’t entirely sure If it was something I misremembered, but quick search on the internet confirmed that it was indeed the case.

For me, the most telling thing about Stewart is the fact that I haven’t heard a single bad word said about him. That’s not always the case when entertainers pass away. So that speaks volumes.

CHRISTOPHER: It feels so strange to grieve someone I never even saw on stage, but such was his presence in my life. I used to be late for school, or stay up just to hear him talk about X-Men on TV, for goodness’ sake. He would’ve been the first to admit he wasn’t perfect, but he was an ideal father figure, especially for those of us with less than great parents, and cool nerd representation too (let’s not forget how contentious the idea of a bald leading man was when TNG premiered). That extended into real life, with the way he opened up about domestic violence during his childhood, and spoke out on Brexit and other political issues. And even though he was 86, he still had such a lust for life (he still wanted to keep playing Picard, and presumably Xavier if Marvel asked), that his death from Alzheimer’s and Lewy body dementia feels especially cruel.

I think Stewart should be an example to us all to continue to always be open-minded and curious, to be playful and joyful, and to speak out about what matters, even into old age. I struggle to think of how many younger prominent actors can fulfill the similar role of an older role model someday, and that also saddens me. Even now, something like his love for his local football team (Huddersfield Town) is making me consider if I should remain as antipathetic towards sports as I am. As the saying on his signature series goes, he lived long and prospered, and I only wish he’d been with us for even longer.

GEORGE: I had always hoped I would run into him one day so I could thank him for being the catalyst for my wife and me connecting. Thank you Sir Patrick.

Z.: If you haven’t seen photos and videos of Patrick Stewart with rescue pit bulls, stop reading and go do that now. He seemed to be a man of both gravitas and lightness, wisdom and silliness. And each new layer he revealed touched me in some way. He was my captain.

OLLIE: Everyone else has something deep to say — and I second all of it. I will add that if you didn’t think this man would become a major sex symbol, then you’ve never seen the photo below of him in Shakespeare.

issues.title: Updated Xbox PC app promises 60% faster loading and easier access to games, but CEO Asha Sharma says there's "plenty more to do"
issues.summary: The Xbox PC app hasn't had the best track record in recent years, but Microsoft is promising that it's now much faster and easier to use than before. Read more
issues.author: Kaan Serin
issues.content_html:
The Xbox PC app hasn't had the best track record in recent years, but Microsoft is promising that it's now much faster and easier to use than before.

Starting today, anyone part of the Xbox Insiders program can try out the new improvements. According to Microsoft, the updated Xbox PC app now boots up 60% faster, several pages can launch up to 50% faster, and in-app windows can open up to 65% faster. The company acknowledged that performance can vary based on your set up, internet connection, device, and so on.

The rest of the update involves "simpler navigation, updated filters, and new ways to organise your games," according to Xbox Wire, while social features are now included in the main navigation menu so you can start playing or chatting with friends quicker.

A faster Xbox PC app is certainly nice for players who regularly use it, though it's still missing a lot of the features that make Steam the go-to place to buy PC games. CEO Asha Sharma called the update "a meaningful improvement," but acknowledged there's still "plenty more to do."

Microsoft also said "it's easier to find what you're looking for" using the app's search function, and refreshed game cards and animations should give the platform "a cleaner look and feel."

Elsewhere, the revamped cloud gaming setup will roll out to even more people using web browsers, and more Xbox Insiders should hear about the program over the next few weeks. "The updated experience also makes it easier to find and play your games," the company said while bringing attention to its new light and dark modes. Supported smart TVs and VR headsets will get the updated cloud experience, as well.

Earlier this year, the console maker brought a selection of 'classic' games to PC for the first time ever - Blinx: The Time Sweeper, Conker: Live and Reloaded, Crimson Skies: High Road to Revenge and Fuzion Frenzy led the first batch. Mythic Achievements - the Platinum Trophy equivalent - went live for all Xbox players, too.

issues.title: The Relationship Between Comedy, Democracy, and AI
issues.summary: “Humor, more than anything else in the human make-up, can afford an aloofness and an ability to rise above any situation, even if only for a few seconds,” Viktor Frankl wrote in recalling the role of humor as a lifeline to sanity and survival in the Holocaust. Humor is a…
issues.author: Maria Popova
issues.content_html:
“Humor, more than anything else in the human make-up, can afford an aloofness and an ability to rise above any situation, even if only for a few seconds,” Viktor Frankl wrote in recalling the role of humor as a lifeline to sanity and survival in the Holocaust.

Humor is a fundamental human freedom: To laugh is to protect ourselves from all that dehumanizes us — tyranny and transactionalism, captivity and commodification. Humor is also fundamental to free societies, to freedom of thought, to democracy: To laugh together is to harmonize our deepest humanity.

Because humor is the art of surprise, it exists beyond the reach of — and is an antidote to — the artifices of predictive computation we mistake for intelligence.

In her altogether fantastic manifesto for breaking free from the prison of predictive technologies, Carissa Véliz argues that humor thrives in the same “spaces of indeterminacy” where creativity and innovation also thrive. (“Whatever inspiration is, it’s born from a continuous ‘I don’t know,’” the Polish poet Wisława Szymborska observed in her magnificent Nobel Prize acceptance speech.) With an eye to the emotional attunement of sharing laughter, Véliz considers the relationship between humor, democracy, and AI:

Our sense of humor is a dialogue, and when we delegate the conversation to AI, we lose the personal relationship with another human being. Democracy itself is a conversation. If we give up our seat at that table and give it to an AI, we will lose our voice.

Comedy is not inconsequential for democracy. Comedy sets the tone for freedom. It gives us courage. A documentary about comedy clubs in war-torn Ukraine reminds me that humor is not a luxury; it’s indispensable. “When I went to Sarajevo to a film festival,” Cleese says, “people were talking about the early ’90s, when Yugoslavia was falling apart. Sarajevo is down in a valley, and the Serbs were up in the hills throwing shells down, and telescopic snipers were shooting people crossing the street. And they told me that they had found an underground car park, had turned it into a cinema, and they would show comedies, including Monty Python, and they would laugh. When they came out, an hour and a half later, they felt better. Nothing had improved. But they were better able to deal with their situation.” Comedy can be an ally in our challenge to defy the odds.

Humor, like creativity, works by defying expectation. It is a felicitous violation of the norm. Societies thrive and progress by continually challenging the norm, the given, the status quo. Every revolution, every change in regime, is the story of turning the old order from terrible to laughable.

donating = loving

For seventeen years, I have been spending hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars each month composing The Marginalian (which bore the outgrown name Brain Pickings for its first fifteen years). It has remained free and ad-free and alive thanks to patronage from readers. I have no staff, no interns, no assistant — a thoroughly one-woman labor of love that is also my life and my livelihood. If this labor makes your own life more livable in any way, please consider lending a helping hand with a donation. Your support makes all the difference.

issues.title: SAG-AFTRA introduces new process for hiring union actors in game pitches
issues.summary: SAG-AFTRA actors can now be recruited for vertical slices, demos, and other forms of content needed to pitch games.
issues.author: Imran Khan
issues.content_html:
SAG-AFTRA, the Screen Actors Guild-American Federation of Television and Radio Artists, is the foremost American labor SAG-AFTRA, the Screen Actors Guild-American Federation of Television and Radio Artists, has released today a new framework for using union actors in pitches and other pre-release content titled the Pre-Funding Pitch Interactive Media Agreement, specifically designed for developers creating full-featured gaming pitches. This new framework provides an opportunity for developers to use SAG-AFTRA actors in pre-production work. Previously, there were no specific union guidelines for using union actors in a pitch expected to be used to try and get a project greenlit by a publisher.

"The Pre-Funding Pitch Interactive Media Agreement streamlines the hiring of professional union talent, and that can help give devs that extra edge to get the backing they need in an extremely competitive industry," said SAG-AFTRA National Executive Director & Chief Executive Officer Duncan Crabtree-Ireland.

Related:Zelda producer: Ocarina of Time remake helps junior staff learn classic insights

Crabtree-Ireland's comments hit on the head of how increasingly difficult it is to bring an in-development pitch to publishers and the agreement itself hits on how hiring union talent for a pitch or vertical slice is becoming more necessary.

"This agreement allows developers to up their game by bringing in professional voice and motion performance talent earlier in the process to create a higher-quality product, with the goal of capturing both imaginations and funding," said SAG-AFTRA President Sean Astin, who also played Samwise Gamgee in Peter Jackson's Lord of the Rings movies.

There are a handful of rules deciding if a project is eligible for union rules, however. Any game with more than 30% of its initial production funding secured is out, as well as anything that is going to be commercially-released—which doesn't happen often, but is explicitly against the rules here.

These rules are may be an effort by the guild to ward off use of generative AI voices for pre-production use in video games. The agreement gets actors involved in the process earlier and encourages developers to avoid growing reliant on AI voices used in early development, which could lead to situations wherein AI voice acting feels like an asset that can be iterated on without the actors.

Ultimately, SAG-AFTRA's strategy may ensure that actors have leverage from word one, rather than feeling only tangentially involved to the project later on.

Can our mummy detective and his vampire sidekick escape the dungeon before a demonic cult commits mass murder and unleashes Hell?!

Kill The Dream is the latest graphic novel from cartoonist Clio Isadora, following sisters Amethyst and Parsley Mire as they return to their mother’s funeral in the isolated desert town of Jupiter Rock. Their mother, Blanche, abandoned the family years earlier to pursue her obsession with unlocking the spirit realm’s three doors of life, death and rebirth. But her followers have other plans. As the sisters discover, Blanche’s students are searching for a new vessel for her soul, pulling them into a supernatural nightmare. Following her debut Sour Pickles, Isadora delivers a contemporary horror story inspired by dysfunctional families, psychological horror,  and the lasting impact of a parent’s beliefs. Inspired by a fictionalized version of Joseph Merrick’s life, the series blends historical folklore with superhero conventions, secret identities and supernatural mysteries. What happens when the person you left behind becomes the only one who can help you survive? The Estranged is a sapphic horror thriller from writer Jason McNamara and artist Matthieu Pereira, following Heather and Albion, two former best friends whose relationship was cut short by a brutal killing in their hometown of Braddock, Texas. Thirteen years later, Heather returns, hoping to rebuild her life and reconnect with Albion, but a sinister presence has awakened, and locals are once again disappearing. An exquisite collection of historic horror fiction illustrated by Julie Doucet, with an introduction by Carmen Maria Machado.

What happens when the home meant to protect you becomes the source of your greatest fears? Death Is a Room brings together nine gothic horror stories by groundbreaking women writers, including Virginia Woolf, Kate Chopin, Frances Hodgson Burnett and Charlotte Perkins Gilman. Illustrated by award-winning cartoonist Julie Doucet, the collection features haunting black-and-red linocut artwork, alongside an introduction by Carmen Maria Machado exploring the lasting influence of gothic horror. issues.title: Mass Effect-like RPG The Expanse: Osiris Reborn ropes in David Gaider, the original lead writer of Bioware's Dragon Age series
issues.summary: The Expanse: Osiris Reborn looks like it's carrying the best bits of Mass Effect forward, and in an encouraging move, the developers have been collaborating with David Gaider. Read more
issues.author: Kaan Serin
issues.content_html:
The Expanse: Osiris Reborn looks like it's carrying the best bits of Mass Effect forward, and in an encouraging move, the developers have been collaborating with David Gaider.

Of course, David Gaider is best known as the lead writer on Dragon Age: Origins, Dragon Age 2 and Dragon Age: Inquisition - he's also often credited as the architect of its dark fantasy world Thedas. Gaider's post-BioWare career saw him open his own game development house Summerfall Studios, which most recently released an ambitious roleplaying musical called Stray Gods.

But he's now lending a hand to a game that's not too dissimilar to BioWare's other hugely famous roleplaying series, while still working on his own games at Summerfall.

"Alongside my work at Summerfall, I've also been collaborating with the Owlcat Games team on The Expanse: Osiris Reborn, focusing on certain aspects of the game's narrative. The Expanse has long been one of my favourite series, and so obviously I jumped at the opportunity to be involved," he wrote on BlueSky.

"The Owlcat team has been so great, it's really such a treat. One thing I enjoy is how responsive they are to the fans," Gaider added, pointing to how the studio recently recast the male version of its protagonist in response to feedback. The game's reworked and re-designed Martian Captain is now voiced by Blythe Melin.

The Expanse: Osiris Reborn shouldn't be confused for the other very Mass Effect-y RPG coming out next year, Exodus. Though it's good to hear that both upcoming projects have some BioWare veterans on board, especially after the famed developer was shut down and had its own promising, actual Mass Effect game cancelled.

Bertie enjoyed what he played of the upcoming game in Eurogamer's The Expanse preview, but also had some concerns about the developer's use of generative AI.

On that note, here were a few of our favorites this week.

  1. AI on the Ballot. This week’s elections delivered Democrats the largest Congressional majority either party has enjoyed in 36 years, and coupled with a variety of similar results at the state level (particularly in Texas), not to mention plenty of data center opposition among Republicans, the future of the AI buildout is now fraught with more regulatory uncertainty than ever. I wrote about X, 2024 symmetry, and the more political aspects of the election for Sharp Text, while Ben’s Article on Wednesday built on his data center warnings from April and provided 10 takes on the post-midterms landscape for tech companies. — Andrew Sharp
  1. A Google State of the Union. Last week Google reported earnings and saw growth in search revenue slow for the first time in five quarters. Given the appearance of mortality in what might be the greatest business in the history of digital commerce, investors were predictably spooked. However, I think the company deserves time to see if AI Mode ends up like Stories and Reels did for Facebook: if anyone can monetize AI with ads, it’s going to be Google. On Sharp Tech, we also got into why Google’s AI bet is about more than AI Mode, and why I find myself impressed by Google’s fortitude, even if the rest of the Internet is a casualty. — Ben Thompson

  2. And What About China? Elections have consequences, as they say, so what might a Democratic Congressional majority mean for the next two years of U.S.-China relations? We tried to answer that question on Sharp China this week, including predicting factional foreign policy fights between the left and center-left, highlighting the profound unknowns concerning President Trump’s posture after this week’s defeat, and offering one safe bet in the new environment: life is about to get a lot more complicated for Jensen Huang in Washington. — AS

Presented by

I spend a lot of time trying to figure out what is happening to businesses on the internet. What I often find I’m missing is a view across the economy itself. With more than 1.7% of global GDP running on Stripe, working with them means I can bring some of what they’re seeing to Stratechery. They are, in a sense, a barometer of the economy.

Take the “SaaSpocalypse”. Earlier this year, nearly a trillion dollars in enterprise software value disappeared amid fears of AI eating its lunch. Stock prices only tell us what investors think will happen, and not necessarily what is happening. In this case, Stripe recently built a SaaS Index using payments data from 72,000 non-AI SaaS businesses. Looking at their actual performance, we can see that while SaaS stocks were selling off, revenue growth was actually accelerating.


Year-over-year growth is now over 30%, with some of the fastest growth coming from the youngest SaaS companies. I suspect there are a lot more interesting things hiding in Stripe’s data, and I’m excited about having an excuse to go look for them.

Stratechery Articles and Updates

  • Google Earnings, Facebook Déjà Vu, The Agent Play — Google’s earnings miss looks a lot like Facebook’s, and that’s a credit to Google. The company is being more aggressive than they get credit for.
  • Apple Earnings, Memory Problems, The Hardware Company Regression — Apple’s earnings suggest that the company’s hardware business is doing better than ever, even in the face of memory challenges. Does the software story help or hurt?
  • AI on the Ballot — Data Centers were on the ballot, and they lost in a major way; what does it mean if American opposition to building is permanent?
  • An Interview With Intuit CEO Sasan Goodarzi About Accounting and AI — An interview with Intuit CEO Sasan Goodarzi about the working for one of tech’s oldest software companies, and how Intuit is leaning into the AI paradigm shift.
