issues.title: Goodbye, Lara as an intertextual queer retelling
issues.summary: This very meta fairy tale retelling both critiques and pays homage to everything that came before it. The post Goodbye, Lara as an intertextual queer retelling appeared first on Anime Feminist.
issues.author: Alex Henderson
issues.content_html:
Spoilers for Goodbye, Lara

Content warning for discussion of metaphorical and literal homophobia; queer tragedy

Goodbye, Lara is a story about stories. As a retelling of Hans Christian Andersen’s The Little Mermaid, the series is clearly in conversation with the original literary fairy tale, but its intertextuality doesn’t end there. It’s also in conversation with queer interpretations of Andersen’s work and the queer allegory many see at the heart of the story, and with the melancholy connotations of that allegory and how it resonates with tropes around queer storytelling. And looming over the whole tale are the genre conventions we’ve come to associate with fairy tales more broadly: handsome princes, good-hearted princesses, and life-altering True Love between them. Goodbye, Lara is keenly aware of all these elements and is able to play off its audience’s assumed knowledge.

Adding another layer is the fact that Goodbye, Lara is not just a retelling of The Little Mermaid but a sequel of sorts, following the mermaid heroine as she’s reborn in Lake Biwa 200 years after her tragic ending. The show is thus dealing with pre-established expectations on multiple levels: the audience knows the story of The Little Mermaid because we’ve read, watched, or otherwise experienced it before, but protagonist Lara also knows the story of The Little Mermaid because she’s lived through it. 

The retelling, then, is an interesting dance in which both the main character and the audience are aware of how this story “should” work. Lara, and the storytelling around her, carefully navigate these familiar narrative patterns to tell a new tale that both critiques and pays homage to everything that came before it.

Once upon a time…

An abstract and multi-layered retelling like Goodbye, Lara works because fairy tales are part of a shared literary language. Even if you haven’t read the original published versions (whether that’s, say, the Grimm brothers’ editorialized transcripts of pre-existing folk stories, or literary fairy tales like The Little Mermaid), odds are good that you know the basic plot beats and elements because they’re so entrenched in literature, film history, and pop culture generally across a multitude of cultures.

This familiarity is what makes fairy tales so ripe for retellings: a few key elements make the story immediately recognizable. Writers can build something new around those waypoints, infusing the transformative work with whatever social commentary, themes, or genre elements they want. Cinderella, for example, can be transformed into anything from a satirical body horror about oppressive beauty standards to a Gothic allegory for chronic illness while remaining legible as Cinderella if those key, familiar aspects are kept intact. The familiarity also means that any changes to the expected formula will be immediately visible to the audience, and the audience can enjoy seeing how and when and why new authors alter things to suit what they’re trying to explore with their new version.

As well as specific fairy tales providing a familiar framework for writers to play in, fairy tale archetypes are also a kind of storytelling language. Stock characters like the princess, the prince, and the wicked witch are shorthand literary devices that the audience understands to represent different traits or cultural ideas. This is how a series like Revolutionary Girl Utena can play with and critique the codes and conventions of fairy tales conceptually without ever referencing or retelling one story in particular. What they use them to say might vary, but a writer retelling an existing fairy tale or invoking these tropes is always starting a conversation with the audience.

Queer allegory under the sea

Naturally, there is a long literary tradition of retelling or remixing fairy tales through a queer lens (which is booming in the English-language novel market at the moment, especially for the YA demographic). The Little Mermaid is arguably extremely well-placed for this kind of adaptation. Reading the tale in tandem with Andersen’s letters, many analysts see it as a queer allegory, interpreting the mermaid’s tragic story as an expression of the author’s own broken-hearted frustration about his unrequited love for a male friend. 

Queer themes resonate out from the story more generally, too, rooted in the mermaid’s marginalization and the way her love is frowned upon by her family and ultimately deemed impossible. As with any story involving magical transformations, there’s also plenty of imagery for trans readers to draw upon. Literary history being what it is, the fairy tale’s tragic ending also echoes a lot of queer storytelling where the gays get buried, whether due to moralistic demands from the publishing house or social mores generally. 

In a queer reading of Andersen’s story, the forbidden and tragic love between the mermaid and the prince is the core of the metaphor for queerness in a queerphobic world. Goodbye, Lara picks up and expands on this, queer-coding Lara’s interest in humans through her family’s extreme stance against it. It may seem a shame to argue that a character is coded as queer because she experiences hatred coded as homophobia, but so much of Lara’s experiences with her family’s prejudice unfortunately rings true. The show’s emphasis on this makes the most sense when read in conversation with queer readings of the original tale.

Lara, like many queer-resonant characters, is an outsider and an oddball, yearning to escape the narrow role she was born into. Lara being stuck under the sea reflects the experience of many queer young people stuck at home with queerphobic relatives. She learns quickly that she shouldn’t express her interest in the surface world and uncomfortably weathers her father and sister’s rants about how all humans are inherently wicked and vile. 

This metaphor is distilled to one harrowing moment in the series finale when Lara’s father uses his trident to slash away her human form, forcing her back into his idea of an acceptable body and social role—essentially forcing her to detransition, in our mermaid-transformation-as-trans-imagery reading. Even after Lara restores the Light and saves the merfolk, she recognizes that it will be difficult to talk to her family once they see her choice to remain on land. It’s only through a fellow outsider, her ostracized aunt, the witch Grace—who gets plenty of her own queer coding during her backstory in Episode 11—that she finally finds someone who can offer her sympathy and support.

Lara’s experience, though rooted in the story’s supernatural elements, resonates with queer reality. Goodbye, Lara’s dedication to bringing the queer themes of The Little Mermaid to the forefront like this makes for a fascinating engagement with the paratextual conversation around the original tale: speaking aloud what’s expressed much more subtly, making a story that already resonated with a queer audience speak to them even more directly. 

It also makes Goodbye, Lara’s decision to let the little mermaid survive this harrowing tale of queer exclusion especially interesting. While all this metaphorical homophobia bubbles inescapably away in the background, the series not only brings Lara back from her seafoamy grave but sends her flying into a meet-cute with another girl. 

Media representation and the hollow promise of the Prince

Now, Lara doesn’t know about Hans Christian Andersen and the long history of queer readings of his work, but she does know about other aspects of the fairy tale she’s stuck in. Naturally, when the reincarnated Lara starts The Little Mermaid 2.0 and sets out on her renewed quest to find True Love, she starts her search by looking for a Prince.

Lara and the audience share a set of expectations here, albeit for different reasons: last time, Lara’s on-land romance was with a human prince, so she figures that’s what she ought to do again. The viewer, meanwhile, understands fairy tale tropes and knows that a Prince and a Princess usually go together. In terms of even broader cultural and pop cultural narratives, the audience understands what heteronormativity is and how it dictates who “ought to” fall in love with whom. It’s an established pattern; it’s the rules; it’s just how stories work. But it soon becomes clear that Lara’s new reality isn’t that simple.

Much like its predecessor Revolutionary Girl Utena—but with a little less violence—Goodbye, Lara explores how the concept of a fairy tale Prince is an empty, false ideal. Its critique begins softly with pop culture commentary. Lara, like many young people looking for instructions and inspiration about what love “should” look like, turns to fiction. She scans through TV shows and movies, searching for what constitutes a Prince in this day and age, coming across various pastiches of overwrought heterosexual romance tropes. 

Her human roommate and rescuer, Mari, is disinterested and cynical about these shows, and clearly finds them annoying while Lara finds them aspirational… perhaps implying that Mari, like many queer viewers, has long since given up hope of seeing herself in this particular romantic dynamic, and finds the whole thing trite and unrealistic.

Meanwhile, when Lara meets a boy named Luca who bears an uncanny resemblance to her previous Prince, she doesn’t get the life-altering love at first sight she’s been told she should expect—in fact, she has a panic response so strong her transformation spell glitches out and she temporarily turns back into a mermaid. It’s a far cry from her goofy, fun meet-cute with Mari and it sets the stage for her disillusionment and disappointment with the Prince. 

To be clear, Luca is… fine. He distinguishes himself from his royal predecessor by knowing and accepting that Lara is a mermaid (perhaps positioning him as a queer ally in our overarching metaphor). Rather than the Prince turning out to be a villain as in Utena, Goodbye, Lara suggests that the Prince is actually Just Some Guy, with no inherent magical life-changing qualities about him. There’s nothing wrong with Luca; at worst, he’s a whiny dork. The narrative makes clear that he’s not wicked nor vile… nor is he the person for Lara. 

As Lara tries to bond with and date Luca, it becomes increasingly clear that despite performing all the correct steps to the dance of courtly love, she just doesn’t love him, no matter how hard she tries, no matter how hard she pushes herself into the pattern she believes she has to fit to save herself and her family. True Love will save the day, and True Love means a Prince, and a Prince means a boy, right? That’s the rules, that’s how the story works. 

But when Lara eventually, awkwardly pushes herself to ask to be Luca’s lover, and he says yes, her gutted reaction is “That’s it?”. Forcing herself to conform to the expectations laid by pop culture and the pattern of her own former fairy tale clearly leaves her feeling empty. It’s a heartbreaking moment for Lara, but it also resonates outwards into a comment on the fairy tale formula itself. 

Its archetypes and their associated romantic framework rely on a set of historic gender roles and heteronormative ideas about how those roles should interact. While not explicitly made as teaching tools, the prominence of these tales and their tropes in the media, especially media aimed at children, has a didactic effect: it models a certain way of being, and a certain way that True Love works, offering little in the way of alternatives. 

Lara is left with no other map to follow when romancing her Prince doesn’t work for her, much in the way that queer young people have no map to follow if their experiences aren’t presented as a normalized, viable, happy option in the media they’re given to consume. For Mari, we can interpret that this has led to her cynicism towards sappy straight romances; for Lara, it’s life-threatening, as she risks turning back into seafoam if she can’t find love, and she has no idea what love looks like if not this. 

Lara assumes her True Love must take a certain form, i.e. be a certain gender and fulfil a certain role, so she almost misses her growing affection for Mari. The one she loves must be a boy in a crown, it couldn’t be a girl with boxing gloves—that would be a deviation from the pattern, and surely the fairy tale must follow its established pattern. And yet, across the series, Mari and Lara are set up as love interests, from big dramatic moments like Lara’s heart-fish exploding out of the lake when Mari playfully teases her in Episode 3; to countless displays of easy affection and camaraderie between them; to promises to stick together forever so Lara can make Mari cakes (cakes popular at weddings, mind you) in celebration of her growing boxing career. 

As the series’ climax looms, every time Lara thinks about what she really wants and who she really loves, all signs point to Mari. Which would be excellent news, except that it means she has to kill her.

The looming tropes of queer tragedy

Lara, surely, cannot be allowed a happy ending. By the expectations of the original Little Mermaid, she is a tragic heroine, something she’s already experienced. By the expectations of historical queer narrative, her love with Mari can’t possibly come to fruition. In other words, she’s doomed twice over, and Mari is doomed by association—hence Lara ordering her to stay away from her during the series’ climax. But Mari is determined to break the pattern, and so, it seems, are the writers of Goodbye, Lara. 

Much as the fairy tale formula tells Lara she must find True Love with a Prince, the surreal and eerie lore of the mermaid kingdom posits that she must kill the person she loves with a bitey, fish-shaped blade that manifests from her own heart—a tragic ritual established to the audience during Grace’s own sojourn on land. Lara’s heart-blade has been hanging over Lake Biwa throughout the series like an ominous obelisk, grown colossal to match the size of Lara’s heartache, and looming conveniently in the background of many conversations about how it’s impossible for humans and mermaids to love each other. 

It represents something specific in the context of Lara’s story, but it also represents the broader storytelling concepts that the show is in conversation with: the tropes, conventions, and expected patterns of queer narrative itself, gnashing its teeth and hungry for a tragic ending. That’s the rules, that’s how the story works. 

But Lara isn’t putting up with any more death. The fish kills Mari, confirming Lara’s love for her just as it makes a relationship between them impossible. Rather than mourning Mari and celebrating the spell’s completion, Lara fights back, enduring terrible pain and a new transformation to not only retrieve Mari’s soul but regrow her own legs. If the fish-blade represents inevitable tragedy, Lara actively fights her way out of it, rejecting the narrative patterns she had initially tried so hard to follow. 

And, most importantly, she succeeds, freeing herself from the grip of the original Little Mermaid tale and liberating herself and Mari from the jaws of queer tragedy. This climactic sequence brings all the metaphors and metatext together into an ending that echoes Yurikuma Arashi or Revue Starlight (or, thanks to a boatload of borrowed imagery, with Utena itself). This deviation from the established patterns is brightly visible to the audience just as it’s deliberate on Lara’s part, and thus massively cathartic for both the viewers and the characters. 

The intertextuality of the story is the source of a lot of the finale’s impact: we know the usual rules, we know what came before, and now we get to see a retelling that engages with and pays homage to that while also rejecting some of its more hurtful elements. 

And they lived happily ever after…?

You may ask how the epilogue—a short sequence that takes place after a timeskip and shows Lara leaving town by herself—fits into all this, and whether it clashes with Lara and Mari’s romantic set-up and their trajectory towards a fairy tale happy ending. Once again, Goodbye, Lara is a multi-layered thing, and the question should be what exactly a “fairy tale ending” means. 

Against Andersen’s original story, this is a triumphant finale and a massive subversion. The little (queer) mermaid gets to live this time, no strings attached, no need to wait for Christian redemption: her heart and soul belong to her, and she’s off to explore her beloved surface world on her own two feet. The conclusion of her romantic arc with Mari is at once an homage to the original and a step forward; as Rebecca Silverman suggests, “Having Mari and Lara not explicitly declare their love is a nod to Andersen having to live a life in the closet. That they both live is the greatest indication that their love is real and true.” 

Against the expectations of fairy tales generally, especially the romantic formula associated with fairy tales in modern pop culture, the epilogue ends on a more melancholy note. Usually the conclusion of the romance arc in these stories is a wedding, or at least a relationship-signifying kiss, and the promise of a shared, peaceful future… a far cry from Goodbye, Lara’s final scene, which shows a mournful-looking Mari chasing Lara’s train car until it vanishes. 

Again, both girls get to live, and we can’t discount the power of that as a narrative statement and a rejection of queer tragedy. The subversion of those expectations is cathartic for an audience that relates to these characters; the subversion of the romantic Happily Ever After… not so much. If this feels unharmonious to viewers, perhaps it’s a case of the different texts and traditions the show is in conversation with talking over one another, as it were. 

Personally, I see the epilogue as adding a slightly disjointed coda to the series without subtracting from its earlier brilliant work. The series remains a beautiful and fascinating intertextual queer retelling, engaging in themes of narrative and tradition, audience expectations, the importance of representation in pop culture, and the way that stories shape our understanding of the world and our own selves. 

Goodbye, Lara’s first episode ends with a title card announcing that the series is in tribute to Hans Christian Andersen, and I think that shines through: it subverts the original without outright rejecting it, showing a tender appreciation for Andersen’s story and its cultural impact while also putting a new, more hopeful spin on it. Hope was impossible for the original Little Mermaid, but Lara, reborn as the heroine of a transformative work, gets a second chance to navigate her own story. The joy of that is shared across both the character and her audience, making the series a wonderfully meta exercise as well as a powerful story in its own right.

issues.title: Report: Silver Lake and the Saudi Arabia PIF hold talks with Unity to explore acquisition
issues.summary: The investment partners recently acquired Electronic Arts and are now reportedly turning their gaze toward software engine Unity.
issues.author: Imran Khan
issues.content_html:
Unity Software, the company behind the Unity game engine, is in conversations with Silver Lake and the Saudi Arabia Private Investment Fund, according to new reporting from Reuters. Both Silver Lake and the PIF just recently finalized an acquisition of Electronic Arts, taking the company private in a leveraged buyout.

The Reuters story states that a consortium of investors are involved, with the biggest being Silver Lake—owned by United States President Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner—and Saudi Arabia's Private Investment Fund, which has been investing in numerous video game and technology companies internationally. Silver Lake already owns eight percent of Unity, but Reuters reports that PIF approached both Unity and the investment firm to make an offer for a full buyout.

The sources for the Reuters report also state that the deal would take the form of a leveraged buyout, much like the Electronic Arts deal which purchased the company with funds that would need to be recouped by its operating profit. While not being the record-breaking numbers the EA acquisition boasted, this would still be one of the biggest leveraged buyouts in history.

Related:Nintendo confident in memory supply in new financial report

Unity's game engine is used, by their own accounting, in over half of all mobile games and a large proportion of console and PC games. Scopely, which is already owned by the PIF and Silver Lake among others, uses it to power titles like Pokémon Go and Monopoly Go.

Unity has expanded to an AI-prominent structure, recently launching a prompt-based tool in collaboration with Google to create games entirely from user prompts called Unity Spark.

The company unveiled a new policy of Runtime Fees in 2024 which was intended to charge developers a per-install tariff, but a monumental backlash to the idea from developers forced Unity to undo the planned policy. Declining stock prices were perhaps the reason then-Unity CEO John Riccitiello—also former CEO of Electronic Arts—resigned from his position. The current CEO, Matthew Bromberg, was also a former EA executive who acted as General Manager of BioWare, a studio which the publisher recently shut down as it attempts to pay off the leveraged buyout from Silver Lake and PIF.

The backlash that unseated Riccitiello shows that Unity is not inured to revolt from its client-facing business, unlike Electronic Arts which does not deal directly with individual developers at a similar scale. A buyout from new, controversial owners could lead to an upheaval in Unity's core business, potentially putting the company's operating profit at risk.

Related:Tripwire Interactive expands publishing business to focus on smaller developers and games

issues.title: IDW and Official Cellar launch limited edition Godzilla Premium Agave Spirits
issues.summary: IDW has announced another collaboration with Official Cellar for GODZILLA Premium Agave Spirits featuring limited edition, numbered bottles.
issues.author: Isaac Swindle
issues.content_html:
IDW has announced another collaboration with Official Cellar for Godzilla Premium Agave Spirits. This new line of spirits follows IDW’s previous releases for The Rocketeer American Whiskeys, celebrating the 35th anniversary of the film, and the Wynonna Earp Kentucky Straight Bourbon Whiskey. This limited edition release features seven different spirits, two pour spouts, and limited and numbered bottle collections to be enjoyed responsibly.

The collaboration features three base Godzilla-themed bottles ranging from $65 to $75– Blanco Agave, Smoky Agave, Reposado– and then a limited tier of numbered bottles at a higher proof with “master aging.” The limited tier includes:

  • Godzilla Cask Strength: Reposado Smoky Agave Spirit ($125, 51.7% ABV)
  • Godzilla Cask Reserve: Reposado Smoky Agave Spirit ($100, 45% ABV)
  • Godzilla Cask Strength: Reposado Agave Spirit ($125, 56.8% ABV)
  • Godzilla Cask Reserve: Reposado Agave Spirit ($100, 48.5% ABV)

Collectors can also choose from the Godzilla: Complete Collection or the Godzilla: Legacy Collections. The Complete Collection comes with one of each bottle, as well as the two gold and silver pour spouts, and is priced at $779. The Legacy Collection, of which there are only 40 sets available, includes the same contents but each bottle has a matching number. These sets are guaranteed to fall within the 11 and 50 range and are priced at $879. There is also the Origins Collection featuring the three base bottles for $210, as well as the ultra high-end Vault Collection. The Vault Collection is limited to 10 sets and includes bottles numbered between 1 and 10. The Vault Collection is priced at $999.

IDW CEO, Davidi Jonas, had this to say about the most recent collaboration, “Creating a spirit worthy of Godzilla is an order as tall as the King of the Monsters itself, but IDW and Official Cellar are always up for the task of honoring and celebrating the fans with every new bottle. We’re proud of these spirits — the best I’ve tasted in every category being sold, that’s what it takes to be an Official Cellar branded spirit — and we know the carefully designed bottles will look great as collectibles. Enjoy responsibly!”

Collectors can find these limited time collections or individual bottles on the Official Cellar website, available now. For more on what the King of the Monsters has been up to, check out The Beat’s interview with Godzilla creators Nick Marino and Oliver Ono, or the upcoming Kai-Sei Era crossovers. As always, The Beat encourages readers to drink responsibly.

issues.title: Is This Old News? Feedly Is An AI Threat Intelligence Company Now?
issues.summary: Huh??
issues.author: Nicole Carpenter
issues.content_html:
This may be old news to some of you, but it is not to me: Feedly, once a RSS feed reader, is an AI-driven threat intelligence company now. Apparently this has been in the works for some time. As of January, the Feedly website advertised the company as three things—threat intelligence, market intelligence, and a news reader. Months later, Feedly all but scrubbed market intelligence and its news reader from its website. (A small button, "Go to News Reader," remains on the top of the front page.) I suppose this is news to me because I never actually go to the Feedly website; I just go straight to my RSS feed.

Feedly has been kind of bad lately, which is how I found out that it made the baffling pivot to AI: My partner mentioned it after I complained about how much Feedly sucks, and I then found a news story from TechCrunch in which Feedly claimed its summer slowdown was a bug and not because of AI. In the last year, Feedly Classic stopped working. The Feedly app is broken. It seems to be slowly disabling its news reader features. The company had seemingly been doing nothing to address this stuff. (Some of this stuff has been fixed, apparently. But Feedly still sucks for me.)

“Despite the pivot to cyber threat intelligence, fixing the basic RSS functionality is still a priority because our CTI community uses the news-reading capability,” Feedly CEO Edwin Khodabakchian told TechCrunch. “Our goal has been to maintain the Feedly News Reader as fast and streamlined as possible.” Sure!

I understand that this is a niche issue; overall, I think there's a very small population of people who still use RSS feeds. But they’re helpful for me as someone who reads a lot of news, since it’s near impossible to keep up with everything as a journalist without some sort of collation. Feedly has never been a good option, but there are very few options, and nothing ever really hit like Google Reader did. 

I can't even really tell what Feedly is supposed to do as a threat intelligence product. It actually looks a lot like news reader Feedly. Apparently you can use its AI agents to look at the dark web for security vulnerabilities? "Deliver STIX-formatted threat intel to your entire security stack and stakeholders?" What the fuck? 

It's expensive, too. It starts at $1,600 per month and goes up to $2,400 monthly. I simply don't understand. It's the sort of mind boggling pivot that I attribute to Allbirds selling off its shoe business to do something with AI.

I don't know, guys. I don't think I'd trust AI to help me with internet security. There's a whole Wikipedia page about cyberattacks from rogue AI agents! Last month, AI exploited a bug that created a big ol' crisis with a PHP vulnerability. A security research company did find the bug in this case, but the ability of AI to very quickly do these sorts of things makes it much easier for people to use it to create chaos, steal information, and generally wreck havoc on the internet.

issues.title: Real-time strategy game The Fertile Crescent 2 is an isometric odyssey inspired by Age of Empires, with the 1.0 release out now
issues.summary: Age of Empires-influenced real-time strategy game The Fertile Crescent 2: Collapse of the Bronze Age leaves early access today, publishers MicroProse have announced, with the 1.0 version adding the final chapters of the singleplayer story. You'll also get your grubby fingers on…
issues.author: Edwin Evans-Thirlwell
issues.content_html:
Age of Empires-influenced real-time strategy game The Fertile Crescent 2: Collapse of the Bronze Age leaves early access today, publishers MicroProse have announced, with the 1.0 version adding the final chapters of the singleplayer story. You'll also get your grubby fingers on the very same map editor developers Wield Interactive used to design the campaign.

I'm new to The Fertile Crescent 2 myself. I do like the sound of a strategy sim in which you guide a fugitive community through the Late Bronze Age Collapse. The land has been thrown into turmoil by the arrival of the Sea People, this being a loose historical term for assorted ocean-going migrants who, I gather, are often blamed for the crumbling of the Hittites among other once-glorious Bronze Age powers. I don't have much scholarly insight to share - I thought the "Sea People" referred to expansionist mermaids, at first - but I do have a trailer.

issues.title: HULK relaunch by Condon and Cappuccio will be Marvel’s only 2027 Comics Giveaway Day release
issues.summary: Ultimate Wolverine creators Chris Condon and Alessandro Cappuccio will reunite for Bruce Banner's post-Infernal Hulk series, releasing for free on May 1, aka Comics Giveaway Day.
issues.author: Christopher Chiu-Tabet
issues.content_html:
Marvel Comics has revealed it will release only one Comics Giveaway Day title in 2027: a brand-new Hulk #1, by Ultimate Wolverine writer Chris Condon and artist Alessandro Cappuccio. Picking up from Phillip Kennedy Johnson and Nic Klein‘s Infernal Hulk, the series will see Bruce Banner be confronted with the prospect of finally curing himself of the Hulk, even though it would come at an “unholy price” that would bring about “his final damnation” as well.

The full, official synopsis (which reads as if the Hulk is interjecting) says, “Bruce Banner is left with the curse he’s spent his life trying to escape… and he’s done running. UNTHINKABLE FREEDOM. AN UNHOLY PRICE. An impossible temptation promises a permanent cure, placing Banner’s salvation within reach, but bringing his final damnation one step closer. LURKING IN THE SHADOWS, A NEW MONSTER RISES. Banner’s desperate hunt for a cure will reveal how much he’ll sacrifice to bury the Hulk forever.”

Condon says, “Dreams do come true, it seems, even if it comes at the suffering of poor Bruce Banner. I am beyond thrilled to be a part of the team chronicling the next era of the Jade Giant at Marvel.” He adds, “I’ve loved the Hulk since I was a kid and that love has continued to this very day, so I hope people know that what we’re crafting is in tribute to everything from [Stan] Lee & [Jack] Kirby‘s initial debut to Phillip Kennedy Johnson, Nic Klein, & company’s horrifyingly brilliant Infernal Hulk saga. We are taking things in an exciting new direction for our day and age, but don’t worry, HULK STILL SMASH.”

Cappuccio also says, “There are characters you meet professionally, and others who, in some way, stay with you. The Hulk definitely belongs to the second category. Behind his immense strength lies a universe of fragility, conflicts, and contradictions that continues to fascinate me. He’s a character who seems to have an endless supply of stories to tell, and that’s exactly what makes him so special. Having the opportunity to explore this universe means a great deal to me.”

Issue #1 will be available on Saturday, May 1. Marvel editor-in-chief Stephen Wacker says of their Comics Giveaway Day decision, “[Our] offering should not only give people a reason to run to their comic shops, but also a reason to come back! That’s why we’re choosing it to launch Hulk, giving away the entire first issue of his new ongoing series. We believe strongly in what Chris and Alessandro are building here and while PKJ and Nic are definitely a hard act to follow, we want as many people as possible to get their huge green mitts on the Hulk’s next adventure!”

Variant covers for the issue will only be available in blind bags. Special 20-bag display boxes will also be available, each containing 19 blind bagged copies, and an exclusive “gamma irradiated” glow-in-the-dark cover by Patrick Gleason. In the meantime, Johnson and Klein’s Hulk War: Infernal Rage will begin the end of their run (which started in 2023) this February, and the latest prelude issue, Infernal Hulk vs. Spider-Man, is available now.

issues.title: Not Even Anakin And Asmongold Could Stop The Bluenami
issues.summary: 'What was Asmongold doing? Fucking malding for eight hours in his decrepit house'
issues.author: Nathan Grayson
issues.content_html:
If you aren’t a fascist (or fascist affiliate), this has been a great week. If you are, well, a) kinda crazy that you’re reading Aftermath, and b) hopefully you've learned some hard lessons. Turns out, no amount of reverse-engineering fandom from first principles or listening to the deranged ramblings of a racist roach king could salvage a truly dire midterm slate. How did the online right so badly misread the room? On the latest Aftermath Hours, we discuss. 

This time around, we celebrate the stunning series of midterm wins Democrats picked up across the country, but don’t worry, this is still a podcast about video games and other nerd stuff, so we keep things close to home: Why did the right (or at least, brain-poisoned X users) think memes about Anakin Skywalker and a gender-swapped version of Draco Malfoy would turn the tide in their favor? And what was the end result of right-wing media spending a full election cycle fixating on Hasan Piker, a Twitch streamer, instead of their own candidates?

Also, less significant but still funny: How did we end up in a situation where Halo composer turned sexist, homophobic asshole Marty O’Donnell lost an election while former Dragon Ball Z composer Nathan M. Johnson won a separate election? Lastly, Chris extols the virtues of Queen’s Domain, and we talk about our favorite video game secrets. 

You can find this week's episode below and on Spotify, Apple, or wherever else you prefer to listen to podcasts. You can also watch it on YouTube. If you like what you hear, leave a review (or sub to our YouTube channel) so that we don’t have to become composers who ultimately pursue a career in politics.

Here’s an excerpt from our conversation (edited for length and clarity):

Nathan: Hasan’s stream attracted over 200,000 concurrent viewers, and meanwhile you had Asmongold—who for the better part of Trump 2 has been at least in terms of raw viewership (with bots included) beating Hasan—at 50,000. That’s a big number on Twitch, but he was dwarfed by Hasan’s coverage of all of this.

I think there are a few reasons for that. One is definitely the vibe shift away from Trump. His second term has been a miserable disaster, and a lot of people are jumping ship. But the other part is that Hasan has been deeply involved in a lot of these campaigns and actually goes outside and does political activism at this point. In so doing—and because of the way he’s been treated by mainstream media and by Republicans and Democrats alike—he’s become kind of a main character in this whole news cycle as well. 

So of course people were like “How is he going to react to this?” They weren’t just watching purely for coverage; they were like “He’s one of the characters, too. He’s firsthand.” If you look at how things played out on election night, Hasan’s viewership was second only to, like, NBC, which is absolutely crazy, but also demonstrative of how things work now. 

Gita: He also had amazing guests on his stream. He had Ro Khanna on there, and he was talking directly to people who were about to win or just won. That’s content. What was Asmongold doing? Fucking malding for eight hours in his decrepit house. 

Nathan: Which is what he always does, and that gets old. Even if you’re looking at people like Hasan as entertainers, [his broadcast had more entertainment value]. I think he’s transcended [the label of entertainer]. For a long time, if you asked him, he’d be like “I’m a political entertainer. I’m not a political figure. I’m not running for office obviously, etc.”

Chris: He wears a suit now. 

Nathan: He does wear a suit. But I think in terms of the extent to which he and his community have gotten involved in political campaigns, you no longer can make the argument that he’s purely an entertainer. But even on that basis, I would say that he’s more entertaining than someone like Asmongold, because Asmongold just sits in his house all the time and doesn’t really do anything beyond complain and play video games. 

Chris: The joke I made is that the rat on his windowsill got up and started doing “Hello! Ma Baby” like Michigan J. Frog [in Looney Tunes]. 

Nathan: The rat’s woke now, too. 

Chris: The rat’s awake. The rat is dabbing on you.

Gita: Asmongold has been eaten by rats. All the rats are sick. They’ve thrown up all over.

Chris: The rats are gay, too.

issues.author: Julian Benson
issues.content_html:
I may be very late to the party with this discovery, but I only just realised you can connect your Steam Wishlist to a third-party deals tracker. The beauty of which is that, once hooked up, you can see what games you've been pining for are going cheap not just on Steam but through any major shopfront across the internet.

I worry that I will be coming across as 'Use this one trick to save money – greengrocers hate it!', but it's already helped save my nephew more than £40. Even if it meant using a slightly underhand method.

issues.title: Sony insists its next-generation console plans are still on schedule
issues.summary: As part of the media giant's quarterly financial report, Sony states that progress toward the next generation of consoles is proceeding on schedule.
issues.author: Imran Khan
issues.content_html:
In Sony's Q2 financial report, the company announced that it's lifting its full-year profit forecast by 9 percent, 2.6 million PlayStation 5 units were sold this past quarter, and that it does not fear the ongoing memory crisis. Sony is, in fact, moving ahead with plans for next-generation hardware in the next fiscal year with confidence.

"Looking ahead to next fiscal year, we aim to continue to enhance user engagement and further strengthen monetization through the release of strong titles and the expansion of our service," the financial report reads. "We also intend to make solid progress in preparing for the next generation platform."

Later in the Q&A, which you can review here, one investor asked Sony CFO Lin Tao if the company's next-generation hardware plans were still on schedule.

"So this is a next-generation R&D," Tao answered. "We are progressing as scheduled. So for the next-generation investment, so the second half would be a large impact of the investment amount. And the development itself is on schedule."

Related:Xbox CEO says console demand is outstripping supply—but sales continue to drop

Another investor from BofA Securities asked how Sony is dealing with the rise in memory prices and the effect that will have on profitability going into a new generation. Tao also fields this question, stating that they have to assume that their production pipeline will be capable enough to produce units, with executive officer Naoya Horii chiming in that Sony has a deal with TMSC to assuage concerns of supply limitations.

The PlayStation 5 itself has reached a 97.9 million units shipped milestone, a virtual guarantee to cross the 100 million units threshold in the coming quarter. Marvel's Wolverine sold 2.4 million copies in the two months since release, which puts it in dire straits when directly compared to games like Marvel's Spider-Man 2, which Sony reported as selling 2.5 million copies on its first day of release. A more recent comparison, Ghost of Yotei, sold 3.3 million copies in its first month, also according to Sony.

Mutant superheroes aside, the quarterly results paint a rosy picture for PlayStation, but the looming discussion of price for the next generation of hardware hangs over any excitement over upcoming plans. While Sony seems confident that the memory crisis won't affect next-generation ambitions, it is difficult to see how that can truly be the case when you consider Sony CEO Hiroki Totoki expressing skepticism for just that reason a few months ago.

issues.title: Marianne Moore on the Three Elements of Persuasive Writing
issues.summary: Several years ago, rummaging through the archives of the Academy of American Poets, I came upon a box labeled “Ballots 1950” — the record of the secret vote by the chancellors the year the Academy’s prestigious fellowship was awarded to E.E. Cummings, catapulting him into…
issues.author: Maria Popova
issues.content_html:
Several years ago, rummaging through the archives of the Academy of American Poets, I came upon a box labeled “Ballots 1950” — the record of the secret vote by the chancellors the year the Academy’s prestigious fellowship was awarded to E.E. Cummings, catapulting him into renown. The voting process is a black box — no one outside the Academy ever finds out who else is in the running and by how much the winner wins.

Leafing through the ballots, one other name appeared over and over, so much so that I was impelled to count.

Marianne Moore had lost by one vote, never knowing how close she had come. It would be many more years until, at 77, she was finally awarded the fellowship.

Long before that, before she won the Pulitzer Prize and the National Book Award (sharing a table with Rachel Carson at the ceremony), Moore had set down her views on writing in a series of essays later collected in the out-of-print gem Predilections (public library). Pulsating through them is a reckoning with the impossible task of the writer — to weave tapestries of truth and meaning from the tenuous thread of words on the ramshackle loom of language.

In an essay titled “Feeling and Precision,” Moore writes:

Feeling at its deepest — as we all have reason to know — tends to be inarticulable. If it does manage to be articulate, it is likely to seem overcondensed, so that the author is resisted as being enigmatic or disobliging or arrogant.

How we name what we feel is not so much a matter of our writing style as of our style of being, because in order to articulate something we must first apprehend it and we apprehend every smallest thing with the whole person — with the frame of reference that is our entire life, the sum of our experience and memory. When “one of New York’s more painstaking magazines” asked Moore to distill her poetic style into a formula, she fought back the “dictatorial” reflex to quip:

You don’t devise a rhythm, the rhythm is the person, and the sentence but a radiograph of the personality.

And yet a personality can write with more or less persuasion — that is, write more or less well — depending on what the person brings to the writing. In another essay from the collection, Moore identifies the three psychological elements necessary for persuasive writing: “humility, concentration, and gusto.” A generation after Mark Twain assured his friend Helen Keller when she was accused of plagiarism that “substantially all ideas are second-hand, consciously and unconsciously drawn from a million outside sources,” she writes:

Humility… is armor, for it realizes that it is impossible to be original, in the sense of doing something that has never been thought of before. Originality is in any case a by-product of sincerity; that is to say, of feeling that is honest and accordingly rejects anything that might cloud the impression.

By “concentration” Moore means a kind of discipline — annealing the essence of the sentiment by cutting away all superfluous explanations, elaborations, and distractions of stylistic posturing, being maximally truthfully in the most minimal way possible. Observing that there is always a “helpless sincerity which precipitates a poem” and that a good poem is always “a concentrate,” she writes:

Concentration — indispensable to persuasion — may feel to itself crystal clear, yet be through its very compression the opposite… I myself would rather be told too little than too much.

Long before we had the language of extrinsic and intrinsic motivation, of finite and infinite games, Moore uses a lovely word, now dusty, for that peculiar private zeal propelling all creative work with its twin dynamos of discipline and deliverance: “gusto.” Echoing Rachel Carson’s abiding advice on writing — “If you write what you yourself sincerely think and feel and are interested in,” she had counseled a young writer, “the chances are very high that you will interest other people as well.” — Moore offers:

Gusto thrives on freedom, and freedom in art, as in life, is the result of a discipline imposed by ourselves. Moreover, any writer overwhelmingly honest about pleasing himself is almost sure to please others.

She maps the fundamental relationship between the three:

Humility is an indispensable teacher, enabling concentration to heighten gusto.

When creating in integrity with these three values, it ceases to matter how the work is received because the process of locating and articulating the truth as you feel it, the world as you see it, is its own reward. In what may be the best advice I have encountered on how to orient to your own work, Moore writes:

There are always objecters, but we must not be sensitive about not being liked or not being printed… The thing is to see the vision and not deny it; or care and admit that we do.

Complement with Walt Whitman on how to keep criticism from sinking your soul and Mary Oliver’s advice on writing, then savor the moving story of how Marianne Moore saved a rare tree with a poem.

issues.title: Terrific fantasy RPG Queen's Domain gets first proper update, adding a new throwing weapon and options to make puzzles "less frustrating"
issues.summary: Extremely good King's Field-style RPG Queen's Domain – or is it a Metroid Prime homage? Or a stealth Morrowind-up? We hacks simply cannot decide – has received its first proper patch, adding a hitherto "missing" throwing weapon, the Grave Knife, alongside a bunch of…
issues.author: Edwin Evans-Thirlwell
issues.content_html:
Extremely good King's Field-style RPG Queen's Domain – or is it a Metroid Prime homage? Or a stealth Morrowind-up? We hacks simply cannot decide – has received its first proper patch, adding a hitherto "missing" throwing weapon, the Grave Knife, alongside a bunch of quality-of-life fixes.

They've stirred in the ability to disable screenshake, alongside some new icons to make status effects more obvious. They've also introduced "options to make some late game puzzles less frustrating", though they don't specify which. How frustrating! Still, it's a tidy overhaul for a game that has rapidly become one of my 2026 favourites.

issues.title: What to build next? With Bill Gross, IdeaLab.ai
issues.summary: “This is my way to have 12,000 companies at once.“
issues.author: Marija Gavrilov
issues.content_html:
This week, I hosted the legendary Bill Gross, founder and chairman of Idealab, for a conversation with the Exponential View community about building businesses in the AI age.

Bill recently founded Idealab.ai, which uses AI to explore vast spaces of potential business ideas, evaluate them against real-world problems, and help founders pressure-test and refine them.

What stayed with me was his emphasis on iteration and speed. At Exponential View, we think about this a lot. AI can help generate ideas and handle more of the mechanics, but founders still need to listen to customers, exercise judgment, and adapt. Bill joked that he should have called his company “Iterate Lab.”

issues.title: Tokyo International Film Festival 2026: Weaving Cultural Threads
issues.summary: Highlights from this year's Tokyo International Film Festival.
issues.author: Katie Rife
issues.content_html:
Three years into covering the Tokyo International Film Festival, and this was the first time my slate was filled almost entirely with Japanese films. The festival’s programming didn’t change—it’s featured a similar ratio of domestic and international films as long as I’ve been coming to Tokyo. The jury awards favored international selections, bestowing the sardonic, surreal Macedonian “Parasite” riff “Sister Brother Manhole Cover” with this year’s Grand Prix, the festival’s top prize. In fact, there was only one Japanese movie among the winners on the main competition slate. 

And, to be sure, there were some non-Japanese films that caught my attention at this year’s TIFF (the Tokyo one, not the Toronto one, as one often has to clarify in conversation). The sweet, bookish Tamil drama “The Paper Flower” stood out, as did “Fuxi: Four Tales of Feasting,” by Chinese contemporary artist Qiu Jiongjiong, “Fuxi” is what you’d call a “big swing,” and it was divisive, at least among the foreign critics with whom I gathered after hours at the many smoky izakayas filled with plastic stools and jars of wooden chopsticks near the festival headquarters. (I’m partial to the one that’s literally underneath the shinkansen tracks, although they all have their charms.) 

A Japanese film, “The Intertwining,” was more popular. Director Akira Yamamoto’s style can be compared to that of Ryusuke Hamaguchi, pointing in a roundabout way to another popular topic of conversation in Tokyo: The divide between Japanese popular cinema (mostly consumed domestically) and Japanese arthouse films like “All of a Sudden” (which tend to break out abroad), and how to bridge it. 

These talks inevitably came back to “Godzilla Minus Zero,” which managed to have it both ways: Takashi Yamazaki’s “Minus One” follow-up premiered to critical acclaim at the New York Film Festival and then opened to big box office in Japan and abroad. TIFF held a special centerpiece screening in the middle of Hibiya, an area that was basically turned into a gigantic immersive advertisement in the days before “Minus Zero” was officially unleashed. (Not that I’m complaining.)

One reason why this question was so prominent in my mind is that watching 11 new Japanese movies (and three classics) in one week, as I did at this year’s TIFF, gives you a pretty full view of the spectrum of what’s being made in the country today. Festival opener “Sukiyaki” is on one end of the scale, an unabashedly mainstream work of cinema from a director with a background in artsy pink movies. (More on those in a minute.) Given how catchy the original song was, though—I had to restrain myself from whistling it in a packed elevator after the screening—maybe the popular route is appropriate for a movie about its composer. 

Speaking of pinku, 2026 marks the 55th anniversary of Nikkatsu’s “Roman Porno” series, a Japanese softcore subtype that was designed to draw adult filmgoers back into theaters amid the rise of television in the early ‘70s. These were typically character-driven, artistically shot works, and “Wet Weekend,” a more obscure but equally challenging (in a good way) entry into the cycle, was no exception. Director Kichitaro Negishi and star Junko Miyashita were present for a post-film Q&A, and although they both joked about how strange it was to watch the film after so long, especially at a film festival, Negishi in particular spoke fondly about the creative freedom he enjoyed on the project. 

Like their American B-movie counterparts. Roman Pornos were places where, as long as you fulfilled your quota—here, a sex scene every 10 minutes—you could do pretty much whatever you wanted with the rest of your film. By comparison, the Amazon/MGM “Boys Love” romance “Monster in Sheep’s Clothing” had fewer sex scenes, and took fewer artistic risks. But it was still interesting to see such a distinctly Japanese phenomenon (although it’s gaining popularity abroad—insert mandatory “Heated Rivalry” reference here) in the context of an international festival. 

“One Cut of the Dead” director Shinichiro Ueda is a filmmaker who’s accustomed to working independently: His debut feature was famously made on a budget of ¥3 million (currently around $19,000). Since then, he’s expanded into the world of so-called “vertical dramas,” the latest of which was so well received that it was recut and repackaged as a standalone feature film. Despite Ueda’s thoughtful efforts, you never really forget that you’re watching a film that originated on TikTok. But the story, about a film director diagnosed with early-onset dementia trying to recall his first movie—and his crush on the girl who starred in it — is absorbing enough to transcend it. In the end, “Earthlings in Love” is both liberated and restricted by its vertical-format cinematography and twisty, melodramatic storyline. 

Although they’re both odd birds, in many ways the Japanese competition title “The Canary’s Lullaby” is an inversion of “Earthlings in Love.” Here, director Akira Ikeda takes the fairy-tale route, telling a story (it’s not quite a fable, as there’s no real moral) about an old woman in a timeless East Asian village who finds what can only be described as a really weird-looking baby threatened by a monster. Ikeda’s style of absurdity is very deadpan—one character’s laugh sounds like a dry cough—which I love.  But while it’s controlled and beautifully composed, it never quite comes to a climax.

Another form of Japanese popular entertainment I’ve been trying to learn more about is anime, as it’s an ideal example of an extremely popular type of cinema—both in Japan and abroad—that doesn’t often get the critical acclaim that it should. I had a great time watching “Grotesqqque,” an animated anthology revolving around three different Japanese teen-girl subcultures; the last segment, about a wandering band of Sapphic vampires in post-apocalyptic Japan, gave me all the Halloween I needed in a city that’s been cracking down on visible celebrations of the imported American holiday. (There’s a good reason for it, but don’t worry—the parties continue in underground clubs.) 

But the best animated film at Tokyo IFF this year—and my favorite movie of this year’s TIFF, period—was “Cherry and Virgin,” which was recommended to me by virtually every critic I talked to at the festival. And it delivered. Director Masanao Kawajiri crowdfunded this rotoscoped feature, about two illustrators—a guy who draws horny manga and a lifelong fujoshi—in their late 20s who meet on a dating app, and who share an embarrassing secret: They’re both virgins. Kawajiri’s direction on the story of these two nerds’ (said with love, of course) halting first romance is outstanding, animating each of the main characters in a different style that reflects their respective creative and emotional worlds. As they grow closer, the styles start to merge. But the visual storytelling, as brilliant as it is, wouldn’t work as well as it does if the story didn’t feature genuine connection and emotional vulnerability. 

A similar thread of longing runs through “Two Cigarettes, Three Nights,” whose English title is adapted from the more evocative, but harder to translate, Japanese title “Otoko Tomodachi,” meaning “Male Friend.” In both languages, there’s an implied question: Can men and women ever really be just friends? Our protagonist’s boyfriend doesn’t seem to think so, looking on jealously as she spends first one night, then another, then another, hanging out until dawn with a (male) former college classmate. But while the sexual tension is riveting, what really stands out about director Yukiko Mishima’s filmmaking is the attentiveness she gives to our heroine’s work as an illustrator as well as her love life. It’s also just a beautifully shot movie, one that depicts the internal worlds of women—romantic, creative, or both—with loving care. 

The question of tying together the many threads of contemporary Japanese cinema—popular and arthouse, domestic and international—was also very present at TIFFCOM, a parallel content market that took place during the Tokyo International Film Festival. Held in the same week in a different high-rise building by a strain station just a few blocks away from TIFF, the market was full of people on the afternoon when I went to walk around and see some panels, multiple of which were about the possibilities of international co-production and exporting Japanese IP.

These ideas came together at the Tokyo edition of the Fantasia Film Festival’s famous Frontieres pitch sessions, where filmmakers give a presentation in front of a crowd of financiers and foreign distributors about why they should invest in their movie. I’ve attended the Fantasia market in Montreal, so it was surreal—and also exciting—to see that same format unfold in a packed screening room at a Tokyo post-production house. Pitches came from all over Asia, but the most popular one was from a group of filmmakers based in Tokyo (with a little help from a Toronto-based Japanese producer) plotting a sequel to the 1999 rockabilly-zombie cult classic “Wild Zero.” 

But perhaps the most striking case study in the divergent threads of Japanese filmmaking at home and abroad is Shinya Tsukamoto’s “Mr, Nelson,  Did You Kill People?,” which opened to lukewarm reviews at the Venice International Film Festival but has since gone on to become a persistent, if modest, box-office force in its home country. It just entered its sixth week in theaters in Tokyo, and a masterclass that Tsukamoto’ gave at this year’s TIFF spent as much time on the director’s recent anti-war work as it did the cyberpunk movies that made him famous. 

At the talk, Tsukamoto said that he wouldn’t have a career without international film festivals, but that his primary focus going forward will continue to be anti-war cinema that’s meant to counter what he sees as a rising tide of militarization in Japan. As a result, he said that he imagines that he’ll remain an independent filmmaker for the rest of his career, but he doesn’t mind: “Filmmaking is the culmination of everything I love,” he said, adding that it combines acting, visual art, and editing, which he sees as a natural extension of the art of storytelling. And when movies themselves are a kind of co-production that takes different modes of expression and weaves them together into an entirely new and different art form, why shouldn’t the threads of cinema be tied together in other ways as well?

issues.title: “Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4” is the Best in the Series in Years
issues.summary: “Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4” is the best game in this franchise in years.
issues.author: Brian Tallerico
issues.content_html:
2007’s “Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare” was one of the most influential shooters of all time, a game that redefined expectations for a multiplayer experience and really put “CoD” on the map. It won a bunch of Game of the Year titles and was the top-selling game of 2007. As someone who is old enough to remember, it was the kind of game-changing title that really doesn’t happen as often anymore, and that certainly can’t happen in a franchise like “Call of Duty.” And yet a variation on this title may be lucky for Activision, because 2026’s “Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4” is the best game in this franchise in years.

Part of the joy of “MW4” could be comparative. Last year’s “Call of Duty: Black Ops 7” was a stinker with one of the worst campaigns in the history of this series (never forget the plant monster) and lackluster map design and overall gameplay in the multiplayer portion of the experience. 

“MW4” makes up for its predecessor’s missteps. First, the campaign is as cinematic and engaging as nearly any in the series, with impressive gameplay variants and even engaging mo-cap performances from actors including Young Mazino (“Beef”), Luke Tennie (“Shrinking”), and the singular Mads Mikkelsen.

It opens in present-day Hajin, South Korea, where Private First Class Park (Mazino) has to rescue survivors and flee enemies after a brutal attack by the North Korean Army. In a world that has shifted enemies a number of times, the North Koreans (and a few shots at the Russians) are the acceptable bad guys in 2026, although the writers of “Modern Warfare 4” are careful to emphasize that the real villains are the amoral people willing to sell anyone out for the right price. 

A friend asked me recently if “CoD” was “kinda MAGA,” and there’s a definite throughline of tough-guy patriotism through many of the campaigns and an ethos that believes in might over negotiation, but the writers are most interested in corruption, the politicians and arms dealers who don’t consider the human cost of their actions, and that’s depressingly apolitical.

Reflecting the temperature of a world with never-ending wars, the writers of “MW4” are arguably more brutal than ever. In an early mission, you’re in a Korean village, forced to root out a defector by any means necessary. At almost every turn in this game, you are forced to take the most violent action, and the developers want to remind you that you’re doing it. For example, you will be ordered to shoot a defector in the head in Kora and given a button cue to do so. If you wait it out and don’t take action, you die. 

This means there’s no real choice here, and yet the writers didn’t just make it into a cut scene, forcing you to do the tough work of “modern warfare”. Many missions share a similar bleakness, and several end in a remarkably misanthropic way. Sure, you can get object X through all these enemies to the endpoint, but it will just get taken, and you’ll just get shot anyway. The whole campaign has a “futility of war” theme that’s impressively oppressive.

Most importantly, it’s all so engagingly conceived and executed. The developers constantly shift the gameplay instead of just dropping waves of enemies behind well-placed cover. Some missions require stealth; some even emphasize melee. Of course, gunfire is still the main aesthetic, but even that feels more strongly considered than some outings with smarter enemy AI and loadout variation. There’s a lengthy mission in the final act of the game that’s almost open world, where you complete objectives across a big map, gather supplies to upgrade weapons, and return to a base between goals. While it’s a fun game-within-the-game, it should have come earlier, since it derails the momentum it builds now.

Of course, most “CoD” players don’t even start the campaign, spending all their time in the award-winning multiplayer portion of the game. Here’s where differences between each annual edition can feel minor on their own but add up to major variations in the overall experience.

First, the map design, something this old video game critic has always pointed out as the most important aspect of a game like this. You can give people 100 new toys and weapons, but if the maps suck, the game does too. The maps definitely do not suck here. There’s a bit of sameness, since a lot of them at launch look like abandoned Korean weapons facilities, but what really matters is the variation within the maps. Tight corridors give way to open spaces that shift their usage based on the mode (for the record, I’m a Domination and Kill Confirmed guy, with dashes of Hardpoint), and each map has inventive elements that keep it from getting stale. The loadouts and upgrades are also strong, although that can be hard to judge until the battle pass drops.

Second, the physics are top-notch. Nothing is more annoying than a shooter in which it feels like bullets aren’t connecting consistently, or weapons don’t perform as they should. That’s rarely the case here, as “MW4” has a chunkiness to movement that’s just right. Of course, it’s still a game based more on twitch response (especially in the fan-favorite, returning “Shipment”) than strategy, but it’s important that a game like this feels customizable and one that people can master across multiple play sessions, and that’s the case here.

The public response to “Call of Duty” in the 2020s has been interesting to watch. What was once one of the most beloved games in the world has lost some of its cultural cachet because annual updates felt like little more than map packs for $70, and because the developers seemed to take the fan base for granted.

There are certainly some annual games that have taken their insane popularity for granted and recycled instead of sought progress (looking at you “NBA2K,” even though I can’t stop playing), and I worried after the 2025 iteration of this game that the 2026 outing would do little more than provide a minor riff on the same. The irony of saying this about a game that’s so intensely nihilistic doesn’t escape me, but this “Call of Duty” actually gives me hope. [85/100]

The Publisher provided a review copy on PS5. It’s also on Xbox, Windows, and Switch 2.

issues.title: 🔮 Don’t waste a good backlash
issues.summary: Voters smashed the build-out at the ballot box. Democrats could turn it into a dividend.
issues.author: Azeem Azhar
issues.content_html:
The market ran for cover after the Democrats won the midterms. More than $2.5 trillion was wiped off the Nasdaq as investors fled the picks-and-shovels part of the AI trade. The Democrats made it clear that artificial intelligence would now face the scrutiny we would expect most technologies to face. Some said it more forcefully.

Those concerns are around AI safety, its impact on labor markets, the concentration of power and, of course, the pushback on data centers.

The data center revolt could be the sanest thing to happen to the AI build-out this year. Voters in the US passed 43 of 44 local measures to slow data centers down. This isn’t the death knell of AI, but the price to make it better.

Hyperscalers will pay almost anything for speed, and the places willing to move faster will be in the driving seat. And they should turn that leverage into lasting benefits for their communities.

Data centers were not why the vote went the way it did. The war, the cost of living, and gas prices did more, according to JD Vance. But data centers were on the ballot, and they lost almost everywhere.

Before the midterms, I said on ’s podcast and on Ezra Klein’s show that this revolt against these suburban monoliths was genuine democratic engagement: on many issues, including about how AI is arriving in our lives.

Data centers had become less popular than ICE. Getting the wrong end of the voters’ ire is not a reason to stop building everywhere. It is a reason to strike a deal.

Subscribe now

Time is power

High energy prices don’t really matter. Taxes and levies don’t really matter. Time to energize does.

Data centers make tons of money. But to get the cash spigot opening, the data center needs to be a data center.

The most important thing for developers—especially hyperscalers—is turning them on. So a pause on development hurts the best tenants, the hyperscalers, hard. Every B300 AI chip plugged in can make about $8 an hour, according to Silicon Data. It can pay for itself in less than a year. Every B300 sitting in a queue is simply lying idle, not yet adding to the depreciation bill but not paying its way either.

A 1 gigawatt data center of the type coming online now might have around 400,000 B300 chips. The total cost would hit about $40bn. But the annual operating expenditure is under 2.5% of the upfront CapEx bill for a 1GW site, roughly $800m a year. About two-thirds of that is the electricity. The shell might take just 18-24 months to build, while the average US wait time for a power connection is four years. Until the electrons flow, no money can flow. And that is an extraordinary point of leverage.

In Lanarkshire, on the outskirts of Glasgow, where Scotland’s 20th-century industrial heartland transitions to the rolling southern uplands, small towns built around UNESCO-heritage 18th-century cotton mills offer the Democrats a template to turn this into a win.

In this case, DataVita, the data center developer, has agreed to pay up to $100,000 per megawatt per year to a local fund for community initiatives like skills and training, education and food banks. When the data center reaches its 500MW capacity, this will mean a $50m-a-year fee. North Lanarkshire, the local council, has annual income of £1.17bn (or $1.58bn), so this is a 3% boost. Over the fifteen-year lifetime, it will run to up to £543m.

By comparison, Oracle sought residents’ approval for a data center in New Mexico, with nearly $1bn in new contracts to local businesses, $155m to offset utility costs, a $50m commitment to water facilities, and a $10,000 grant to a local sports team. But most of this Oracle needed to spend on building, rip that out and you end up at $205m in total. Compared to the Scottish deal, this was a miser’s bargain. Across the campus, it was $84,000 per megawatt, not per year, but as a one-off fee, nearly 18 times stingier than the Lanarkshire compact. If Oracle had met that benchmark, its 15-year bill to the community would have run to $3.5bn.

If the North Lanarkshire benchmark held, every GW of connection could yield $100m to a local community. Infrastructure companies can make $10 to $40 billion per gigawatt of energized AI compute. SpaceX’s surge deals with Anthropic and Google earn nearly $50bn per GW per year. There is plenty to go around. $100m per GW is 0.2% of what a gigawatt can rent for at today’s surge prices. At three or four times that, the levy is still under 1%.

Lanarkshire is a principle. US counties sitting on a four-year grid queue have more leverage. They should ask for more.

This isn’t to say locally negotiated levies are the only thing to aim for. Reducing energy and water bills clearly matters too.

So too does giving something to the local community when construction workers leave. The truth about data centers is that they don’t really employ anyone for every billion dollars sunk into the ground.

While Meta’s Louisiana data center investment grew five-fold to $50 billion, permanent staff numbers only doubled, to 1000. That’s around 20 people per billion spent. Anthropic’s $50bn of builds in New York and Texas will bring 800 permanent jobs. Sixteen people per billion dollars.

Transient construction workers don’t really create healthy, thriving communities—just watch Landman to see that.

But locally negotiated levies can create an annuity stream that communities can use to support local businesses, regenerate, and develop their own internal heat. Go back to Lanarkshire, where running the data center will likely employ 220 people. As part of the politically mediated agreement, the AI Growth Zone plans to create around 600 jobs for “AI researchers and coders”. As the chart below shows, this nudges that jobs-to-capital ratio up a little, but it's still far from modern manufacturing.

Smart data center policy can turn this revolt into a durable win for Democrats and their communities. Get the full playbook as a paid subscriber.

issues.summary: This week’s links, below, is, as Disturbed would have it, currently down with the sickness (ooh wah ah ah ah). The post Nurds of November — This Week’s Links appeared first on The Comics Journal.
issues.author: Clark Burscough
issues.content_html:
This week’s links, below, is, as Disturbed would have it, currently down with the sickness (ooh wah ah ah ah), so, while coughing oneself awake at 2 a..m on a regular basis, it’s nice to be up and about in the wee hours during a period in which, thanks to the joys of time differences, the vast majority of the terminally online population has been posting their way through what is admittedly a very funny run of election results. Novocaine for the soul, indeed.

“Triceratops at Ueno”(2025)

— 生田目和剛(Nabatame Kazutaka) (@nabatamekazutaka.bsky.social) 2026-11-03T08:47:09.127Z

This week’s news.

• Now that the dust has settled from the failed legal blocking actions against the festival, announcements were made this week about what form the new iterations of annual comics events in Angoulême will take, with the reveal of the newly (and pithily) titled Angoulême Bande Dessinée, which will take place from 28-31 January 2027, under the stewardship of the Morgane Group’s subsidiary, M:BD.

• In memoriam, remembering those the world of comics has lost, as ICv2 shared the news of the passing of librarian, writer, and comics advocate Katharine Kan, who has died at the age of 71.

The Comics Courier is a special project for me, and has become, I hope, a way for folks to slow down amidst all the noise and read about comics from new perspectives. The Courier 5 is going to be a really special issue, and it has an absolutely stellar team. Pledge for it now. comicscourier.com

— Tiffany Babb Thought Bubble (@explodingarrow.bsky.social) 2026-11-01T17:01:12.112Z

This week’s reviews.

TCJ

• Hagai Palevsky reviews the broad strokes of Paradise Systems’ SYSTEM 01: Hot Net Hotel — “Perhaps unsurprisingly, the stories that offer the most detail about their characters and the worlds they inhabit — in the way of central metaphors — are also the most overtly political pieces in the book.”

• Whit Taylor reviews the lush layers of Ulli Lust’s Early Man Was a Woman: Book 1 — Reclaiming Prehistory — “There’s a lot of complex text, which takes time to sit with and absorb- it’s a slow read. In fact, much of this book took me back to being an anthropology major in college, and is a great primer for anyone interested in that field of study.”

AIPT

• Alex Schlesinger reviews the shallow start of Joshua Williamson, Carmen Carnero, et al’s Iron Man: A New Nightmare.

• Chris Coplan reviews the familiar framework of Dan Watters, Brian Level, et al’s Mad Science Division #1.

• Kevin Clark reviews the tantalising setup of Homero Rios, Diego Yapur, et al’s Red Sonja/Barbarella #1.

• David Brooke reviews the compelling continuation of Pornsak Pichetshote, Alberto Ponticelli, et al’s Exquisite Corpses: Lone Gunman #1.

• Collier Jennings reviews the charged emotions of Spencer Ackerman, Antonio Fuso, et al’s No One Escapes the Dialectic #1.

• Colin Moon reviews the masterful storytelling of Ross Murray’s Bedford Street.

• Rory Wilding reviews the toothless action of Joe Palmer’s Destination Kill: Deluxe Edition.

The Beat

D. Morris reviews the big ideas of Chip Zdarsky, Marco Checchetto, et al’s Avengers #1.

Book and Film Globe

William Schwartz reviews the dense strangeness of Ben Katchor’s Hotel & Farm.

Broken Frontier

• Lydia Turner has reviews of:

  • The delightful world of Ellie Durkin’s Seed.
  • The imaginative weirdness of John Chalmers and Sandra Marrs’ Wilomina: The Land of Dreams and Nightmares.

• Gary Usher has reviews of:

  • The fresh takes of Professor Raco et al’s Everybody’s Happy Nowadays. 
  • The talented cartooning of Agata Wawryniuk and Robert Sienicki’s Freshly Grown Gardener #1-3.
  • The hilarious interactions of Nick Bryan,Flo Woolley, Len Gogos, Elena Cerisciola, Elena Artese, Jodi Perez, et al’s The Collected Letters of Courier Z Volume 2.

• Andy Oliver has reviews of:

  • The meta layers of Donald Calabrese’s Coady.
  • The honest reflections of Katriona Chapman’s Katzine: The Catch-Up Issue.
  • The pertinent punches of Nikesh Shukla and Camille Aubry’s Mad Villain #2.
  • The rich details of Anna Readman’s One Day in the Life of Xero Slingsby.
  • The enthusiastic fun of Leeds Comics Collective’s Warriors of Junk Food.
  • The slapstick delights of Sheena Dempsey’s Pablo and Splash.
  • The expressive characterisations of Gemma Plum’s adaptation of Ivo Van Woerden’s The Great Marc Evers.

Comics Grinder

Henry Chamberlain reviews the perfect mix of Shawn McBee, Maciej Jankowski, Nicolas Nieto, Matias De Vincenzo, et al’s Westron #3; and the rollicking weirdness of Jean Pleyers’ The Children of Light.

Far Out

Liam Gaughan reviews the bold visuals of Phuong Mai Nguyen’s animated adaptation of AJ Dungo’s In Waves.

Financial Times

Lucy Scholes reviews the harrowing testimony of Chris Hedges and Joe Sacco’s Requiem for Gaza.

FreakSugar

Jed W. Keith reviews the sharp dialogue of Rob Williams, Nil Vendrell, et al’s Hidden Springs #1.

House to Astonish

Paul O’Brien has capsule reviews of Marvel Comics’ X-Men #40, Fantastic Four #18, Bishop #5, Tomb of Apocalypse #3, Gambit: Gone #2, and Alien vs. X-Men #2.

The News-Gazette

Deb Aronson reviews the satisfying conclusion of Victoria Jamieson’s The Whole Wide World of Mabel Mulligan and the resonant story of Pedro Martin’s Mexikid.

RetroFuturista

Dominique Musorrafiti reviews the insightful indictment of Camila Kerwin’s Soft Targets: Guns in America and the Kids Caught in the Crossfire.

Solrad

Hagai Palevsky reviews the oppressive concentration of Rea Irvin’s The Smythes.

Winnipeg Free Press

Candida Rifkind reviews the metafictional intrigue of Paul B. Rainey’s Murder School.

Yatta-tachi

• LB Bryant reviews the fantastic visuals of Kozue Amano’s Colori Colore Creare Volume 1, translated by Andria McKnight.

• Kai reviews the shallow romance of Enhi’s Give Me a Hug, Mr. Frog!, translated by Margaret Ngo.
