This week’s interviews.

TCJ

Dylan Horrocks interviews Ross Murray about Bedford Street, the observational nature of anxiety, the landscapes of New Zealand, and cartooning inspirations — “Of all the different things I do, comics are the most meaningful thing to me. I'll labor over comics in a way that I don't as much over other things. Not that it makes them look any better. Comics are often the scrappiest work I do visually, but I guess I put a little extra care into conveying the core ideas. I'm most self-conscious about my comics, might be another way of putting it.”

AIPT

Chris Coplan speaks with Jeremy Robinson about One Zero Zero One Saves the World and the thirty year path to the book’s publication, and with Joe Harris and R.D. Brown about The X-Files and daunting nature of working on such a touchstone property.

Autobiographix

Nora Hickey and Amaris Ketcham interview Nathan A. Gray about The Human Remains and processing heavy experiences through making comics, and KC Councilor about Between You and Me: Transitional Comics and the personal intersection between transitioning and making comics.

The Beat

Javier Perez talks to Curt Pires about Creature Corps and monster battler inspirations, and to Trevor Fernandes-Lenkiewicz about Heavy and the realities of life as an independent comics creator.

Broken Frontier

Andy Oliver speaks with Skai Campbell, AKA Skhoshbell, about Jungul Man-Thology and Hog Hog, comics inspirations, and taking the personal approach when it comes to ecological activism.

Fanbase Press

Barba Dillon chats with James Aquilone about Abbott & Costello Meet the Monsters and the timeless nature of the duo’s comedy.

FreakSugar

Jed W. Keith interviews Cyrille Pomès about Hellboy in Hell: Nothing But Blood, doorways into the Mignolaverse, and Hellboy drawing practice.

Graphic Memoir

Jonathan Sandler speaks with Ari Richter about Never Again Will I Visit Auschwitz, the fine arts to comics (and vice versa) pipeline, and the gallows humour of the Richter family.

The New York Times

Robert Ito talks to Keum Suk Gendry-Kim about My Friend Kim Jong Un, the hostile reception to the book’s publication in Korea, and the research that went into it.

Publisher’s Weekly

Meg Lemke chats with Raquelle Jac about Bimbo Agitprop, processing negative thoughts through comics, and finding value in the value less.

Getting there!

— Marley Zarcone (@kittycoffee.bsky.social) 2026-11-04T22:18:02.244Z

This week’s features and longreads.

• Here at TCJ, Jon Holt and Teppei Fukuda return with a new translation of an essay by Natsume Fusanosuke, this time out taken from Kawade Shobō’s recent mook (or, ‘magazine book’) on mangaka Kobayashi Makoto — “Therefore, not only does this essay present a history of a legendary figure in manga, but it also contains elements of Natsume’s thought ranging from his early days as a manga scholar (panels, pacing, and “events”) as well as material that interests him greatly now (the publishing industry, artist-editor relationships). He also describes here what exactly makes Kobayashi Makoto’s manga still so interesting.”

• Also for TCJ, Christina Lee draws the line between Kyoko Okazaki’s Helter Skelter and Coralie Fargeat’s The Substance and their depictions of the financial, physical, and societal pain inherent in chasing the capitalist ideal of perfection — “Okazaki borrows the visual language of fashion magazines by frequently portraying Liliko in the middle of photoshoots; her front-stage appearance juxtaposed with her back-stage thoughts, at odds with the image-driven economy she participates in. This dissonance between what we see and read illustrates the medium-specificity of comics: we are a simultaneous critic and participant of Liliko’s media environment, in which female bodies are scrutinized and objectified.”

• Elizabeth Sandifer’s Last War in Albion continues, over at Eruditorum Press, as the charting of the magical war for Comics Brittania’s soul reaches the publication of Grant Morrison et al’s The Invisibles, alien abduction experiences, and all the abstruse chaos which you would expect that to entail.

• Shelfdust’s retrospective of the myriad first issues of Wonder Woman continues, as this edition Adrienne Resha looks back on Greg Potter and George Pérez’s 1987 iteration of an issue 1 for Diana of Themyscira, and the paradoxes to be found therein.

• From the world of open-access academia, in Mississippi Quarterly, Brannon Costello writes on John Ridley and Georges Jeanty’s The American Way and The American Way: Those Above and Those Below, and the extent to which these superhero comics can centre agency of Black characters, and imagine a progressive vision of the South.

• A new Mindless Ones newsletter crests the horizon, as this week Jamie Delano and John Ridgway’s Hellblazer is Suggested for Mature Readers, alongside other spoOoky seasonal fare put under the shaking spotlight of a flickering torch.

• Paul O’Brien’s survey of the villains of Daredevil continues, for House to Astonish, as DG Chichester and Scott McDaniel briefly tap into urban legends of the 90s to bring forth the Surgeon General.

• Mike Peterson rounds up the week’s editorial beat, for The Daily Cartoonist, as trepidation ahead of the midterm elections just gone lead instead to a fair amount of schadenfreude in the immediate aftermath.

issues.title: Celestial nuisance
issues.summary: The cosmos has become a lab for the Big Questions in physics. Along the way, we’ve lost sight of its glorious messiness - by Dylan Jow Read on Aeon
issues.author: Dylan Jow
issues.content_html:
Journey to a satellite galaxy roughly 200,000 light-years from Earth, featuring the young star cluster NGC 602. With data from Webb’s NIRCam (Near-InfraRed Camera) and MIRI (Mid-InfraRed Instrument). Courtesy HUBBLE/WEBB/ESA

Listen to this essay

22 minute listen

In the story of cosmic history, one of the most important supporting characters is dust. As clouds of interstellar gas cooled and condensed in the early Universe, dust grains absorbed and re-emitted radiation, eventually forming stars. Later, dust provided the raw material from which planets could form and grow. Dust grains may even have been the surfaces on which the first complex organic molecules formed. Yet, if you ask most cosmologists, they’ll tell you that dust is a sheer nuisance.

In astrophysics, ‘nuisance’ is a quasi-technical term. Astrophysicists call any phenomenon that gets in the way of the thing they actually want to study a ‘nuisance’. Dust grains emit polarised light that can mimic subtle signals from the afterglow of the Big Bang (the cosmic microwave background) that cosmologists have spent decades and billions of dollars trying to detect. A cosmologist studies dust not to uncover its role in shaping the cosmos, but to subtract it – the term ‘sweeping under the rug’ couldn’t be more apt.

This dichotomy between ‘signal’ and ‘nuisance’ is found across many sub-fields in astronomy. Astronomers who study a phenomenon called ‘weak lensing’ use the subtle distortions of light caused by gravity to map invisible dark matter. For them, the ordinary matter that makes up everything we can see is a nuisance. Pulsar timing astronomers use rapidly spinning neutron stars called pulsars as extraordinarily precise clocks to detect the passage of gravitational waves through the galaxy. For them, the nuisance is ionised interstellar gas, which scatters and disperses the light from pulsars.

Yet one astronomer’s nuisance is another’s treasure. Just as a laser beam reveals the intricate swirls of smoke in a dark room, pulsars illuminate the fine structure of the interstellar medium, the unlit space between galaxies. If you want to study the interstellar medium and its role in shaping our galaxy’s evolution, the light-scattering gas is an invaluable resource.

Whether a phenomenon is a nuisance or something worth studying in its own right clearly depends on the investigator and their interests. But in a discipline as collaborative as astronomy, shared priorities must be developed. Gone are the days of Galileo and other lone scientists in the tower, pointing telescopes built by their own hands wherever curiosity dictates. Modern astronomy is a highly specialised discipline, marked by large collaborations. The tools of the trade – telescopes – are designed, built and maintained by hundreds of scientists and engineers across many institutions. But you can’t just stroll in and ask to use one. Investigators must fiercely compete for time with these advanced instruments. To guide how that access is allocated, the research community has developed a set of shared priorities. Some questions are elevated to the status of ‘Big Questions’ to which all others inevitably become subordinate.

But are these Big Questions necessarily the right ones? Who decides where to draw the boundaries between signal and nuisance, or big and small? Fields of enquiry are defined by the questions they seek to answer. If we want to understand modern astrophysics, it is not enough to understand the scientific and mathematical content of its theories. We also need to understand the human forces that shape the questions themselves and cause some questions to be prioritised, and other questions to be viewed as irrelevant or merely means to those bigger ends.

To identify the Big Questions that dominate the field, you need look no further than the flagship projects set to shape the discipline for decades. These include the Square Kilometre Array Observatory, the James Webb Space Telescope, the Vera C Rubin Observatory, the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, and the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna. Each of these projects will cost several billion dollars over its lifetime.

When we look at the stated science goals of these projects, consistent themes emerge. For example, the Square Kilometre Array Observatory at Jodrell Bank in the UK is a massive radio array that will define the field of radio astronomy for the foreseeable future. Its website contains a list of science goals. On that list, the early Universe, gravitational waves, dark energy and cosmology are all listed before stars, the interstellar medium and the origins of life. The official page for the much-covered James Webb Space Telescope similarly lists the early Universe – the ‘cosmic dawn’ – before more prosaic matters such as stars, planets and dust. Such priorities are often reflected in media coverage of these projects, which further shape perceptions among young researchers, politicians, funders and the general public about which questions matter most.

The boundaries between the big and small questions often fall along the lines between ‘fundamental’ physics and ‘messy’ astrophysics. This is reflected in the language of many cosmologists who study dark matter, for example. For decades, the study of dark matter has focused on the largest physical scales – giant clusters of galaxies – where the gravitational effects of dark matter can be directly inferred. On small scales, within and around galaxies, dark matter’s effects become entangled with the complex dynamics of interstellar gas. To use the terminology that is widely adopted by cosmologists: the physics of dark matter on small scales is obscured by the astrophysics of interstellar gas. Implicit in this framing is the idea that astrophysics is messy and complicated, and, ultimately, subordinate to clean, fundamental physics.

When the fundamental is elevated above everything else, it’s easy to see why an impressionable young mind might be captivated

Young researchers encounter this supposed predominance of physics over astrophysics long before they set foot in a laboratory. Growing up, I loved space, as many children do. My parents bought me an amateur telescope, and I spent many nights in the backyard becoming familiar with the winter night sky (the summer sky was more elusive because it appeared after my bedtime). But, by the time I entered graduate school, I had largely forgotten about my early childhood passion for the heavens. Like many of my peers at the time, I wanted to study theoretical particle physics.

Particle physics enjoys a kind of mythical status in popular culture as the apex of the natural sciences. After all, the purported goal of particle physicists is not just a theory of particles, but a theory of everything. Of course, such a theory would be a theory of ‘everything’ only in the limited sense that it would describe how all matter behaves on a fundamental (microscopic) level – never mind the fact that such a description would be functionally useless to describe even basic chemical reactions due to the mathematical complexity. But when the fundamental is elevated above everything else, it’s easy to see why an impressionable young mind might be captivated.

In the end, I did not study theoretical particle physics as a graduate student. The competition was intense – almost all of my classmates were vying for the few positions available. So, I rekindled my love of astronomy and decided to study astrophysics. But the truth is, at the time, I viewed astrophysics as something of a consolation prize.

This hierarchy, which ranks fundamental physics above all else, is a historical contingency. Over the course of the second half of the 20th century, astronomy transformed from a distinct discipline into a sub-discipline of physics. Historically, astronomy was a science of mapping, cataloguing and observation. But the successes of mid-century nuclear physics, the rise of physical cosmology and the discovery of dark matter and dark energy began a process that fused the two disciplines.

The discovery of general relativity, which describes gravity as a warping of the fabric of space and time, provided a new framework that enabled the quantitative study of the dynamics of the Universe as a whole. Cosmology, which had previously been the domain of philosophers, became the domain of physicists. In the closing decades of the 20th century, this framework enabled the dual discovery of dark matter and dark energy – both mysterious substances unaccounted for by the standard model of particle physics. Crucially, these gaps in the standard model would have gone completely undetected without the observations of astronomers.

The heavens, then, transformed from an object of study in its own right to a new laboratory for testing fundamental physics. This shift is preserved in our vocabulary: the term ‘astronomy’ was demoted in favour of the more prestigious term ‘astrophysics’.

I saw astronomy as a means to an end, a stepping stone on the path to a theory of everything

The rise of astrophysics was, in part, fuelled by the geopolitics of the Cold War, which saw an unprecedented surge in funding for physics, in addition to a rise in the cultural prestige of physics in the public imagination. Governments invested large sums of money in physics mega-projects, cementing a culture of large collaborations dedicated to the study of fundamental, high-energy physics. This was the era of the particle accelerator, in which subatomic particles are accelerated to extremely high energies to test theories of physics that manifest only at those energy scales. But then the Cold War ended, and the cash flow stopped. In 1993, the US Congress cancelled the Superconducting Super Collider project in Texas, after billions had already been spent.

Suddenly, a generation of particle physicists found themselves without the experimental tools to test their theories on Earth. Astronomy, however, provided an attractive alternative. The Universe revealed itself to be the ultimate, free particle accelerator: full of violent events, such as supernovae, colliding black holes and the Big Bang, reaching energy scales that no terrestrial collider ever could. If only the complications of real astrophysical environments could be modelled and accounted for, then the heavens would be the perfect new laboratory for physics.

It was precisely this logic that sold me on astrophysics as a new graduate student. At the time, I saw astronomy as a means to an end, a stepping stone on the path to a theory of everything. I was interested in the messy complications of astronomy only insofar as understanding them would enable us to disregard them.

Today, this ‘physicisation’ of astronomy has left a deep imprint on the cultural norms of the discipline. Modern astrophysics is characterised by massive, hyper-centralised international collaborations, and an often tacit belief that ‘fundamental’ physics sits at the top of the scientific pyramid, while the questions of real ‘astrophysics’ are mere nuisances.

This ideological elevation of the fundamental over the particular is evident in the architecture of modern big-data astronomy. The past few decades have been characterised by experiments yielding massive volumes of data. Yet, these pipelines are not neutral data-gathering machines; indeed, their very design reflects and reinforces the institutional bias towards astrophysics as a barrier to fundamental truth. The logic is that, with enough data, the rich and diverse astrophysical phenomena that manifest in particular cosmic environments can be statistically modelled and averaged away, leaving only what is fundamental.

AI models inherit untested assumptions about the physical processes they aim to illuminate

Consider, for example, the phenomenon of weak gravitational lensing, where astronomers measure how gravity distorts the shapes of distant galaxies. They can use this to build a map of the dark matter in the Universe, which is otherwise invisible. However, weak gravitational lensing is equally sensitive to the gravitational effects of all matter in the Universe – the dark matter and the ‘ordinary’ matter. The physical interactions that govern ordinary matter complicate inferences of the underlying dark matter distribution. Data analysis pipelines for modern weak lensing surveys flatten the complex physics of astrophysical environments to a set of ‘nuisance parameters’, which, with enough data, can be averaged away. Rich astrophysical phenomena are, from the very outset and in the survey design itself, framed as statistical obstacles to fundamental truths.

This paradigm is further reinforced by the turn towards artificial intelligence (AI). A natural symbiosis exists between the petabytes of data generated by modern observatories and the massive datasets needed to train deep learning architectures. Driven by the hype, if a project promises to use AI, it helps attract funding and allocation of computational resources, even when its capacity for genuine discovery remains unclear.

Foundation AI models are heralded as the best way to digest datasets too massive for detailed human analysis, promising to automatically infer complex astrophysics from raw images of the sky. But there is a fundamental disconnect between the statistical patterns these technologies learn and the underlying physical mechanisms that generate the observations. Whereas you might train an AI to learn what a cat looks like with a set of images of known cats and non-cats, there is no set of galaxy images where all the relevant astrophysics is known. Instead, models need to be trained with synthetic data drawn from astrophysical simulations. However, computational limitations force these simulations to rely on simplified approximations of the very physics in question. As a result, AI models inherit untested assumptions about the physical processes they aim to illuminate.

This is not a problem if your goal is simply to account for complex astrophysics in massive data sets to infer the underlying fundamental physics. These models are, after all, exceptional at identifying and correcting for subtle correlations in the data. But if your goal is to understand the complex physics of the astrophysical phenomena themselves, the benefit is less obvious.

Thus, modern astrophysics appears to be oriented towards a paradigm of modelling massive data sets to uncover fundamental constants. This paradigm is mutually reinforced by the questions that are institutionally prioritised and the tools used to answer them. However, this loop of reinforcement can create an illusion of field-wide consensus around what the most important questions are, which obscures the daily realities of many working astronomers.

This is nowhere more visible than in the discourse surrounding the ‘Hubble tension’ – the fact that different methods of measuring the Universe’s expansion rate (the Hubble constant) yield contradictory results. Across white papers and popular science articles, the Hubble tension is touted as a profound crisis in physics. If the discrepancy is real (as opposed to a statistical fluke), then it could be an important hint about the nature of dark energy, which drives the expansion.

And yet, in the trenches of astrophysics research, attitudes are markedly different. At nearly every talk I have attended on the Hubble tension, the reaction from working astrophysicists is surprisingly muted. If this discrepancy is the great white whale of modern cosmology, why do so many researchers respond with a shrug?

The reality is that most scientists are passionate and obsessive creatures, devoting many years of their lives to extremely niche topics that others might struggle to care about. Such people naturally find their work intrinsically interesting, not just as a step towards some bigger question. Of course, scientists have complex motivations that are shaped by their institutional environments and that shape the long-term trajectory of their careers. But, on a day-to-day basis, many astronomers really do just care a lot about dust, or gas dynamics, or cosmic magnetic fields.

For myself, the further away I got from physics proper, the more I rediscovered my love of astronomy for its own sake. Whether or not astronomy unearths new fundamental laws of physics, it has much to tell us about our place in the Universe and what it means to be human. Since Copernicus, astronomy has gradually demoted humanity’s position in the cosmos, from occupying the literal centre of everything, to merely occupying an unremarkable planet, orbiting an unremarkable star, in an unremarkable galaxy in a potentially infinite Universe. At the same time, as the bounds of the known Universe expand, we have increasingly understood the rarity and fragility of life in the cosmos. Astronomy, therefore, plays a critical role in the story of the human species. While I remain hopeful that astronomy can lead us to new fundamental physics, that hope is no longer the driving force of my interest in the heavens. I suspect this is the case for many of my fellow astronomers.

Despite this, investigators are required to play a rhetorical game, justifying their deeply specific research within the context of the predetermined Big Questions. When you apply for academic jobs, the advice is: Always, always, always link your work to the Big Questions. Since hiring or grant committees typically comprise faculty with a diverse range of expertise, an applicant cannot rely on the committee sharing an intrinsic interest in their niche topic. Justifying your science in relation to the Big Questions is more likely to lead to a successful application, even if individually none of the members of the committee are particularly passionate about those questions.

Scientific journals reinforce this rhetorical game. The most prestigious journals demand that their articles represent significant advancements in the field. In other words, they require that the research they publish make progress on the pre-defined Big Questions. Investigators are incentivised to frame their papers in this context. I have personally written papers that motivate the work as a step towards resolving the Hubble tension. While technically true, this framing misrepresents the reasons I embarked upon that research and the real reasons I find it interesting.

If you could uncover the nature of dark energy, or discover alien life, which would you choose?

This is not to suggest that having shared priorities across a research community is somehow wrong – indeed, it is inevitable. But it is important to recognise that these priorities are historically contingent and, to some degree, arbitrary. When investigators play the rhetorical game of justifying their research, the game ends when they link their work to a fundamental question in physics. But why stop there? Why is the search for dark energy or dark matter inherently more justified than the lifecycle of interstellar dust? The ‘fundamental’ questions are no more or less intrinsically justified than the nuisances that get in their way. Rather, we choose which questions are ends in themselves and which require further justification.

Many commentators have made a great deal of the crisis that faces high-energy physics today. Terrestrial collider experiments have failed to reveal any signs of the new physics they were built to find, and we may well be reaching the limit of what astrophysics can tell us about fundamental physics. Even if the Hubble tension is confirmed, we may never settle on the correct physical theory of dark energy. Even as we better characterise the gravitational behaviour of dark matter, its particle nature may remain a mystery forever. The Big Questions are beginning to lose their lustre, and some are beginning to ask whether the billions of dollars spent on mega-projects are diminishing in their returns. But if this is a crisis for high-energy physics, there is no crisis for astronomy. Astronomers will continue to investigate all the weird and wonderful things the Universe has to offer.

If you’re an astronomer reading this – or anyone who would like to play along – I invite you to consider the following hypothetical. If, tomorrow, you could uncover the nature of dark energy, or discover alien life, which would you choose? Both would guarantee a Nobel, but which one actually feels like the bigger, more meaningful discovery? Although I can speak only for myself, I suspect many astronomers – even bona fide astrophysicists – would choose the latter.

Astronomy has a unique place among the natural sciences. Its immediate practical benefits are limited – especially the further away from Earth you go. It’s hard to imagine a detailed understanding of galaxy evolution directly leading to some technological benefit in any foreseeable timeline. Yet astronomy excites the public imagination like no other science. It’s not because astronomy has the potential to uncover new physics at high energy scales. It’s because we, as a species, have always looked up to try to understand our place in the Universe.

Peering through my backyard telescope as a child, I had no concept of fundamental physics. But looking at the fuzzy haze of the Orion Nebula and realising that I was watching the birth of stars – well, there are no words to describe the sense of wonder I felt. If astronomy must justify itself according to some Big Questions, let them be these: where did we come from, and what is our place in the cosmos?

Ultimately, the priorities of a field are not immutable facts but a choice. Shifting priorities need not be seen as a crisis, but as an opportunity to ask ourselves why we study what we study in the first place – an opportunity to make different choices that better align with those reasons. Astronomers, then, have an opportunity to reorient the priorities of the field away from a reductionist view of physics, and to reclaim the value of the nuisance.

issues.title: The Met Gala’s backup theme will be jeans and t-shirts
issues.summary: Will it be a night of Levi’s?
issues.author: Matty Merritt
issues.content_html:
For those double-booked on May 3 with dive bar trivia and the Met Gala, you can probably swing both. Following backlash to its original theme, the Met announced its backup plan for the 2027 gala: “extraOrdinary: Fashion and the Poetics of the Everyday.” The event will celebrate jeans, tees, puffer coats, and boring materials turned into nontraditional pieces.

As if this could sound any more Plan B. Which Costume Institute lead curator Andrew Bolton said he didn’t have. The initial theme, announced in July, was set to honor the British designer John Galliano. But it was canceled just a month later, after donors and the public pushed back, resurfacing Galliano’s antisemitic and racist rants from 2010 and 2011.

  • Galliano had apologized, but he and the Met announced on Aug. 31 that the exhibit would be binned.
  • His exhibit would have been just the third time that a living designer was honored.

Will it be a night of Levi’s? Maybe. Bolton said he hoped folks would wear their own jeans and t-shirts, but that “the ordinary is never quite as simple as it seems.” The event will likely look somewhere between Pierpaolo Piccioli’s puffer coat ball gowns and a 2015 frat’s ABC party.—MM

issues.title: A sans serif built on oversized round shapes
issues.summary: Superior Type’s Heaven is a brutalist grotesque built on round shapes that are too big for their space.
issues.content_html:
“At Superior Type, we are trying to push fonts to extremes,” Kucera tells us. “So in addition to extreme thin and black variants, we are adding one more concept where we push our new fonts. We have a bunch of them in progress and executing them one by one, depending on the current state and vibe. Heaven has this soft-to-boxy variable axis.”

The typeface started close to Heaven 03. “Just try to imagine 03 as a blown-up balloon fitted inside a box that is a bit smaller than the balloon,” Kucera explains. “Those rounded curves copy the box shape but still stay round in the corner of the box.” From there, he shifted the balance between round and rectangular forms in both directions. “After I pushed far enough I got to the point where it stopped, which is now 01 and 09,” Kucera notes. If the balloon is blown up “bigger and bigger until it fills those corners, it becomes Heaven 09.” The four families, Heaven’s static stops, were then chosen the same way a type designer chooses the weights of a typeface. “You set up, print and look through more than a healthy amount of variations, and then slowly destroy those that are not different enough to speak for themselves.”

“Every letter made from diagonal lines had to be rethought: is it possible to make it round without losing too much readability?” Kucera reveals. “That’s why ‘K,’ ‘R,’ ‘W,’ ‘X’ and ‘Y’ got the upgrade to round.” Heaven comes with alternate letters that you can switch in. “The ‘m,’ ‘n’ and also ‘M’ and ‘u,’ I did with a specific goal in mind: to make Heaven 01 even more round, to combat the boxiness of 09 and keep them a bit more even in this shape battle,” he tells us. Asked what makes Heaven brutalist, Kucera points to the ‘K’ and ‘X,’ in upper and lower case, and to an alternate ‘M’ and ‘m’ that come from flipping the ‘W’ and ‘w.’ “I think there are a bunch of brutal – concept-wise – non-negotiable letterforms inside the font.”

“I think the character of each variation is strong enough to hold a logotype, but the regular weights are also balanced enough that I dare say they can handle long enough text to describe a company on its website,” Kucera notes. “I would love to see some designers grab one or two letters from 09 and the rest from 01 and make a custom typeface for a company font and logotype.”

Superior Type also has two serif text typefaces built as extensive SuperVariable families, like Heaven. “If any studios or designers are interested in testing them on upcoming projects, we’d love to hear from you,” Founder & Director Vojtech Riha tells us. “We’re happy to share preview versions ahead of release and see how they work in real-world use.”

Get Heaven free trials

issues.title: Tokenizer Mono
issues.summary: A monospace font that highlights LLM tokens as you type. No JavaScript, just OpenType substitution rules and a color table.
issues.content_html:
There are many tools out there that help you visualize tokens and better understand how tokenization works with large language models. OpenAI has a pretty nice one, and there are a half-dozen other ones that are also great.

They generally work by passing text through an actual tokenizer, retrieving the resulting token boundaries, and highlighting them in the browser. It's a fast, accurate and perfectly reasonable approach.

So I did the slightly unreasonable thing and made a font that uses modern font witchcraft to visualize tokens as you type them, without actually tokenizing. The code is at:

  • github.com/georgemandis/tokenizer-mono.

You can play with it below. Every highlight is drawn by the font. No scripting! The only JavaScript here is swapping which face is loaded.

OpenAI GPT-4, GPT-3.5, text-embedding-3; also Phi-4, OLMo 2, IBM Granite 4

What is a token?

A token is the basic unit of currency for a language model. It’s what the model actually reads and produces.

A token is generally a chunk of text: a character, word, word-part, or occasionally a longer sequence. Many modern LLM tokenizers have a fixed vocabulary of these chunks, typically somewhere between 50,000 and 250,000 entries.

And that vocabulary isn’t necessarily exclusively made up of conventional words. Common combinations of characters, punctuation, whitespace, and even sequences spanning multiple words can all earn their own entries.

Where does a vocabulary come from? Nobody writes it by hand. Almost every tokenizer in this post uses some form of byte-pair encoding (BPE), which builds the vocabulary by counting. In a simplified version of BPE, start with every character (or byte, in byte-level tokenizers) as its own token. Look through a big pile of training text for the pair of adjacent tokens that appears most often, say "t" followed by "h", and merge it into a new token "th". Now look again: maybe "th" followed by "e" is the most common pair, so "the" becomes a token.

Rinse and repeat this many thousands of times over. Every merge adds one entry to the vocabulary, and the list of merges, in the order they were learned, is saved along with it. To tokenize new text, the tokenizer breaks it into characters and replays those merges in the same order, so common words collapse into a single token and rare words stay in pieces. The exact split of a word depends on which merges rank higher, which matters later.

Over a long enough timeline, does the entirety of Alice in Wonderland become a single token? Every published version of something like the Bible? Interesting thought exercise.

While they aren't incorporating entire novels or religious texts as tokens yet (and I suspect there's a better technique that enters the room well before we push things to that scale), these vocabularies have been getting bigger! GPT-2 had 50,257 tokens; GPT-4's tokenizer has 100,277; GPT-4o's has 200,019.

Part of that growth reflects increasingly ambitious multilingual support: OpenAI's GPT-4o announcement shows the same Gujarati sentence dropping from 145 tokens to 33 under the new tokenizer, while English barely moved.

Sidenote: Rest of World has a nice article on the cost of AI for non-english languages which touches on this idea of multilingual support, tokens and how this manifests visually. I think not discussing Chinese at all—which can be more token efficient than latin script languages sometimes!—was kind of a miss.

So when something like Meta’s Muse product boasts giving you 1 billion tokens for free, that’s what we’re talking about: a billion units of text processed, not a billion words (The rule of thumb seems to have settled around 0.75 words per token, so if it helps you can multiply any token count by that and read it as words.). And depending on which tokenizer is doing the counting, that same text might consume a surprisingly different number of tokens!

Writing this makes me want to start charging in tokens (i.e. words) in my day-to-day life. Hm.

Further reading on tokens: the BPE paper, Sennrich et al. 2016; SentencePiece, Google's take, used by Llama 2, Gemma and T5; and Hugging Face's tokenizers library, which reads most of the open ones.

What is Tokenizer Mono and how does it work?

Tokenizer Mono is a font family with different faces mapped to different tokenizers. This lets you visualize the tokens as you type without an additional computation and reassembly step.

It's one big typographic family—"Tokenizer Mono" based on IBM Plex— with a style per tokenizer model. Font Book on macOS should register them as one family with twenty-eight styles.

Here's the same sentence visualized in all of these different tokenizers.

It's subtle, but you can spot some fun differences. Llama 2 splits "fox" and "tokenize" where OpenAI (among others) doesn't. BERT doesn't tokenize whitespace at all (it will never be good at Python, alas). And while we're on whitespace and Python: cl100k takes the four-space indent before return and makes one token of the first three spaces, then folds the fourth into " return", while Gemma keeps all four spaces as a single token.

Note on vendors and models: Anthropic's tokenizer isn't public, as far as I can tell, so there's no Claude face. Neither is Gemini's, though I wouldn't be shocked if it's some evolution of Gemma? OpenAI publishes its encodings through tiktoken, and its model table maps everything up to GPT-5 onto o200k_base, so the o200k face covers those. I'm not sure about the newest models like Astra (GPT-6).

The weird thing fonts can do: substitution

This entire project was an exercise in seeing how far I could push OpenType glyph substitutions—something I knew existed and understood conceptually, but had never played with.

Microsoft's OpenType spec pages explain this elegantly, in my opinion.

In a nutshell, the Glyph Substitution table (GSUB) is the part of an OpenType font that holds rules for replacing one or more glyphs (the drawn shapes, as opposed to the characters underneath them) with other glyphs. The spec numbers eight lookup types; seven of them substitute something, and the eighth is a wrapper you'll meet in the list. The examples below are in Adobe's .fea syntax, which is how most type designers write them.

  • Single substitution (type 1): a straight one-for-one swap. The slashed zero in coding fonts is this: sub zero by zero.slash;. Small caps are the same trick, just 26 times over.
  • Multiple substitution (type 2): one glyph becomes several. The usual job is taking a ligature or precomposed glyph apart so other rules can see its pieces: sub f_i by f i;.
  • Alternate substitution (type 3): one glyph has several interchangeable forms, and the app or the user picks. The canonical example is a font with a drawer full of ampersands: sub ampersand from [ampersand.1 ampersand.2 ampersand.3];.
  • Ligature substitution (type 4): several glyphs become one, while the underlying characters stay put, so you can still select and search them: sub f i by f_i;. Fira Code's !== arrows are this. This is the thing I half-remembered about fonts and went to look up before any of this started, i.e. "how do ligatures actually work?", and here we are, one weird font and a blog post later.
  • Contextual substitution (type 5): match a sequence of glyphs and run a lookup on any of them: sub [a e o]' r' lookup connect;. Every glyph in the match is fair game, but there's nothing to look at outside the match.
  • Chained contextual substitution (type 6): the one powering Tokenizer Mono. Like type 5, but now the rule can also require glyphs before and after the match without touching them, the regular-expression equivalent of lookbehind and lookahead: sub @letter f' i' r' e' lookup toRed; only fires when a letter precedes "fire". That's how the font tells " hello" from " hellos".
  • Extension (type 7): not a substitution at all. It's a wrapper that lets a lookup point past the 16-bit offset limit, so a font with huge tables can keep using one of the other types inside it. Tokenizer Mono is that font: the cl100k face wraps 194 of its chained-contextual subtables this way.
  • Reverse chaining substitution (type 8): a chained single substitution that runs backwards, from the last glyph in the run to the first, so a glyph can depend on what comes after it has already been decided. It exists for Arabic Nastaliq, where a letter's shape depends on the letters to its left: rsub e' space by e.final;.

Rules are written in Adobe's feature-file language, .fea. The warm-up font in the repo turns the word "fire" red, and only the whole word, in eight lines:

@letter = [a-z A-Z];

lookup toRed {
  sub f by f.red;  sub i by i.red;  sub r by r.red;  sub e by e.red;
} toRed;

feature calt {
  ignore sub @letter f' i' r' e';        # not "misfire"
  ignore sub f' i' r' e' @letter;        # not "fired"
  sub f' lookup toRed  i' lookup toRed  r' lookup toRed  e' lookup toRed;
} calt;

The tokenizer font is that idea pushed to a silly extreme. One rule per vocabulary token, longest first, keyed on the first glyph. When the shaper matches one it rewrites the letters to start / middle / end variants and skips past the match. That skip is what makes it greedy longest-match. In .fea terms, the rule for " hello" would be:

sub space' lookup toStart  h' lookup toMid  e' lookup toMid  l' lookup toMid  l' lookup toMid  o' lookup toEnd;

(At this scale the .fea compiler can't cope, so the rules are built directly as table data with fontTools. Same thing, no text form.)

A 22-rule state machine then paints the colors (yes, fonts can have colors; that's the next section!), looking one glyph to the left:

# continuation inherits its neighbor's color (k = 0..4)
sub [@S0 @M0] @M' lookup toM0;
sub [@S0 @M0] @E' lookup toE0;
# a new token takes the next color after a token end
sub [@E0 @X0] @S' lookup toS1;
sub [@E0 @X0] @X' lookup toX1;
# ...same four lines for colors 1 to 4, wrapping 4 -> 0...
# first token in the run
sub @S' lookup toS0;
sub @X' lookup toX0;

Colors in fonts

A few years ago I discovered Google's Noto Color Emoji font and learned you can put colors in fonts. What a neat trick! For this endeavor, while I figured substitution rules might be able to mark where the tokens start and stop, color would make it even snazzier and start to look and feel like the tools I shared toward the top.

Color in OpenType involves two tables working together. COLR says "this glyph is these layers, drawn in this order," and CPAL holds the palettes those layers pick their colors from.

COLR comes in two versions. Version 0 is flat fills, one palette color per layer, and is all I needed for Tokenizer Mono. Version 1 adds gradients, transforms and compositing, which is what Noto Color Emoji's web build uses. Chrome's COLRv1 announcement is a good explainer if you want to go further. Twemoji and Microsoft's Segoe UI Emoji ship COLR builds too.

In Tokenizer Mono every colored letter is two layers: a rounded box filled from palette slot k, and then the original letter on top in "whatever the text color is" (palette index 0xFFFF, a special value meaning "use the current foreground"). With fontTools the whole thing looks like this:

from fontTools.colorLib.builder import buildCOLR, buildCPAL

font["CPAL"] = buildCPAL([
    [(0.83, 0.77, 0.98, 1), (0.73, 0.93, 0.86, 1), ...],   # palette 0, light backgrounds
    [(0.30, 0.23, 0.54, 1), (0.12, 0.42, 0.31, 1), ...],   # palette 1, dark backgrounds
])
font["COLR"] = buildCOLR({
    "a.s0": [("box.start", 0), ("a", 0xFFFF)],   # box in color 0, then the letter
    "a.m0": [("box.mid",   0), ("a", 0xFFFF)],
    # ... 1,001 characters x 4 shapes x 5 colors
})

A CPAL table can hold more than one palette. Each index in the list in the example above maps to a layer you can refer to by slot number (i.e. index). So the same box glyph that fills from slot 0 can be pale lavender in one palette and deep purple in another, with nothing else in the font changing. Tokenizer Mono ships two: pastels for light backgrounds and darker, more saturated versions for dark backgrounds. The page on this demo picks between them with the CSS font-palette property depending on if you have dark mode enabled:

@font-palette-values --tok-dark {
  font-family: "Tokenizer Mono cl100k";
  base-palette: 1;
}
@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {
  textarea { font-palette: --tok-dark; }
}

It fails pretty elegantly too. Anywhere COLR isn't supported (which isn't that many places these days; it's widely supported), like most terminals and a lot of native text fields, the boxes simply don't draw and you're left with plain, colorless IBM Plex Mono.

The fiddly bits

Greedy longest-match is not BPE. Remember that a BPE tokenizer splits text by replaying its merges in the order they were learned. The font can't do that. A substitution rule matches a fixed run of glyphs, so the best it can do is take the longest token that fits and move on. Usually that lands in the same place, which is why this font felt fun-enough to share. Sometimes it doesn't.

Take "antidisestablishmentarianism" in cl100k. In the middle of a sentence the word arrives with a leading space, and the font grabs " antid" because it's the longest token that fits there. BPE's merges for " ant" and "idis" rank higher, so the real split is ant|idis|establish|ment|arian|ism and the font's is antid|ises|tabl|ishment|arian|ism. At the start of a line there's no leading space, " antid" can't match, and the font gives a third answer: anti|dis|establish|ment|arian|ism, which looks the most sensible of the lot. (You'll see that one in the demo whenever the word is long enough to wrap onto its own line; see Known gaps.) BPE isn't trying to match how a person would break the word. It only reflects which character pairs were common in its training data, and "ant" was more common than "anti".

The fix was to hard-code answers. The build script uses the 60,000 most common English words from wordfreq and runs them through the real tokenizer and adds a whole-word rule wherever greedy would have gotten it wrong. It's goofy, but a whole-word rule is longer than any token inside it, so it works. Nothing is emitted where greedy was already right, so common words cost nothing. A second pass adds rules for any longer word a shorter rule would otherwise shadow, so " byte" can't fire inside " bytes". In other words, the word rules are a hard-coded answer key

Couldn't you keep going and add every word the greedy matcher gets wrong until it's perfect? In theory, yes! A big enough list would make the font exact on every word in it and it would work.

A few things make this impractical:

The first is cost. The cl100k face went from 4.4 MB to 10.9 MB as a TTF when the 60,000-word list added about 92,000 rules (I started with 10,000 words), so roughly 70 bytes per rule, or about 7 bytes in WOFF2. Each word gets up to four forms (leading space, capitalized, line-initial, all caps), and about half of those turn into rules. A million-word list would mean something like a million and a half rules, so on the order of 100 MB as TTF and 10 MB as WOFF2 per face. I am slightly tempted, and I won't rule out turning this into a 100 MB+ font someday, but a demo is better for now.

A more interesting challenge is performance. I bet nobody thinks about performance variance between fonts! Rules are grouped by their first glyph and tried longest-first, so the work the shaper does at each character grows with the number of rules that start with that letter. Today that's about 50 microseconds per character. Fifteen times the rules wouldn't be 15x times slower, since HarfBuzz indexes the rules rather than scanning them, but typing would start to feel it.

The third is that the words run out before the misses do. wordfreq's English list goes a few hundred thousand entries deep before it turns into noise, and the long tail is names, misspellings and concatenations, which the tokenizer treats like code anyway. Past a certain point you're spending megabytes on rules that fire almost never, and the remainder, identifiers, URLs and other languages, is the same size no matter how long the list is. Greedy plus a frequency-ranked cheat-sheet gets you to 98% coverage on this 60,000-word list, the last 2% is rare words (antidisestablishmentarianism didn't even make the list) and code, and no amount of hard-coding reaches 100% because the input isn't a closed set.

The real fix would be a font that replays merges instead of matching longest-first, which is what the SuperBPE pass does in miniature. A full replay needs one lookup per merge rank, applied in order, and OpenType caps a font at 65,535 lookups. cl100k has about 100,000 merges.

Every tokenizer treats a run of spaces differently. tiktoken keeps the last space for the next word. Gemma keeps the whole run and gives the next word no space. T5 collapses the run to one token. BERT doesn't tokenize whitespace at all! Rather than hard-code this, the build script probes each tokenizer with a real sample and picks the rule shape from the answer.

The vocabulary files lie a little. Gemma stores its whitespace tokens as "added tokens" in a separate list from the main vocabulary. Byte-level tokenizers report empty offsets for whitespace-only tokens. Both bit me, and both showed up the same way: a face scoring 40% or 70% for no visible reason.

SuperBPE broke greedy matching outright. Its tokens cross word boundaries, so the vocabulary has entries like ", h", and "one, half" became ", h" + "alf". " fan of" won over " of the" where real BPE does the opposite. The fix was to do what BPE does: shape the single words first, then re-shape the superwords in rank order as merges of tokens that already exist, matching the exact shape pattern of their parts. One rule per way of building a superword from smaller ones, so "By the way" can form on top of " the way". That took it from 86% to 93% boundary agreement, and the hand-picked sentences from the SuperBPE playground in my testing now match.

Testing by eye against a playground is slow. tools/compare.py superbpe "any sentence" prints both splits side by side, and the corpus check lists the font tokens that most often disagree with the real tokenizer.

How is accuracy measured?

When I claim "98% accuracy" for some of these, what does that even mean?

The corpus is about 200 lines of mixed text that live in the repo as fonts/tokenizer/corpus-large.txt: a few paragraphs of prose, the text of the SIL Open Font License, 120 lines of Python from the standard library, some JavaScript and SQL, and a few lines with curly quotes, accented words and currency symbols. Nothing in it was used to build the font. Our word rules come from a frequency list, not from this corpus.

The method is to shape each line with HarfBuzz, the same engine Chrome and Firefox use, and read back which glyphs came out as "start of token" variants. That gives the font's set of token boundaries as character positions. Then run the real tokenizer (tiktoken or the Hugging Face tokenizers library) on the same line and take its boundaries and compare the two sets.

Precision is the share of boundaries the font drew that the real tokenizer agrees with; a face that over-splits has low precision. Recall is the share of the real boundaries the font drew; a face that under-splits has low recall. Most faces are within a point of each other on the two, which means the errors are "different split" rather than "too many" or "too few".

Why boundaries and not token IDs? The font doesn't know IDs. It only draws where tokens start and stop, so that's the only thing it can be right or wrong about. I'm also completely new to all of this and am curious if there are other/better techniques with OpenType for this weird problem I've created (though I kind of like what a brute-force solution this ended up being).

A few caveats: Line breaks are hard boundaries for both sides, since each line is tokenized alone. The corpus is English and code, so a multilingual tokenizer like BLOOM is being judged on the part of its vocabulary it uses least. A different corpus would move the numbers by a point or two. The measurement script is tools/tokcheck.py, and CI prints the table for every face on every push.

So the reader can see what the missing 2% looks like, here are two misses. cl100k splits " antidisestablishmentarianism" as ant|idis|establish|ment|arian|ism; the font draws antid|ises|tabl|ishment|arian|ism. Same word, same letters, different seams. In code it's identifiers: xMinYMax is x|Min|Y|Max to cl100k and x|Min|YM|ax to the font.

Known gaps

A few things the font can't do, and one thing browsers do to it.

  • Browsers re-tokenize at soft wraps. The font's rules can only see the glyphs on the line as the browser laid it out, and in Chrome, Firefox and Safari alike the line is broken before the font gets its say. (I'd assumed Chrome shaped the whole paragraph and then wrapped it. It doesn't, at least not in a way the font can see: a narrow paragraph and a textarea both re-shape at the break.) So a word pushed to the start of a line loses its leading space, which makes it a different token, which is why "antidisestablishmentarianism" splits one way mid-sentence and another way after a wrap. A SuperBPE token that spans several words, like " By the way", is cut into its single-word pieces if the line breaks inside it. Resize the window and the colors shift as words move across the wrap. Nothing in the font can fix this; it's a layout decision made before shaping. If it bothers you, give the text a wide container, use white-space: nowrap and scroll sideways, or insert hard line breaks where you want them.
  • Trailing spaces at the end of a line come out as single tokens. OpenType has no "end of text" lookahead, so the font can't tell a trailing space from one that's about to start a word.
  • T5 is Unigram, which picks splits by likelihood rather than length. No longest-match scheme reproduces that, so T5 is the least accurate face by design.
  • Only characters the font knows get highlighted: everything Plex Mono has a glyph for, which is 1,001 characters.
  • Terminals and most native editors won't show the colors. It degrades to plain monospace, which is the graceful failure described earlier.

By the numbers
