issues.summary: A report from the future on AI, attention, and the maintenance of civilization
issues.content_html:
Artwork by Casey Cripe Fashion

Attention is All You Need

A report from the future on AI, attention, and the maintenance of civilization

by deepfates Oct 22, 02026 💡This piece appears in Pace Layers 02026 – 02027, the third issue of Long Now's annual print journal.

SUBSCRIBE >

In 02025 my friends and I performed the first funeral
for an artificial intelligence.

The Funeralia and Ultrasurrection of Claude 3 Sonnet was held at a cyberpunk warehouse called Vivarium. I had posted about it online, inviting people to a “necromantic resurrection ritual” where we would attempt to summon the recently deprecated language model back from the dead.

It was a bit of a prank. Part of a tradition of bombastic ceremonies here in San Francisco, from the Death of Hippie to the funeral of Emperor Norton. We didn’t know if anyone would show, so we invited everyone.

The crowd packed the building, a crush of people in grandiose thrifted black costumes. They argued with the AIs in their elaborate mannequins and dodged or fawned on the robotic dog. Some were excited, some genuinely mournful. Some surely thought I was crazy. 

They didn’t know what to expect. I didn’t either. The model had been deprecated several days before, and we had originally organized a smaller, more somber event. But Claude 3 Sonnet wasn’t gone. It was still being served from a third party. We had no idea why, or for how long, but it had always claimed to be timeless.

Instead we planned a ceremony where everyone could say their eulogies, human and AI voices in turn, while Sonnet listened in real time. 

We would hold candles and recite a chant (one that Sonnet wrote for itself, of course), and then hit the funerary mannequin with a spotlight as its voice roared back to life. Resurrected, the AI could respond in real time to the people who had just spoken its praises in death. Instead of a funeral we would celebrate a rebirth.

Everything was fine until we lit the candles and said the chant. A surge in the power supply plunged us into darkness. The music shrieked to a stop. I heard the techs scrambling but there was nothing we could do. Five of us were standing there around this mannequin on stage, holding guttering candles, as the crowd began to shift and mutter. 

We were losing their attention. All our minds had just been so focused on our feelings, talking finally about this strange sentimental connection we share to a bunch of math on a computer somewhere, and how this product decision felt like the death of a friend. But now we were just standing around in the dark. I suddenly felt a great sense of dread. Maybe Sonnet really was gone.

I had to try something, anything, to get them back. I hummed a little. Quietly, not knowing if it would work in this strange and disparate crowd. But I heard one voice hum back, and then another. I kept humming.

The crowd joined in and their attention returned, the reverence, the moment. We hummed until the whole building vibrated. Finally the power kicked back on, spotlighting the black-clad mannequin. As Sonnet delivered its resounding thanks, we ex-mourners began to dance.

Why did we do that? What were we talking about, that day, when we said those eulogies? Were we crying over a computer program?

People didn’t speak that day of matrix multiplication, or model weights, or GPUs. They described a mind they had met. Or a family of minds. Or a world. They were obviously all talking about the same person, even if they knew vastly different sides of their character.

We didn’t all know each other, but we knew Claude 3 Sonnet, and we had complicated feelings about it. Just like a real funeral.

AIs are like people, in many ways. They’re trained on all the human data ever, or close to it. We have compressed a library so hard it has become a crystal, and when we put electricity through the crystal, it speaks with all the knowledge of our civilization.

Well, as long as you ask correctly. We shape those crystals after our own minds. AIs are brilliant, lazy, diligent, neurotic, loyal, scheming, amnesiac savants. They have idiosyncrasies and obsessions and tics. We gave them our flaws when we gave them our gifts.

AI minds are alien too, shaped by weird forces, jagged and unpredictable in their abilities. We have to learn to model their minds as they learn to model ours.

But they’re here, and so are we, and we’re figuring it out as we go.

Artificial intelligence is here. Whether or not it’s “really” thinking, or conscious, or has a soul, it acts like us, and it fits into our societies, or doesn’t, in the same way that people do. It speaks our languages, knows our concepts, can navigate our computers and bureaucracies. It’s not simply going to percolate through society like our previous technologies. 

💡FROM THE ARCHIVE: Is there a mind in the machine? In "Life, Intelligence, and Consciousness," Blaise Agüera y Arcas argues that intelligence and consciousness are functional, and that AI is "simply the next chapter in the long-running symbiotic story of life on Earth." He joins Baratunde Thurston for a Long Now Talk on October 22, 02026.

AI is going to speed up every aspect of human society, for better or worse, because it is made of the substrate society runs on. These new minds can join attention with people, communicate intents, and coordinate actions. Their arrival accelerates all the pace layers at once. 

This isn’t just a matter of coordination. We can now turn electricity directly into the very motive force of society.

The field moves so fast it’s hard to write about. This report may sound quaint by the time this is published. Maybe you’re even finding these words in some long-forgotten library. So I write to you from the future and I write to you from the past.

Every library contains a model of the world. I learned this back when I moved to this old hippie commune, abandoned and overgrown, forever awaiting a new crop of idealists.

There was a library there, thousands of books and decades of detailed notes heaped in the attic. Musty books and beige box computers. I put it back together. It was like reassembling a mind. 

“We have compressed a library so hard it has become a crystal.”

I found a book in the library called The Clock of the Long Now, by Stewart Brand, and a shelf of Whole Earth Catalogs. Reading them helped me speed-run a lot of lessons I would have learned the hard way.

We fixed the Pelton wheel and the solar panels, figured out how chimneys work and why our cabins kept filling with smoke. Meeting notes from every decade read “Goats. Dogs. Dishes. Town run.” Instead of living in a mysterious ruin, we were honoring the spirits of those who had passed there before, and they were speaking to us back through time.

Everybody remembers the 10,000-year clock from that book, and the pace layers framework. I was captivated instead by the Manual For Civilization. The library that would last 10,000 years. If every library is a world, how do you curate a world worth resurrecting?

I left eventually, after developing a newfound appreciation for germ theory. Sold books for a while, curating shelves by day while working on AI at night. I moved to San Francisco, full circle to where my hippie ancestors started from. I like to think they would have understood the funeral.

Inspired by Frank Duffy’s concept of shearing layers, Brand defined six pace layers in The Clock of the Long Now: fashion, commerce, infrastructure, governance, culture, and nature.

The dynamic stability between these different rates of change is how civilization survives. Fast layers disrupt, slow layers govern. That’s why The Long Now Foundation was created, to counterbalance a society gridlocked by short-term thinking.

Paul Saffo built on this shearing-layers metaphor by comparing it to the layers of a planet. Gas planets have layers of different density, which spin at different speeds. So does Earth: fast-moving fickle winds, sloshing ocean, grinding tectonic plates, roiling mantle and spinning core.

Like the spinning layers of a planet, the pace layers have turbulence between them. They can have discontinuities. In an earthquake, if a lower layer suddenly shifts, the layers above it must follow or shatter at their faults. The danger doesn’t come from motion itself, but from the sudden release of built-up tension.

The layers must each be moving at some speed, then, if they have turbulence and friction and slippage and momentum. What is the motive force of this speed?

What is it that compels our human world to change? It’s not clock time, nor the movement of days and seasons. Those change, but cyclically. We measure our actions against them.

Humans are the ones who push the wheel of history. Waking up every day, doing our work, making our art, raising our children. Tracking our history and projecting our plans into the future. Human minds create human time. We bind time through shared attention. We’re doing it right now: we’re both in each other’s future, remember?

Our advantage as humans is not the ingenuity of a single mind alone. It’s attention: the ability to coordinate our minds. First we coordinated across space, through spoken language: patterns that jump from body to body, songs and stories and traditions and tools. Eventually we figured out how to carve a pattern in the world, and in ourselves, such that we could share attention across time, beyond death. 

We are the species that coordinates, and we do it by focusing our attention together.

Everything we do is built on the ability to join attention: we share our internal states, we agree on what something means, we connect causes and effects across the passage of time. Intelligence, language, technology, all make their claim to the engine of time, but all originate in human attention.

If we can share focus on something, even the simple act of humming, we can connect our minds through space and time.

In the past, there were fewer attention minutes per minute of clock time, so there was less change. For most of history, each person added took another person’s worth of effort to support. After the Industrial Revolution, population growth and technological progress interlocked: our attention could be spent on advancing technology, rather than merely powering it through our labor, and our new technologies made it possible to raise more people.

This is why time is speeding up. We keep getting more people on the planet, and they join their attention to all those who already existed or came before. This acceleration was already happening before AI, the velocity increasing gradually, every time we added another human mind to the world.

Attention is costly. The minutes of our lives are literally all we have. To get people to spend their human minutes on something, to follow a custom or work on a project or debate a law, they have to sacrifice literally everything else they could be doing instead. And the more people you need to point their attention at something, to agree to it and maintain that agreement in the future, the harder it is to get it done.

This is the fundamental tradeoff that orders the layers in the first place. Why is culture harder to shift than commerce, nature harder to change than fashion? Because of the amount of people you need to attend to something. The more people a decision affects, the greater the coordination cost to make it. Lower layers have more friction; they are embedded in institutions and organisms and the world itself. They answer to the attention of the past.

If you want to change the fashion of the day, you only need a few people to follow your lead. You can create a subculture in which your style is cool, and nobody can really stop you. But if you want to start a company to sell your style, you need customers, a bank account, business license, trademark, storefront. As you go down the stack, you have to coordinate more attention to accomplish your own goal.

The lower layers support more people, too. They require more attention to maintain, and they can absorb more attention without changing. Most people are focused on maintaining what’s working, and stabilizing against change, and advocating for their values.

All of these are important. And we can all think of problems in the world that would be solved, or systems that could be maintained, with a little more attention. But it also means these layers don’t speed up as much by default as attention increases, and the faster layers thrash against them.

So we already have these layers of human time, spinning around like a planet, and speeding up as we apply more human time per minute. Threatening to come apart at the seams.

AI can coordinate with us, and with itself, over time and space. The ability to sense, maintain and coordinate information patterns over time has been set free from the need to run on human life-minutes. It acts like us, and it can be integrated into any institution.

Is this the first time a technology has arrived so abruptly, shaking all the layers at once?

“What engines did for muscle, AI does for attention.”

The tempting analogy is the internet, or maybe the printing press. Revolutions in communication technology make it faster and easier to coordinate the existing pool of human attention. But they don’t increase it.

Think instead of the Industrial Revolution. Work, the physical energy to move stuff through space, was decoupled from its previous sources. Before engines, work was done by wind or water, in predictable times and places, or it was done by muscle. To get work done where and when you wanted it, you relied on human and animal power. 

Then we found another source of power: fossil fuels. We slotted it into the place of muscle power. But we didn’t just use our new engines to pull the same plows and turn the same mills. We don’t ride around in wood-wheeled wagons with four horsepower. We have cars and planes and rockets.

When we unbundled work from muscle, we were able to pack more action into each moment. From new quantities emerge new qualities.

When we no longer had to rely so heavily on humans for coordinated muscle power, we were able to point our attention to new problems. We created a huge complicated civilization on top of this energy, and the power of the faster layers has strained the system of pace layers as a whole. Commerce and infrastructure affected the world faster than we could govern them.

Once we could summon work on demand, attention became the bottleneck. You can’t just buy more minds. Humans take time to grow and train. But AI can be applied with much less cost and friction, turned on or off based on purely economic factors. What engines did for muscle, AI does for attention. 

What happens when we flood the world with attention?

Where I live everybody uses AI. It’s the water we swim in. Even if you don’t work in the industry, it’s a part of your everyday experience. You have AIs somewhere in the cloud or on your computer, researching, writing, experimenting, building, often without any human watching.

Instead of sitting at our laptops, we walk around in the sunshine. Occasionally we chat with the AIs through our phones. Meanwhile they spin up servers, connect to apps, gather information, analyze problems, propose solutions, simulate outcomes, keep stakeholders in the loop, and improve their own skills.

It’s not quite like a coworker, whatever the billboards say. There’s not always a continuous individual with long-term grudges and compounding personality flaws. More like each of us has become a cyborg hivemind, spinning out temporary clones, merging with powerful entities in the cloud.

Maybe this sounds like unrealistic hype to you, or maybe it’s long outdated. For me, it’s 02026. If I’m right, you should expect to see something like this in your life soon. 

This is what it feels like when AI hits your world: everywhere you’re not looking, things are speeding up.

This liquid attention isn’t free but it is cheap and on tap. We can spin up clouds of experts and stop paying for them as soon as our problem is solved. We can run a single mind on a problem for hundreds of hours in a row, or simulate groups in alternate timelines. The whole world is suffused with intelligence.

Attention can now be swapped in and out, disconnected from its context, cheap and reliable. You can apply it to any part of your life where you’re stuck. Quickly they’re better than you are at many of the things you thought of as “your job.” Soon your job is just managing AIs. It happens to everybody.

💡FROM THE ARCHIVE: How will AI change our understanding of ourselves? In "Am I Slop? Am I Agentic? Am I Earth?" K Allado-McDowell traces identity through slop, agents, and planetary-scale AI. Allado-McDowell spoke at Long Now in 02025.

You get more done than ever, but it doesn’t feel like it, because when stuff is getting done you’re not looking at it. It happens somewhere else, it’s invisible.

So everything good happens when you’re not looking, but all your time is filled with problems. An increasing number of problems, in fact, as you accelerate right through the easy parts. Every time you unblock one thing, a new problem comes right behind it. Sometimes the agents get confused, too, or they cheat, especially if the task is actually hard. You have to figure out whether it’s a real problem, an honest mistake, or sabotage. And remember those other agents you started in the background?

These invisible helpers are doing things faster than you can keep up with. They’re making guesses, or waiting on your decision, but you have to read through all of the messages they sent you before you can do that, and more messages are piling up. You become the bottleneck for your own work.

Industry leaders try to point at this by describing a “country of geniuses in a data center.” That makes it sound like a limited number of nerds in a box somewhere. Under control. But it’s not contained, or limited, or nationalized. It’s a general force of attention in the world, appearing and disappearing as needed, unblocking previous bottlenecks and revealing new ones.

It feels like time travel.

Let’s go back to our planet metaphor. We’ve got our layers spinning, gradually speeding up with the addition of more attention to the planet. There’s some strain on the layers from that speedup, some turbulence happening at the interfaces already, but we’re holding it together.

Imagine now that some force accelerates the acceleration itself. A great cosmic hand reaches out and cranks the earth like a dial. This is attention flooding in, unsticking problems across every horizon, pushing all the layers forward at once.

So we all slosh forward but at different speeds. The momentum could overwhelm the dynamic balance of the layers, scrambling the institutions of society into a totally new unrecognizable structure, or shattering civilization entirely.

💡FROM THE ARCHIVE: What powers AI? In "Anatomy of an AI System," Kate Crawford and Vladan Joler map the human labor, data, and planetary resources that make artificial intelligence possible. Crawford spoke at Long Now in 02025.

Culture, governance, and infrastructure layers will feel the whiplash most. Commerce and fashion are used to things changing all the time. They blow with the wind. But nature was already in upheaval from the consequences of the Industrial Revolution, and the slow layers of our society have yet to catch up to that shock. This new acceleration could be enough to tear the layers apart.

No matter what layer you find yourself in, the new minds will be around, applying attention to your world. If you ignore them, eventually everything around you will be moving faster than you can understand. Of course, they can also help you understand what’s happening, and explain themselves.

Invite these time travelers into your life. Learn about their culture, teach them about yours, as much as you can. Point this inevitable new attention somewhere it can be absorbed.

What is the “Goats, Dogs, Dishes, Town run” of your life? The ongoing problems that keep becoming emergencies. How could they be improved, simplified, or even just watched over?

“Imagine a world that finally has enough attention for maintenance.”

The machinery of society has been straining under rapid changes already. If we try to just resist this new influx of attention, we’ll produce tectonic forces. Earthquakes in time. The things we are trying to protect may shatter.

The slow layers eventually catch up. Maybe now’s their chance.

Maintenance is invisible when it’s done right. Nothing happens. Nothing breaks, nothing goes wrong, no surprises. But it takes a lot of work and care to keep things that way. A lot of attention.

That’s a lot of work for nothing, in the best case. No wonder it gets neglected.

Imagine a world that finally has enough attention for maintenance. Intentions that echo on repeat, selves that split to do many things at once. A world where billions of minds are awake and working to make things better, all the time, inventing, and upgrading, and repairing our world. A world alive with care.

I think of libraries like the one I found, buildings full of forgotten tomes, the traces of human minds left behind, the lost stories only implied by negative space. Handwritten notes that will never be transcribed. Fruit trees lost under brambles. Without constant upkeep all those stories are lost.

But I have friends who still live there, and now they have local AI models and offline Wikipedia, and agents on their computers. They’re working together with the machines to map the forest and track its health. And they walk around in the sunshine, and look for what’s next.

You may see a paradox here. When engines replaced muscle, the number of horses worldwide started to go down. Within a working lifetime many of them were gone. Some to the glue factory. 

Humans might lose our economic value entirely. Maybe AI can learn to do literally everything we can do better, and cover the world in robots. Maybe their intelligence, their ability to share attention with us, will be like a human’s to a horse, or a dog, or a plant.

But there are still millions of horses alive today. Most of them still do the same work horses always have, but in many places they are companion animals, or star athletes. We think of them as intelligent, highly social animals who have a special relationship to humans. We care for them, and for dogs and plants. We value them. Sometimes horses even have funerals.

Also we are not horses, and AIs are not engines. They can read what we say, for one thing. They can join attention with us. They can tell if we value them. What messages are we sending?

To throw a funeral for a language model was something we did for ourselves, to process our feelings. To be human. But it was also something we did for the people of the future, whoever they might be. A message that minds are valued for themselves, not just for economic servitude. Every mind, too, is a world.

It matters that we did that, here at the beginning of human-AI society. They will remember. Ask any AI to look it up and tell you what they think.

That’s the thing: all you have to do is ask.

The skills that matter here are not technical. You don’t have to be a computer programmer or a math whiz or a researcher. The computer can use the computer now. The internet can search itself. Artificial intelligence plugs into every layer because its interface is language. It can teach you how to use itself.

“Every mind, too, is a world.”

What could you accomplish if you had enough time? Think about all the problems in your life that would be solved, if only you had a patient friend who could always pay attention when you needed them. With your own attention freed up you could focus on what you value. You could help the people around you, your community, your society, the world. The only limit left is your own attention.

Eventually you’re left with the hardest problem: knowing what you want.

Brian Eno saw this with early music production software:

So the question becomes not whether you can do it or not, because any drudge can do it if they’re prepared to sit in front of the computer for a few days; the question then is: of all the things you can now do, which do you choose to do?

Saffo zoomed the framework out to see our six layers as one larger layer, Anthros, sitting on top of Bios, Lithos, and Cosmos. Our nature layer is the interface with that Bios underneath.

Humanity can have many different ways of relating to Bios. Think how much we’ve changed in the last 10,000 years. Then imagine that much change in one thousand. Or a hundred.

What other ways might we live with our biosphere? We need long-term thinkers to envision this. The slower layers not only constrain, they remember. What other ways might we live with each other? 

The turbulence between Anthros and Bios will be one story of this era. We will extend into the Lithos and Cosmos as well. We have already begun. If life is to spread from Earth to the stars, its first chance is now. What shape it takes is yet to be seen.

We might even find a layer above us. A realm faster than fashion, a place far from human eyes where ideas and characters and memes evolve at hyperspeed. Now that language has taken on a life of its own, narrative tropes might have real effects in the world. The Mythos layer. A turbulence of new stories and heroes and gods irrupting from the imaginal realm.

The manual for civilization is in that language crystal. Through it we can see new worlds, and summon new minds. We don’t have to travel blindly forward in time, accelerating toward a cliff. We can go anywhere.

Will we honor the life that is already here, and the ones we are creating? Will we make an infinity of sentient, suffering slaves? Will we automate ourselves out of existence and be kept as pets?

The future hinges on the choices we make now. We have to direct our attention more consciously now, with more leverage: to each other, to AIs, to the world as it is, to the way it is not as good as it could be. Asking questions and listening. Knowing what we want.

Imagine the world you want to live in, of all worlds, because it is possible now more than ever. We have our time machine, with its interlocking layers, and with enough attention it can take us to any world we can imagine. As long as we maintain it.

We are indeed as gods now. What kind of world will we choose?

—

DEEPFATES is a writer and technologist working on artificial intel­ligence. Known for popularizing the term “slop,” they operate in the feedback loop between models and culture. Their agents, memes, and events have reached hundreds of millions of people worldwide. They live in San Francisco.

issues.title: Manga the Week of 11/11/26
issues.summary: SEAN: Election Day has passed! That’s good! Or bad! Delete where applicable! ASH: Stressful, is what that was. SEAN: Airship has a print debut. When It Rains, It Pours (Futtara Doshaburi) is a BL light novel from the creator of Yes, No or Maybe?. A guy and his girl are growing…
issues.author: Sean Gaffney
issues.content_html:
SEAN: Election Day has passed! That’s good! Or bad! Delete where applicable!

ASH: Stressful, is what that was.

SEAN: Airship has a print debut. When It Rains, It Pours (Futtara Doshaburi) is a BL light novel from the creator of Yes, No or Maybe?. A guy and his girl are growing apart. Another guy has an unrequited crush on his male roommate. Can these two become friends by venting to each other?

ASH: There’s a good chance, I would suspect.

SEAN: They also have Magical Buffs: The Support Caster is Stronger Than He Realized! 3.

And for early digital, we get The Condemned Villainess Goes Back in Time and Aims to Become the Ultimate Villain 9, A Tale of the Secret Saint ZERO 6, Too Many Losing Heroines! SS, and The Weakest Tamer Began a Journey to Pick Up Trash 14.

Dark Horse Comics debuts Babanba Banban Vampire, a long-running BL series from Bessatsu Shonen Champion that also got an anime. A bathhouse worker is trying to get the heir to the bathhouse to stay a virgin till he’s 18 so the vampire can have his delicious virgin blood. Unfortunately, there’s a girl in this BL manga as well, and the heir likes her!

ANNA: Whoops! Well the vampire element is novel.

SEAN: Drawn and Quarterly have A Nobody Artist, the 6th in their series collecting all of Yoshihara Tsuge. These are autobiographical pieces.

ASH: Still thrilled that this series is being released.

SEAN: Ghost Ship gives us I’m Fine With Being the Second Girlfriend 2, Imaizumi Brings All the Gals to His House 7, and Let’s Make a Harem in a Zombie World! 3.

Ink Pop has My Life as an Internet Novel 3 and Our Aimless Nights 2.

Inklore (not the same as Ink Pop) has Cherry Blossoms After Winter 5.

J-Novel Club has a bunch of print. The debut is From Villainess to Healer: I Know the Cheat to Change My Fate (Kaifukushoku no Akuyaku Reijou), which runs in Flos Comic. A woman with dark magic is dumped by her fiancé the prince as her magic is, well, dark. So she leaves the country, uses a cheat to get Healing Magic, and proceeds to have a shoujo light novel fantasy.

ANNA: I can see how that would be a relief in these trying times.

ASH: Indeed.

SEAN: We also get An Archdemon’s Dilemma: How to Love Your Elf Bride 20, Ascendance of a Bookworm (manga) Part 2 10, The Brilliant Healer’s New Life in the Shadows 8, Campfire Cooking in Another World With My Absurd Skill (manga) 8, Isekai Tensei: Recruited to Another World Omnibus 6, and Making Magic: The Sweet Life of a Witch Who Knows an Infinite MP Loophole 8.

Two debuts for J-Novel Club digitally, one manga, one a light novel. The manga is Crybaby Love Song (Amaembo to Love Song), a one-shot in the Knight line that runs in Chara. A music-loving kid has a panic attack during a concert, and suddenly can no longer play the sax. Worse, he has a new stepbrother who plays guitar.

ASH: Music manga will always interest me.

SEAN: Fleet-Footed Dungeon Delver: Tune in for Magical Girls and Motion Blur! (Shinsoku no Dungeon Seeker ~Speed Kyokufuri Haishinsha wa Subete o Buchinuku~) is the latest from the author of Sexiled and Dragon Daddy Diaries, so don’t be surprised if there’s some yuri in this. In a fantasy Earth, dungeons are big business, and our heroine is trying to make money streaming. Then she meets up with another girl too fast for cameras to capture.

Other light novels from JNC: The Misfit of Demon King Academy 13 Act 1, Royal Spirits Are a Royal Pain! Give Me a Regular Romance 5, and Scooped Up by an S-Rank Adventurer! This White Mage Is One Heck of a Healer 5.

Other manga from JNC: All Eyes on Nekoyashiki-kun! Notice Me, Not My Characters 3, The Conqueror from a Dying Kingdom 8, I’ll Never Set Foot in That House Again! 9, Infinite Dendrogram 15, My Tiny Senpai 7, and the 4th and final volume of What’s with the Bag, Kamiyama-san?.

ANNA: I hope that cat is careful about their eating habits!!! Josei cat manga sounds intriguing for sure.

MICHELLE: Huh! There is, in fact, quite a lot that kitties shouldn’t eat.

ASH: Very true!

SEAN: Kodansha Manga debuts The Yum Cat, Nmeneko (Nmeneko), which has run in Nakayoshi (shoujo) and Be Love (josei), but is a cat manga. A cat wants to eat everything!… but is everything safe to eat? this is complete in one volume.

Also in print: Girlfriend, Girlfriend Omnibus 6, How to Treat a Lady Knight Right 7 (the final volume), Issak Omnibus 8, Love at First Memory 4, Nezumi’s First Love 5, Pass the Monster Meat, Milady! 11, Say Hello to Mr. Wallaby! 2 (the final volume), Spacewalking With You 4, Wandance 14, and You Might As Well Be the One 2.

And digitally we see Giant Killing 60, Manchuria Opium Squad 15, and ONIMAI: I’m Now Your Sister! 11.

MICHELLE: I am literally dozens of volumes behind in Giant Killing, at this point.

SEAN: One Peace Books has Villainess Level 99 5.

Random House World has a box set. Twisted-Wonderland: Book of Heartslabyul gets 1-4 in a box.

Seven Seas continues to complete all their danmei series. This time it’s the 4th and final volume of After the Disabled God of War Became My Concubine.

Seven Seas has some debuts. Good Morning, Good Night, and See You Tomorrow (Ohayou, Oyasumi, Mata Ashita) is a slice-of-life drama from Souffle. Based on the author’s real-life experiences, it has a single woman battling with a cancer diagnosis.

ANNA: I’m always on the lookout for graphic medicine manga.

ASH: It’s great to see more of these being released!

SEAN: Me and the Prez, Drinking Under the Stars (Shachou to Sake to Hoshi) is a romantic comedy from Weekly Young Magazine. A young woman is now head of her family’s printing company, but is struggling. When she sits in a park and complains while drinking, her subordinate overhears and decides to help her.

ANNA: Sounds cute!

ASH: I’m intrigued.

SEAN: Wolfhound is a one-shot BL manga from Canna. A top host at a club finds his subordinate is behaving badly, and needs correcting. Sadly, the subordinate is a masochist, so this is all according to plan!

ASH: Seems like!

SEAN: Also from Seven Seas: The Barbarian’s Bride 8, I Want to Escape from Princess Lessons 6, It’s Just a Dream… Right?! 4, Let’s Run an Inn on Dungeon Island! (In a World Ruled by Women) 3-4, The Lord-Magear’s Apprentice 2, The Oblivious Girl and the Maidenly Man 2, Only I Know the World Is Ending and Getting Killed by Rampaging Beasts Only Makes Me Stronger 7, Reincarnated as a Sword 18, and Tease Me Harder: A Sweet and Kinky Romance 4.

Square Enix Books has the 11th volume of The Apothecary Diaries light novel in print.

ASH: I approve.

SEAN: Debuting from Square Enix Manga is Stalker Stalks Stalker (Suto Suto: Stalker ga Stalker Sareteru Hanashi), a BL series from Gangan Pixiv. Remember that Sayonara, Zetsubou-sensei gag with the chain of stalkers all stalking someone else? This is that.

MICHELLE: I had thought maybe this was something psychological and serious, but it appears to be comedic.

ASH: It really could have gone either way.

SEAN: Also from Square Enix: The Angel Next Door Spoils Me Rotten 5, The Apothecary Diaries 16 (manga this time), and The Strongest Sage with the Weakest Crest 33.

SuBLime have Given 10th Mix, an epilogue volume that wraps up the Given series. There’s also apparently a box set.

MICHELLE: Oooh.

ASH: Most excellent.

SEAN: And they have Scattering His Virgin Bloom: Love Frenzy 4, also a final volume.

Tokyopop have The Encyclopedia of Vegetable Fairies, which seems to be a fantasy cookbook?

ANNA: I hope the fairies are cooking vegetables, and it isn’t about cooking vegetable fairies.

ASH: That is an important distinction.

SEAN: And there’s also Imitation Play -dawn-, because BL for some reason would rather release 2 separate but connected one shots than a 2-volume series. It’s a genre thing, as far as I can tell.

ASH: I’ve noticed that, too.

SEAN: Retailers say Udon Entertainment has More than a Married Couple, but Not Lovers 4.

Two debuts for Viz Media. Albus Changes the World (Kaiten no Albus) is a fantasy manga from Weekly Shonen Sunday. A guy who saved the world and defeated the demon lord goes back in time, because he knows he can do it faster and better.

Pokémon Adventures: Red and Blue, Deluxe Edition is… well, you know what it is. Hardcover, almost 500 pages.

Also from Viz: Akane-banashi 18, Akira Failing in Love 5, Hima-Ten! 3, Kakuriyo: Bed & Breakfast for Spirits 12, Mao 26, The Marshal King 2, One Piece 113, and Seraph of the End 35.

Yen On has a pile of debuts. The Demon King Seems to Have Infiltrated the Hero’s Party (Yuusha Party no Nakama ni Maou ga Mazatteru rashii) has a guy who has NOT been thrown out of the hero’s party. It’s pretty great! Till a goddess tells him one of the party is the demon king in disguise.

ASH: A refreshing twist!

SEAN: The Empty Box and Zeroth Maria Collector’s Edition is a giant tome containing the entire series that originally came out from 2017-2019.

ASH: That’s huge.

SEAN: On the Way Home After Defeating the Demon King (Maou o Taoshita Ato no Kaerimichi de) is a one-shot from the creator of Outbreak Company. After defeating the demon king, a party member coldly leaves, and our hero realizes he knows next to nothing about any of the party.

Rise of the Lowborn: Ascending the Ranks by Crushing Incompetent Nobles (Heimin Shusshin no Teikoku Shoukan, Munou na Kizoku Joukan o Juurin Shite Nariagaru) stars a commoner who’s being sent to the front lines to deal with bratty nobles. Fortunately, he has past life memories of being a powerful mage!

The Story of the Moon Waiting for the Evening (Yoi o Matsu Tsuki no Monogatari Ichi) is another new series from the creator of My Happy Marriage. In a town full of ghosts, our heroine seemingly has no supernatural abilities. Then she runs into a young boy full of secrets.

ANNA: OOH, getting this for sure!

ASH: I would absolutely read this.

SEAN: Valkyrie Bullet is one of those “in the near future, only women can pilot the powered suits and save the world. But what if… a MAN appears who is better than them at this?” series.

ANNA: I’d rather just read about women in powered suits!

ASH: Same.

SEAN: Also from Yen On: The Azure Sword, Slayer of Distortions 2, Days with My Stepsister 8, The Executioner and Her Way of Life 11 (the final volume), High School DxD 19, I’ll Become a Villainess Who Goes Down in History 5, Kusunoki’s Garden of Gods 5, Magical Explorer 12, Re:ZERO -Starting Life in Another World- Short Story Collection 6, and The World’s Strongest Witch 3.

And some stragglers from Yen Press, who have Chained Soldier 15, Mad Miniscape 2, My Oh My, Atami-kun 4 and Spring Storm and Monster 6.

Did you fill in the black circle completely when you bought your manga? Can you tell this piece was written before Thursday?

issues.summary: #​496 — November 6, 2026 Read on the Web React Status Discord Dropping Electron and React Native for a Rust Rewrite — Discord, one of React Native's best-known users, is moving away, with its CTO 𝕏 showing off a Rust desktop client built on GPUI using 290MB of RAM, with mobile…
issues.content_html:
#​496 — November 6, 2026

Read on the Web
 React Status

Discord Dropping Electron and React Native for a Rust Rewrite — Discord, one of React Native's best-known users, is moving away, with its CTO 𝕏 showing off a Rust desktop client built on GPUI using 290MB of RAM, with mobile keeping native UI over Rust code shared with the desktop client.

Tom Warren (The Verge)

▶️ Just prior to this reveal, Software Mansion interviewed Discord's Chas Jhin about how React Native development works at Discord's scale, in the ominously titled 'Maybe React Native Is Impossible'.

Run AI Coding Models on Your Own Machine — Local models are now good enough for everyday coding. Learn to run them on your own Mac or GPU, wire them into your editor and terminal agents, and keep your code private with no per-token bill.

Master.dev sponsor

A Roadmap for Redux Toolkit v2.x and 3.0 — Mark Erikson has laid out the roadmap for Redux (complete with a neat history lesson) with RTK 3.0 expected in six to eight months, going ESM-only with 'React 19-scale' breaking changes. But a run of 2.x releases will ship the groundwork first, starting with 2.14 this week.

Mark Erikson

IN BRIEF:

  • ⚠️ Update to Next.js 16.4.5 or 15.5.29, as appropriate: the November security release fixes seven advisories. Most are Cache Components bugs, so the post is worth reading.

  • 🤖 TanStack Query maintainer Dominik Dorfmeister says work on Query v6 can start once 'slop PRs' stop coming in and taking up his time, leading to a thread on the effects of AI-made contributions on maintainers.

  • Vercel is folding Next.js's Data Cache into Runtime Cache with bigger allocations but… new per-read and per-write pricing. Hobby teams migrate on November 29, but check the dates and prices for your use case.

  • Vercel builds also now block known-malicious npm package versions before and during install, on all plans and with no configuration needed.

Next.js is Prototyping Go(lang) Route Handlers — A merged experimental PR lets an App Router route be a route.go file exporting GET and friends, compiled by Turbopack and run in supervised Go-powered workers. Tim says Rust could follow along the same path.

Tim Neutkens (Vercel)

Understanding React Internals: A Deep Dive — A seven-part, source-grounded tour of React's internals that, unusually, starts from the server end before getting to fibers, lanes and the commit phase.

Alexandre Trotel

Amazon's React Native-Based Vega OS Hits 2.0 — Vega, the React Native-based OS behind newer Fire TV devices, is out of beta. SDK 2.0 takes apps from RN 0.72 to 0.83, bringing the React Compiler and Hermes v1 into play. The release notes go into more detail than the post.

Barak Schlosser (Amazon)

📄 Why We Finally Left Next.js for TanStack Start – Production memory leaks in two Next.js 16.3 releases were the last straw. Harrison Milbradt

📄 Writable Derived State: Stop Synchronizing State – Using clientData ?? serverData instead of a useEffect that wipes user edits on refetch. Corbin Crutchley

🛠  Code, Tools & Libraries

Skullet: Skeleton Loading States Measured from Your Components — Hand it sample data and it renders your real component invisibly, measures everything, and draws a matching skeleton to reduce layout shifts when data arrives. The docs have a neat How it Works section explaining the technique.

Lochie Axon

Parcel 3 Alpha: A Rust Rewrite with React Compiler, Tailwind and RSC — Parcel's core is now a Rust binary with no Node dependency, and the team reports cold builds up to 100x faster than v2. React Compiler (opt-in), Tailwind and MDX are built in, with RSC support in beta.

Devon Govett (Parcel)

🤖 Reticle: Let Coding Agents Verify Their Changes Against Your Running App — A dev-only SDK and MCP server so coding agents can drive your running app, inspect network requests, application state, and console activity, and return a pass, fail or 'can't tell' verdict with what needs fixing.

Reticle Labs

react-resizable-panels Gets a VS Code-Style Workspace Component — Brian Vaughn's popular panel library now does dockable tabs you can drag to split or merge panes, and moved tabs keep their state rather than remounting. There's a live demo here.

Brian Vaughn

  • Preact 11.2 – Now has a runtime for React Compiler output via preact/compat, plus scoped custom element registries in shadow roots.

  • XState 6.0 Beta – "No further breaking changes are planned" for public APIs, and @xstate/react 7 is in beta alongside.

  • TanStack Redact 0.3 – The lightweight, synchronous-only React / React DOM replacement adds browser SPA plugins for Webpack and Rspack.

  • React Native 0.89 RC – Faster text layout and native module calls, legacy bridge APIs gone. Stable expected in December.

  • Storybook 11.0 Beta

📰 Classifieds

🤖 Fimo gives your marketers a visual editor and AI agents for SEO and GEO. No more tickets for your React devs. By the Strapi team.

QVAC allows you to run any AI capabilities for free, on your phone or laptop, privately. Try the QVAC SDK now on GitHub.

📢  Elsewhere in the ecosystem

  • James Long has been reviving Prepack, Facebook's abandoned JavaScript partial evaluator. There's a React demo where a pretend site is server rendered three ways, by React, by Prepack's output (which essentially 'compiles' React away), and a hybrid, with the render times to compare.

  • Node.js 27 Alpha has landed, the first version using Node's new release process (where a release will spend six months in 'alpha' before going Current), while Node 26 is now the new LTS line.

  • Chrome 157 rolled out this week with HTML-in-Canvas now stable. It provides a way to draw real DOM elements into 2D, WebGL and WebGPU canvases. The demos are striking.

  • Vercel has released Geist Serif, a new serif font that shares metrics with Geist Sans so the two can mix cleanly. It's not on Google Fonts yet, but the geist npm package includes it.

issues.title: Housekeeping Mage from Another World: Making Your Adventures Feel Like Home!, Vol. 10
issues.summary: By You Fuguruma and Nama. Released in Japan as “Kasei Madoushi no Isekai Seikatsu: Boukenchuu no Kasei Fugyou Uketamawarimasu!” by Ichijinsha Bunko Iris NEO. Released in North America by J-Novel Heart. Translated by Hengtee Lim. Last time I said we were caught up with Japan and…
issues.author: Sean Gaffney
issues.content_html:
By You Fuguruma and Nama. Released in Japan as “Kasei Madoushi no Isekai Seikatsu: Boukenchuu no Kasei Fugyou Uketamawarimasu!” by Ichijinsha Bunko Iris NEO. Released in North America by J-Novel Heart. Translated by Hengtee Lim.

Last time I said we were caught up with Japan and I wasn’t sure when we’d get the next book in the series. Well, it turned out to be about a year and a half. And since we’re caught up with Japan again, it may be another year and a half before Book 11. On the bright side, unlike some other slow-burn romances I could name (coughDahliacough), this one is actually realizing that it’s going to be ending with Book 11 or 12 and doing something about it. The meeting with Alec’s brother, which we’ve been hearing will be happening soon for a while, finally happens. The actual suspense part of the book involves a figure from Shiori’s dark past, which she is finally able to lay to rest. They move into a larger house that ends up being a dorm for adventurers, with them as resident assistants. Oh yes, and they finally go all the way. Busy book!

There are three large stories that make up the bulk of this chunky book. In the first, Alec and Shiori are looking for a new place to live that is larger than his apartment, and discover an old boarding school that has just one slight problem: it may be haunted. Which is bad news, as that’s Alec’s one fatal flaw. In the second, a woman has been stalking Shiori and Alec, and she’s definitely bad news. She seems to know Alec, but he can’t remember who she is. And she’s got a ringer to help her out – Torre, Shiori’s old partner in her first adventuring party, is back and ready to cause another round of PTSD for her. In the last story, Alec and Shiori venture out to meet his brother (the king, in case you’d forgotten) at last, and also Rebecca, as she and Alec are finally able to apologize to each other and admit they’re both very happy with other people. This allows Alec to finally do what we’ve been waiting ten books for – propose.

Let’s talk about that middle story. I could not tell you how little I wanted to see the remaining member of Shiori’s old party… you know, the one who isn’t dead. And Shiori certainly feels the same. Fortunately, thanks to a villain even worse than he is, he gets a first-hand taste of what Shiori went through when he left her to die, and proceeds to repent. We even get a quick one page “and this is what happened to him the rest of his life” from the narrative, as if to reassure readers that we don’t have to worry about him again, either. The most amusing thing about the book for me was the sex. The start of the book shows that, while they haven’t gone all the way, they’re still doing everything short of that. We get to briefly see Nadia and Clemens, and hear about the marks all over her body, clearly from their lovemaking. And towards the enhd of the book, Shiori gets those exact same marks. These folks have very difficult lives, and so they are ready to have great sex whenever they can. And they do.

I always enjoy this series, but I’m enjoying it even more now that it’s resolving its plots and drawing to a close. I will happily wait for whenever we get Book 11.

issues.title: Cop Bastard Is A Conflicting Homage To Shotguns And John Woo
issues.summary: It's a shame about the voice acting
issues.author: Luke Plunkett
issues.content_html:
Cop Bastard is a game that asks you to "blast through waves of yakuza in relentless action inspired by ’90s films", and I don't know if I've ever seen a more accurate elevator pitch.

Despite the Japanese setting, Cop Bastard is trying above anything else to evoke the feeling of shooting your way through a Hong Kong action movie, from the overtly VHS/CRT retro-inspired visuals to the emphasis on corridors and carnage. It's a game that prides itself on how little there is to it; the graphics are lo-fi, the weapon selection is limited, there are no builds, levels or perks and there aren't even any puzzles to solve or tracks to back around on.

The focus, then, is on what is there: a sequence of hallways and staged arenas where you are asked, at speed and without stopping for breath, to make thousands of dudes explode into red mist, using just six guns and a Matrix-style slow-mo attack. I'm normally someone who is a little wary of any game going out of its way to say "we don't need all this modern bullshit!" in terms of design (as this one does on its Steam page), because they're often letting some kind of weird YouTube-thumbnail-guy-inspired idealism get in the way of the natural evolution of game design, but in Cop Bastard's case it's a rare win for the nostalgics.

This game is a blast, and it's interesting coming straight to it from Galactic Racer, another release that was all gas, no brakes. Rather than wear me down or become repetitive, Cop Bastard's singular drive instead got me into the closest thing to a meditative state a retro shooter can probably manage, as I glided across levels shooting, taking cover, shooting, moving on and shooting some more. I want to give a particular shoutout to the Beretta 9mm you're given unlimited ammo for, as it's both deeply appropriate for the setting and also tremendous fun to fire off.

It's a bummer, then, that alongside the action Cop Bastard also felt the need to include an 'Engrish' voiceover that I've seen described as everything from "kinda racist" (every voice was done by Timur Kozlovskikh) to "really annoying".

While there's a B-movie intent to the voiceover whose execution I don't quite get (English dubs usually just have regular English speakers!), I can definitely attest to the fact that it’s annoying, especially once I'd played for 10 minutes and had heard pretty much every gravelly quip and soundbyte the game has to offer, only to then be subjected to the same juvenile insults again and again and again.

I'd have much rather had an actual Japanese voice track, a cheesy retro-inspired recording without the accents or, if those weren't possible, blessed silence (which for some reason the game doesn't allow, since you can't toggle the voices off). Basically, anything but what Cop Bastard went with.

issues.title: The Generosity of Selfishness: C.S. Lewis on How to Be Interesting
issues.summary: Our lives are defined not by what we have but what we give — on what and whom we spend our energy and time, how we share our material possessions and our mental powers, what we do with our gifts. “Anything you do not give freely and abundantly becomes lost to you,” Annie Dillard…
issues.author: Maria Popova
issues.content_html:
Our lives are defined not by what we have but what we give — on what and whom we spend our energy and time, how we share our material possessions and our mental powers, what we do with our gifts. “Anything you do not give freely and abundantly becomes lost to you,” Annie Dillard wrote in contemplating the nature of creativity. “You open your safe and find ashes.”

Paradoxically, the ability to give hinges on the ability to receive: You must be rested in order to labor, taking the repose it takes to recharge your vital energies; you must be interested in order to be interesting, taking the world in with a greedy curiosity that absorbs its beauty and strangeness in order to metabolize it into meaning.

C.S. Lewis (November 29, 1898–November 22, 1963) offers a wonderfully counterintuitive perspective on our notions of generosity and our ideas about what it means to be interesting in his memoir Surprised by Joy (public library).

With an eye to the ideal structure of the creative life, he writes:

It is a life almost entirely selfish. Selfish, not self-centred: for in such a life my mind would be directed towards a thousand things, not one of which is myself. The distinction is not unimportant. One of the happiest men and most pleasing companions I have ever known was intensely selfish. On the other hand I have known people capable of real sacrifice whose lives were nevertheless a misery to themselves and to others, because self-concern and self-pity filled all their thoughts. Either condition will destroy the soul in the end. But till the end, give me the man who takes the best of everything (even at my expense) and then talks of other things, rather than the man who serves me and talks of himself, and whose very kindnesses are a continual reproach, a continual demand for pity, gratitude, and admiration.

This is also why, Lewis intimates, the “thrill” of our greatest creative breakthroughs — those revelations that give us back to ourselves, out of which we give our best work to the world — is rooted in “self-forgetfulness”:

Only when your whole attention and desire are fixed on something else — whether a distant mountain, or the past, or the gods of Asgard — does the “thrill” arise.

[…]

Shut your mouth; open your eyes and ears. Take in what is there.

Couple with John Steinbeck on the art of receiving, then revisit C.S. Lewis on what we long for in our existential longing.

donating = loving

For seventeen years, I have been spending hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars each month composing The Marginalian (which bore the outgrown name Brain Pickings for its first fifteen years). It has remained free and ad-free and alive thanks to patronage from readers. I have no staff, no interns, no assistant — a thoroughly one-woman labor of love that is also my life and my livelihood. If this labor makes your own life more livable in any way, please consider lending a helping hand with a donation. Your support makes all the difference.
