issues.title: Nintendo confident in memory supply in new financial report
issues.summary: As part of the company's quarterly financial report, company president Shuntaro Furukawa affirmed that Nintendo is not suffering due to the ongoing memory crisis, and is confident it has enough supply.
issues.author: Imran Khan
issues.content_html:
Despite rising memory costs worldwide, Nintendo president Shuntaro Furukawa stresses that the company is in a position to secure sufficient quantities for its Switch hardware. Said during a quarterly financial report captured by Reuters, Furukawa says there has been no major change to the memory situation from Nintendo's point of view, indicating that while the memory crisis is not getting better, it is at least not getting worse for the company.

The worldwide rise in memory component prices has driven price increases and launch uncertainty across the industry, largely impelled by those components going to data centers. With Furukawa's confidence that the company has a handle on supply for the time being, the Switch 2 price is seemingly not in immediate danger of another price increase, though Nintendo has warned not to rule it out in the past. The Switch 2 received a price increase in the United States in September, bumping the per-unit pricetag up from $450 to $500, an increase driven by the price of components like RAM going up.

Related:Report: Silver Lake and the Saudi Arabia PIF hold talks with Unity to explore acquisition

This year's price hike may be to blame for a slowdown in Switch 2 hardware sales with a 32.7 percent drop from the previous quarter, though the Switch 2 still remains a higher seller than its Switch predecessor when launch-aligned. A Bloomberg report quotes analyst that place the blame for the console unit slump on a lack of major blockbuster titles for Switch 2, as little on the console beyond Nintendo's own Mario Kart World has crossed the six-million sold barrier—though, due to the way Pokemon Pokopia is split between publishers depending on region, it has likely crossed that threshold in a way Nintendo does not report.

Software sales, meanwhile, did increase significantly overall, with a healthy boost year-over-year for both Switch 2 and Switch 1—the latter benefiting greatly from titles like Tomodachi Life and Rhythm Heaven Groove. It is also worth noting that the quarterly results were reported the day that The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time was released on the Switch 2 as the company's most notable holiday title. So while the title’s debut aligns with this financial report’s release, any actual monetary impact from Ocarina’s launch won’t be visible until the Q3 report in January.

The Switch 2 itself sold 2.67 million units in the last quarter, while the Switch 1 sold 610k, a number certain to decline next year as Nintendo plans to stop selling the 2017 console in Europe in February. Despite the price increase and slower sales this past quarter, Switch 2 forecasts remain unchanged, with the company planning for 16 million units overall in the financial year. At the moment, the Switch 2 retains its current superlative of being the fastest-selling console of all time.

Related:Tripwire Interactive expands publishing business to focus on smaller developers and games

On a milestone note, Mario Kart 8 Deluxe—the Switch version of the 2014 Wii U title—has reached 72 million copies sold, marking it as one of the company's most successful titles in their decades-long history.

issues.title: Early Man Was a Woman: Book 1 (Reclaiming History)
issues.summary: Early Man Was a Woman: Book 1 (Reclaiming History) by Ulli Lust, The Experiment 2026, reeviewed by Whit Taylor. The post Early Man Was a Woman: Book 1 (Reclaiming History) appeared first on The Comics Journal.
issues.author: Whit Taylor
issues.content_html:
If you read any of Ulli Lust’s graphic novels, whether personal memoir or otherwise, you’ll see a consistent theme- a genuine yearning to examine what it means to exist as a woman in, and in spite of, the patriarchy. Her latest graphic novel, Early Man Was a Woman: Book 1 (Reclaiming History) takes a step back and asks us to reconsider what we have been taught: namely, what if the history of early mankind was actually driven by women?

The book starts with a personal anecdote about gendered shame. Little Ulli, who grows up with two sisters in 1970s Austria, is proud to be a girl. And she is baffled at society's rigid expectations for her. She points out that (Western) history has normalized reverence for male bodies (such as the “grotesque” renderings of Jesus that she sees in church) while treating the female body as taboo. Thankfully, Lust discusses these observations in a way that avoids gender essentialism. As she comes of age, pursues the arts, and spends time in museums, she observes that the fossil record does not reflect what she has been taught. “History is written by men!” she exclaims walking past the Ancient Greek statues at the British Museum. Because, why is it that female figurines, what we’ve been colloquially referred to as “fertility goddesses,” have been found throughout the globe for over 30,000 years? 

Lust delves into this question, immersing herself in years of study of anthropological and archeological research, to present an alternate narrative of Human Evolution and Paleolithic cultures. Hominids had to make a “tradeoff” in that babies had to be born premature compared to other animals, so that their large heads (and disproportionately big brains) could pass through the narrow birth canal.  Child-rearing, mothering, and bonding with human children has historically been much more risky and labor intensive compared to other species, as a result. Lust asks, what if empathy, nurture, and other pro-social traits often maligned in modern patriarchal cultures, are in fact natural behaviors that are ultimately responsible for the successful and sustainable growth of culture and society? 

She documents the egalitarian and cooperative cultures of the San/Khoikhoi, southern African hunter-gatherer societies, as an example. As one of the oldest known peoples, the story of the San people is commonly taught in anthropology, part “case study” of traditional hunter gatherer societies and part “cautionary tale” of what happens when indigenous groups are forcibly displaced from their native lands by colonial powers. Lust does not explicitly remark on the legacy of colonialism and its connection with patriarchy, but shows it in her portrayal of modern day San people struggling with the deterioration of their traditional way of life. 

Like Lust's earlier works, the writing and art is lush, layered, and dense, but with a more “academic” slant. There’s a lot of complex text, which takes time to sit with and absorb- it’s a slow read. In fact, much of this book took me back to being an anthropology major in college, and is a great primer for anyone interested in that field of study. Lust successfully harnesses the power of visual storytelling to bring to life a topic that has the potential to be dry. But there’s a clear reverence for the material objects that she draws: fossils, artifacts, and examples of early human art. We also see this care in her depiction of Paleolithic peoples, animals, and their habitats. The warm color palette is muted, soft, and nostalgic with pops of Red Ochre (an important current throughout the book.)

Lust examines early art making and storytelling through Sulawesi cave art and the Swabian Jura ceramic artifacts of now-southern Germany. She reviews the rare documented instances of Paleolithic burials, asking what the remains tell us about those cultures. The last few chapters are dedicated to reexamining early human behaviors historically attributed to men, including shamanism, hunting, and the documentation of time. Lust returns to the topic of female shame at the end. We are back in the present as Ulli talks to a film producer about the secrecy and shame around menstruation in modern society. Suddenly, we are back with the Pavlovian People of the now- Czech Republic, reimagining: what if menstruation was a coming of age step to be celebrated? Publicly? Brazenly! What if we underestimated the value of menstrual blood itself (this may have been in the news recently…) Lust plays with these ideas, not presenting them as fact, but as enlightening possibilities. 

The book ends as the nomadic tribe of the Last Ice Age moves on to their next Mammoth hunt. I look forward to where Book Two will lead us. 

The post Early Man Was a Woman: Book 1 (Reclaiming History) appeared first on The Comics Journal.

issues.title: Helter Skelter, The Substance, and the Horror of Having a Female Body
issues.summary: Christina Lee on Kyoko Okazaki's Helter Skelter and Coralie Fargeat’s The Substance. The post Helter Skelter, The Substance, and the Horror of Having a Female Body appeared first on The Comics Journal.
issues.author: Christina Lee
issues.content_html:
I’d like to start with a trite question: Are we becoming a more superficial society? When I look at art, I feel it’s becoming emptier: aesthetic without concept, optimized for consumption on a 6” screen for a hit of dopamine instead of provoking thought. Alongside the rise of Ozempic and low-rise jeans, my body dysmorphia has reached peaks akin to what it was like when I was 16 years old. It also doesn’t help that I’m getting married this year. I’m approaching my mid-30’s, and it's a time of profound life changes involving career and family. Maybe I’m becoming obsessed with the way I look to avoid making big decisions, or maybe it’s resulting from my increasing fixation with youth; becoming stronger each and every day as I watch the younger generation try on the “vintage” and “retro” clothing and music I grew up with. 

In Louis Theroux’s 2026 documentary, Inside the Manosphere, which I recently watched while riding a Peloton at an airport hotel gym, Justin Waller, a self-proclaimed “alpha male” and business associate of Andrew Tate, argues that, “...women are born with their value. It’s their beauty, their youth. A 20-something woman can hop on luxury cars and yachts for free. Men cannot.” If we accept this inane premise as true, it’s all the more terrifying to have an aging, female body: what are we left with when we are stripped away of our youth and beauty? With dark satire, Kyoko Okazaki’s 1995 manga series Helter Skelter and Coralie Fargeat’s 2024 film The Substance portray the horrors of narcissism, capitalism, and gender expectations associated with having a female body, while providing no easy answers to the aforementioned question.

Kyoko Okazaki is a manga artist, active during the 80s and 90s, until her career was tragically cut short after becoming paralyzed as the result of being stuck by a drunk driver in 1996. She remains in physical rehabilitation to this day. Influenced by New Wave manga, Okazaki’s comics are characterized by a willingness to portray transgressive topics such as incest, sex work, and death through a playfully delicate visual style. Her slice-of-life stories depict young women navigating the rapidly changing cultural and economic landscape of late 20th century Japan. Okazaki’s 1989 series, Pink, follows the life of Yumiko, who works as both an office secretary and call girl to make ends meet in an increasingly expensive Tokyo. Helter Skelter, serialized in josei magazine, Feel Young from 1995-1996, shows the mental unraveling of Liliko, an aging supermodel who regularly undergoes a mysterious medical procedure to keep herself looking young. Her reliance on this surgery contributes to her descent into drug use, crime, and abusive behavior; a huge price she's willing to pay for maintaining a youthful look.

If this premise sounds familiar, it may be because Coralie Fargeat’s 2024 film, The Substance, tells a similar story: after middle-aged actress Elizabeth Sparkle gets fired from her job as an aerobics TV show host, she starts to inject herself with a black market drug to make herself look younger. It transforms her into Sue; a younger, “better” version of herself. However, each dose starts to come at a greater and greater cost to Elizabeth. Both Helter Skelter and The Substance show society’s poisonous gold standard of youth and beauty; illustrating women who equate their net worths to their looks, and the perverse financial, mental, and physical lengths they will go through to maintain their bottom line. Okazaki and Fargeat deploy satire and the visual language of mass media's upholding of misogynistic beauty standards in such a way as to make their audiences feel both uncomfortably introspective and duplicitous. They suggest that the only way for us to escape our self-imprisonment is by exiting society; a defiant path to self-acceptance and peace.

Capitalism pressures the protagonists of Helter Skelter and The Substance to preserve their appearances. We witness Liliko and Elizabeth experience job precarity due to their age: Liliko starts to lose gigs to the newly-arrived teenage model, Kozue, and Elizabeth gets fired from her TV show (by a producer named “Harvey”) after her 50th birthday. Beauty products and surgical procedures are presented as the healing salve for their career bumps: in Helter Skelter, when Liliko gives her assistant, Hada, a Lancôme, mask, we are presented with the model’s thoughts on a stark, flat black panel, “Cosmetics are like crack. The more you use, the more you crave the strong stuff. It just escalates.” While Hada is overjoyed with the gifted product, Liliko spirals into existential panic as she discovers sore-like bruises on her face; a side effect of too long a lapse betweeen secret beauty procedures.

Elizabeth also encounters the futility of beauty products as she gets ready for her date with Fred, a former high school classmate, in one of my favorite scenes from the film. She attempts to leave her apartment four times; each resulting in a false exit and return to her bathroom mirror as she confronts images that shake her confidence: an unavoidable view of a massive billboard of Sue in a barely-there unitard outside her apartment window, an unflattering warped-mirror reflection of herself on her front doorknob. In her final attempt at applying makeup, she violently wipes off her lipstick, leaving a huge red smear on her face à la Joaquin Phoenix in Joker. Elizabeth fiercely scratches away at her face and hair; angry at the mirror's reflection, upset that these products don’t do what she wants them to do: she wants them to transform her back into the young Sue.

It’s perversely comical to see the quantity of psychological and physical damage these women inflict upon themselves through these medical procedures: I think about how in these days, once arriving at a certain age, it is almost expected one will get a neurotoxic protein injected into the face every few months (I certainly have been toying around with this idea in preparation of my wedding), or yield to a surgical skin-stretching and muscle-tightening of the face. Public validation is as addictive, and when we’re hooked, we’ll go through nearly anything to get a fix.

The cost of achieving physical perfection is not only financially extravagant, it is also disgustingly painful. Liliko must go to the clinic repeatedly for maintenance, or else her body will start to peel, shed, and deteriorate. Each time we see her go through the process, she folds into distress; crying and writhing in pain. Liliko’s clinic is investigated by an unnamed male detective, led there by a string of suicides related to the medical practice. The victims are female patients who, unable to continually afford their expensive treatments, kill themselves. In Okazaki’s Tokyo, capitalism is such an unrelenting force that when women are priced out of looking young, they’d rather die than look old.

Both Okazaki and Fargeat lean into satire and are not afraid to make their audiences complicit through staging. Okazaki borrows the visual language of fashion magazines by frequently portraying Liliko in the middle of photoshoots; her front-stage appearance juxtaposed with her back-stage thoughts, at odds with the image-driven economy she participates in. This dissonance between what we see and read illustrates the medium-specificity of comics: we are a simultaneous critic and participant of Liliko’s media environment, in which female bodies are scrutinized and objectified.

Okazaki's use of visual repetition, contrasting colorful, breezy commercial-style illustrations with panels of anonymous high school girls admiring modeling photos, or, most compellingly, sudden portrayals of industry, construction cranes and factories. The cycle of these images' sequencing makes me think about how women sacrifice their bodies for capital: how capitalism produces goods for the female body, and how it uses the female body to sell the same goods.

Similarly, Fargeat references the language of mass media by adopting the male gaze and exaggerating it to the nth degree when we first see Sue perform the updated Elizabeth Sparkle aerobic routine. The outfits are smaller, and the routine has been transformed into a skimpy, gyrating circus: the camera focuses on Sue’s derriere for a good 2 minutes. But nothing here is unusual; in fact, this is all boilerplate. Despite the hyperbole, the visual staging of Liliko’s photo shoots and Sue’s dance routine is familiar. This appropriation throws us off-kilter and makes us examine if we and the world around us hold Justin Waller’s premise to be true.

Liliko and Elizabeth represent women who have internalized society’s impossible beauty standards and who will go to extreme lengths for external validation, and the real horror is in how their stories function as a mirror reflection to society and ourselves. At the end of their journeys, they experience freedom from the suffering of wanting by defiantly exiting from the public eye. In Helter Skelter, Liliko’s intensive medical procedures are revealed to the public, resulting in an ironic twist of reinvigorated interest in her career and image (Negative attention is better than no attention at all). In the middle of this media cycle, she abandons a press conference, leaving only a pile of blood and an eyeball behind. Later, it is revealed that Liliko has left the country and has relocated to Mexico. Without access to the clinic, her body is now deteriorating, yet she revels in her new-found anonymity and bodily autonomy.

Like Liliko, Elizabeth exits society, but goes a step further by dying. In the final moments of “The Substance”, as a result of mis-dosage, Elizabeth transforms into a seeping, gruesome creature. Only after this transformation does she finally accept her appearance, we see her contentedly look in the mirror. In a scene reminiscent of The Elephant Man, she appears on a stage alongside topless showgirl dancers. The audience starts to heckle her, yelling and screaming, until she spontaneously combusts into a gory mess, the explosion producing a never-ending shower of bloody rain onto the spectators. In a 2024 interview with Vogue, Fargeat says, “The audience [in the film], which stands in for all of us as a society, screams and hates her for this, and I wanted to portray how violent that reaction can be. That the only real moment of relief that she has is when she doesn’t have a body anymore, I think, says it all.”

Helter Skelter and The Substance present cautionary tales of internalizing societal gender expectations, and no easy solutions to escape them. Despite the blood, guts, and gore of both stories, I find the subtler scenes the most impactful and reflective of the current times in which we live. In the final pages of Helter Skelter, in the pursuit of perfection and beauty, those anonymous high school girls from mid-90s Japan express their desires: “...Prada’s the only good designer now”, “I want an Air Max!” Okazaki ends this scene with the following statement: “Everyone quickly forgets about everything. Only desire is ever present. It comes along using a new name each time”, which makes me go back to the original question I posed at the beginning of this piece: Are we becoming a more superficial society? And in response to that question in 2026, I wonder if we have just always been this way. 

The post Helter Skelter, The Substance, and the Horror of Having a Female Body appeared first on The Comics Journal.

issues.title: It Gets Harder Before It Gets Better: Netflix’s “North of North” Returns For a Warm Second Season
issues.summary: Still a sitcom, but its charm, warmth, and pathos make it something truly unique.
issues.author: Nandini Balial
issues.content_html:
In its second season, there is a predictable rise-and-fall structure to the writing on Netflix’s “North of North.” Siaja (Anna Lambe), trying to bring vibrancy to her community during winter, concocts several plans—all well-meaning but a little half-baked—and things go sideways.

Were this a lesser, duller show, this would be grounds for complaint. But not in Ice Cove, the fictional Inuit town that is a microcosm for the world at large: specific in its customs, yet universal in its experiences. It is one of the few TV series right now that uses costumes, production design, and color to enhance the storytelling this effectively. Many storylines, even comedic ones, double as commentary on much larger issues, though you never feel hit over the head with A Message. “North of North” is still a sitcom, with slightly more traditional trappings this season, but its charm, warmth, and pathos make it something truly unique.

A lot has changed for Siaja. The good news: Her ex-husband Ting has moved to a different town, so their daughter Bun commutes between both parents. The bad news: Standing up for herself and her ideas at the community center where she works remains a challenge for Siaja. Compounding the problem is her boss Helen (Mary-Lynn Rajskub), who favors the blonde-haired, blue-eyed influencer Alexis (Taylor Hickson)—girlfriend to Siaja’s crush Kuuk (Braeden Clarke)—as a more PR-friendly representative of Ice Cove’s tourism offerings. 

In more bad news, Siaja is at odds with her mother Neevee (Maika Harper), with whom she has no choice but to live, and whom she is pressing to take a DNA test. The results, Siaja hopes, may help them find Neevee’s firstborn daughter, whom she gave up for adoption when she was struggling with alcoholism. Neevee insists she has put this part of her life behind her, but Siaja isn’t so sure.

Though “North of North” is clearly meant to follow Siaja’s journey, Neevee sometimes emerges as the show’s most interesting character. Season one explored her guilt and shame over her past struggles with addiction, and her shock at the arrival of her ex, Alistair (Jay Ryan), who also happens to be Siaja’s father. A complex resentment has been simmering inside Neevee: after all this time, time that she spent raising Siaja alone, Alistair now enjoys a relationship with his daughter and granddaughter, has set up a home in Ice Cove, and is even dating an attractive, age-appropriate, self-possessed romance writer. It’s enough to upset any woman. 

Another subplot, which starts off funny but has more to it than meets the eye, involves the offerings in Neevee’s general store. The shop is an extension of her personality: tough, rugged, the bare essentials and little besides. Why, asks a visitor, doesn’t she sell needle and thread? Why not sell yarn, or beads, or bias tape? But Neevee hasn’t gotten this far in life by being vulnerable. She rejects needs she sees as weaknesses, in others and in herself. This subplot takes both a comedic and a somber turn—elder Elisapee (Nutaaq Simmonds, a bona fide scene stealer) uses devious leverage to secure Ice Cove’s sewing circle’s support for Neevee’s store—and pauses to acknowledge losses the community has faced at the hands of colonialism. All this in a 24-minute sitcom teleplay structure: it’s good stuff.

Zorga Qaunaq and Bailey Poching make very welcome returns to play Millie and Colin, respectively, Siaja’s best friends, full of crackling one-liners and always up for a hijink or two. It’s surprising how quickly Jay Ryan can shift from a smoldering scientist getting cozy with a new girlfriend to a man on the verge of tears, forever soaking up every moment with Siaja and Bun to make up for the years of fatherhood Alistair will never know. Braeden Clarke does lovely, quiet work too, as the long-wandering Kuuk, who may have finally found a sense of belonging. 

And where would this season be without costume designer Alexander Reda? Few TV shows sport more eye-catching or enlightening costumes. Certainly the furs, earrings, parkas, and boots come in luminous colors, shapes, sizes, and prints, but the absence of color and jewelry speaks to each character’s emotional downturns. Conversely, characters not usually seen wearing jewelry come alive in gorgeous accessories. Every piece, it is clear, has been carefully selected to accompany each character’s personality, quirks, and color palette, and each ensemble complements the next. It’s a feast for the eyes, truly unlike anything else on TV this year.

Anna Lambe, meanwhile, finds new layers in her performance. Siaja bungles various plans to bring her community together during winter, as is customary for the bright-eyed, bushy-tailed optimist in a sitcom. But her arc this season, and the arc of “North of North” overall during season two, is about the discomfort of dwelling in the in-between. Yes, she has made progress, but she still feels stuck. Lambe walks a fine line, beaming from ear to ear in Siaja’s trademark joyous grin and determined to believe in the best possible outcome, but she runs up against harsh realities, including mistakes she’s made chasing an ill-defined future. 

The series’ writing remains its greatest strength. Just as things get very dark, someone whips out an uproarious one-liner. Elderly characters provide deadpan beats of physical comedy. Through the long, dark winter, “North of North” wants to say, all we can do is be there for each other. It won’t be pretty, but we have to keep trying. “Do the thing that feels true to you,” says a community member to Siaja, “even if no one claps right away. And whatever you’re searching for, don’t give up.” Words to live by, from a show that’s nigh unmissable.

All episodes screened for review. Currently streaming on Netflix.

issues.title: Season 2 Proves That “Black Doves” Might Be Netflix’s Best Show
issues.summary: A thrilling balance of humor and espionage, and another show that blends the personal with the political in continuously captivating ways.
issues.author: Brian Tallerico
issues.content_html:
Apple TV’s “Slow Horses” has received consistent acclaim and annual nominations from the Television Academy, most of them deserved. Netflix has its own six-episode British spy series that deserves to be alongside the Gary Oldman hit on the medal platform: Joe Barton’s “Black Doves,” a thrilling balance of humor and espionage, and another show that blends the personal with the political in continuously captivating ways.

The second season drops today, and it’s just as good as the first, a study in the inherent trauma of spyhood, a profession that demands that relationships be as tenuous as the pull of a trigger. With some of the most breakneck plotting of any show on any network, “Black Doves” is a rare Netflix drama that justifies the binge model, pushing through twists and turns over six chapters that might even force you to put your phone down while you watch.

A sort of Brit riff on “The Americans,” “Black Doves” is about a woman named Helen Webb (Keira Knightley), the wife of the U.K. Secretary of State of Defence who also happens to be a Black Dove, a mercenary spy organization that gets the shit done that Slough House can only imagine. Having someone undercover in the Cabinet is important enough, but season two promises even more access as Helen’s husband Wallace (Andrew Buchan) is about to become Prime Minister. Helen’s handler Reed (Sarah Lancashire) comes to her with new information … and then promptly disappears. Uh oh.

Meanwhile, Helen’s BFF Sam Young (Ben Whishaw) is hired for a job that goes very wrong, pinning him under the thumb of a mysterious figure played by Sam Riley, who tasks him with a series of assassinations for his and Helen’s freedom. A meeting between Webb and someone on the Russian side who could broker long-delayed peace looms so large on the horizon that it brings in an American representative played by Neve Campbell (kinda wasted but almost impressively just there for the ride) while the great Babou Ceesay of “Alien: Earth” slinks into the proceedings as Helen’s new handler with the Black Doves, and someone who may not be as understanding as Reed.

A brief early plot summary of season two of “Black Doves” barely scratches the surface of what it’s about, in part because some of the joy of the brilliant plotting is in twists and turns that won’t be spoiled, but also because this show moves at a speed that’s unusual in the streaming era. Many modern espionage shows linger in their Le Carré inspirations—“The Agency” being a good example—slow-burning through the day-to-day tension of being undercover. Not “Black Doves.” It constantly shifts and moves, closer to a Bond action movie in its telling of a story that began decades ago in one character’s early spy career. 

The writers here know how to use their relatively large cast, amplifying the roles of Sam’s allies Williams (Ella Lily Hyland) and Eleanor (Gabrielle Creevy), and introducing a new quirky assassin named Laila, played perfectly by Ambika Mod. It’s a big extended cast that never gets away from Barton and his team, giving each of the players essential parts to play in the unfolding chaos, and his team expertly ties its characters together not just narratively but thematically, giving all of them issues related to the classic spy fiction belief that caring is a weakness.

It also smartly doesn’t rely purely on chaos, taking opportunities to ground its characters, often through their action. It helps to have a performer as consistently fantastic as Whishaw, who imbues Sam with growing melancholy this season, playing him like a man who’s accepted he’s tied to the train tracks of a profession that doesn’t let people walk away before they get run over by the train.

Sam’s moral code remains in place, but he’s starting to ask what good it’s done. He will protect Helen at all costs, but that commitment has led to the kind of personal tragedy and immoral decisions that make him the kind of melancholy alcoholic that only Whishaw could play. We’ve seen so many troubled spies in literature and film, but Whishaw makes Sam into one of the most memorable, a figure who is somehow equally haunted and driven.

Whishaw may be the award-worthy standout of “Black Doves,” but the cast has no weak link. Mod makes for a marvelous addition this year as the kind of live wire who will throw a dart at a jerk at the pub; Ceesay oozes as the kind of suit that probably can’t be trusted even while he insists he can; Hyland and Creevy get to have some real fun as a couple of assassins who may find love undercover. That word is essential to the success of “Black Doves”: so much of this show is “fun,” and it always remembers to be as witty in its dialogue as its plotting.

The end run of the plotting in season two of “Black Doves” requires a bit more suspension of disbelief than some of the best spy fiction, especially in a fifth episode that gets so surprisingly heavy on the gunfire that it offers flashes of Michael Bay. But it’s a minor complaint for a show that should be more major in the public sphere. When it ended with a series of scenes promising a third season that will go in a different direction, it’s rarely more exciting to see where a show goes next.

Whole season screened for review. Now on Netflix.

issues.title: Umberto Eco’s Antilibrary: Why Unread Books Are More Valuable to Our Lives than Read Ones
issues.summary: How to become an "antischolar" in a culture that treats knowledge as "an ornament that allows us to rise in the pecking order."
issues.author: Maria Popova
issues.content_html:
How to become an “antischolar” in a culture that treats knowledge as “an ornament that allows us to rise in the pecking order.”

“It is our knowledge — the things we are sure of — that makes the world go wrong and keeps us from seeing and learning,” Lincoln Steffens wrote in his beautiful 1925 essay. Piercingly true as this may be, we’ve known at least since Plato’s famous Allegory of the Cave that “most people are not just comfortable in their ignorance, but hostile to anyone who points it out.”. Although science is driven by “thoroughly conscious ignorance” and the spiritual path paved with admonitions against the illusion of thorough understanding, we cling to our knowledge — our incomplete, imperfect, infinitesimal-in-absolute-terms knowledge — like we cling to life itself.

And yet the contour of what we know is a mere silhouette cast by the infinite light of the unknown against the screen of the knowable. The great E.F. Schumacher captured this strange dynamic in the concept of adaequatio — the notion that “the understanding of the knower must be adequate to the thing to be known.” But how do we face our inadequacy with grace and negotiate wisely this eternal tension between the known, the unknown, the knowable, and the unknowable?

That’s what Lebanese-American scholar, statistician, and essayist Nassim Nicholas Taleb explores in a section of his modern classic The Black Swan: The Impact of the Highly Improbable (public library) — an illuminating inquiry into the unknowable and unpredictable outlier-events that precipitate profound change, and our tendency to manufacture facile post-factum explanations for them based on our limited knowledge.

Taleb uses legendary Italian writer Umberto Eco’s uncommon relationship with books and reading as a parable of the most fruitful relationship with knowledge:

The writer Umberto Eco belongs to that small class of scholars who are encyclopedic, insightful, and nondull. He is the owner of a large personal library (containing thirty thousand books), and separates visitors into two categories: those who react with “Wow! Signore professore dottore Eco, what a library you have! How many of these books have you read?” and the others — a very small minority — who get the point that a private library is not an ego-boosting appendage but a research tool. Read books are far less valuable than unread ones. The library should contain as much of what you do not know as your financial means, mortgage rates, and the currently tight real-estate market allows you to put there. You will accumulate more knowledge and more books as you grow older, and the growing number of unread books on the shelves will look at you menacingly. Indeed, the more you know, the larger the rows of unread books. Let us call this collection of unread books an antilibrary.

Eco himself has since touched on humanity’s curious relationship with the known and the unknown in his encyclopedia of imaginary lands, the very existence of which is another symptom of our compulsive tendency to fill in the gaps of our understanding with concrete objects of “knowledge,” even if we have to invent them by the force of our imagination. Taleb adds:

We tend to treat our knowledge as personal property to be protected and defended. It is an ornament that allows us to rise in the pecking order. So this tendency to offend Eco’s library sensibility by focusing on the known is a human bias that extends to our mental operations. People don’t walk around with anti-résumés telling you what they have not studied or experienced (it’s the job of their competitors to do that), but it would be nice if they did. Just as we need to stand library logic on its head, we will work on standing knowledge itself on its head.

Noting that his Black Swan theory centers on “our misunderstanding of the likelihood of surprises” because we underestimate the value of what we don’t know and take what we do know “a little too seriously,” Taleb envisions the perfect dancer in the tango with knowledge:

Let us call this an antischolar — someone who focuses on the unread books, and makes an attempt not to treat his knowledge as a treasure, or even a possession, or even a self-esteem enhancement device — a skeptical empiricist.

Complement The Black Swan, which is fascinating it its totality, with astrophysicist Marcelo Gleiser on how to live with mystery in a culture obsessed with certitude, philosopher Hannah Arendt on how unanswerable questions give shape to the human experience, and novelist Marilynne Robinson on the beauty of the unknown.

HT Bobulate
