issues.title: Like aliens
issues.summary: Like living metaphors, these self-contained miniature worlds show us the wondrous and fragile beauty of our biosphere - by Aeon Video Watch on Aeon
issues.author: Aeon Video
issues.content_html:
For his ‘Biosphere Project’, the Argentinian artist and engineer Joaquín Fargas isolates ‘natural ecosystems in completely sealed containers where the only interaction with the environment is through heat and light’. These small, self-contained worlds are meant to comment on the fragility and deep interconnectedness of life on our own planet. The project reflects Fargas’s enduring commitment to creating engaging, accessible art that speaks to the urgency of the climate crisis. In his portrait of the ‘Biosphere Project’, the Argentinian filmmaker Nico Muñoz captures Fargas’s process with his own artistry, melding inventive camera angles and patient observation with archival footage from space missions and the dreamy piano of Claude Debussy’s ‘Clair de Lune’.

Via Labocine

Director: Nico Muñoz

Website: El Mano Films

issues.title: Following Kobayashi Makoto’s footsteps through manga history
issues.summary: Translated by Jon Holt and Teppei Fukuda “Manga-shi ni okeru Kobayashi Makoto no ashiato o tadoru” — from Kawade Mook: Kobayashi Makoto (Kawade Shobo, 2026) pp. 170-175. If there is one thing America needs to copy from Japan, it’s the mook. “Magazine Books” are special-issue…
issues.author: Natsume Fusanosuke
issues.content_html:
Translated by Jon Holt and Teppei Fukuda

“Manga-shi ni okeru Kobayashi Makoto no ashiato o tadoru” — from Kawade Mook: Kobayashi Makoto (Kawade Shobo, 2026) pp. 170-175.

If there is one thing America needs to copy from Japan, it’s the mook. “Magazine Books” are special-issue magazine printed on great quality paper, usually with lots of color photos and illustrations. The publisher Kawade Shobō usually issues a mook showcasing the career of prominent cultural figures, like writers or manga artists, on a semi-monthly basis. They come with interviews, essays on the person’s works, a timeline of their career, and lots of interesting side pieces about the person. Another publisher, Shogakukan, also issues their own mook series and in 2019 they released a special Takahashi Rumiko mook, from which we translated an essay about her written by Natsume Fusanosuke and published on TCJ in 2021. In June, Kawade Shobō published a mook about Kobayashi Makoto (born 1958), the creator of the popular manga What’s Michael? Kobayashi is a true master of both gag manga and martial-arts manga. Natsume Fusanosuke contributed a five-page essay about his career, his works, and their relationship to developments in manga from the 1970s to the present. We present our translation of that essay for TCJ.com readers.

Working through the translation, it became apparent that this essay pairs well with another Natsume essay, also published on TCJ.com. As in his article on the “gallant” women in Yoshinaga Fumi's manga, Natsume here breaks down how the artist can use panel layouts to convey humor. Like Yoshinaga, Kobayashi can be very nuanced in his panel placements or repetition to entertain the reader, often triggering explosive laughter instead of the more dry or sober kind of jokes that Yoshinaga creates. Although Natsume does not use the term here, the repetitive panels he likes and sees in Kobayashi’s style (see Figure 2), is also what Natsume describes elsewhere as “events” (jiken), where manga can often become very “interesting” as Japanese artists will risk using the same or similar panel twice or three times to quietly or subtly show the impact of the moment. Even though the iterations do not immediately suggest some large dramatic punch (i.e., they look the same so might seem boring), in reality the artist conversely creates an “event” through the most unlikely panel layouts. This is one of the fruits of manga — one of Natsume’s larger points from his book Why Is Manga So Interesting? (1997).1

Therefore, not only does this essay present a history of a legendary figure in manga, but it also contains elements of Natsume’s thought ranging from his early days as a manga scholar (panels, pacing, and “events”) as well as material that interests him greatly now (the publishing industry, artist-editor relationships). He also describes here what exactly makes Kobayashi Makoto’s manga still so interesting. Like Natsume, we regret he could not discuss more than he does here the artist’s most recent manga, JJM: Girls’ Judo Club Story (co-written by Emoto Yuko; serialized originally in Evening from 2016 to 2023; now running since 2023 in Comic Days), which is a very funny manga that begs to be translated for audiences outside of Japan.

As always, we thank Natsume-sensei for letting us publish his work in English here. — Jon Holt and Teppei Fukuda

***

Kobayashi Makoto’s Debut

Kobayashi Makoto was born in 1958. In 1978 he made his debut with his short story "The Fighting Brothers Trio" (“Kakuto san-kyōdai”) in the pages of the Weekly Shōnen Magazine. He soon won Magazine’s newcomer award and in the same year began serializing 1-2 and 3 Shirō (1-2 no Sanshirō, published in trade paperback in 1983).2 By 1981, he took home Kōdansha’s Manga Award for the Shōnen category. He got on a roll with his chaotic fighting (kakutō) gag style. At that time, Kobayashi was 20 years old. I had already become a fan of his and would laugh out loud at the way he drew Japanese high school girls on the way to school in a forced gag-comic way, saying things like, “Good morning, Inoki-ko!” and “Morning, Baba-ko!” (Figure 1); I was utterly charmed by the way he would make his characters do strange poses and loved his dirty characters like Iwashimizu (in Go, Go, Iwashimizu! [Sore ike Iwashimizu], a spin-off series he did from 1980-81 in Monthly Shōnen Magazine) (Figure 1). Iwashimizu was a total jerk but someone you could not really hate and he was based on a kind of an inverse version of [the male lead in] Love and Sincerity (Or: Ai and Makoto [a very popular romance manga by Kajiwara Ikki and Nagayasu Takumi (1973-1975)]. Iwashimizu had a strong character, a combination of Mizuki Shigeru’s Rat Man (Nezumi-Otoko) and Azuma Hideo’s Bukimi-kun with his face never showing emotion.

But when it comes to really strong people in Kobayashi’s works, he always has his heroines with a certain peculiarity. Shino was a cool leader-type character from "Fighting Trio Brothers," but when she reappears in Sanshirō as the cool leader — she transformed into a purely funny character who cries dramatically with an infinity- shaped mouth. Like Sanshirō, she undergoes physical changes, physically “breaking character,” and this surely is one reason why she makes this work so popular. In manga with the sports-and-school setting (supōtsu-gakuen-mono) of that era, Shino was a really distinctive female character, whom I loved. She was sexy, too.

In that same year of 1978, we see Takahashi Rumiko begin to serialize Urusei Yatsura. That work and then Touch (Tacchi) [by Mitsuru Adachi] started the love-comedy (rabu-kome) boom in shōnen [manga] magazines. By bringing into shōnen magazines the style elements from shōjo, they opened the way for a new path to story humor (sutorii-gyagu, i.e., long-running stories with humorous bent). In his manga autobiography A 1978 Manga Bookworm (1978 no manga-mushi [published by Shōgakukan in 2023]), Hosono Fujihiko has a scene that shows how his college student protagonist was shocked by the appearance of a girl who had an “anime-like look” of Lum [from Urusei Yatsura]. This was the period that marked the beginning of changes in the portrayal of female characters in boys’ manga magazines.

At the start of 1-2 Sanshirō, Shino is running late for school and collides into Sanshirō at a street intersection. To make matters worse, her skirt gets caught and rips apart, which shows just how clumsy she is. You see it, right? This part of the story immediately shows how it is a parody of love comedies. With this in mind, as one keeps reading, it becomes clear that this manga about earth-shattering fighting actually was inspired by a love comedy lurking in the background. So, if one reads 1-2 Sanshirō as a love comedy, the whole manga gets turned upside down and thrown into the different, crazy world of love comedy by the power and charm of Shino. Moreover, in the final episode, there is a coming together of the feelings the two main characters have for each other. They try to go into a love hotel in order to consummate their feelings with a kiss, but they get caught by Iwashimizu, who photographs them and they end up appearing in the newspaper. What kind of love-comedy world is this when our hero and heroine get caught going to a love hotel? This manga is an anti-love-comedy. (It is so good at reversing the conventions of love comedies.)

Before their date begins, Shino is waiting for Sanshirō to arrive. Kobayashi takes three panels to depict Shino turning to see Sanshirō arrive wearing a full three-piece suit and even a hat. It is characteristic of Kobayashi Makoto to break down the panels to get "beats" (ma) (Figure 2). What he does is very different from the kind of skillful use of intervals that Adachi Mitsuru is good at. Kobayashi has a technique that triggers laughter in his reader.

Although it looks like excessive play with the panels, here we can also see how it was reflective of the period in manga where serialized manga were allowed an increase in the number of pages. This kind of appealing power that 1-2 Sanshirō had only gets even more polished when Kobayashi returned to the sequel, 1-2 Sanshirō 2 (published in Young Magazine, 1994-1998), where Sanshirō and Shino become a married couple. It was a really fun turn of events for fans, and here is a good point that shows Kobayashi had transcended the love-comedy genre: having your protagonist get married is just something I cannot recall seeing, except in Dragonball (Weekly Shōnen Jump, 1984-1995).

From shōnen to seinen

When Kobayashi graduated from shōnen magazines and moved to seinen (young male) magazines like Morning and Evening with works like Fighting Spirit Production (Tōkon Purodakushon [serialized from 1982-83 in Morning]) and How to Draw Manga (Manga no egakikata [1983-1984, Evening]), he underwent a phase of trial-and-error in his style and depicted the underbelly of the manga world. How to Draw Manga also features a precursor of his famous character cat, Michael. The group of readers who followed Kobayashi since 1-2 Sanshirō now had grown up into adults. During this period, Kobayashi’s drawing skill improved to an unbelievable extent; plus, he became a master of “funny faces” (kaogei), precisely capturing facial expression with things like distortions in mouth shapes.  At the graphic level, he improved even more in the reality of the movement of his characters’ bodies when he drew them in melee scenes. But, on the other hand, he could also expertly show those obligatory reaction shots that immediately follow a fight and then betray them with a “What the hell?” reaction that undercut the drama. It was just in this short period that, once he was reborn in seinen manga, he marvelously came to occupy his own place there.

In the 1970s, manga underwent a huge and sudden expansion of its market, and postwar manga, which had become a true industry, would change so that by the 1980s, it was seinen manga magazines that grew into its own huge market, where it would nearly monopolize more than half of all the marketplace. Manga readership kept on shifting to people in their thirties. It makes sense that Kobayashi’s manga fan base overlapped with that readership.

It was in this period of the 1980s that Kobayashi suddenly started drawing cat manga. I’m talking about What’s Michael? (Howattsu Maikeru?, [serialized in Evening from 1984-89]).3 This huge hit greatly expanded his fan base. What Kobayashi did was draw the cat not as some anthropomorphized feline, but instead with a real physicality and life so that he maintained a persuasive quality, making his readers think, “Yup, cats do stuff like that.” Previously, Kobayashi mainly had had a legion of male fans through his use of the fighting subgenre, but thanks to Michael becoming such a bit hit, Kobayashi was probably able to add female readers to his base.

Despite the marketplace shrinking, Kobayashi finds success

During the latter part of the 1980s, Japan suddenly entered its bubble economy and the manga industry also showed its biggest expansion and increased its influence on the society. However, after some time passed, the bubble burst and the manga market suddenly shrunk. The years 1995 and 1996 were the peak years in the industry with paper-printed manga, but then there was a sudden drop in the circulation of Shōnen Jump. Thereafter, the sales and units of magazines continued to fall, showing nothing but a downward trend. This was also the period in which we see the growth of the internet. With the core focus having been the magazine format, Japanese comics came to a turning point.

Sometime before this, Kobayashi published his series Judo Club Story (Jūdō-bu monogatari [serialized in Young Magazine from 1985-91]). He shed his skin, moving away from using powerful brute character types, like Sanshirō. Instead, he drew “a manga that makes you read” the play-by-play depictions of judo martial arts. This was a work that set itself apart from other Kobayashi works in that it is a coming-of-age story, much calmer and definitely less crazy (!) than Kobayashi’s other works, as he carefully developed a story about the growth of his character. In an interview, Kobayashi said, “Judo Club is 100% all my planning … while I was drawing What’s Michael? I found myself wanting to do something entirely different. I think I wanted to tell the world, ‘Dammit, I’m not some artist who does trendy manga!’”4 In other words, Michael stuck him with a reputation as an artist of cute manga, so he reacted to that by putting out Judo Club. I suppose that Kobayashi is the kind of creator who is always trying to break away from what is fashionable and normal in manga.

One of the ways he was able to avoid getting caught in the downward trend in manga sales during the 1990s was to draw 1-2 Sanshirō 2 [i.e., the sequel]. Even when I read it these days, it strikes me as an extremely interesting manga with a high level of density. It makes me wonder where Kobayashi gets all of that energy. On the other hand, it also proves that when manga publishing was going through such a dangerous period, Kobayashi sailed through it with this work,  his unbreakable fighting gag manga. With this, he was really able to advance his craft, particularly in the sense of tension from his linework (Figure 3).

After that, he produced a really strange work called Chichon-manchi (serialized in Young Magazine Uppers from 1998 to 2002).5 Kobayashi had heard an ero-manga artist say “I never get bored drawing them. I can’t help feeling happy doing this kind of work,” so he wanted to try to draw an ero-manga himself. Even though his linework here serves the subject of sex, his drawing never feels indecent. Even when he makes the art distorted, he shows the female protagonist experience pleasure with her saying things like, “Oooooh, yessssss!” Kobayashi makes the work feel less like a porno manga — it reads more like a fantasy gag manga. I would rank this work highly for his achievement, but I just don’t get why others don’t feel the same way I do. It is a pretty darn amazing manga.

An unconventional artist keeps thriving

When I’ve met Kobayashi Makoto, he seemed to me a shy person who does not talk that much, but looking now at all the transformations that have happened throughout his oeuvre, I see that he is an artist who can render delicate expressions with great care while simultaneously doing works that are totally off the wall in the Japanese manga scene. And yet, at the same time, he has been able to maintain a clean and clear drawing style that allows him to put care into depicting nuanced expressions for his characters. The kind of raw, unfiltered expressions and reactions his characters give is completely off the charts. Even so, he does not do raw and rough work. Instead, he usually restrains his emotions in his manga. And then, just when you gets to a place where there should be this burst of emotion, he immediately undercuts the drama with a joke. Even when he works on a quintessentially serious story, he maintains a certain level of emotional power.

Proof of that is in his Hasegawa Shin series (serialized in Evening from 2009 to 2014), but even more surprising and powerful than that work is his prior series, The Young Days of Shōnen Magazine 1978-1983 (Seishun Shōnen Magajin 1978-1983 [published in Weekly Shōnen Magazine in 2008]). He serialized it to coincide with the 50th anniversary of the magazine's founding, but it also reads like Kobayashi’s autobiography. The series begins with a line: “In May of 1978, there was a young man dreaming of becoming a manga artist, having come from Niigata prefecture, but he was on the brink of dying.” It features a number of important people, such as the 29-year-old editor who discovers Kobayashi, or Ono Shinji, who got an honorable mention prize because of Kobayashi. There is also the newcomer Ōwada Natsuki, who starts at the same time as Kobayashi. We also see Yanagisawa Kimio, who was a popular artist already at this time; plus, legends like Tezuka Osamu, Kajiwara Ikki, and Chiba Tetsuya. Kobayashi becomes drinking buddies with Ono and Ōwada. One might think this is a quintessential comic of age (i.e., seishun, youth) manga — they all get dogged by work assignments and never get to sleep. Kobayashi depicts how they were having their life energy drained by drawing manga. On a veranda, the protagonist finds a part of himself wanting to jump off, but he cannot let go of the handrail.

Ōwada gets in the bathtub and feels like he could let himself sink and drown, so he holds onto the edges of the bath with both hands. Ono’s liver goes bad and he develops splotches all over his face. Eventually his fingers stopped working, so he taped them together with tape so he could keep drawing (Figure 4). He ends up being unable to walk without the use of a cane.

It is the story of a cruel place to work, where an artist will grind down his body to work. Ōwada commits suicide. Ono ends up being hospitalized and he dies there. At this point in time, so many autobiographical works about manga artist and manga editors have been published, but they are all of the type that only celebrate the successes. However, Kobayashi here depicts the lives and deaths of his two good friends and he shows the cruel truths about the industry. He reminds us that in a world that produces a select number of big winners and successful people, tragic stories like this also exist. Lurking in the shadows of the success of manga, there are many people who suffer much frustration and even die early deaths. And to do this, Kobayashi returned to Shōnen Magazine. For those who know these truths about the industry, he makes us keenly feel for these artists.

Even though I’ve just barely scratched the surface of discussing his work, you can sense the happy-go-lucky brightness Kobayashi brings to his manga. For his readers, there is a sense of elation and relief one gets from them. But he is also the rare artist who lets his readers know that lurking behind that is distress and frustration, invisible to the bystander.

Golly, I have now run out of space to touch on [his most recent work] The Story of JJM Girls’ Judo Club (JJM jōshi jūdō-bu monogatari). Mr. Kobayashi, forgive me!

The post Following Kobayashi Makoto’s footsteps through manga history appeared first on The Comics Journal.

issues.title: AI on the Ballot
issues.summary: Data Centers were on the ballot, and they lost in a major way; what does it mean if American opposition to building is permanent?
issues.author: Ben Thompson
issues.content_html:
Listen to this post:

Log in to listen

From Bloomberg this morning at 2 a.m. Central:

Democrats won control of both chambers of the US Congress in a midterm election landslide that amounted to a rejection of President Donald Trump following widespread voter discontent with the economy and the war in Iran. Across the country, Democrats scored victories in GOP strongholds, flipping at least seven Senate seats and winning House races in districts Republicans easily carried in 2024. Several news organizations projected that Democrats would win the House, while Decision Desk HQ projected they took the Senate.

I have no doubt that Iran and the economy played significant roles in this election; what stood out to me, however, was very much Stratechery fodder. Specifically, I watch a lot of sports, and particularly this fall, watched a lot of baseball. My Milwaukee Brewers — excuse me, my World Champion Milwaukee Brewers — demanded my full attention, which also meant I saw a lot of campaign ads, and by far the most common topic, at least here in Wisconsin, was data centers. Moreover, it was never entirely clear which way it cut politically: both parties were anti-data center, accusing their opponent of being the opposite.

Meanwhile in Texas, from Yahoo Finance:

A strong showing by Democrats in Texas swept Gina Hinojosa into office as the state’s first Democratic governor since 1990 in a contest closely watched by Big Tech companies. The state is considered a bellwether for government restrictions on AI data centers…Hinojosa, Texas’ first Latina governor, has pledged to impose a moratorium on data center construction in Texas, which accounts for more than 25% of planned US capacity by 2030.

Republican incumbent Greg Abbott, I would note, already declared a moratorium on new data-center permits in September; that’s how much of a hot-button issue this is, including in the state that is the biggest opportunity and beneficiary of the data center buildout. So yeah, this is a Stratechery topic of concern.

The Data Center Veto

Earlier this year, while writing about data center opposition, I said:

There really wasn’t widespread opposition to data centers when they were being built for the Internet generally; indeed, local governments would compete for them, eager for the economic benefits that came during their construction and the long-term tax benefits once they were operational. In other words, it seems pretty clear that the current wave of opposition can’t be divorced from AI — you know, the technology that in the best case scenario is going to take everyone’s jobs, and in the worst case scenario end the human race.

I do not, I don’t think, need to explain to you why this is not a very compelling message, and, in the very long run, I do think that humans will have economic value. At the same time, it’s hard to explain the huge amount of investment that is going into AI, not just at the model level but also in terms of data centers, without admitting that a big part of the thesis is that AI can not just increase the top line for companies, but also increase the bottom line — i.e. replace the jobs of some number of humans. Again, I’m generally an optimist here, but this already happened with the first wave of IT.

That leads to an interesting contrast to globalization: when companies were closing down American factories and laying off workers and moving operations to China, none of the affected towns or workers had a say. They just suddenly no longer had a job, and a huge number of cities across the Rust Belt no longer had a reason to exist. People simply had to move, or worse, retreat to things like alcohol or drugs. AI, however, is the opposite: building data centers requires permission, which is to say that people actually have a say. Again, I am not at all saying that these people are well informed about data centers, or about the economic impact on their communities, much less the economic impact of AI generally; what I am noting is that people who didn’t have a say in globalization are suddenly finding they do have a say about AI, and it’s not a surprise they are expressing their disapproval by blocking data centers.

That message was loud and clear last spring; now it is deafening, and it’s tempting to say that tech, particularly the frontier labs, have no one to blame but themselves. In fact, however, some of the biggest culprits may, in the long run, be some of the biggest beneficiaries of the anti-data center wave.

My thesis — driven not just by national results and the Texas governorship, but also the fact that, as this thread documents, nearly every relevant local ballot measure opposing data centers won or is winning (the only exception so far was in North Dakota) — is that the constraint on AI dispersion has shifted once again. First we were short on compute, but that ramped; now we are short on memory, but that will ramp; we were coming close to being short on power, but that will be rectified. The final constraint is political, and that may be the most imposing constraint of all. Not only is it harder to solve, but it actually interferes with solving the other constraints. Many of the theories about AI assume that it becomes a commodity; I think it’s just as likely we are looking at scarcity for much longer than we expected, which will have ripple effects on everything.

Ten Takes

To that end, here — with the caveat that nothing leads to hot takes you regret like an election — are ten perspectives on what a permanently impaired ability to build might mean. To be clear, I’m not declaring permanency — look at how our elections swing back and forth — but it’s worth considering what the implications might be if Americans don’t change their minds about data centers.

1. The AI Trade Got It Right

The most obvious reason why the stock market has been rocky over the last few weeks is the tightening of credit markets, which I wrote about this summer. We are, needless to say, full on into the equity funding era (and while I’m here, I haven’t written about Anthropic’s updated S-1, but it strongly affirms my initial analysis). At the same time, it seems clear that this outcome is very bad for the AI trade in the short term, but much of the pain may have already been endured.

2. Neoclouds on the Edge

The Neoclouds have been at the forefront of credit concerns, and from a certain perspective, being unable to build data centers has a silver lining in that they couldn’t get the money to pay for them anyways. Moreover, Neoclouds with facilities that are already permitted now have an asset that is going to be scarcer than expected. At the same time, it’s Neoclouds that need new sites and new permits, even as they are likely to have much less political sway than the hyperscalers — who already have more sites they can repurpose or rebuild. It was already getting harder to get capital, relative to the hyperscalers; now you have to layer on that it’s going to be harder to get permission, too.

3. Hyperscalers Are Winners

The downside for the neoclouds is upside for the hyperscalers, who are more likely to grow their share of AI compute than they were before. Moreover, investors may be pleased if the hyperscalers’ ambitions are somewhat curtailed; political opposition is an excuse to moderate spending, knowing that everyone else is in the same boat.

4. Nvidia’s Mixed Bag

Nvidia will almost certainly be a short-term loser. Fewer data centers mean fewer Nvidia chips generally, and a weakened Neocloud set is particularly harmful not only because Neoclouds almost exclusively use Nvidia full-rack systems, but also because Nvidia is back-stopping a huge number of them. It’s the hyperscalers, meanwhile, who are Nvidia’s biggest long-term threat, given their scale and ability to invest in their own chips.

At the same time, a constrained world makes Nvidia’s offerings more compelling. CEO Jensen Huang actually spent an entire keynote making this point back in 2025; I wrote in an Update:

When Huang says “iso power” he means that power is the constraint; the question is how many tokens can you generate given a fixed power envelope, and Blackwell can generate a lot more. These were the numbers Huang gave for a 100 MW data center:

What this means is that the first order of business for an ASIC maker is to match that level of efficiency. That, though, means keeping up with Nvidia’s product development cadence; The Information has a post about Amazon offering instances using its latest Trainium ASIC at a significant discount to the H100. Huang, though, spent this keynote insulting the H100! You can almost hear him speaking to Amazon directly: you spent all this money, and are offering these huge discounts, just to entice developers to lock themselves into an inferior chip, even as reasoning models are going to swamp your available power generation…

Huang is issuing a challenge to every cloud provider tempted to make an ASIC: do you really think that you can keep up with this, and risk running out of power capacity because your chips aren’t efficient enough? Don’t even try.

A world without power or data center constraints is one where it is, in the very long run, very difficult to maintain Nvidia’s margins; once those constraints start to bite, however, an advantage in tokens/megawatt is worth a lot of money. Go back to my point about the hyperscalers: one way to generate more tokens is to build a new data center; another way is to rebuild a data center with new Nvidia chips.

5. Advantage China

China is the inverse of the scenario that Huang laid out: the country has plenty of power and the ability to build a lot more, but they don’t have leading-edge chips. Some of the advantages of leading-edge chips, however, can be overcome by simply throwing tons of electricity at the problem. From a 2025 Update about the Huawei CloudMatrix 384 supercomputer:

The CloudMatrix 384, which is a supercomputer consisting of 384 chips, takes up dramatically more space, uses dramatically more power, is almost certainly dramatically more expensive to make, and is dramatically more brittle than Nvidia’s NVL72; there is no one in the world who would choose the CloudMatrix 384 over the NVL72 if they had the choice.

That’s the thing, though: China doesn’t have the choice, because of U.S. export controls. The country’s saving grace is that they are operating on different constraints than the U.S.…China — which actually builds power generation — is not iso power; they are iso compute: Huawei’s goal with the CloudMatrix 384 is to get as much compute as possible, power efficiency be damned.

In the fullness of time — i.e. as China figures out leading-edge chips — this may be an insurmountable advantage.

6. Data Centers in Space

When SpaceX released their S-1, I explicitly pointed to political opposition to data centers as one of the company’s most significant upside scenarios:

The third question about data centers in space is if there is a stick. Specifically, while I think that racks-in-space are both a lot more viable than people think, and a lot more relevant to agentic inference than current modes of compute, it is at the end of the day cheaper and easier to build on earth, all things being equal.

All things are not equal, however: right now we are at the very beginning of the AI buildout and already one of the biggest constraints is not just power (expected), but zoning (unexpected). I wrote in an Update last week:

I already posted the relevant excerpt above. Continuing:

In that Update I made the case that data center builders — and by extension the companies that use them — should straight up pay people for permission to build data centers in their communities. At a minimum, however, that increases the costs of terrestrial data centers. What seems very plausible in the long run is that the demand for compute ends up being so large that there eventually is nowhere left to build, making the vast expanses of space not just an alternative but in fact the only choice.

This is where I come back to my experience watching these campaign ads: this isn’t a partisan issue, where the pendulum will swing back in two years. Both parties see opposition to data centers as a winning cause, and not just nationally: that thread has multiple examples of local officials straight up recalled for approving data centers in their localities. Space will be incredibly difficult, but difficulty is all relative! Moreover, to the extent opposition is permanent, the more this actually reduces the risk of data centers in space, because investors will have more confidence in there being enduring demand.

7. The Frontier Labs Benefit

If the hyperscalers had a red queen problem, the frontier labs have it even worse: the biggest revelation from Anthropic’s S-1 was that their inference margins were very high (good!), which meant that their massive compute costs were actually in R&D; this is bad because that R&D spend is governed by competition with the other frontier labs, and absent constraints, that spend looked set to surpass revenue sooner rather than later. Now, however, it is the public that is effectively demanding that the frontier be paced, which is great for the frontier labs’ financial outlook.

The upside goes further than that: the point about efficiency being more important in a world of constraints doesn’t just matter for chips, but also for models. Devoting limited compute to inefficient and costlier-to-serve Chinese models is a poor trade if there isn’t enough compute. Moreover, open models may be at greater regulatory risk, as Democrats seem much more likely to pass laws that ultimately favor the frontier labs.

There are some counter-arguments. First, if compute is constrained, and thus more expensive, then that will increase the drive to right-size models for jobs, which is a big argument in favor of open models; the fact that compute won’t be a commodity means that the frontier labs’ lower cost to serve will never come to bear on the low end of the market. And, it’s worth noting, it will be harder for the frontier labs to build their own compute, leaving them dependent on the hyperscalers; big tech wins again.

8. Apple Gains

The most obvious advantage for Apple is that in a world of constrained compute, inference on the edge will be that much more important. Another advantage is that any slowdown in the dispersion of AI is good for a company that dominated the previous paradigm.

The biggest advantage of all, however, is that any slowdown in the AI buildout offers hope that the memory crunch will ease. This will take a while, to be sure, but no company would be a bigger beneficiary of the world running out of places to put AI chips than Apple.

9. Startups Suffer

AI has drawn a great many battle lines, not just in terms of data centers, but also within AI, and between AI and the rest of tech. Specifically, anything that strengthens the frontier labs is likely bad for the rest of the startup ecosystem. In a world with fewer data centers, startups will have less access to cheap compute, even as a slowdown in capabilities both means it takes longer to build compelling products and also gives the frontier labs time to actually build products that secure their ownership of the end user.

10. The Human Factor

One major fear that investors have had about the data center buildout is that there would be too much capacity, causing prices to plummet and investors and creditors to lose their shirts; that scenario, however, would be great for users, who would suddenly have access to incredibly cheap compute. Of course most users aren’t going to use AI directly; what they will miss out on is the equivalent of the Web 2.0 wave of free Internet services that were predicated on compute being free. Now there’s a good chance that AI is going to have meaningful marginal costs for a long time to come.

At the same time, while I have been an optimist about humans in an AI future, there is no question that we were and are facing a wrenching change as intelligence becomes a commodity. It follows, however, that if it doesn’t become a commodity — or if that change takes longer than expected — that humanity will have more time to adapt. Maybe this is a break we needed; what is increasingly clear is it’s the break Americans wanted.

That noted, there is a long history of citizens demanding the ends and opposing the means, and it’s the demand that wins in the end. The big difference today is that, unlike the first few waves of tech, the industry is going to need to do some convincing, and break the habit of assuming everything it does will get the benefit of the doubt. AI wasn’t technically on the ballot, but it was implicitly, and will be forevermore.

Presented by

I spend a lot of time trying to figure out what is happening to businesses on the internet. What I often find I’m missing is a view across the economy itself. With more than 1.7% of global GDP running on Stripe, working with them means I can bring some of what they’re seeing to Stratechery. They are, in a sense, a barometer of the economy.

Take the “SaaSpocalypse”. Earlier this year, nearly a trillion dollars in enterprise software value disappeared amid fears of AI eating its lunch. Stock prices only tell us what investors think will happen, and not necessarily what is happening. In this case, Stripe recently built a SaaS Index using payments data from 72,000 non-AI SaaS businesses. Looking at their actual performance, we can see that while SaaS stocks were selling off, revenue growth was actually accelerating.


Year-over-year growth is now over 30%, with some of the fastest growth coming from the youngest SaaS companies. I suspect there are a lot more interesting things hiding in Stripe’s data, and I’m excited about having an excuse to go look for them.

issues.title: Meeting the “Sentenced to Be a Hero” Creators and Cast at NYCC 2026
issues.summary: "Ever since I was in elementary school, I drew a lot of sketches. Dragon Ball, Naruto, the popular shows at the time. I would draw at school. My friends would be impressed and it gave me pride and joy, so I continued to draw." - Mephisto Meeting the “Sentenced to Be a Hero”…
issues.author: Seth Burn
issues.content_html:
• Interview Location: New York Comic Con 2026
  • Interview Format: In-person, One-on-One

Anime Herald: Now that Ace Combat 8 is out, has it inspired any future arcs for the series?

Rocket Shokai: It is very easy to be influenced, but if this were to inspire an arc within a story, I would choose a different story. An imitation becoming real would be a story for a different time.

Anime Herald: That is an interesting pen name. How did you choose it?

Mephisto: In Japan, we have a term, “middle school illness.” (chunibyo) It comes from middle school kids thinking of themselves as more powerful and important than they are. When I was in middle school, I was into foreign legends, fairy tales. I was reading Dante, Milton’s Paradise Lost, Faust. Within Faust, there is the devil Mephisto. I thought that was so cool, so I’ve been Mephisto since middle school.

I want to make it clear that I am not Satanic. No devil worshiping. (Laughs)

Anime Herald: What do you do to mentally get into character to play Xylo Forbartz?

Yohei Azakami: When it comes to voice acting, there’s no movement. There are no visuals, no body element that we can use to convey what the characters are doing or feeling. The damage to the body, the dirt, the scent, what all of the senses that the character is feeling, they all have to be conveyed by voice. What I focus on is not necessarily how to provide the depth of the character, but rather, what is this character truly experiencing at that moment, and how do I let that carry through using only my voice. I don’t know if I am doing a good job, but that’s what I hope I’m doing.

Anime Herald: What do you do to mentally get into character to play Teoritta?

Mayu Iizuka: What I hope to be able to convey is, going back to my childhood, I always try to help other people. As I get older, it is harder to do that, to have that opportunity to reach out. That pureness, that innocence, of offering help because you can, because you want to, is something that I am calling upon again through reliving that innocence that Teoritta has.

Anime Herald: George R.R. Martin has generally treated life as cheap. Do you feel the same way about life in Sentenced to Be a Hero?

Rocket Shokai: Maybe it is my perspective on this, but I feel like George R.R. Martin is asking “What is more important than life? What is worth giving up your life for? If not life, what is left?” That is a consistent philosophy I always ask myself as well in my perspective of this.

Anime Herald: What is it about Rhyno that makes him your favorite character from Sentenced to Be a Hero?

Mephisto: Most importantly, Rhyno is super unique. He has a storyline like no other. What I think is absolutely adorable is that he tries so hard to be accepted by mankind. He tries so hard to be loved by mankind. And yet, everything he does makes him look stranger and like more of an outcast. I think that’s adorable.

Anime Herald: If you were sentenced to be a hero, what is the crime you would have been accused of?

Yohei Azakami: Too many! Lots!

Laziness.

Laziness is definitely the crime. Luckily, voice acting has allowed me to challenge myself. It really motivates me. I feel so lucky to be here in New York because of it. If I didn’t have work, I’d be in big trouble.

Rocket Shokai: What do you think my crime would be?

Yohei Azakami: No comment. (Laughs)

Anime Herald: On a scale of one to ten, where one is not caring at all, and ten is equal to Teoritta, how much do you enjoy praise?

Mayu Iizuka: Ten, with confidence.

Yohei Azakami: Me too!

Rocket Shokai: I’m about a five.

Mephisto: I’m self motivated.

Mayu Iizuka: I feel very fortunate that I can enjoy praise. That makes me feel like there were lots of people who found good things in me and feel that I was praiseworthy. I feel fortunate to be able to say I like praise because it is the love I have received.

Anime Herald: What would you like our readers to know about Sentenced to Be a Hero?

Rocket Shokai: In the anime so far, we haven’t necessarily seen how lovable these penal heroes really are. That is coming. Please stay tuned to see these characters really come to life.

Anime Herald: What is your origin story? How did you decide you wanted to be an artist?

Mephisto: Ever since I was in elementary school, I drew a lot of sketches. Dragon Ball, Naruto, the popular shows at the time. I would draw at school. My friends would be impressed and it gave me pride and joy, so I continued to draw. In high school, smartphones and social gacha phone games became popular. That allowed illustrators to design characters and push their content to a much larger audience. That made me realize there was a future in making a career out of illustration. That’s what propelled my career.

Anime Herald: What was your initial impression of Sentenced to Be a Hero?

Yohei Azakami: I’ve always preferred dark heroes over traditional, clean heroes. There’s definitely an element of that. But more so, this is a story where a lot of characters with faults come together to make success happen. It ties all of the pieces of the puzzle together, so that they can succeed. Yes, Xylo is the main character, but he is not the one with all of the superpowers. He doesn’t just swoop in and save the day. He has to use wit. He has to use his team. He has to collaborate. There are no clear answers. Everything is complex. That makes the storyline so exciting and enjoyable for me.

Anime Herald: What was your initial impression of Sentenced to Be a Hero?

Mayu Iizuka: I already knew I was assigned to play Teoritta when I first studied the source material. I found Xylo an interesting character. To me, heroes were Anpanman, Precure. Clean, classic heroes of justice and good. But Xylo is very human. That raw emotion that drives him is so new for the concept of a hero. It is intriguing and something that gets deeper as the story develops.

Anime Herald: Thank you very much.

Meeting the “Sentenced to Be a Hero” Creators and Cast at NYCC 2026 - Seth Burn

issues.content_html:
Most of my ideas turn into sketches, research notes or brief videos for the team. Some of them finally make it into or .

But most — because of the time it takes to polish them — simply remain internal as tools to push our thinking forward.

We’ve been wondering just how valuable it would be for readers to peek at the artist’s sketchbook, even in its raw, unfiltered form.

The advantage is that you’d get to see things I think are important but, for whatever reason, we don’t finish or publish. Maybe they go out late, much, much later, or they don’t survive the cut.

These sketches are more raw than anything we’d normally publish. For example, it’s interim research I’m doing as I think through a thesis. I’ve judged it good enough for my thinking but not yet ready for your reading. But perhaps I’m wrong. Examples from the past week include:

issues.title: Lenny’s Newsletter holiday gift guide 2026
issues.summary: 100+ gift ideas—all things I actually use, love, and recommend
issues.author: Lenny Rachitsky
issues.content_html:
👋 Hey there, I’m Lenny. Each week, I share deeply researched product, growth, and career advice. For more: Lenny’s Jobs | Lenny’s Podcast | Lennybot | How I AI | AI/PM courses.

Subscribe now

P.S. Get a full free year of Cursor, Notion, Replit, Lovable, Wispr Flow, Linear, ElevenLabs, Factory, PostHog, Granola, Brain.fm, Waking Up, and more, by becoming an Insider subscriber (while supplies last). Learn more.

The holidays are fast approaching, so I’m back with my sixth (!!) annual gift guide. It started out as a random post idea, but now you’d be surprised how many people ping me as early as September asking when the new list will be out.

These guides take a lot of work to do well, and ever since the first edition, my secret weapon has been my wife, Michelle. She finds the cutest stuff, makes me cut the slop, and she’s the best gift-giver I know. Dare I say, she’s got taste. 🤌

I’ve included a mix of practical stuff with a lot of fun and delight, from high-end products to very affordable items. As always, there are no affiliate links here, I’m not benefiting from recommending any of these products, and I’m an investor in only two of these companies (marked with 🏦). I’ve marked returning champions—products I’ve mentioned in past guides—with a medal icon 🎖️.

If you’re looking for even more ideas, check out my previous gift guides from 2025, 2024, 2023 (for new parents), 2022, and 2021. And enjoy!

P.S. If you’re based in the U.S., go vote today!

Some fun, delightful sh*t

  1. Be Nice cap from artist David Shrigley. The world needs more nice. If you’re in the EU (or unconcerned with $30 in tariffs), buy directly from the artist’s store here.

  1. Dandelion Chocolate. Dandelion is a San Francisco–based company that makes their chocolate at their own factory in the heart of the city. The founder left tech to study chocolate-making traditions in France, started making his own chocolate in his garage 16 years ago, and became one of the best-known small-batch chocolate makers in the U.S. Unlike most chocolate, it’s made from just two ingredients: cocoa beans and organic cane sugar. They have many beautiful (and delicious) gift options (the Advent calendar is a popular choice), and the site clearly states allergens for each product.

  1. Avian Visitors. A framed e-ink display that dynamically updates to show a collage of the birds heard most recently near your home. You can order a kit that you assemble yourself or this ready-made version, while supplies last. This is a one-man hobby project, so he may sell out fast.

  1. Applause Machine. For the underappreciated PM in your life. As the designer puts it, “for when your ideas are great but no one else agrees.” It’s like VCBrags but IRL. P.S. High price point. It’s art!

  1. Flowers for Things I Don’t Know How to Say by Tucker Nichols. A touching gift for someone who’s going through a hard time, plus some funny entries that add levity. The spread pictured hits close to home for me and my misophonia. 🫣

  1. BonBon’s Sour Blackberry Fish. The most delicious, addictive, memorable candy I’ve had in a while. We discovered this at the very cute Jenner Outpost while on a road trip and had to agree not to get any more bags on the return trip. Gluten-free, vegan, no dyes, possible crack.

  1. Ugmonk 15-minute sand timer. “No notifications. No glowing numbers. Just sand moving through glass.” Can be used to give your kid a time limit without having to use a screen. Or for yourself. Thanks, Chris, for the tip.

  1. Blunk Cups. These cups are a West Marin trifecta of “something old” (original JB Blunk design), “something new” (third-edition collaboration with Oakland artist Stephanie Intelisano), and “something blue.” Too pricey? Try this cobalt blue mug from East Fork’s Matisse Collection.

  1. Bathing Culture certified-organic “mind and body wash.” Smells great, looks pretty, and comes in refillable glass bottles.

  1. MD Notebook. Just a really nice minimalist notebook with smooth-to-the-pen pages. The blank version is Michelle’s go-to. Another silky-paged favorite: Mnemosyne.

For the friend always talking about microplastics

  1. Aarke stainless-steel hot water kettle, Rishi glass teapot, and Five Mountains stainless steel strainer. Michelle and I are tea drinkers, and we stopped using tea bags about a year ago, so we only have tea advice. If you’re a coffee drinker and have plastic-free coffee equipment recommendations (especially espresso machines), please share in the comments! Caveat on the kettle: there’s black silicone on the inside of the lid but nowhere else.🎖️

  1. Hestan for baking, and stainless steel Made In for pots. We started with one pan and are slowly replacing all our cookware with these.

  1. Vera Salt. Did you know sea salt can be full of microplastics? Here’s Huberman talking about it. Vera Salt is 100% microplastic-free, “hand-harvested in the foothills of Spain.” Fancy. This has become our go-to sea salt. 🎖️

  2. Seatopia. Frozen high-quality seafood delivered to your door. Lab-tested for mercury, microplastics, and more.

  1. Ophora water (test results) and Loonen water (test results). Loonen’s sparkling water is just as bubbly as our previous favorite brand that tested high for PFAS.

  2. Fashionable 100% organic cotton clothing from Wax London, Pact, Nads, Industry of All Nations, Faherty, and Mate. For kids: Colored Organics, Pehr, and Mushie. 🎖️

For friends/colleagues who need to touch grass

  1. Online comedy classes from The Second City. They’ve got improv, stand-up comedy, public speaking, and more. The stand-up class is excellent for getting your creative juices flowing, even if you never plan on performing your tight five.

  2. Solgaard carry-on luggage. We’ve used this “carry-on closet” suitcase for years and love it. The MoMA edition has fun colors as a bonus. Tip: Don’t lose the interior closet insert, because you can’t buy a new one without buying a whole new suitcase (we learned the hard way).

  1. K9 dog backpack. We used this every weekend to ride our bikes with our dog before we had a kid. Sorry, buddy.

  1. Garrett Leight sunglasses. I’ve done cheap sunglasses my whole life, and after getting this really nice pair, I’m going the quality route from now on. I just have to not lose them.

  1. The Architecture of Trees by Cesare Leonardi and Franca Stagi. A hearty book to page through when you need a detox from slop scrolling.

  1. Pendleton grab-and-go throw. So cozy. To save some bucks, you can skip the leather carrier and just get the blanket.

  1. Tern electric bike. For riding with your kiddos around town, especially a hilly one. Cargo e-bikes are expensive as hell, and this is among the pricier models, for good reason. Bosch battery system, smooth and easy ride. No kids but have a small dog? There’s an attachment for that.

  1. AllTrails gift subscription. I’ve been a paid subscriber for over five years now.

  2. Giftable Bay Area experiences:

    1. Redwood Nights in Fairfax. Like The Moth but with twinkle-light-strewn towering redwoods, and deer families stopping by to eavesdrop on the stories.

    2. Lightscape at the San Francisco Botanical Garden

    3. Outstanding in the Field. They tour all over the U.S. and are opening the new season soon.

    4. Candlelight concerts in San Francisco (and beyond). Covers of your favorite songs “surrounded by a thousand candles.”

For your friends with kids

  1. Botanic and Luxe 2–4T Bear Robe. Cuteness overload after a warm bath or shower.

  1. Kids’ Glerups slippers or Blundstone shoes. Cuteness overload, continued.

  1. Shameless-plug alert: Charts for Babies and All the Feelings (pre-order), written and illustrated by my wonderfully creative wife, with the goal of introducing the visual language of math at an early age. Yes, I’m biased, but they’re great. Best way to incept your kids into STEM.

  1. Yoto Mini 4th Gen. I recommended this last year, and so many people grabbed one and loved it. We continue to be huge fans, and they just came out with a new model with a larger on/off/pause button. If you’re not familiar with Yoto, it’s a screen-free audio player for kids, with hundreds of music and story options. 🎖️

  1. Rey To Z hat. Get custom hats for your kids and their grandparents, whatever the kids call them.

  1. Little Moonjumper custom blanket. Our favorite new-baby gift. Parents treasure it. We did—thank you, Sarah.

  2. The Hideaway Carry-On Duffel. This has become our go-to travel bag for our kid. It’s cleverly designed, with specific pockets and openings for everything you can think of. They also have a smaller version. 🎖️

  1. Original sketches by Mo Willems, like this one from I Really Like Slop!, and other original children’s-book artwork from Books of Wonder.

  1. Once. For your type A parent friends trying to get their kid to read. It worked for ours.

  2. Nanit. The best baby monitor on the market. Delightful reminders, video compilations, and it just works. A great way to watch your delicious turkey-shaped baby. 🎖️

For the home-and-healthmaxxers

  1. For home air filters, we’ve settled on the IQAir HealthPro Plus for the living room (godawfully ugly, sometimes we hide it), Dyson and Blueair for bedrooms, and this Coway Airmega for smaller rooms, like my office.

  2. Lightwork Home Health. A whole-house toxin health assessment. They come to your house to test your air quality, water, EMFs, lighting, mold, and household products. Not cheap, but we did this (they comped us a visit) and it was eye-opening.

  3. Aranet4 CO₂ indoor air quality monitor. High CO₂ levels allegedly impair your cognition, so I have one of these puppies in my office and open windows when I see it go above 1,000. I’ve also heard good things about this Airthings device. 🎖️

  4. Daylight Labs Deep Amber incandescent lights. The most beautiful and practical light for evenings, to help you slow down at the end of the day. They plug into any standard light socket, or you can grab a couple of the cute wood light fixtures. By the creators of the Daylight computer (a recommended gift in 2024).

  1. Blissoma SPF 30 mineral facial sunscreen. My go-to (face) sunscreen. Zinc-based, no scent, doesn’t turn me into a white-bearded Santa Claus.

  2. Wild Roman face moisturizer. They just got a 98/100 Yuka score. High-quality ingredients, small-batch, and it comes in a glass jar. And smells great. Created by Sahil Bloom. 🏦

  3. Waterpik. I’d always been afraid of these, but my dental hygienist told me it’s the most impactful intervention you can make for your teeth and gum health. I floss with DrTung’s Smart Floss in the evening and Waterpik in the morning. Do it in the shower with warm water—so easy.

  4. Matic robot vacuum. The Apple/Dyson/Tesla of vacuums. Not cheap, but the best and the most delightful. They also just launched the Serene, a quieter, limited-edition version. 🎖️🏦

  1. Kawabon leather/merino wool tray. Cute place to store art supplies. Also works for keeping your keys and wallet near the front door.

  2. CANARY Cardboard Cutter. For opening your packages. I’ve had this on the gift guide since day one, and it’s the item readers thank me most for helping them discover. Some people prefer this smaller version. 🎖️

For the sleep optimizers

  1. Manta silk sleep mask. It looks ridiculous, I know, but after trying a lot of different sleep masks (including my longtime favorite, WAOAW), I think this is the best. Reader Tamara Winter swears by the Sleep Crown Classic, though it’s often sold out. 🎖️

  1. Mack’s earplugs. I’ve tried a bunch of fancy, and even custom, earplugs, but I keep returning to these. So cheap, so easy, so effective.

  2. Moon Juice Sleepy Magnesi-Om. An acupuncturist I’ve been frequenting suggested this, and more than anything I’ve tried, it has helped me sleep better and deeper. It includes a low dose of plant-based melatonin “extracted from organically grown alfalfa and chlorella,” and maybe it’s a placebo, but I do feel like it works. I alternate this with magnesium supplements from Designs for Health.

  1. Oura Ring 5. The model that came out earlier this year is a lot thinner and holds a charge for about a week. It’s been really helpful to see how my sleep is affected by changes I make.

  1. Coyuchi organic cotton sheets. Expensive, but we’ve slowly been replacing all of our sheets with these. You spend so much time on bedsheets, it feels worth it. They also just started creating mattresses 😅. 🎖️

  2. Hooga clip-on blue-blocking amber light. I previously recommended this as a nursery light in my 2023 new-parents gift guide. It still works great as a warm reading light in our kid’s room but also as my own book light. We have several. 🎖️

  3. I’m a big fan of the Avocado side-sleeper pillow. Michelle loves the Tempur-Pedic small profile—so much so that she takes up half her suitcase with it when we travel.

For the workaholics

  1. Mateína Yerba Mate. No sugar, tastes great, and arguably one of the healthiest sources of caffeine. Co-developed with Huberman.

  2. Breath by James Nestor. This book rewired how I think about breathing, which has impacted how I work, speak, and sleep. It’s a quick and engrossing read. To go deeper, our friend Gopika teaches Sudarshan Kriya, on one of the core breathwork techniques described in the book, in the Bay Area (also available online), and I recently discovered these Moonbird devices that help you (and your kids) practice different breathing techniques.

issues.title: 🎙️ How I AI: Grok vs. Dot vs. Muse vs. Duet + How Figma’s PMs actually use AI every day
issues.summary: Your weekly listens from How I AI, part of the Lenny's Podcast Network
issues.author: Lenny Rachitsky
issues.content_html:
Grok vs. Dot vs. Muse vs. Claude Duet: which one crushes the competition?

Listen now on YouTube • Spotify • Apple Podcasts

Brought to you by:

WorkOS—Make your app enterprise-ready, with SSO, SCIM, RBAC, and more

Firecrawl—Give your AI agents web data and beyond

In this solo episode, Claire puts Grok Bot, Dot, Meta’s Muse, and Claude Duet through nine real-world tasks to find out which personal agents are actually worth using. She tests them on everything from Slack replies, inbox triage, and coding to video editing, Figma thumbnails, family projects, and shopping. The results point to a clear split.

Biggest takeaways:

  1. Grok Bot is the strongest all-around personal agent in this benchmark, especially for work. It scored 93% overall and won the Figma, inbox triage, and shopping tasks. For someone choosing one agent for professional workflows, Claire recommends starting here.

  2. Muse is the best agent for personal life. It created the strongest short-form video and family newspaper with almost no prompting and answered a physics question too quickly to time. That speed has led Claire to move more quick Q&A conversations from ChatGPT to Muse.

  3. Speed is central to the product experience. Muse finished first on four of the nine tasks, while Claude Duet was consistently the slowest. When an agent disappears for several minutes, users lose context and stop wanting to use it.

  4. Claude Duet asks for permission too often. It requested approval four times during the benchmark, compared with once for every other agent. That caution may be well-intentioned, but it makes Duet feel like something the user must supervise rather than trust.

  5. An agent is only as capable as the tools it can access. A Codex audit found that Claire’s agents did not have equivalent connectors and skills. Muse lacked Slack and GitHub, which prevented it from completing several work tasks, highlighting the importance of equal setups for a fair comparison.

  6. Grok Bot is the agent Claire trusts most with Figma. Dot and Claude Duet mostly filled existing templates, while Grok Bot proposed fresh headlines and layouts that looked like real YouTube thumbnails. It has consistently outperformed the others across Claire’s Figma tests.

  7. Claude Duet and Dot still showed the strongest coding judgment. Dot came closest to the intended Sentry fix, while Duet found a second bug and avoided duplicating work Dot had already completed. Claire would still choose Claude or Codex for serious coding, just not through Duet’s personal-agent interface.

  8. Dot showed the strongest personal context in one important moment. It was the only agent that asked whether Claire’s Lovable talk was paid and remote, which felt like genuine chief-of-staff judgment. Its poor performance on creative tasks, however, kept it well behind Grok Bot and Muse overall.

  9. The useful takeaway is that different agents belong in different parts of life. Claire’s current split is Grok Bot for work and Muse for personal tasks. Choosing agents by job is more effective than expecting one product to handle everything well.

Blog and detailed workflow walkthroughs from this episode:

Grok vs. Dot vs. Muse vs. Claude Duet: Nine Tasks, Four Agents, No Universal Winner: https://www.chatprd.ai/how-i-ai/grok-vs-dot-vs-muse-vs-claude-duet-nine-tasks-four-agents-no-universal-winner
↳ Generate Novel YouTube Thumbnail Ideas with Grok and Figma: https://www.chatprd.ai/how-i-ai/workflows/generate-novel-youtube-thumbnail-ideas-with-grok-and-figma
↳ How to Create a Branded Product Launch Video with Claude Duet: https://www.chatprd.ai/how-i-ai/workflows/how-to-create-a-branded-product-launch-video-with-claude-duet
↳ Create a Personalized Family Newspaper with Meta’s Muse: https://www.chatprd.ai/how-i-ai/workflows/create-a-personalized-family-newspaper-with-meta-s-muse

How Figma’s PMs actually use AI every day | Ezra Mechaber (PM, Figma)

Listen now on YouTube • Spotify • Apple Podcasts

Brought to you by:

Optimizely—Your AI agent orchestration platform for marketing and digital teams

Jira Product Discovery—Prioritize with insights, build with confidence

Ezra Mechaber is a growth product manager at Figma and one of the creators of PM OS, a shared repository of 31 AI skills used across the company’s product organization. In this episode, he demonstrates how Figma’s PMs use it to manage Slack, gather organizational context, create artifacts, and run more thorough bug bashes with Codex. He also walks through AutoXP, an AI growth PM that runs experiments with a single human checkpoint, and a real-time Jev assistant that improves writing as he types.

Biggest takeaways:

  1. The best place to start with AI is the work PMs routinely skip. Ezra designed PM OS around tasks that fall through the cracks, such as involving support before a launch or documenting meetings. His goal is to establish a minimum acceptable standard for every PM workflow.

  2. Context-gathering skills are the foundation of useful AI at work. At a company with roughly 2,000 employees, even identifying the right collaborators can be difficult. One PM OS skill maps a team and automatically adds the relevant designer, engineering manager, and team leaders as reviewers.

  3. A simple “what’s up” skill can make Slack manageable. Ezra runs it about six times a day to gather relevant threads, projects, open decisions, and people awaiting a response. He archives roughly 10 channels daily because the skill preserves what actually matters.

  4. A basic Git repository can support an entire PM organization. PM OS consists of an AGENTS.md file, reusable skills, and a few command hooks. An automatic version check keeps 60 to 70 PMs aligned, while private subrepositories give each person room to customize.

  5. Successful AI adoption starts with familiar tools, then evolves with users. PM OS began as a terminal interface in Claude Code before gaining a local web interface that was easier to read. Ezra now works primarily in Codex, partly because browser use has become reliable enough for his workflow.

  6. Agents can be more diligent bug bashers than humans. Ezra gives his agent a test account and a FigJam board full of scenarios, then has it document its findings. It has caught edge cases ranging from a text box filled with 1,000 emojis to grammar that changed based on a team’s name.

  7. In growth, wasted traffic is the biggest sin. AutoXP uses three agents to identify funnel drop-off, propose new copy, and prepare the implementation. A human reviews the experiment once before launch, after which the system analyzes results and begins the next iteration automatically.

  8. Fast, inexpensive models can provide feedback that feels continuous. Ezra’s Jev prototype reviews writing whenever the user pauses, flags placeholders and unsupported claims, and finds relevant interview quotes from a research library. The speed makes it feel less like running an AI task and more like working beside an attentive editor.

  9. When an AI conversation goes bad, starting over often beats arguing with it. Ezra treats poor output as a sign of unclear instructions or contaminated context. He opens a fresh conversation, restates the goal, and approaches the model with high expectations: “Buddy, I know you can cook.”

Blog and detailed workflow walkthroughs from this episode:

↳ Automate Software Bug Bashing with a Browser Agent: https://www.chatprd.ai/how-i-ai/workflows/automate-software-bug-bashing-with-a-browser-agent
↳ Build an Automated Growth Experiment Loop with Multiple AI Agents: https://www.chatprd.ai/how-i-ai/workflows/build-an-automated-growth-experiment-loop-with-multiple-ai-agents
↳ Build a Personal PM Operating System with a Shared Knowledge Repo: https://www.chatprd.ai/how-i-ai/workflows/build-a-personal-pm-operating-system-with-a-shared-knowledge-repo

If you’re enjoying these episodes, reply and let me know what you’d love to learn more about: AI workflows, hiring, growth, product strategy—anything.

Catch you next week,
Lenny
