issues.title: DD413 / The lost art of having people over
issues.summary: Issue 413: The lost art of having people over – Read the full issue in the archive.
issues.author: Kai Brach
issues.content_html:
As a kid, I loved our big lunch and dinner parties. There are photos of 30-odd people – friends, family, neighbours – squeezed into our apartment on borrowed chairs around tables that didn’t match. It was chaotic, loud and a lot of fun. They didn’t happen nearly often enough, and I sometimes wonder why something we all enjoyed so much was saved for birthdays and other rare occasions.

Over the years, we’ve actually made them rarer still. Derek Thompson has the numbers to prove it:

“In the last 30 years, Americans have seen double-digit declines in practically every measure of socializing. ... The share of Americans who say they host friends or family at their home at least monthly has fallen from 42 percent in 1975 to 12 percent in 2026 – a 70 percent collapse in a half-century.”

These days, the convenience economy has made staying in so easy that inviting people over feels like a self-inflicted chore.

Elizabeth Oldfield went the other way. For more than a decade, she and her husband have hosted shared dinners every other week, first squeezing eight people around a table in a tiny London flat, now feeding up to 16 at a time in their community house. By her count, around 1,500 people have come through the door. The trick, she says, is putting it in the calendar and refusing to renegotiate:

“This bizarre culture of possessive individualism will always give us reasons not to be together, so sometimes it takes a strong container to push back. ... Always keeping our options open and autonomy over our time sounds good but leaves us lonely and disoriented. Make a commitment and your future self will thank you.”

I love how unbothered she is about the state of the house. As her husband puts it, hospitality is ”not the same as entertaining”:

“To be invited into someone else’s imperfect house is, it turns out, a blessing. I do not tend to find very primped, spotless, Instagram-ready homes especially relaxing to be in. If we are going to move towards each other and build real community we have to let go of the desire to impress people.”

I wrote about the radical act of regular open-door dinners a while back (DD331), and Oldfield’s dinners are about the most practical version of that idea I’ve come across. (Do check out her list of tips in the essay.)

So why don’t more of us do it? Thompson has a pretty good theory:

“Everybody might prefer, in the abstract, a world of dinner parties, neighborhood friendships, and spontaneous gatherings. But on any given Wednesday at 7:45pm., it is easier to look at a screen than to host a party; easier to listen to a podcast while doing yoga than to plan a gathering. This is not so much an individual failure as a coordination failure. ... Compared to TikTok, a dinner party is a terrible leisure technology. It requires matching schedules, cleaning the house, buying food, accommodating children and allergies, tolerating awkwardness, and taking the risk that the evening is mediocre. By contrast, what does television ask of us? Nothing. TikTok? Even less.”

When I look at those old photos and my mum’s kitchen, I notice who’s doing the cooking. Those parties ran on a lot of unpaid labour, mostly by women, and Thompson points out that the social calendar frayed when they took on paid work and the men didn’t pick up the slack. Today’s cost-of-living pressures and two exhausted working parents make the couch and screens combo look very appealing.

Oldfield offers us a way back that doesn’t require a kitchen full of women doing all the work and stressing about being a perfect host. Her dinners run on cheap dahl and wine from Lidl. Guests chop, set the table and stay for the clean-up. Nobody performs, nobody keeps score, and somehow everyone leaves a little less alone.

And now to this week’s discoveries. – Kai

issues.title: Anime Feminist Recommendations of Summer 2026
issues.summary: Summer gave us plenty to chew on, from sweet rom-coms to fairy tale retellings. The post Anime Feminist Recommendations of Summer 2026 appeared first on Anime Feminist.
issues.author: Anime Feminist
issues.content_html:
Summer gave us plenty to chew on, from sweet rom-coms to fairy tale retellings.

How did we choose our recs?

Participating staff members can nominate up to three titles and can also co-sign other nominated shows. Rather than categorizing titles as “feminist-friendly” or “problematic,” they are simply listed in alphabetical order with relevant content warnings; doing otherwise ran the risk of folks seeing these staff recommendations as rubber stamps of unilateral “Feminist Approval,” which is something we try our hardest to avoid here.

The titles below are organized alphabetically. As a reminder, ongoing shows are NOT eligible for these lists. We’d rather wait until the series (or season) has finished up before recommending it to others, that way we can give you a more complete picture. This means we also leave out any unfinished split-cour shows, which we define as shows that air a second season less than a year after the first (often defined by announcing a sequel with an already-secured upcoming air date).

Draw This, Then Die!

Recommended by: Dee

What it’s about: Ai Yasumi fell in love with manga at a young age, thanks to the single-volume cult classic Robota and Pocota. To her surprise and delight, it turns out the manga’s artist is her no-nonsense teacher, Teshima, who claims to hate manga even as she’s drawn to Ai’s passion for it. Ai is inspired to start a manga club and tell her own stories, and Teshima reluctantly agrees to be the club advisor—as long as Ai promises to only draw manga as a hobby and not as a job.

Content considerations: Depictions of burnout and depression; a teenager forces a kiss on her teacher once and it is never referenced again; in flashbacks, a teen Teshima often imagines blowing up buildings or shooting people after they critique her work.

This series may be dressed up as a hobby anime, but it’s also an unflinching, sometimes devastating, ultimately optimistic examination of art and storytelling in the modern world. Through its dual protagonists, teenage Ai and adult Teshima, Draw This highlights the passion that often sparks an artist’s creative light… as well as the grim capitalist reality that often snuffs that light out.

Ai’s arc looks to the future while Teshima’s looks to the past, their narratives weaving together as Teshima remembers the passion that used to burn inside her (and how she lost it) while also clumsily trying to keep Ai and her clubmates from barreling down the same burnout path. Through their twin tales, the series highlights the importance of a creative community and the dangers of isolation; considers the balance between expressing oneself and engaging with an audience; and makes a strong case that independent “hobby” creatives are just as valid and valuable as professional ones.

Draw This is primarily a comedy, but it’s got a lot of heart and some genuinely thoughtful things to say about storytelling, both from a reader’s and a creator’s perspective. As someone who has been both an Ai and a Teshima (sometimes simultaneously), Draw This body-slammed me with grief and filled me with hope in equal measures. I’d recommend this series to pretty much anyone, but especially creatives, newbies and vets alike.

—Dee

Goodbye, Lara

Recommended by: Alex, Dee, Peter, Tony

What’s it about? Long, long ago, a mermaid princess named Lara fell deeply in love with a human prince. In order to be with him, she used a magic potion, but all magic has a cost, and for her, failing to find true love would mean she turned into seafoam. Now, two hundred years in the future, Lara awakens in Japan with one last chance to find love and save herself from a dismal fate… 

Content considerations: fantasy racism; gore/supernatural body horror

Goodbye, Lara appears at first as a whimsical modern-day retelling of The Little Mermaid. It maintains this tone for much of the first few episodes, luring the viewer in with slice-of-life shenanigans and characters learning life lessons through minor conflicts. This belies the much more serious ambitions of the show, which come to the fore fairly quickly: Goodbye, Lara is a powerful condemnation of how the dreams of young women are shaped and manipulated into a force of their oppression.

Goodbye, Lara is in dialogue with a few shows in this vein that came before, with its closest analogues being Princess Tutu and Revolutionary Girl Utena. Lara, like Utena and Duck, struggles against a feminized narrative that uses her capacity for care and love as a source of stability for her community. This struggle is not just external, but largely internal: she has been brought up internalizing the beliefs that the only way for her to protect and care for her community is to fall in heteronormative, romantic love. Watching Lara slowly let go of these beliefs and disentangle what is expected from her from what she actually wants for herself is deeply satisfying, especially because Lara, even in her naivety, often succeeds in helping the people around her confront and let go of their own toxic narratives.

Her female co-lead, Mari, is one of my favorite characters of the last few years. Only Mari, when confronted by a gorgeous girl falling from the sky, would think to put on her boxing gloves and punch her in the face. Mari’s journey parallels Lara’s beautifully as she learns to love without fear, to be vulnerable and open to even being hurt in her openness with her emotions—which she learns through learning the story of a witch, the moral of which is, almost verbatim: “be gay, do crime.” 

Goodbye, Lara is an astonishing feat of storytelling and animation. Pretty much any fan of queer stories well told owes it to themselves to watch it.

—Tony

Jaadugar: A Witch in Mongolia

Recommended by: Dee, Lizzie, Peter, Tony

What it’s about: In 13th century Persia, Sitara is an orphaned slave girl in the city of Tus. When the recently-widowed Lady Fatima buys her at a discount, Sitara find herself in a household of scholars, learning theology, literature, and mathematics and opening up her world despite her circumstances. But Sitara’s life takes a grim turn when the Mongols attack Tus. Can she snatch back control of her fate, even as the darkness of war and conquest threaten to steal away everything she holds dear?

Content warnings: Depictions of slavery, murder, conquest, and forced marriage; Sitara’s backstory leans a bit into slavery apologia and the myth of the “good” slaveowner.

As someone who’s reading the manga, let me first say that this adaptation improves upon the source material in every possible way. It’s Science Saru and Naoko Yamada, so of course the animation and direction are magnificent, but the anime also gives the somewhat breakneck pacing of the manga a chance to breathe, expanding on scenes to create a lusher, more fully realized world and cast.

I am woefully unequipped to discuss the historical accuracy or cultural authenticity of Jaadugar, but I’ll at least say that, from my limited perspective, it feels thoughtful and grounded, particularly in the solemnly beautiful way it depicts the various cultures’ belief systems and religious rituals. There’s a sincere attempt here to engage with historical peoples on their own terms, without judgment or dismissiveness; whether it succeeded is a conversation for the historians in the audience (and AniFem would welcome an article when submissions are open!).

Jaadugar’s greatest strength, though, is the way it handles the complex relationships and perspectives of its cast, and especially its female leads. The series focuses on the marginalized people largely cut from the history books, exploring how women struggled to find agency in a world that treated them as pawns. The bond between Sitara and Töregene—two survivors determined to bring down the empire that robbed them of their homes—is especially affecting, and serves as the beating heart of the series.

The manga is ongoing and only at 6 volumes as of writing this review, so even if we get a season 2, it’ll be a while before there’s enough material for it. Still, even as an unfinished story, Jaadugar is worth your time as a grounded, gorgeous character-driven historical fiction.

—Dee

KAIJU GIRL CARAMELISE

Recommended by: Alex, Cy, Dee, Peter

What’s it about? Kuroe Akaishi wants to be a normal high school girl, but her rare condition that turns her into a Kaiju when she gets emotional makes that pretty impossible. On top of that, she’s got a crush on Arata Minami, the most popular boy in class, meaning that every case of butterflies in her stomach triggers a transformation. How’s a girl to survive when she can’t help but have a monstrous reaction to everything around her?! 

Content considerations: Nudity (typically non-sexual and post-monster-transformation); depictions of bullying and anti-fatness; jokes about unfeminine girls being ugly and/or looking like apes.

Now, why did this goofy series about a flustered teenager turning into Legally Distinct Godzilla make me cry multiple times?

In the words of some of the great poets of our time, it’s so confusing sometimes to be a girl. KAIJU GIRL CARAMELISE is a fun supernatural comedy and an adorable teen romance, for sure, but at its core is a heartfelt character arc about navigating the horrors of a female adolescence where your body is at odds with the ideal. 

For Kuroe, “normal girlhood” is a place she can visit but never live, its borders seemingly immutable. How can she perform this thing called femininity when she grows unladylike spikes and claws at the slightest provocation? How can she ask her crush to find her beautiful when her body is so monstrous?

Well, as Kuroe discovers slowly across the series, the trick is to find people who love you unconditionally and maybe even think your monstrous side is cool—but not in a shallow “just be yourself!” way. Kuroe’s anxieties and body image issues are never swept under the rug, even among all the escapism and comedy hijinks. I have an awful lot of feelings about her depiction and her development across this first story arc. I’ll also take this opportunity to recommend Sylvia Jones’ episode reviews, which read the series’ supernatural shenanigans as an allegory for being a trans woman, and make for an insightful companion piece to the show.

There are some messy elements: contrived jealousy and miscommunication tropes to keep the main couple apart, for example; and a running joke about a girl looking like an ape without her makeup on. (I get it, alright, she’s the King Kong to Kuroe’s Godzilla. It’s still fraught!) But ultimately I feel like Kaiju Girl has its heart in the right place, and brings all of its elements home for a really satisfying conclusion (for now, at least—fingers crossed for a second season!). 

If themes of girlhood and body image intrigue you, and/or if you want a rom-com where the female lead can pick up her love interest in the palm of her big scaly hand, definitely check this one out.

—Alex

You and I Are Polar Opposites

Recommended by: Alex, Chiaki, Dee, Peter

What’s it about? Suzuki’s a high schooler in love, but the object of her affections is her absolute opposite. Yusuke is quiet where she’s loud, stoic where she’s bubbly, standoffish where she wants to belong, and confident… where Suzuki’s not. But that won’t stop her as she tries to overcome her anxiety and just ask him out! 

Content considerations: Light-touch depictions of past bullying, harassment, and social anxiety; one male character has some incel-adjacent rhetoric about gender roles and “social status” that are annoying for a few episodes but quickly unlearned.

It can be difficult to articulate what makes a slice-of-life rom-com so good, because their appeal lies in the portrayal of such ordinary things. How am I supposed to explain why I found an animated hug so charming, or why I found a scene of teenagers hanging out at a convenience store so funny? This is the reviewing conundrum with Polar Opposites, a show that so beautifully depicts a candy-colored comedy version of deeply normal teen shenanigans.

The storytelling expertly balances silliness with sincerity and hits the nail on the head when it comes to the adolescent emotional landscape. All of its characters and relationships feel real at their core, even if their antics are obviously heightened for rom-com purposes. Everyone gets their own nuance, and no one gets stuck in stock roles as The Love Interest or The Cute Girl or The Sad Loner. One hundred gold stars for the handling of Miyu Suzuki, who a worse show would have written as a paper-thin gyaru love interest for the wish-fulfilment of quiet guys who relate to Tani. Instead, she leads her love story with real depth and real heart.

As the ensemble cast expands, the show unpacks a lot of contemporary issues and anxieties facing young people and the relationship dynamics between them. It manages to address things like the importance of communication, navigating jealousy and anxiety, and expressing desires and boundaries. Dare I say it models healthy relationships for its intended teen audience—but without feeling didactic or manufactured. 

If you want to laugh and go awww and enjoy some really solid character work all at once, I can’t recommend this show highly enough!

issues.author: Seth Burn
issues.content_html:
• Interview Location: New York Comic Con 2026
  • Interview Format: In-Person, One-on-One

Anime Herald: What do you do to mentally get into character to play Maomao?

Aoi Yūki: When I play Maomao, when I am in the recording studio, I think of myself as the percussion. I am the downbeat. I want to set the rhythm for the show so everybody can shine when playing their characters.

Anime Herald: What do you do to mentally get into character to play Jinshi?

Takeo Otsuka: I don’t have any particular prep. When recording in Japan, it is very much a team effort. I play off of other characters, and let other characters affect me. I try to listen very well to my scene partners. I try to hold space for my emotions to get affected by others.

Anime Herald: If Yuki-san is the downbeat, are you the upbeat?

Takeo Otsuka: Not Really (Laughs)

Anime Herald: You have described The Apothecary Diaries as a more lenient production. What did you and the rest of the cast do to earn the director’s trust?

Aoi Yūki: There are a lot of actors in this production. When I look at them, and I look at their characters, I feel like their souls are very close with their characters. The colors of their souls are so right, it’s so well cast in that way. There are a lot of new characters, having great places to shine in season three. When you look at the actor, you know which character they are playing. My guess is that the director knew that well enough to cast them in the right spots. That’s how they trust us. On my end, all I can do is work really hard to answer the call with the freedom they have given me.

Anime Herald: Jinshi’s humility hides just how high ranking he is. How do you manage to communicate the nuances of his character to the viewers?

Takeo Otsuka: When the director says that this is the place where you communicate what Jinshi is going through, or make it clear to the audience, I’ll do that. The great thing about this show is that it is very realistic. The characters’ reactions and actions are not so extravagant. I think that is why fans have an easy time connecting to the story and immersing themselves in this fantasy world.

As an actor, I would like to always listen to the director. Not to push it too much, or try to make this happen, but rather immerse myself in the environment and the plot that they are in to play and portray him as Maomao’s partner.

Anime Herald: “Originally, Jinshi was supposed to die. We figured if we killed him off, everyone would get mad so we decided to let him live. The original plan was to have Gaoshun kill him by throwing something at him. It would have been a very different story.” -Hyūganatsu

Why do you think Jinshi became so popular that he gained “plot armor?”

Aoi Yūki: From my point of view, when I look at Jinshi, I think about how too much of anything is a poison. Jinshi is the epitome of that. He is too beautiful. He is too high class. He has everything. That is the definition of “poison” in my mind. From my perspective Jinshi has the hardest time. He has so many struggles. That’s why all the fans, myself included, want him to survive. We are rooting for him because of that..

Takeo Otsuka: We have to check with Hyūganatsu-sensei. I’d be very curious what they would say to answer this question. We all root for Jinshi because he is so honest and direct. He’s a great person. As we move through the seasons and see his struggles, we connect to that and want to support him. That’s why everybody loves him. We’d have to ask Hyūganatsu-sensei how he got here. I think that is why he survived.

Anime Herald: Maomao is a natural born detective. Do you have a similar interest in deduction?

Aoi Yūki: Are you familiar with escape rooms?

Anime Herald: Yes.

Aoi Yūki: Escape rooms are very popular in Japan. I go, but I can never deduct and solve the clues. I end up doing different things to support the group. Someday, I would love to use my mystery solving skills to save my teammates.

Anime Herald: What does Yuki-san do to create a welcoming recording atmosphere?

Takeo Otsuka: She’s wonderful at creating a lively environment in the recording studio. All of the actors have been working together for quite some time now. We know each other very well and get along. We always talk about how we love the story and get inspired by it.

Sometimes, Yuki-san will talk about, “What is your favorite kind of car or truck? What type of construction vehicles do you like?” We’ll go with the flow and talk about stuff like that.

Anime Herald: What wisdom would you like to pass on to the next generation of seiyuu?

Aoi Yūki: Is this for American voice actors?

Anime Herald: Worldwide.

Aoi Yūki: I’ve worked on this show for three seasons. The one thing I think about daily is, there is this word “Tatedokoro” in Japanese. It asks, “Which word within the sentence is most important, what is the core?” I am always looking for the core word in every sentence.

If I can deliver that word, it will reach the audience’s ears very effectively. If I focus on that, the characters will become three-dimensional. The relationships, the relay of the information, will stand up. You can create three-dimensional scenes, if I am really focused on the core. Day to day, I am always thinking about “what is the emphasis, what is the core of each line?”

Anime Herald: That is a very good answer. Thank you.

Takeo Otsuka: Health. We need to stay healthy.

My voice is my instrument. I cannot be nasal. I cannot be hoarse. If I am hoarse, it will be a different character. Health is my #1 priority. For that, sleep is what supports it.

Anime Herald: Again, a very good answer. Thank you. 

The Apothecary Diaries Cast Talks With Anime Herald - Seth Burn

issues.title: Shingo Natsume’s Ghost And Madoka Magica: Walpurgisnacht Rising Shake Up The Status Quo For High-Profile Theatrical Anime
issues.summary: As high-profile anime films continue to trend toward faithful adaptations, Shingo Natsume’s Ghost and Madoka Walpurgisnacht Rising make it an explicit point to expose audiences to unique new ways to tell a story through animation. The landscape of theatrical anime is completely…
issues.author: kViN
issues.content_html:
As high-profile anime films continue to trend toward faithful adaptations, Shingo Natsume’s Ghost and Madoka Walpurgisnacht Rising make it an explicit point to expose audiences to unique new ways to tell a story through animation.

The landscape of theatrical anime is completely different than what it used to be merely a decade or two ago. In 2018, we happened to be present at an event with renowned film director Mamoru Hosoda, who expressed his worries about its future. In his view, what had been a nearly sacred environment led by people like Hayao Miyazaki was being encroached upon by an invasive species: seasonal anime spinoff movies. He may have sounded like a bit of an extremist at the time, but that doesn’t mean he wasn’t already making a solid argument that has been reinforced tenfold ever since.

Theatrical anime had, over its existence, developed a culture that felt distinct from TV projects. It’s worth noting that daytime, long-running franchise films encompassed the majority of offerings—and Hosoda would know that, since he had experience with them. Regardless, it’s undeniable that the idea of anime movie carried with it a greater focus on transformativeness, was supported by productions backed by ampler schedules and an effectively separate pool of talent, and had a purposefulness to the animation tied to the emphasis on actual acting. Even among those franchise films that weren’t necessarily as outstanding, staples like Doraemon or Shin-chan could skew much closer to that theatrical tradition than their TV origins, for reasons more meaningful than the sheer quantity of animation. Exceptions always existed in the form of serialized anime sharing similar sensibilities and teams, but generally speaking, there was more to these films than just being anime on a bigger screen.

For as important in defining the identity of anime as those iconic theatrical works were, depending on such select creative teams made them unsustainable in ways that the last few decades have tragically proven. Production IG classics became fewer and far between, as individuals like Mamoru Oshii shifted focus and their more direct heirs couldn’t establish themselves in the same way; look no further than Hiroyuki Okiura, by all means a household name when it comes to realistic animation, but so particular about his craft that we’re lucky if he can finish one project a decade. With the sad loss of Satoshi Kon, studio Madhouse’s evolution is similar—not a complete erasure of such projects, but a huge loss in prominence that can also translate into debilitatingly limited productions. Even Hosoda has broken what was once the steadiest theatrical production cycle and finds himself in an increasingly undeniable creative slump.

Above all else, it’s the gradual transition to a post-Ghibli paradigm that has changed what we understand as an anime film. While they continue to operate to some degree, and we’re not that far removed from The Boy and the Heron, they’re more of a brand than a fully active animation studio. The desperate attempts by the press to find The Next Miyazaki led to reductive readings of various creators, but no one can deny the humongous, Ghibli-shaped hole in the theatrical space. While you couldn’t take it for granted that there would ever be a straightforward replacement for one of the greatest creative hubs in anime history, there was a need for alternatives; perhaps less centralized, likely sporting different styles, but something that felt like it continued the tradition of a separate culture of theatrical animation. That is what Hosoda was afraid wouldn’t happen, and he was right to be.

Mind you, this isn’t necessarily criticism of the new faces in this space, nor the veterans who still populate it. While you can fault the aforementioned Hosoda for his recent stumbles, there’s no denying that he cares a lot about this field and has contributed to it like few have. As the most direct heirs of Ghibli, Ponoc employ brilliant artists with familiar sensibilities… but they’ve struggled to produce works through the methods that were only enabled through Ghibli’s sturdy fundamentals, and have also had a bit of an identity crisis from a creative standpoint. Relative newcomers like Naoko Yamada could one day hold a similar position to those iconic theatrical directors, but she has yet to commit in full to films. The most unarguable success in recent times is the commercial rise of Makoto Shinkai, but even he faces undeniable issues; more than any of his predecessors, he’s swayed and restricted by producer demands, slowing down his process and diluting what can already be a flimsy thematic intent.

The most notable aspect of this new era is that the floor of theatrical productions has collapsed. Just as important as the way that we now get an endless barrage of seasonal anime spinoff films—be it sequels, recaps, or side stories—is the fact that most anime movies now are made as if they were seasonal TV. They’re created by the same teams, often under conditions that aren’t all that much better, so it wouldn’t be fair to expect the qualitative bump in the delivery that filmgoers once expected.

Fortunately, it’s not all doom and gloom either. There is plenty of room for modest projects to beautifully convey a story, and despite all the trends to push anime toward faithfully reproducing something that already exists, there has been a recent upturn in fully original and thoroughly transformative films. Of course, this doesn’t mean a return to the previous status quo; for one, because it tends to happen along the margins, but most importantly, because the new players tend to have wholly different mindsets.

The irruption of directors like Kenji Iwaisawa and Kohei Kadowaki into the commercial field is bringing forth a wave of new, independent flavor. It’s perhaps even more encouraging that there are institutional pushes for unique films as well, with Shin-Ei Animation’s recent work (Totto-chan, Ghost Cat Anzu, Toritsukare Otoko, Peleliu, even the extended version of Milky Subway) being a fascinating mix of traditional and fresh sensibilities. The rise of new international collaborative partners like Miyu Productions is certainly helping diversify the anime portfolio. Even studio 4ºC, when they’re not too busy reinventing slavery, continue to push for radically idiosyncratic works. There is so much life in the periphery of theatrical anime, even in this era.

As positive as that is, there is inherent value in occupying the highest profile slots, in receiving wide critical attention and catching the attention of countless eyeballs. Even if they become a cult hit, those more modest films will struggle to earn a fraction of the spotlight of the new kings of the theatrical space. The biggest anime movies of the moment are no longer the domain of Miyazaki, who once ruled the box office with an iron fist. They’re also not films directed by critical darlings whose immediate box office numbers were quieter, but whose acclaim was so massive that their works were cemented as must-sees for everyone; think of the likes of Kon, Oshii, or Katsuhiro Otomo. With the notable exception of the aforementioned Shinkai, no current film can compete with extensions of seasonal megahits or older franchises reaching new heights. Again, this is not to imply that those can’t be excellent stylish movies like CSM Reze, nor that they can’t be technical achievements in the way the latest entry of Kimetsu was. But they are, by nature, conforming—potentially excellent films whose business isn’t to expose their viewers to new ways of telling a story with animation.

That aspect is something that two fascinating new films not only embody in their creative choices and motivations, but that has even been brought up by the artists behind them. After the international premiere of Ghost – end of night at the Sitges International Film Festival, director Shingo Natsume replied to a question about getting such a unique original film funded in the current industry, which no longer feels welcoming to the type of idiosyncratic voices we’ve been alluding to. Natsume was conscious that those conforming adaptations and spinoffs are all the rage now, but considered it an important challenge to create a capital-O Original film that would stick with people—whether they like it or not—and showcase it to as many viewers as possible; he even alluded to a potentially wide distribution, talking about more theaters than are currently listed. He’s very aware of the weight that his name still carries thanks to massive hits like One-Punch Man, and will happily use that to expose moviegoers to unique forms of art.

What’s so unusual about this film, though? Well, describing Ghost isn’t easy. You can look at it as a modern version of Jean-Luc Godard’s Alphaville, sharing similar worries about a techno-dystopia where supposed advancements have undermined our collective and individual agency. Its level of energy, though, is closer to the downtime in Oshii’s The Sky Crawler. And yet, it’s neither of those films—nor is it the direct, theatrical evolution of Sonny Boy that one might have expected. Mind you, that is unsurprisingly the anime it most resembles; of course that Natsume’s previous philosophical musings in a sci-fi package share DNA with his newest philosophical musings in a sci-fi package. However, from its relationship with the audience to their fundamental artistic choices, Ghost feels cut from a bit of a different cloth.

Due to the larger scope of the story, its episodic nature, and a premise that egged Natsume to imagine dozens of quirky worlds, Sonny Boy may appear like the more outrageous work of the two on paper. And yet, it was also quite the communicative series; its bending of space-time may have been hard to wrap your head around, its narrative beats were anything but conventional, but the show still looked at you in the eye and verbalized what was going on.

In contrast to that, Ghost is a quiet film that rarely faces the viewer; literally so, as there are a handful of wide shots where characters are obliquely seen in the background, having conversations that you’re not privy to. There is much going on in its world, but the film challenges you to piece it all together. While this may paint the picture of a completely inscrutable work, its beauty is that its core ideas are so tight that its message comes across clearly even if you miss many details about the convoluted plot. This amusing dichotomy is embodied by the way that Natsume himself talks about the film. Before the screening, he joked that it was a big struggle to make his team understand what the hell they were supposed to do. But at the same time, once the movie was over, he didn’t hesitate to say that he believes it to be a simple film—and I would agree with his judgment. Regardless of any obfuscation and all the complicated mechanics at play, Ghost is unquestionably about permanence and purpose.

The film presents a world where technology has advanced to the point where working isn’t needed. According to capabilities determined by that same tech, people are divided between the few elites driving society forward and the vast majority of needless humans. Through the automation of everything, the latter don’t have to work, as they’ll have access to food, housing, and key services regardless. And yet, plenty of them develop routines doing technically pointless tasks, often under the guidance of elite members. An overly literal read into this premise may seem like Natsume is implying that working is what makes us human, but that’s clearly not the director’s intent. At the Busan animation festival, he mentioned the impending destruction of jobs by AI and how that has repeatedly happened across history, noting that his interest is the ways people find to live in such times.

Our two main points of contact with that world are 15-year-old Neekei, an elite among the elite who protects the dead etched into stars, and a chill lesser citizen by the name of Mass. Neither of them sits comfortably in this dull dystopia; the former’s forms of resistance are initially akin to a gifted child lashing out, whereas Mass’ everyday departures from the world’s clinical norm are those of an adult carrying grief, one who’d rather not forget what it was to be human. Their meeting brings change to both—most visibly for Neekei—but if you expect this to be conveyed through explicit, loud and clear depictions of human emotion, you’ve shown up to the wrong film.

I believe there are two main reasons why such a tortured approach ends up working. For one, there is the fact that Ghost’s deadpan nature is very much by design. It feels natural for a heartless techno-dystopia to feel languid, especially in the way this film manages to blend that into the delivery. The camera itself appears detached, preferring wide, long shots. The tempo is slow and the direction can be cruelly uncaring; at one point in the film, a work accident kills a needless worker, with neither the characters nor the storyboard visibly acknowledging anything more than the need to clean up the floor. The film’s colors are more often than not muted, as is the usage of sound. There is a generally dispassionate, hard-to-read feeling to everything, which ties to the way that the characters themselves feel in a fascinating way.

Among the many futuristic inventions that define Ghost’s society, there is a widespread one that allows for lossless neural communication, making it so that you can perfectly convey your feelings to others. Useful as that may sound to some, this supposed convenience is rejected by the main characters. Just like the viewer, they must rely on reading the cues, which have also become hazier in a world that doesn’t exactly encourage expressivity. If you’re not entirely sure how they feel, worry not, you’re not alone; one of the most shocking scenes comes as Neekei catastrophically misreads Mass’ affection, something that would have never happened if either of them digitally transmitted their exact feelings. However, it’s in mistakes like this that the movie finds humanity.

The upside of such deliberate restraint is that the film’s occasional flares of intensity land even more strongly. Quiet as Ghost can be, its excellent soundtrack doesn’t hesitate to make itself known when it’s needed. Similarly, a more traditionally affective narrative thread involving cats can break the sterile routine. The muted palettes come to life as Neekei and Mass enjoy an afternoon together, with the storyboards themselves becoming more easily readable in moments when they connect.

When it comes to these dashes of liveliness, the MVP may be visual director (映像演出) Akane Fushihara. One of her known strengths as a director of photography is precisely accents—her ability, for example, to make effects animation dazzling without obscuring the core aesthetic of her shows. With Ghost, she has fine-tuned a look akin to the Boogiepop teaser that never was, but with a darker look to it, occasionally pivoting to the pleasant serenity you may find on Frieren instead. The most striking example of that ability to accentuate visuals, though, is Neekei herself. The protagonist works in the dark, but thanks to design choices like her bright eyeshadow (always coordinated with her stylish clothes!) and Fushihara’s processing, she stands out in memorable fashion.

Given Natsume’s pedigree, you may also be wondering about the animation itself. It comes as no surprise that it’s one of the most interesting aspects in Ghost, though not in the way many will be imagining. Gosei Oda earned himself the title of lead action animator, but as impressive as his work is, it’s mostly concentrated in one scene that hardly counts as exciting fun. While you may think that the focus of the production is instead on elaborate character acting, that would actually be a bigger misassumption. Following the same trend as every other aspect of its delivery, the animation of Ghost is often sterile and impenetrable, making it a point not to be overly expressive; as it should be, since we follow inexpressive characters in an expressionless world. Sakuga discourse is so obsessed with action that, conversely, any moving character who isn’t throwing a punch is said to be acting. In the same way you wouldn’t call a person who isn’t purposefully conveying something an actor, you shouldn’t do so with character animation. Ghost doesn’t only underline that, but also proves that stoicism can be pointed as well.

Mind you, dryness isn’t all there is to praise about Ghost’s animation. Natsume relied on Norifumi Kugai to adapt Natsume Ono’s original designs, following in the footsteps of ACCA: 13-Territory Inspection Dept. Although that makes the characters feel familiar, Ghost’s tone pushes them in a sharper, sleeker direction compared to the often affable feeling of their predecessors. Despite Natsume’s framing occasionally demanding to draw them in tricky angles, the polish is absolutely impeccable; something that could have pushed the animation in an overly stiff direction, but Kugai’s work retains some of his characteristic organic linework to balance things out.

In the age of ridiculously large armies of artists assembling anime, Ghost’s focused production stands out even more. The clarity of ideas is evident in how the qualities of the animation directly connect to every other stylistic precept, and its credits and schedule tell a similar story. Madhouse star animation producer Yuichiro Fukushi gathered a moderately sized team, made up of pretty much only his regular acquaintances. Even the small exceptions, like the few animators brought over from Takopi by ENISHIYA’s Kei Igarashi, are so familiar with this crew that they could understand Natsume’s tricky demands. This allowed them to have time to spare: the film wrapped up quite early in 2026, effectively a full year before the projected premiere.

If the navigation of restraint is one of the film’s greatest weapons, the other one is how on-point its choices of imagery and motifs are. In what Natsume described as a stationary road film, Ghost follows the two lead characters as they meet people who have found different answers to the question of what do you do when doing things isn’t required? For many individuals, this leads to a desire to leave something behind—a key idea embodied by many of these motifs. Neekei is in charge of a system that takes the common belief of the stars representing the dead and literalizes it, trying to maintain an idealized record of all who’ve passed. On the other hand, we have Mass choosing to leave a more physical imprint on himself, gradually covering his skin in tattoos. From burials that aren’t meant to happen to dancing routines, many people in that world choose an avenue to achieve permanence, to leave something to be remembered by. As eclectic as its ideas appear, the way this ties everything together makes the movie click into place.

It’s worth noting that, for such a unique film, Ghost is not the most visually outrageous anime by any stretch; it is unlike anything else, but it achieves that from a restrained angle rather than a loudly eccentric one. This is quite the contrast with Sonny Boy, which had plenty of tricks up its sleeve and was much more open about its artifice. The show would often exploit its picturesque art direction to abstract character layers into paintings, using the supernatural aspects of the story to toy with the assets. The one major exception in this film is the return of CG visual programmer Ryu “kezzardrix” Kanda, whose highlight is a climax reminiscent of his kaleidoscopic work in Sonny Boy’s finale. For the most part, though, Ghost is an unorthodox storytelling exercise relying on techniques that don’t read as radical on their own. If you flip those tendencies the other way around, you get Puella Magica Madoka Magica Walpurgisnacht Rising: a more traditionally told story on paper, given form through more overtly radical visuals.

We introduced Ghost through Natsume’s wish to expose more and more people to unorthodox art, and thanks to its daring style and 15 years of existence, Madoka is living proof of how valuable that is. Speaking to Famitsu, Walpurgisnacht main animator and visual concept designer Kazuki Kawata recalled how he felt when he saw the TV show in his youth. Above all else, what Kawata—and as he imagines, many other people—felt was huh, anime can do this? Within the context of studio SHAFT’s work, it’s not as if the series was a complete abnormality; in another recent interview, their president Mitsutoshi Kubota instead refers to it as the culmination of 00s SHAFT, since its core team was mostly composed of artists they’d gathered in that era. For many viewers, though, the sum of the studio’s quirky house style and the clinically deployed, unique collages by Gekidan Inu Curry were eye-openers. A decade and a half later, it’s now Kawata’s work—not just within the film, but also in additional material like the otherworldly key visual he drew—that will help broaden the horizons of younger viewers.

A reason why Madoka is particularly effective in that sense, in addition to its massive popularity, is its ability to regulate and sell its visual eccentricity. I don’t subscribe to the idea that any avant-garde technique must have an explicit justification any more than pedestrian ones do, but there’s no denying that seeing why an unorthodox choice has been made helps many people digest it. In that regard, there’s excellent affinity between Madoka’s central concept and its representative creators. Although the discourse about the show being a deconstruction back then was rooted in ignorance of the genre’s history, there’s no denying that it deliberately contrasted the cute and hopeful promise of magical girls with a much darker underside. In the same way that pairing Aoki Ume’s adorable characters with Gen Urobuchi’s ruthless script embodied that duality, so did Gekidan Inu Curry’s bewitching work all on its own.

In a previous write-up introducing the troupe’s origins and members, we explained how their influences sparked a wondrous but also eerie style. 2White Dog and Doroinu’s shared fondness for Czech puppet animation and filmmakers like Jan Švankmajer cultivated a trademark style characterized by its use of mixed media, twisting fairy tales and family-friendly imagery into the uncanny valley between creepy and cute. This is to say, the exact perfect register to depict Madoka’s witches: the wretched, grotesque forms of corrupted magical girls.

Had the show locked the viewer into Gekidan Inu Curry’s surreal dimension from the start, though, it may not have been the historic hit it became. Instead—and this very much continues into Walpurgisnacht—the direction led by Shinbo and Yukihiro Miyamoto has always excelled at modulating the idiosyncratic expressions to reinforce the narrative. While this may sound like common sense, it’s quite the contrast with the early stages in the career of SHAFT’s figurehead; it’s well-known that Madoka was conceived as a spiritual successor to Le Portrait de Petit Cossette, an OVA series where Shinbo places wild experimentation much higher in the priority list than tangible, explicit storytelling. If you intend to understand his evolution as a creator, no two works offer a clearer answer than these two sibling anime.

To be more specific, that regulation of eccentricities involves not just Gekidan Inu Curry’s work but the art direction as well. Even in its less magical corners, Madoka’s world was never all that concerned with strict realism. Turn your head around, and you’d come across an impossible pastiche of structures borrowed from every corner of the globe, complemented with all sorts of sleek neo-futuristic structures. A glance at the protagonist’s house alone told you enough about the way that its interior design defied logic, being more interested in symbolism than in making material sense; the very first conversation in the family bathroom was about confidence and the persona we ought to project outward, hence the endless mirrors. The same school that had come across as minimalistic could grow a gothic cathedral on the roof for a lavish recap film—again, depending on whether it was convenient to lean toward superficial, perhaps even fake peacefulness, or accompany the lead characters as they opened their eyes to a more hostile reality.

Despite bordering on surrealism with those architectural choices, the first stages of the TV show managed to cling to a sense of normalcy. After all, it was a collage of distinctly human environments, where we caught glimpses of regular people’s routines. Thanks to the concept of the witches’ labyrinths or barriers, Gekidan Inu Curry’s incomprehensible dimensions were clearly separated from the semblance of normalcy in regular scenes; again, a successful trick to acclimate broad audiences to unorthodox techniques. As the situation gradually worsened and grew more chaotic, what once were segmented oddities began to take over the entire screen. The 2013 film Puella Magi Madoka Magica: Rebellion picked up that trend in a calculated way; familiar stylizations in the corner of your eyes evoked a sense of dread, telling you that something was off and building to the reveal that everything was now inside the world of a witch.

What is Walpurgisnacht like on that stylistic level, then? Given the changes in the setting, the specific type of dark, stop-motion fairy tales we’ve come to expect from Gekidan Inu Curry aren’t as ever-present as they were in its predecessor; mind you, that was a film where they were absolutely everywhere. To make up for it, its radical artistry is more diverse in the choices of texture. Rather than having one go-to mode of surrealism, Walpurgisnacht can whimsically switch from the insertion of live-action footage we see in Kawata’s opening segment to the heavily industrial imagery brought over by a certain storyboarder and concept artist.

Even a specific concept like paper-cut animation can take clearly different forms, whether it’s the physical material we’d seen in previous iterations or f4samurai’s CG sequences also present in this film. This allows each type of supernatural being to have its own visual language, and feels representative of what Madoka has become. What once was a TV show with one expression of otherworldliness designed by Gekidan Inu Curry is now a more complex franchise, requiring 6 additional alternate space designers, multiple concept artists, and distinct pipelines to depict its world. If you feel nostalgic for those simpler days and familiar stylizations, though, worry not: a reveal about a certain character’s nature is accompanied by unleashing them back, turning it into one of the most satisfying moments in the film.

Given that this is a film that fans have waited an entire decade for, I’d rather not venture into spoiler territory—we can return to the movie again once it’s widely available anyway. That said, there’s no harm in pointing out that it’s an interesting follow-up that feels slightly held back by the very concept of a franchise. Madoka’s original TV series was all about hope, and by its ending, it made the executive choice to operate on a purely thematic level. It’s not as if it didn’t work as a character story, of course; the specific ways it developed a massive fandom demonstrate that it clicked in that way for many viewers. However, in choosing to culminate with the protagonist sacrificing herself to become the ideal of hope, its ending leaned heavily toward the conceptual.

The last thing you could accuse Rebellion of is being too objective and bereft of ideas, but as the title indicates, it was literally about characters rising up against an outcome that had been uplifting… on paper. But for them, as individuals? Of course there would be some lingering regrets, plenty of unfulfilled wishes; yeah, hers too. In particular, the insurrection that the film surprised everyone with in the final act still stands as one of the most fascinating, bold choices in an anime of this caliber.

Considering that history, it’s comforting that Walpurgisnacht doubles down on its predecessor’s stances, further developing them into a movie that is about salvation and selfhood. In attempting to do as much as it does, it certainly struggles to address all the returning characters. It has neither the tightness of the original show nor the self-contained potency of Rebellion, and it feels the cumbersome weight of being a franchise. And yet, it is a successful sequel, one that introduces new characters as vectors to explore these central ideas. It’s only once it has done so that it begins the ongoing process of interrogating the two lead characters, in a way that helps you understand why it both begins and ends with a call for help. Perhaps more than ever, it left me dying to know what will come next.

The way it wrestles with the idea of a sequel makes Shinbo’s choice of sole storyboarder feel particularly smart—make way for fan favorite Tomohiro Furukawa, of Revue Starlight fame. Back in Rebellion, this role went to a safer but admittedly quite fitting pick: Shinsaku Sasaki. He had been one of the most regular storyboarders in the TV show and is quite compatible with Shinbo’s more aggressive side, for what was a very intense film. Rather than looking for a similar comrade, this time they swerved hard into an individual they hadn’t worked with.

As I mentioned, however, there was plenty of reason to believe they were making a great choice. Revue Starlight was, for starters, a Madoka-conscious work; look no further than the black-haired transfer student privy to unsettling information, as well as the time loop shenanigans. As fellow Dezaki-inspired directors (through his master Kunihiko Ikuhara in Furukawa’s case), his style was going to feel at home as well. I believe that what makes it fully click is the thematic links between the theatrical sequels for both series. Urobuchi has admitted to struggling to follow up a TV show conceived as a self-contained work, and the path he eventually found has involved the characters themselves opposing the original thesis. Similarly, the Revue Starlight film is about the very concept of a sequel, about the self-immolation of the artist who can’t help but step into a new stage. And again, in doing so, it directly confronted the idealism of the TV show.

It’s worth pointing out that, because Walpurgisnacht is a movie that subverts expectations and isn’t afraid to ruffle some feathers, social media campaigns have been quick to manufacture staff controversies. While it has mostly been about Urobuchi’s role, something he has been very honest about, fingers have also been pointed at a potential rift between Furukawa and the studio. While the former did joke that (because of Shinbo’s corrections) people couldn’t have guessed he boarded the film if he went under a different name, that is a perfectly natural occurrence that has little to do with the aspects that have upset some viewers.

Although few regularly take it to the extremes we can see under Shinbo, it is the job of a chief director to revise storyboards if need be, and near full redraws happen more often than is made public—understandably so, since it’s a touchy subject for everyone involved. Upon first watch, Walpurgisnacht came across as a fluctuating film: entire sections came across as essentially unfiltered Furukawa work, best seen in the staging of a certain fight in the skies, while in others the cadence and posing make Shinbo’s presence rather clear. I can see why this might have saddened a director with a vision as precise as Furukawa’s, but I believe it made for an ultimately more interesting hodgepodge.

Of course, neither film is beyond reproach. Deliberate as it may be about its choices, Ghost places itself in a somewhat contradictory position in regard to the audience. Its mystique is alluring, and ultimately, its intent comes across with surprising ease. However, it’s undeniable that it demands the viewer to sit and digest the film carefully, with certain aspects—especially in regard to the mechanics of the narrative—feeling like they’re meant to be absorbed through repeated watches. And yet, it’s also a daring film that embraces the emotional distance in the society it depicts, then projects it to the audience. Without definite storytelling hooks in the traditional sense and with an often-dispassionate ring to it, it makes quite the gamble in expecting you to care enough to give it the time it needs. Which, for the record, I was delighted to do; so much so, that I’ve been craving an opportunity to watch it again since the day of the international premiere.

Similarly, Walpurgisnacht offers plenty of angles for criticism. Chief among them all is the lack of finality, which feels uncharacteristic of Madoka. While other areas where it subverts expectations come across as purposeful, bold stances, this new film’s transitional nature feels subservient to the financial needs of what is now a fully established franchise. The original TV show was structured like an ultimate message of hope, not meant to be followed up upon. In a way that Urobuchi himself jokingly refers to as cheating, Rebellion managed to formulate a reply that felt equally definitive; sure, its epilogue left a door open that Walpurgisnacht has capitalized, but the film would have never felt like an incomplete piece if it hadn’t been followed up on. In contrast to that, this new entry not only leaves you with a bona fide cliffhanger, but also can’t shake off the feeling that it’s merely the first half of a larger sequel package. A fascinating one so far, yet one that doesn’t stand on its own with the same aplomb Rebellion did.

Flaws and all, Ghost and Walpurgisnacht take the wildly unique irreverence that we tend to see limited to the sidelines onto the grand stage. While these two films won’t change the norms for high-profile anime movies in the current era, let alone turn back the clock and restore the theatrical standards of old, the ecosystem is healthier when there’s space for artists to rampage around like this. We’ve seen how the creators behind them believe that doing so can broaden the horizons of the audience, perhaps even encourage them to become daring artists as well. I believe they make a good point, but even beyond such broad goals, there’s a more immediate charm: it’s films like this that make going to the cinema surprising, so we should treasure them.

issues.title: 2026 Fall Premiere Digest
issues.summary: While this autumn doesn't offer as bountiful a harvest of anime as earlier in the year, there are still hopefully some series to look forward to. The post 2026 Fall Premiere Digest appeared first on Anime Feminist.
issues.author: Anime Feminist
issues.content_html:
While this autumn doesn’t offer as bountiful a harvest of anime as earlier in the year, there are still hopefully some series to look forward to.

Which shows do you review? 

We don’t review shows that are direct sequels, shorts, or (generally) for very young children. Anything not licensed and/or immediately available is off the table as well; series that are dropped in batches (the binge/Netflix model) won’t receive are a premiere review but are eligible for recommendations at end of season. Shows with late release dates will be reviewed separately from the digest.

While shows may change category as they continue to air, for ease of reference this is the order that will be used when discussing shows on our mid-season and wrap-up podcasts. Please note that any shows released in batches/by cour rather than weekly will not be discussed on the mid-season podcast.

How do you write the reviews?

Lizzie, Alex, Vrai, Cy and Tony split the majority of shows, with Chiaki and Dee stepping in to pinch-hit. The titles were divided by each reviewer’s preferred workload and choice. Caitlin is at ANN for seasonal work, so you can check out her reviews over there.

Once we have more funding, we’d like to change our current model to provide a wider range of perspectives on more episodes. We’re a long way from that goal, but it’s been a personal wish of ours since launch and we hope to make it happen someday.

What do your reviews focus on? 

This varies by writer to some extent (some of us are more focused on visuals, others on narrative, and so forth), but as a feminist site it’s of course essential that we raise any issues of intersectional feminist interest.

When you read an AniFem review, you’re likely to learn about female character designs, queer representation, analogies to real-world marginalization, and so on. If you think we missed something, please comment under the review and let us know!

Why do you categorize them?

The purpose of these reviews is to give you, our readers, information to help you decide if you want to try a show. There’s greater access to anime than ever before, and we want to help you find series you can truly love, without wasting your time on a show that contains an automatic deal-breaker, be that fan service, queerphobia, the sexualization of children, and so on.

Individuals can find value in any series, and we will never lead a boycott of a particular show, but we want to make it easier for you to get the most out of your limited time. In our digest, feminist-relevant themes and ideas take precedence, with overall narrative quality coming second and personal preference a distant(ish) third.

Premieres that seem to contain progressive themes are at the highest end and those featuring regressive ideas (or out-and-out hatefulness) are at the lowest. We expect some disagreement and welcome debate, so if you have any objections to our lists then by all means let us know in the comments!

issues.title: Talking GalaXic Baseball with Acky Bright at NYCC 2026
issues.summary: Anime Herald: I overheard that you’re a fan of Spider-Man. Do you know what baseball team Spider-Man roots for? Acky Bright: I don’t know off the top of my head, but in chapter six there will be a spider-ish character coming in to play. Anime Herald: Got it. Just to share…
issues.author: Seth Burn
issues.content_html:
• Interview Location: New York Comic Con 2026
  • Interview Format: In-person, One-on-One

Anime Herald: I overheard that you’re a fan of Spider-Man. Do you know what baseball team Spider-Man roots for?

Acky Bright: I don’t know off the top of my head, but in chapter six there will be a spider-ish character coming in to play.

Anime Herald: Got it. Just to share, Spider-Man roots for the New York Mets. The same team Kingpin roots for.

You’ve been working on the GalaXic Baseball League manga for quite some time. Can you share the backstory?

Acky Bright: This was a few years ago. It was originally an idea from the MLB Players Association. They had their IP and wanted to do something. Two years later, we have this, but there were a lot of contracts to be signed in that time. For them it was their stage one of a big IP. Now, after all of the contracts, we finally have the manga.

Anime Herald: Roughly how many issues do you think the manga will run?

Acky Bright: With the current tournament, I foresee it being about five volumes. But, that is just the tournament. That’s not getting into the league. We can think of the tournament arc as season one. There is the potential for season two and season three once we get into the league. If people keep buying it, I will keep writing it.

Anime Herald: I am curious about something. The GAIA on the player’s uniforms is crisp and clear. On the poster for the tournament, it is not. What was behind that decision? Did you want to show how run down it was?

Acky Bright: When we first see team GAIA, it’s very run down. Luna comes in to do a full renovation. The poster is handwritten. When we first meet team GAIA, they are the underdogs. Once Luna comes in, there is a full refresh.

Anime Herald: Who was your favorite player to draw? It could be from any team, it doesn’t have to be team GAIA.

Acky Bright: That is always a hard question. In general, I would say the characters who are fun and it is easy to express their movements. A lot of the times, the characters that make it to cover are like that. But honestly, I need to have love for all of my characters. I have leanings, but I can’t point to a specific character.

Anime Herald: I can say Kiba is my favorite character. I was very sad when he gave up the home run.

Acky Bright: It makes me happy that you already have a favorite.

Anime Herald: What would you like our readers to know about the GalaXic Baseball League?

Acky Bright: If you love baseball and are an MLB fan, it is very easy to get into it. But, I also want people who don’t know baseball, people who might not have watched a game in their entire lives, to know that this is also for them. As a manga artist, I have those folks in mind. To make it accessible for everyone.

I also wanted to make it accessible specifically for kids who love baseball. I’ve kept them in mind.

Anime Herald: Given the popularity of (Shohei) Ohtani-san, how much did you have to resist making him a main character?

Acky Bright: I actually do treat everyone equally. When I think about Ohtani, he wouldn’t want to be the star here. It’s baseball, it’s a team sport. Naturally, from game to game, the hero of each game is going to change. Everyone gets to be a main character during the games. As I am writing the story, there are times I am surprised at who becomes a hero throughout the storytelling.

You saw that the players have the powered suits. They’ll have special abilities that will emerge. José Ramírez is the first one. I hadn’t planned that. That was something that occurred naturally once I was telling the story. Once these characters start moving, they take on their personality and tell me what the story is. That’s when it is really fun and interesting for myself, and the audience. I don’t know what to expect. Currently, they are down by ten runs. What is going to happen next? I don’t know, and neither does the audience. The characters will tell me.

Anime Herald: As someone known primarily as an artist, how did it feel to be able to flex your writing muscles?

Acky Bright: As a writer and storyteller, I’d actually already been doing that. I think this is probably a unique way of living life. With this work, and all of the other past works in my mind, I’ve always been thinking like a mangaka from the get go. Doing this has felt natural for me. It’s a muscle that has always been there.

Anime Herald: Do you have any questions for us?

Acky Bright: We’ve had a long relationship. You know me, I know you. I want to ask you, as this is my first manga, what do you think?

Anime Herald: I know what I hope will happen. It doesn’t have to do with which team wins. I just want you to lean into the wackiness. Like when the ball smashes through the huge glove. Keep it wacky.

Acky Bright: I’m glad you pointed that out, because that is exactly why I wanted to write this manga. To have those wacky crazy moments. You know my work. I think I will meet your expectations in the future.

You’ve been following me since before anyone in the US knew me. For you to say that, that’s something I will always keep in mind. This relationship is very big for me. Thank you for following me from the very beginning. I will think about that input and folks like you as I keep writing the manga.

Anime Herald: Thank you.

issues.summary: #​495 — October 30, 2026 Read on the Web React Status Putting MUI, Mantine, Ant Design and React Spectrum Under Load Den Odell wanted to see how popular design systems cope when you give them real work, so he timed ten of them, including MUI, Mantine, Ant Design and React…
issues.content_html:
#​495 — October 30, 2026

Read on the Web
 React Status

Putting MUI, Mantine, Ant Design
and React Spectrum Under Load

Den Odell wanted to see how popular design systems cope when you give them real work, so he timed ten of them, including MUI, Mantine, Ant Design and React Spectrum, and profiled the slowest cases. "Performance belongs on the design system team's priority list, next to accessibility," he says. Some highlights:

  • 📊 With the CPU slowed 4x, opening a 249-country dropdown took 84ms in Mantine and 134ms in Ant Design, but over 200ms in MUI and React Spectrum, both of which froze the UI past his 100ms budget.

  • 🔍 React Spectrum's problem was React Aria measuring options one at a time and forcing layout for each. Den filed an issue and a fix is in review.

  • ⚖️ Framework alone didn't decide the results as non-React Ionic was by far the slowest to open (1,266ms) yet was quick at checking 100 checkboxes, while MUI handled them in 70ms compared to Ant Design's 421ms.

  • 🧪 Want to try this on your own components? Den's Playwright tests are available on GitHub.

Agentic Mobile Development Needs Mobile AI Infrastructure — Your agent writes mobile screens fast. Getting them built and into the App Store is where it stalls. Expo is mobile AI infrastructure: native builds, store submits, over-the-air updates and workflows your agent can run. Start free.

Expo sponsor

TanStack Redact: A Smaller React for the Browser — A drop-in replacement for React/React DOM in the browser. Add it to your build config (Start, Vite, Vinext and Next.js are supported) and ship less JavaScript. But it renders synchronously, with no time slicing, so the compatibility guide is handy.

Tanner Linsley

💬 Does Redact pay off? On r/reactjs, commenters pondered who needs it and how it differs from Preact, while one tester found re-renders cost about twice the CPU across two production sites.

IN BRIEF:

  • ⚠️ Next.js has a security release scheduled for November 3, fixing seven medium-severity vulnerabilities. Advisories will be published with the patches.

  • Dan Abramov is fuzzing React's Flight protocol, the format behind Server Components, by streaming random value graphs through the real server and client. It's turned up six stream bugs and three writer bugs so far.

  • TanStack AI 1.0 is stable: a vendor-neutral AI toolkit with React hooks like useChat(), 23 provider adapters and MCP support.

  • 📱 React Native Windows 0.85 completes its move to the New Architecture, and there's more React Native on the desktop with Expo Desktop (an independent project – not by Expo) and Legend Spark for macOS.

React.lazy, Suspense and the Hidden 300ms Startup Delay — A lazy component can suspend on its first render even when its code is already loaded, and React can throttle reveals of suspended content to once every 300ms. Here's how one team traced the delay, and what fixed it.

Matthew Wong (Tab Widgets)

TanStack DB 1.0 RC1, and How 'Oracles' Found Its Bugs — The reactive client data layer is now API stable, but check the migration guide, as mutation handlers, hooks and errors have changed. Kyle explains how agents, checked against simple reference models, found many of the bugs fixed.

Kyle Mathews (TanStack)

🤖 Ship Less JavaScript in Next.js with Your AI Agent – A new skill hunts bundle bloat using Turbopack's module graph. Will Binns-Smith (Vercel)

📄 Porting 287,000 Lines of React to Foldkit in 3 Days – Focuses on how they built a harness to ensure visual and behavioral parity. David Granzin (Maple)

📄 Async React and Progressive Server Actions – How to keep server action forms working before hydration, even with optimistic UI. Jacob Ebey

📊 React Compiler in Next.js 16.4: Babel vs Rust, Benchmarked Waseem Anjum

🛠  Code, Tools & Libraries

Puck 0.24: The Visual Page Editor for React — A drag-and-drop page editor you embed in your own app, using your own components. 0.24 lets you lay out a component's settings panel as you wish, improves drag and drop, and more. GitHub repo.

Fede Bonel Tozzi

react-window 2.5: Virtualized Lists That Scroll with the Page — Brian's long-standing virtualization library adds a scrollElement prop, so lists/grids can scroll along with the page or an ancestor, plus a headless useVirtualizer() for building your own virtualized layouts. Docs and demos.

Brian Vaughn

Vinext 1.4: The Vite-Powered Next.js Reimplementation Gets Faster — A Vite plugin that reimplements the Next.js API so you can deploy anywhere. 1.4 focuses on performance, with a Hacker News clone example now using 43% less server CPU per request vs 1.3, putting it slightly ahead of Next.js in that test.

James Anderson

  • OpenTUI 0.8 – Terminal UI library with React bindings that powers OpenCode. Now repaints only what changed each frame.

  • React Hook Form 7.91 – Lots of useFieldArray and async validation fixes, plus fewer re-renders. v8 is also now at beta 5.

  • React-Toastify 11.2 – Popular toast notification library. Now with theme="auto" to follow the OS color scheme.

  • emoji-picker-react 5.1 – Full-featured customizable emoji picker. Live demo.

🎃  And finally…

Halloween is almost upon us, so how about a round of Graveyard Pinball? It's built with React Three Fiber, with skulls, cauldrons and a skeleton mage. Its creator explains more about how it works here, including how the 3D table actually uses 2D physics.

issues.summary: The producer (and William Greaves’s granddaughter) speaks with the filmmaker about the newly resurrected portrait of the Harlem Renaissance
issues.author: Michael Blair
issues.content_html:
The producer (and William Greaves’s granddaughter) speaks with the filmmaker about the newly resurrected portrait of the Harlem Renaissance

  • Apple Podcasts
  • Spotify
  • Amazon Music
  • Audible
A standout of this year in films, Once Upon a Time in Harlem is an extraordinary feat of resurrection. In 1972, the director William Greaves gathered luminaries of the Harlem Renaissance at Duke Ellington’s house in New York for a party and then filmed their lively conversations—spanning history, politics, and culture. That footage lay in the archives until recently, when William’s son David (credited here as co-director) and granddaughter Liani Greaves (producer), along with producer and editor Anne de Mare, restored and restitched it into an exquisite time capsule that offers a doubly retrospective portrait of Black America—allowing us, the audience of 2026, to witness a gathering from half a century ago of artists who themselves were reflecting on events they lived through another half-century prior.

For this week’s episode, Film Comment Editor Devika Girish spoke with Liani Greaves and filmmaker Barry Jenkins about the making and significance of the film and the immense and unparalleled legacy of the late, great William Greaves.

This story is part of the Fall 2026 issue of Film Comment.
