issues.title: KPop Demon Hunters’ Saja Boys Talk With Anime Herald at NYCC 2026
issues.summary: "I think it goes back to the cultural authenticity. There are so many global fans, even Korean Americans, that are so American that they are not intertwined with the culture from the motherland. Things that the global audience connects to are authentic, and they don’t even know…
issues.author: Seth Burn
issues.content_html:
• Interview Location: New York Comic Con 2026
  • Interview Format: In-person, Roundtable

Unknown Outlet: How did you get involved with the movie (KPop Demon Hunters)? This is a little bit of a different role for you.

Rich Ting: I’ve been an actor and producer in Hollywood for over twenty years. That has allowed me to explore a lot of different paths in the business. So, what am I doing here, why am I associated with KPop Demon Hunters? I opened up a production company, and one of the verticals is talent management. I’ve been able to work in Korea on the acting side. Through that, I have great connections with the KPop world.

One of my first films in 2010 was with the #1 KPop artist, BoA. BoA is associated with SM Entertainment. They are the founding company of KPop in Korea. With my network there, I was able to get into contact with Andrew Choi, the lead singing voice of Jinu. I was able to plug him into some different projects I was involved with. That evolved into a manager-talent relationship. I now represent Andrew and Neckwav. Through that experience, I’ve been with Andrew since before when Huntrix debuted.

I know Maggie (Kang), I’m friends with a lot of the voice actors and actresses. I’ve seen this evolution of this global phenomenon. Through that, I’ve been next to them throughout this entire process. For me, it has been a phenomenon. Going from someone who stood in front of the camera, trying to express and share my culture through all of the roles I’ve played, where we never had a seat at the table. Trying to provide the audience a glimpse of what I’m about, what my culture is about. I’m Chinese/Japanese, and a fourth-generation American. That’s confusing right there, because I look like this.

Now, the fans want it. They are demanding culture, they are demanding K-this, K-that. To me, it is mind-blowing, to see the 180. Before we were asking to tell them a bit more about our culture. Now the fans are saying that they want it. It’s been fantastic to have a first-person view for this journey.

The Culture Collective: What went through your mind seeing KPop represented on the Oscar stage and seeing audiences around the world connect with these characters?

Rich Ting: Two things. One, like I just mentioned, it is going from the late ‘90s, early 2000s, even mid-2000s. We had no seats. When I say “we,” I’m talking about Asian and Asian-American leading men. We didn’t have seats at the table. We were trying to convince people that we could play a role. We could play a police officer, we could play a firefighter.

I grew up in California. I’ve seen Asian-American first responders. I’ve obviously seen Asian-American dads, husbands, boyfriends. But yet, we never fulfilled those roles on TV or in movies. And if those roles ever were available back in the day, they went to Asia and got whoever was the biggest superstar in Hong Kong at that time. They never looked in their backyard.

Seeing a movie like KPop Demon Hunters, where it’s the flip. Now the fans demand it. They want it. I’ll give you a quick anecdote on the side. I do a ton of voice acting, as well. From animations, to TV shows, to movies, as well as dubbing. I can speak Korean, even though I am not Korean. I speak Chinese, I speak Japanese. I would think, as an Asian-American voice actor, that you would want some authenticity with the accent. We can speak in a Western American accent in English, but then when you say a certain word, you would want to hear it the way it’s authentically pronounced. But now, a lot of streamers will say, “No, we want it in a Western American accent.”

That’s fine. We’ve gone from that, which was painful to say, to the point where we are now revisiting shows I’ve done years ago. We’re not only saying it with an accent, but we’re replacing the English words with the actual words in that language. What I mean by that is we’re calling Korean foods by their real names. We’re not saying “rice porridge.” The global audience doesn’t know what that is. But they know what the Korean word is.

To me, to see that happen in front of me, and with me being the person who did the original version. Now, I am going back to remix it. It’s mind-blowing. I think it all stems from being authentic. And I know that word is overused. Instead of trying to conform, trying to be more Western, it’s gone in the opposite direction where we’re just going to be true to our culture. That is what has sold.

SWO Productions: Was there a moment you realized it was going to be the phenomenon it ended up becoming?

Rich Ting: Having been on a few Netflix productions myself, I kind of know the behind the scenes, regarding the press, the media, the marketing side. Whether it is HBO, whatever. When word got out that they were going to release it on the platform, I had an instinct, “This is either going to be crazy in a good way, or it is going to be a failure.” I don’t think that was strategic. I think it was one hundred percent budget related.

I’ve seen it with other shows. If you talk to Andrew (Choi), if you talk to Neckwav. If you talk to Arden Chow, the voice actress for Rumi, she’s a good friend of mine, they all tell the same story. They had no idea. If anything, I can speak for my artists Andrew and Neckwav, they kind of forgot about it. They did the recordings, they did these catchy songs, and then they forgot about it.

Neckwav will tell you a story. He didn’t even know which character he was playing until it got released. They wouldn’t tell him. They told him he had pink hair. Well, there are two characters with pink hair. He had to watch the film to see which character was his based on the music.

No one had an expectation. If we think back to last year, Huntrix didn’t debut until October of last year. The film was released in June. They weren’t ready to debut. It was a cultural phenomenon.

(Editor’s note: I believe he was referring to the Jimmy Fallon interview as the debut of Huntrix.)

BET/Hot 97: What do you think KPop Demon Hunters understands about KPop culture that made it resonate with people who aren’t traditional KPop fans?

Rich Ting: I touched on it a little bit earlier. I think it goes back to the cultural authenticity. There are so many global fans, even Korean Americans, that are so American that they are not intertwined with the culture from the motherland. Things that the global audience connects to are authentic, and they don’t even know that it is authentic. I’ll give you a perfect example.

There are a group of old women in the film. They are fans. In Korean, they are called ajummas. These fans exist. I have a lot of personal friends who are huge idols in Korea. I’ve been to their concerts, I’ve been on stage with them. There is a front row of these women, who are probably in their sixties or older. They are diehard fans. The fact that they are able to put this demographic into an animated film and give them this representation that really is there. We laugh and think they are cute. They’re real. The food is real.

I’ll give you another example. The manager. That’s a manager. When I saw the character, I started laughing because my manager in Korea is identical. I’m not trying to be racist or stereotypical. I’m just saying he looks identical to my manager. All of these things are so real, but no one knows. There’s some kind of emotional connection that exists that’s based on the realness of it.

Anime Herald: Rich told us a story that you did not know who you were playing in the movie until you saw the movie. Can you elaborate on that?

Neckwav: I did not. When I was recording “Soda Pop” and “Your Idol”, the musical director for the movie was kind enough to explain the plot and he said, “You’re the guy with the pink hair.” But there are two pink-haired Saja Boys, Romance and Abby. For the longest time, when I was recording the song, I thought I was Romance. I was wondering, “Why am I not synching with audio and visuals? Oh, nevermind, I’m the guy with the abs.”

When the movie first came out I was trying to see who I was, “Oh, I’m the dude with the abs, making people’s eyes turn into popcorn.” It was amazing. I can’t complain, I love it.

Unknown Outlet: What has the movie done for your singing career?

Neckwav: I started off as a singer, trying to make my way into becoming an artist. That didn’t work out when I first started off. I switched my career into being a songwriter for KPop. All of these boy bands and girl groups were selling out stadiums, selling records. That helps songwriters survive. The movie opened up so many doors as a songwriter.

“You’re the voice of Abby?” They recognized the voice. Maybe another songwriter was writing a song and thought that my voice might be a good fit. That opened up a lot of doors. My own music, as well. Fans are digging through the music I released years ago. Now, I am releasing more of my music. They want to hear more of Abby, so I am trying to get them into my music as well. I plan to release more singles in the future.

The Culture Collective: Has the success of KPop Demon Hunters and your experience with it changed you as an artist or influenced the music you are making now?

Neckwav: Absolutely! It feels like I am repeating myself, but as a songwriter, you can’t complain about the genre you are making. You get leads from companies. The genres we make have to be tailored to their tastes. What we make is what they want. I realized that, since I’ve been both singing and rapping, the fans loved the deeper voice of Abby, so maybe that appeals more than my singing voice of Abby. I’ve been trying to aim for the “Your Idol” moment from the beginning of the song, as well as my verse in “Soda Pop.” Trying to see what they like, not necessarily what I like.

SWO Productions: What is the difference to you between doing voice over work versus your singing work? Did you have to adjust anything versus your regular procedure?

Neckwav: Absolutely. Normally, I would not be in a room with many people when recording. Usually, a producer who wrote the beat, and a couple of songwriters. A maximum of four or five people in the room. I don’t feel that pressure. But when I recorded for KPop Demon Hunters, Ian (Eisendrath) and the team were all in New York. There were maybe ten to fifteen people listening to me sing. That was nerve-wracking in the moment. At the same time, usually I am singing songs I wrote, so I know where to go. I can just take the key and drive.

Singing, rapping, and recording under Ian’s direction was amazing. I could see his vision, where he wanted us to go. That was amazing, getting direction from someone who has been in the industry, did amazing work for movies. This was my first movie ever. It was my first voice-acting and singing role. It was a whole new experience that changed everything that I am doing right now. It’s been really fun.

BET/Hot 97: Do you think the success of the Saja Boys says something about where pop culture is heading next?

Neckwav: Absolutely. I’ve been receiving leads from different big companies, like SM Entertainment, JYP Entertainment, HYBE. They are sending out leads where the reference songs, the guidance, includes our songs. People want more of “Your Idol” and “Soda Pop.” That’s been a change.

People are trying to imitate the sounds and the looks of the Saja Boys. It’s been amazing to see.

Anime Herald: What is your origin story? How did you get from there to being a Saja Boy?

Neckwav: Oh wow… I started to take my musical career seriously in 2017, 2018. I came back to Korea. I had been here for college. I came back to Korea around that time, right before COVID. I was working very closely with a Korean singer named Johan Kim, shout out to him. He was very good friends with one of the producers for KPop Demon Hunters. She urgently called him, “Do you know anyone who sings and raps in Korean and English? I need him now.”

I heard that there were so many last minute changes. I didn’t hear the details. I was just told to record “Soda Pop” and “Your Idol” to audition for this. They wanted to hear my voice. Ian really liked my voice. He had me come in and record. I recorded for six or seven hours. Then I forgot about it, because it was a year before the movie came out. I was singing to stick figures. This was before the animation.

When the movie came out, my Instagram started blowing up. Next thing you know, I’m here at New York Comic Con. I was at San Diego Comic Con. It’s been incredible.

Unknown Outlet: Is there a moment that stands out as the most surreal? The Oscars or Comic Con?

Neckwav: The Oscars was something I still cannot fathom to this day. That I was on the same escalator with these celebrities that I’ve watched in movies from my iPad. Like, “What is going on in my life right now?”

It started off when I was shopping in a store in Korea with my mom. Someone stopped me and asked, “Are you one of the Saja Boys?” Surprisingly, KPop Demon Hunters is not as big here as it is in Korea. It was amazing to see. My mom asked, “Are you something big now?” I said, “I guess. I’m going to the Oscars in March.” She asked, “Wait, is this the same Oscars that we know? I said “Yes, the Oscars.” Then I went.

I think those are the two experiences that stick with me. Andrew (Choi) and I still talk about it “Did we really go to the Oscars?” It was an amazing experience.

The Culture Collective: Has this experience with voice acting changed you? Do you want to pursue more of it?

Neckwav: Absolutely. I think the reason that KPop Demon Hunters was such a huge success was the songs. They were that good, starting with “Golden” and “Soda Pop.” I think the movie and the songs worked together. I would love to be part of a movie with musical elements involved. To be completely honest, I’m a terrible actor. I’ve never tried voice acting, but in my opinion I don’t think I would be good at voice acting. But, I would love to give it a try.

Andrew and I were talking about it, “Maybe we should audition for movies with more musical elements.” We could sing and voice act at the same time. I believe Baby Saja (Danny Chung) has the same singing and acting voice. He had “Goo goo” and “gaga” lines. If it is that easy, maybe I can give it a try for a role in the future.

SWO Productions: Who are some of your musical inspirations?

Neckwav: That is so difficult. I started off listening to a lot of hip-hop and rap. I went to middle school in San Diego. The West coast hip-hop influence has been deep on me. It started with Dr. Dre and Snoop Dogg. Then, I went to high school in Boston, so there were East coast influences there. Then I went to college in Atlanta, so there was the Southern experience.

By the time I was in college I had gotten into R&B, so artists like Brian McKnight. Old school R&B artists. And all of the great KPop artists that are out there now. It’s hard to name one artist.

BET/Hot 97: If you had to explain the Saja Boys phenomenon, what would you say?

Neckwav: I would have to say it is an interesting KPop boy band that tries to take your soul by looking and sounding so good. They finally reveal their identities as demons with a darker song. They just have two songs. One bubbly, bright song that makes you think of them as a regular boy band. Then later, they reveal themselves as demons trying to take your souls. I would say they are a boy band with two faces.

Anime Herald: Did you know Andrew before the movie?

Neckwav: Yes. I’ve been a fan of Andrew’s since I was in college. He was in a show called KPop Star, which is like an American Idol for Korea. He was top three. I’ve practiced my singing listening to him. He’s been my go to singer that I’ve listened to. He’s had so many great KPop cuts before the movie. I think he was the only one I knew of, but I didn’t know any of them personally.

KPop Demon Hunters’ Saja Boys Talk With Anime Herald at NYCC 2026 - Seth Burn

issues.title: DD412 / Breaking up with Gmail
issues.summary: Issue 412: Breaking up with Gmail – Read the full issue in the archive.
issues.author: Kai Brach
issues.content_html:
On a visit to Google’s HQ in Mountain View in 2007, I watched people run almost their entire working lives out of a browser. Gmail was still new-ish, and the Googlers I met were doing clever things with labels, aliases and filters that made my Outlook setup look like an old filing cabinet.

When Google started offering a paid Gmail version with custom domains, I made the move and Gmail slowly became the app I spent most of my days in. Docs, Sheets and Google Maps followed.

By the time I started feeling uneasy about Google, I was thoroughly entangled. The thought of dragging hundreds of thousands of emails somewhere else, and giving up some of Gmail’s then-unique features, sat in the too-hard basket for almost a decade.

But earlier this month, a friend reminded me of the EFF’s Opt Out October, and that finally gave me the nudge. I know plenty of you are in the same boat, so here’s a quick rundown of how it went.

My emails turned out to be the easy part, which is annoying given how long I spent dreading it. My shortlist came down to Proton, Fastmail* and iCloud. I liked Proton a lot when I trialled it, but its (admirable) emphasis on security means calendars and contacts won’t sync with the native apps on my iPhone. iCloud now supports custom domains, and since I’m already deep inside Apple’s walled garden, it would have been the path of least resistance. It would also have meant handing more money to a different Big Tech company.

So I went with Fastmail, a small Melbourne company (represent!) with a solid reputation. Its migration tool pulled everything across via IMAP in a few hours and mirrored my Gmail labels. On my laptop I use the web interface and don’t miss a single feature. On my iPhone, I can still use the native Calendar and Contacts apps, and Fastmail’s own app for email (it’s good). When I made a mistake during my custom domain setup, an actual human replied to my support request within a day with an answer that helped. I’d forgotten that was possible.

Google itself isn’t disappearing from my life any time soon, though. Too many clients and collaborators live in Docs and Sheets. But, I learned that once you remove your custom domain from Google Workspace, it takes Google about 20 days to ‘release’ it, after which you can sign up for a free Google account with that same custom email address.

What you can’t do is bring your other stuff with you. Ugh. Drive files have to be exported and re-uploaded into the new account. Maps and YouTube have no migration path at all, so I’m rebuilding those from scratch, one saved café at a time. Google Maps’ reviews are hard to beat, sorry Apple.

So yeah, Google does remain a fixture for a handful of ‘free’ apps. But the elephant in the room – my big fat inbox – walked out the door far more willingly than I’d expected. All up, it took a few hours over a couple of weekends. Years of dread, overcome by two weekends of mild admin. Shoulda done it ages ago. (And yet, I was just in time.)

And now to this week’s discoveries. – Kai

* This is a referral link that gets you 10% off your first year.

issues.title: TanStack Start is finally stable
issues.summary: #​494 — October 23, 2026 Read on the Web React Status TanStack Start Reaches 1.0 After a year as a release candidate, TanStack Start 1.0 is officially stable. Tanner Linsley explains how it grew out of TanStack Router, and is candid about RSC, which felt like "this box we had to…
issues.content_html:
#​494 — October 23, 2026

Read on the Web
 React Status

TanStack Start Reaches 1.0

After a year as a release candidate, TanStack Start 1.0 is officially stable. Tanner Linsley explains how it grew out of TanStack Router, and is candid about RSC, which felt like "this box we had to check to be taken seriously as a React framework", and which tanstack.com itself no longer uses. Plus:

  • 📊 The same app in Start and Next.js 16.4, benchmarked – Start handled 2.9x-8.6x more dynamic requests and built ~1.7x faster with type-checking included.

  • 🚚 Moving over? There are official guides for migrating from Next.js and from the RC. Sarthak Mishra moved his site over from Astro (and explains why) and Lovable offers older projects a migration option (here's how one went).

  • 💬 Ryan Carniato called it "a React metaframework with an architecture I can get behind", while in the r/reactjs thread Tanner explained why '1.0' is listed as 1.169 on npm.

TypeScript in the Age of AI — Knowing TypeScript deeply is how you get better code out of AI. Adam Rackis of Spotify shows you how to steer AI toward simpler, correct types and catch the mistakes it slips in.

Master.dev sponsor

IN BRIEF:

  • ⚠️ Last week, Next.js patched two critical RCEs, one rooted in React Server Components, and a public PoC is now out. Update Next.js to 16.4.1 or 15.5.28; for other RSC setups, update the react-server-dom-* packages to 19.3.1 (or 19.2.9/19.1.10/19.0.9).

  • React DevTools for agents now has official docs, covering how it exposes profiling and component data to coding agents through Chrome DevTools MCP.

  • 📱 Expo SDK 58 is out, using the new React Native 0.88, targeting iOS 27 and ready for the iPhone Duo on day one.

  • React Native for Web has active maintainers again and is moving to the React Foundation's GitHub org.

  • TypeScript 7.1 is now in beta, adding a programmatic API and more speed. Type-checking MUI's docs is 1.9x faster and uses half the memory.

Improving Navigation Experience in v0 with Next.js 16.4 — How the Next.js team used Partial Prefetching, intent-based prefetching and the new navigation() API to cut loading skeletons across its v0 AI app builder.

Aurora Scharff (Vercel)

React Only Where Needed: Owner's Next.js to Astro Move — Owner's 10,000+ restaurant sites now run on Astro and Cloudflare Workers, keeping React for interactive islands. Menu-page p75 LCP went from 5.4s to 0.7s.

Selden and Hanford (Owner)

Dead Code Shouldn't Exist — The slides and transcript from a popular talk Dominik has given at several conferences this year on how Sentry removed 28K lines of unused code with Knip.

Dominik Dorfmeister

🤖 Testing AI-Generated Code: Lint the Pattern, Test the Decision – Structural lint rules and shared harnesses beat a test beside every component. Robin Wieruch

📱 Apple Didn't Invent the Foldable. It Might Make You Support One. – Getting a React Native app ready for the iPhone Duo's three compatibility tiers. Sean Barker (Infinite Red)

📄 Loading a 9MB WebAssembly Module Earlier Made Recraft's Editor 17% Faster – Suspending components left the module's download waiting its turn in the React tree. Sergey Patrakeev (Recraft)

🛠  Code, Tools & Libraries

Pixel: Build Graphical Applications in the Terminal — Like Ink, but with "pixel perfect" graphics. It's a React renderer that draws rounded corners, gradients and proper fonts in terminals that support the Kitty graphics protocol, and that can even embed Chromium WebViews to run web apps in a pane(!)

Rob Pruzan (Zenbu Labs)

TanStack Hotkeys Beta: A Type-Safe Library for Keyboard Shortcuts — Hotkeys takes care of the fiddly, cross-platform edge cases of keyboard shortcuts, sequences, and user-recorded hotkeys. The beta adds scopes, so that, say, a dialog's Escape doesn't close the panel behind it. Try the demo on the homepage.

TanStack

React Router 8.5 Hands View Transitions Over to React — Its own view transition APIs are deprecated in favor of React 19.3's <ViewTransition>. Migrating starts with wrapping an <Outlet> and removing the old props and state styling. There's also an unstable 'API-only' mode that serves static HTML but keeps a server for loaders and actions.

Remix Team

env.style: Style Every Environment with Colors or Custom Icons — A utility that wraps your Next.js config or Vite setup to tint the favicon per environment at build time, so you can see at a glance where you are.

Ryan George

Tamagui 3: One React UI Codebase for Web and Native — A styling system and UI kit for sharing one codebase between React web apps and React Native. v3 adds an opt-in (beta) C++ native runtime that applies theme changes without re-rendering, plus React Strict DOM and Tailwind-style syntax.

Nate Wienert

  • Hydrogen 2026.10 – Shopify's commerce toolkit is now a library you can drop into existing Next.js or React Router apps.

  • Morphicons 2.0 – Spring-physics morphing between SVG icons. Now filled icons morph too, not just stroked ones. See it in action on its homepage.

  • Unistyles 3.6 – High-performance React Native styling library. Now with an experimental zero-config Metro integration instead of the Babel plugin.

  • Motion 14.6 – Adds keyboard grab-and-move to Reorder lists, plus stepFrames for deterministic animation testing.

📰 Classifieds

issues.title: DD411 / Nothing personal, just grifting
issues.summary: Issue 411: Nothing personal, just grifting – Read the full issue in the archive.
issues.author: Kai Brach
issues.content_html:
A couple of years ago, my mum nearly sent $1000+ to someone on WhatsApp who was pretending to be me. A (human) bank teller saved her by suggesting she call me first.

This isn’t to mock my mum. We’re all potential victims. But some days I’m surprised nothing worse has happened, given how much of the internet has become fertile ground for scams, fakery and plain nonsense.

Merritt K thinks the only sane response is to go back to the suspicion of the internet’s early days. She writes:

“We must return to 1990s-type hysterics with regards to the internet. Refuse to take anything or anyone at face value. Assume that everything you see is a falsehood tailor-made to mislead or manipulate you. If it seems too good to be true, if it reinforces your beliefs in a neat little way, it’s probably AI-generated.”

I remember those hysterics. I was just on the other side of them. When I first got online, there were pretty much two kinds of people. There were the curious tinkerers, thrilled by ‘right-click, view source’, and then there was a much larger group of sceptics who saw the whole thing as a waste of time and assumed anyone merely mentioning the exchange of money was up to no good.

Scams and dodgy sites have always been part of the furniture, of course. But back then the elaborate cons sat at the edges. Hardly anyone typed their credit card details into a random website, mostly because hardly anyone was selling anything.

Today everyone is selling something. Everywhere we look, someone is scrambling to profit from whatever they can push into the tubes, and that desperation doesn’t stop with the scammers.

One of the comments under Merritt’s piece captures this well. Most of the people chasing attention for a living now have to feed the machine with engagement bait, outrage, contrarianism and half-baked takes, whatever keeps the show rolling. News outlets do it too, the legitimate ones as much as the ones rehashing everyone else. And once honest people have to perform as well, the line between real and fake stops meaning much.

Spend two minutes on Product Hunt and you’ll see how much of what gets celebrated is the plumbing for this desperate economy: tools to generate posts at volume or to spin one idea into fifty variations. Fakery used to be the exception you had to spot. Now authenticity is the exception you have to verify.

Worse, curiosity itself has become something to fake. I see it in my inbox every day. A dozen AI-generated pitches pose as loyal subscribers, all running the same prompts to get my attention. I can live with the volume and the extra admin. What bothers me is the pretence. It’s interest that’s been automated and scaled. All the right words, none of the curiosity.

As I’ve written here before, I’m wary of romanticising the early web. It was narrow, mostly white, mostly male. But I miss its honesty, its naivety. Sure, many small, personal corners of the web will survive, but it’s hard not to grieve, just a little, for a web where most of the people talking to you actually meant it. And were, you know, actually people.

And now to this week’s discoveries. – Kai

issues.title: DD410 / Design: frictionless, flawless, forgettable
issues.summary: Issue 410: Design: frictionless, flawless, forgettable – Read the full issue in the archive.
issues.author: Kai Brach
issues.content_html:
Whenever I come across yet another ‘why does everything look the same’ essay on modern design, I tend to roll my eyes. Not that I disagree. I just think the sameness they complain about isn’t a glitch but the logical endpoint of our operating system. When markets and algorithms decide what is good, and efficiency decides what gets made, convergence is the result.

I’ve grown pretty tired of design discourse overall. For all the noble language around craft and care, the discipline’s main job is usually just to help grease the engine of consumption – with better kerning.

So I was sceptical about Ezra Klein’s conversation with designer Debbie Millman on why the modern world looks so drab. I admire Millman’s podcast, but to be honest, her answers here fell flat for me. Klein raises some interesting questions, though.

He says modern apartment buildings, cars or even some municipal infrastructure make us feel nothing. Much of the built environment has been smoothed into something frictionless, functional and inoffensive – convenient, but increasingly hard to distinguish from anything else.

“I actually think some of the drabness that we’re talking about comes from people living in a world that has been smoothed for them, such that it, on the one hand, works really well, and on the other hand, it doesn’t feel alive to them. It just sort of has been like flattened into a kind of soulless service.”

Klein makes a great point: some of the reasons for this drabness are actually positive. When it comes to housing, we now know how to make buildings more energy efficient, thermally comfortable and safer in earthquakes or extreme weather, and those technical requirements inevitably narrow the range of forms and materials.

And, sadly, housing has become a tradable financial asset. For many people it’s a stepping stone, not somewhere they expect to stay for fifty years. Painting your house flamingo pink might express your personality, but it won’t do your resale value any favours.

The charming old streets we romanticise for their beauty are mostly what’s left of housing built for people with money. The workers’ cottages were largely bulldozed or thoroughly renovated. It’s a bit like judging how people live today by watching Grand Designs.

So everything is being nudged towards the inoffensive middle. But there’s a counterforce now too: attention. In a desperate attempt to stand out, design has swung hard the other way – loud, oversized, garish, deliberately grating. Millman describes it as ‘vulgar’ design. The Cybertruck is the perfect example.

Most design these days feels as though it passed through a branding agency. The new ugly cuts through the noise because it feels like somebody made it, rather than a committee approved it. It provokes a reaction, good or bad. That’s a rare feat in a world gone numb.

“It’s not that the market hates beauty. It would love to sell you something beautiful. But the intentionality of the market is to sell product.”

Every bargain has its price. In houses, we traded character for comfort. Instead of our grandmother’s soulful dining table that lasts generations, we buy a flatpack we can carry up three flights of stairs to our tiny apartment where we live for a couple of years until the landlord wants to sell.

Beauty is still possible. It’s just that the freedom to build a world around your own tastes and expectations of quality is largely reserved for those who can afford it. As it always was.

And now to this week’s discoveries. – Kai

issues.title: Jaadugar: A Witch In Mongolia Production Notes #07-12 – A Star-filled Ending (For Now)
issues.summary: Rather than merely limping to the goal line, allowing its gripping narrative and careful cultural research to carry it, Jaadugar fought back against production exhaustion. To do so, they gathered their most luxurious lineup of lead creators to tackle this final arc, making its…
issues.author: kViN
issues.content_html:
Rather than merely limping to the goal line, allowing its gripping narrative and careful cultural research to carry it, Jaadugar fought back against production exhaustion. To do so, they gathered their most luxurious lineup of lead creators to tackle this final arc, making its ending (for now) as evocative and fulfilling as possible.

Our previous article about Jaadugar: A Witch in Mongolia covered the genesis of its anime adaptation. We recalled how its team came together, shared what their priorities and philosophies regarding historical fiction happen to be, and then analyzed how their mindsets manifested across the first six episodes. That stopping point wasn’t just a convenient halfway landmark, but also a pivotal narrative beat for the series altogether. The staff understood as much, given that it was entrusted to as high-profile a guest as you could imagine. That’s no exaggeration, mind you; while we’re in an era where recognizable names tied to action blockbusters are used as promotional tools, enlisting meticulous theatrical animation maestro Masashi Ando as the sole storyboarder was genuinely shocking. It was in fact the first time anyone—specifically, his friend and equally renowned designer Kenichi Yoshida—had convinced Ando to accept such a request, but his affinity with the material at hand couldn’t have been any clearer.

Apart from bringing us up to speed, it’s worth bringing up the feat they’d just accomplished to better understand how Jaadugar‘s final stretch subverts expectations. After all, what would you reasonably expect after such an ambitious episode that acts as a paradigm shift within the narrative? Most of the time, that would lead into a modest production effort to preserve energy, and even a slower storytelling rhythm to get viewers acclimated to the new chapter in the story.

Most of the time indeed, but not in Jaadugar, which is a beautifully backloaded season of television.

Of course, there is still a sense of prioritization, and taxing episodes like the preceding one are always going to have repercussions; especially in the context of a production that, like we’ll be forced to talk about yet again later, has had its share of scheduling issues. That said, there’s a concerted effort by its team to put extraordinary effort into the final stages of the show, counterbalancing the creeping exhaustion and then some. This season of Jaadugar was always going to be an excerpt of a larger story—one that stands on its own, but only if you’re capable of connecting its two halves without losing too much energy in the process. No matter how good the first episodes are, if the rest of the broadcast had lacked punch, the inconclusive narrative might have left people deflated rather than dying for a sequel. Fortunately for everyone but our patience, we can celebrate the exact opposite outcome.

Following up a prestigious outsider guest like Ando, episode #07 returns to closer associates to Science Saru. Right after reminiscing about Sitara and Töregene’s alliance, forged in the pain inflicted by the same empire, the framing makes it clear that Yujiro Abe storyboarded the first half of the episode. Though not to the same degree as his previous appearance, where the light raining down from above had been a major theme, the usage of overhead shots reminds us of the inherent link between Jaadugar and the heavens… and of course, of Abe’s own propensities. If you add to that other familiar choices like the depiction of tradition and myth through Ryoko Tanaka’s papercuts, his own fingerprints become so obvious that the official confirmation of the storyboarding splits felt superfluous.

When it comes to his delivery, though, it’s two aspects derived from the show’s evolving narrative that stand out the most. One of them may seem like a minor detail, but it’s quite telling about the series directors’ philosophical approach to the adaptation. Although it’s an attitude that has manifested across the entire show, chief director Naoko Yamada addressed it quite plainly in a recent interview with CREA: she’s not particularly interested in historical events, at least not on their own. Although working on Jaadugar has been stimulating, constantly sparking her interest in learning more about various cultures and their history, this is something that has always happened as a consequence of her actual interest. That is, the curiosity about how real people felt, thought, and tasted at the time.

This humanistic angle, shared to a large degree by series director Abel Gongora, easily explains why the Jaadugar anime has thus far been so sparing with aspects like maps. It’s not until they’ve fully sold the personal dimension of this conflict, framed predominantly through Sitara and Töregene’s bond, that we’re starting to see military and political scheming take over both the narrative and visuals. As it starts to lean more in that direction, the show issues a new challenge to its directors: it asks them to turn impersonal concepts like army diagrams into visually engaging sequences. Abe is the first one to give it a spin, with his most amusing attempt being a masked transition between a certain warmonger’s plans and his own theatrics to promote that campaign.

It’s precisely that character who embodies Abe’s sharpest direction. In contrast to the fairly neutral delivery in the manga, his storyboarding demonstrates why Tolui’s natural charisma threatens to destabilize an entire empire. Leaning into an angle that the anime has used before, which is to link that figurative dazzling presence into a literal one, his accidental hijack of the conversation about the Mongol plans constantly puts him in the spotlight.

The following episodes make it clear that, for as ruthless as he is in battle, Tolui is truly committed to his family and the empire altogether. Despite looking like a figure placed on this board to attempt a coup that could earn him the throne once occupied by Genghis Khan, Tomato Soup’s story reads him in an entirely different fashion. However, Jaadugar—and this episode in particular, given an earlier scene between siblings—also understands the importance of optics in politics. Tolui may not intend to betray Ögedei, but for as long as he is an incredibly charismatic figure with access to military might, schemers will read his mere existence as a potential vector of attack. Tweaking the lighting in his favor and framing him in low-angle shots that aggrandize his presence are simple tricks, but they go a long way to convey his powerful presence. If the Great Khans have been linked to stars, Tolui is the Sun itself.

As the episode progresses, we get a taste of the unraveling political conflicts, as well as their ties to that personal dimension that motivates the series directors. The benign veneer over the otherwise brutal Mongol regime pushed by Ögedei frustrates Sitara, who wishes they were a perfectly evil opponent to fuel her revenge. Two parallel scheming factions begin to develop, and it’s through their moments of intimacy that we’re introduced to them. On the one hand, we see Töregene’s willingness to show vulnerability in front of Sitara, who exposes her true self to her as well. On the other, it’s time to introduce Great Khatun Boraqchin, with a quietly imposing presence that can only be disarmed by the earnestness of fellow Ögedei spouse Möge. The likes of Yamada have praised Tomato Soup for her ability to imagine so much interiority and interpersonal chemistry within the gaps of recorded history, so it’s no surprise the anime adaptation treats these moments with such care.

It’s also worth noting that, after Abe’s solid first half, Nick McKergow made his storyboarding debut in the second one. Although it helps that inherently funny character dynamics come into play, the comedy feels particularly sharp under his pen; not just through the expressions and poses, but also with clinical pauses that exploit Sitara’s amusing cunning. Down to the tiniest details like a parasol lagging behind the person it’s meant to shield, McKergow’s attentiveness as an animator feels like it can translate to this new position.

Speaking of emerging talent, episode #08 features Asami Murakoshi as the storyboarder and episode director. Given that she’s a massive fan of Yamada whose entire life pivoted because of Liz and the Blue Bird (not much of a secret), it’s not a surprise that her most inspired work thus far has been in the chief director’s collaborations with the studio. Despite appearing modest when compared to Jaadugar’s more obvious highlights, Murakoshi turns a transitional beat into one of the most delicate yet sharp episodes in the whole show. The finesse in the execution feels way beyond her still limited degree of experience, but it’s a quietly brilliant outing from the conceptual stages already.

It’s worth pointing out, for example, how Murakoshi’s imagery depicts knowledge as something universal and more tied to nature itself than to any specific civilization. Much to Sitara’s chagrin, Jaadugar has constantly emphasized the value of cultural exchanges, the commonalities between different peoples, and how we can advance by combining their answers to similar challenges. Our protagonist is quite adept at stumbling into problems and then using her lived experiences to navigate through them, which is exactly what occurs as she finds a cure for Boraqchin’s poisoning. Murakoshi’s storyboards don’t just connect her eureka moment with Muhammad’s lesson to Sitara about preparedness, but also stylize the spilled water as a perfect mirror of the stars. All humans exist below the same skies, no matter how far apart we are. It’s this connection through the world itself that will always allow us to repurpose other people’s knowledge.

As mentioned before, the execution of those ideas is just as refined. There is a delightful flow to the palette; Boraqchin’s surroundings are lifeless when she’s locked inside, you can sense Möge’s kindness in the evening colors when she begs for help, Sitara appears in their life as if she were a new light for the Great Khatun, and ultimately, Boraqchin’s world becomes more vivid than ever when she regains her health. You can sense Murakoshi’s passion for Yamada’s work in certain areas, like the conversations with characterful acting rooted in the storyboards themselves, rather than in the flamboyant traits of a specific animator.

In the aforementioned CREA interview, the chief director framed this adaptation as an attempt to fill the gaps in the original work. And the best, most meaningful way to do so in her eyes was through more intricate depictions of the characters’ daily lives, as she has always seen that as the ideal way to communicate someone’s personality and cultural identity. While his angle is a bit different, perhaps more anthropological in a utilitarian way, Gongora shares a similar viewpoint; hence why he greatly values all the practical knowledge about everyday life in Mongolia, which they acquired through careful research and a much-promoted scouting trip.

Following that philosophy, one of the most interesting additions to this episode’s script—and of course, something successfully fleshed out by Murakoshi’s storyboard—is the preparation of urum. The viewer casually experiences Sitara’s process step by step; the people she would meet along the way, how to present the dish, and the way to eat it as well. At the same time, the scene still accomplishes the more tangible narrative intent it had in the manga: showing Töregene’s jealousy as she notices Sitara orbiting around Boraqchin a lot amidst her scheming.

That growing rift between the two becomes an important source of conflict during the final stages of the show. Like many other challenges Sitara ends up facing, this is a result of her hubris. As she grows more confident in her machinations to destabilize the empire, she fails to realize what she’s unleashed upon the Mongolian steppe by healing Boraqchin and encouraging her ambition. All the shrewd political moves that follow appear to up the stakes; we have the developing war against Jin, Ögedei mysteriously falling ill in a way that incriminates Töregene, and a potentially dangerous ceremony to save his life that must involve his siblings. Curiously, many happenings that benefit Boraqchin, who in one fell swoop could save her husband, get pests like Tolui and Töregene off the board, and secure another asset like Sitara firmly in her pocket.

Despite the overarching narrative being so dyed by human machinations, dragged through the mud of personal agendas, episode #09 is conversely defined by the immaterial. The lead creators behind Jaadugar have explained over and over how much weight they put on respectful, accurate cultural representation. Sure, they are open to an occasional white lie that reinforces the evocativeness even if it comes at a slight cost of accuracy, but those are interesting curiosities more than a betrayal of their stance. Their mindset has been palpable from the design stages to the animation work; after all, we just praised a sequence extensively showing how a specific food would have been prepared at the time. Lots of effort went into replicating tools, clothes, architecture and art, and also into approximating their manual processes and behaviors.

And yet, is that physical dimension enough to capture a culture as it was hundreds of years ago? You shouldn’t be surprised to hear that Jaadugar’s staff thought that they shouldn’t stop themselves at that. Yamada noted, for example, that the scenes where we visualize Sitara learning about astronomy shouldn’t feature imagery (a dark void universe, a blue Earth) rooted in modern conceptions. In this way, the team wasn’t just trying to be accurate when it comes to the scientific understanding at the time, but also to keep people’s imagination grounded in their reality.

It’s as an extension of that idea that the adaptation does an exceptional job with the spirituality of Jaadugar. Tomato Soup succeeds in explaining the beliefs of various civilizations, but with the brisk pacing of the manga, the delivery of the customs derived from them can be rather matter-of-fact. In contrast to that, the anime consistently emphasizes these ceremonies, aggrandizes their atmosphere, all while still adding new mythological imagery rooted in historical research. Above all else, it’s committed to making the viewer feel as bystanders would at the time; not only presenting the results that could explain why certain beliefs were held, but also selling the overwhelming, magical, sensorial experiences that turn feelings into faith.

Back in the sixth episode, we highlighted director Kotaro Matsunaga as a particularly apt figure to handle otherworldly matters. He has an affinity for larger-than-life material, and within an environment like Jaadugar, his approach tweaks the rules just enough to make his episodes stand out. In short, Matsunaga is invested in modulating the lighting as a storytelling tool. Although that’s something that this show has consistently attempted—the literalization of Tolui’s brilliance continues across this arc—his emphasis on digital effects and photographic tendencies is unusual for this cel-forward production. While he doesn’t betray the show’s aesthetic to an uncomfortable degree, he nudges it enough to underline the mystical aura of rituals and ceremonies; shout-out to the sound direction as well, which hypnotizes you during these special moments.

This focus on what lies beyond the objective realities of the characters continues into episode #10, which landed on the directorial lap of Kenji Zenba. While he feels like an equally fitting leader for another venture into the spiritual realm, it’s worth noting that he reaches that position from an entirely different angle. Zenba’s origins are in support studio Azeta Pictures, and yet, he has quickly become perhaps the most authentically Saru-esque figure in their productions. To be precise, he’s the artist most reminiscent of their origins, highly influenced by the style of Masaaki Yuasa. Though not quite as radical as the studio’s founder, Zenba’s work adds a tad more angularity while incorporating plenty of the extreme exaggeration of perspectives, surreal deformations, and aggressive spacing. He’s the type of artist who can make you feel like you’re watching Kemonozume in the actuality, and that’s something to be treasured, because not even Saru can offer that feeling often.

During the release of Summer Time Machine Blues, we praised Shingo Natsume’s ability to turn back the clock. He was merely an associate rather than a core member of that team, and he’d already gone on to establish himself as a uniquely appealing director, but he truly treasured the memories of learning from Yuasa during his pre-Saru heyday. Those feelings fueled an uncanny visual recreation of Tatami Galaxy’s iconic style, to a degree that the studio’s other projects—and arguably Yuasa’s theatrical return to the franchise—couldn’t match. As noted in that article, though, Natsume’s feat didn’t extend to the episodes led by creators belonging to Saru’s younger generations; not necessarily a slight against the show, as Summer Time Machine Blues is a rather different narrative to begin with. The one exception to that? Zenba’s supervision on the third episode, which brought back that nostalgic edge. Even in more commercially-focused productions, Zenba taking the lead gives a particular spice to the drawings.

If that feels like a quality that Jaadugar could put to good use, episode #10 should prove you correct. Thanks to Boraqchin’s Machiavellian plots, we find ourselves in the spiritual realm alongside Ögedei and Tolui. Right off the bat, you can appreciate those Zenba-esque perspective distortions and looser, geometrical forms. A mystical realm, yet in the earthen choices of colors, one that very much feels born in Mongol imagination. One where nature plays a big role, but also where animals are abstracted until they almost become 2DFX, contrary to their physical rendering during regular scenes. These intense stylizations combine with the solemnity that has characterized Jaadugar’s depiction of rituals to make it clear that we’re in a different plane of existence.

Later in the episode, the fit between Zenba’s sensibilities and the comedic side of the series also becomes clear. His characteristic perspective exaggeration and snappier timing follow amusing characters like Töregene’s scaredy-cat son Güyük and the ambitious little runt that is Kyrgyzstani. Through various registers, we witness how the flavor that Zenba adds not only as director but as storyboarder and layout artist can enhance many areas in the show. And yet, those familiar with his work should be able to notice that his radical instincts are being held back.

Popular discourse tends to oversimplify the philosophy behind artistic choices, presenting false dichotomies that are completely detached from the reality of collective creation—and frankly, from art altogether. Sheer ambition and daringness, irreverence and looseness, willingness to stray from visual trends, diversity of techniques, creative freedom for each individual, and any such qualities are blended together under a meaningless banner of true, high art; one that ought to be attached to your favorite show, even if it’s a broadly marketable, conforming hit. With this reductive view, though, you miss interesting nuance like the areas where idiosyncratic anime chooses to be inflexible and restrictive. That’s very much the case with Jaadugar, a production that limits certain stylistic choices because it’s that committed to the identity it has forged.

It’s no secret that Jaadugar wants to minimize the usage of 3DCG; not ban it outright, as it’s occasionally present and still acts as the skeleton for the animation of many digital artists, but it’s not allowed to have a prominent role. Similarly, the show demands sparing visibility for digital lighting effects, wanting to give off the impression that it’s cel and BG layers that convey it. Given the weird stigma around digital techniques when it comes to artistic expression, those likely don’t read as restrictions to many viewers. And yet, Jaadugar is also a show that has very little loose animation and the type of radical deformations expected from artists like Zenba. Mandates to stay close to the design sheets are often associated with creatively barren anime, and yet here we experience that phenomenon in an inspiring series that nonetheless platforms unique styles. Artistic choices are never so simple, and that’s what makes them so interesting.

Of course, the limitations Jaadugar places aren’t arbitrary. The relative shackles on the character art exist because, in conjunction with the approach taken for the backgrounds, the show’s look is meant to evoke something akin to Islamic miniatures and classic Mongolian paintings. The series directors were preoccupied with how to balance its duality of space: the clearly farcical, flat look of Tomato Soup’s manga and a necessarily three-dimensional world, which they’d otherwise struggle to sell as a lived-in setting. In that paradigm, rocking the boat too much with radical distortions of perspective or super loose drawings could have compromised the identity they were after. The regulation of these aspects might not be absolutely perfect—Zenba’s episode suggests there was room for more idiosyncrasy—but it’s important to keep in mind that the restrictions exist because they have a vision, not because they lack it.

Episode #10 demonstrates the value of gradually building a story with that cohesive, focused approach. We’ve written at length about Tolui possessing an aura so dazzling that it influences the politics of an entire empire, and how that has consistently translated into visual choices. Chances are that Zenba personally animated one of the first instances that established this motif, so when he arrives to sacrifice himself for Ögedei, that blinding light feels familiar. His men saw in him the most straightforward heir to Genghis Khan’s supernatural presence, and that allows Jaadugar to reiterate the imagery it had successfully used before when he passes away; another falling star for the death of a larger-than-life figure, elegantly completing the sentence as Sitara finds out about this outcome.

Even in a more self-contained sense, the framing distills the interpersonal conflict brilliantly. Boraqchin set up Töregene to take the blame for endangering Ögedei’s life and indirectly leading to Tolui’s death, and as the oppressive visuals convey, she nearly trapped Sitara as well—quite literally having the protagonist in the palm of her hand. However, a well-timed reminder of Muhammad’s lesson to pursue knowledge to be better prepared to live your life helps her realize that she was never betrayed by Töregene. With an understanding that the two of them had been victims of the same ploy, Sitara faces Boraqchin once more. This time, the sly mask she wears and the stark separation in the storyboard confirm that a line between two factions has been drawn.

With only two episodes remaining before the end, the common approach would be to entrust the final one to the series directors if possible. Instead, Jaadugar commits to allocating material to the most fitting individuals, hence why the storyboarding duties in episode #11 were mostly entrusted to Yamada and Gongora. If you’re curious about what Ryouta Aikei was responsible for, well, so are we; despite also being credited for storyboarding, neither series episode director Takuya Fujikura nor the official accounts alluded to his work, which they’ve been doing for everyone else in similar roles. Given his tendencies, perhaps he’s responsible for certain moments where the camera takes an uncharacteristically proactive role.

Either way, it’s clear why Yamada seized control for the first half, while Gongora did the same for the second one. Episode #11 is the final chance to establish why these people fight, so each series director focused not only on their favorite character, but the aspects of their personality they excel at conveying. In Yamada’s case, that means fleshing out her beloved Boraqchin. For all the ruthless schemes that have earned her the title of witch in Sitara’s eyes, her extended backstory in this adaptation paints a very human picture.

Its original introductory scene shows her as a woman fascinated by natural phenomena; just a cute moment with her wondering about the snow, but it organically builds up to her later obsessions with the alchemical properties of minerals and the concept of mortality. It’s this fundamental curiosity that resonates with Ögedei, who in turn shares a dream for a vast empire connecting civilizations that strikes a chord with Boraqchin. This is delivered especially well in the anime, which turns a regular speech into a bright vision taking shape. While that aspect of her personality and Ögedei’s encouragement are what fuel her more ambitious plans, the individual who grounds her and provides emotional stability is clearly Möge. More than ever—especially under a director like Yamada, who was born to storyboard such a cheerful person—you can feel Boraqchin’s love for her, and the quiet sadness when she pushes her away as if not to taint her.

As we move on to the second half, we transition to Gongora’s storyboards. And, on a character level, back to Sitara’s point of view. The adaptation emphasizes her worries about Töregene through both the script and the animation, leading to some of the most characterful sequences in the entire show. As valuable as that is, the most striking and thematically important scenes come near the end. Reality can be so cruel that victims may need to process their misery in a simplified way, giving them singular enemies as an outlet for their pain and hatred. Jaadugar isn’t merely a story about the ruthless Tolui slaying Sitara’s city to claim a book for his whimsical wife Sorghaghtani, even though he was indeed ruthless, and she is far from sinless. Having lost everything to incomprehensible tragedy, though, Sitara’s only way forward was to put a target on their backs. And that has all fallen apart.

The book she sought to recover is in her hands, but what meaning is there to it? Boraqchin was the one who recovered it and forwarded it as a bribe, and Sorghaghtani immediately gave up on everything after Tolui’s death. To her, who lost everything and fought to rebuild a semblance of a life, a more privileged enemy’s quick capitulation is one of the most infuriating experiences in her life. Gongora conveys that fury through flashbacks of Sitara’s lost family and the moment she decided to blame Sorghaghtani for their deaths, flowing so choppily that you can feel the overwhelming rage. Beyond the effectiveness on a character level, this connects with what Gongora has always seen as the main theme of Jaadugar: freedom. He began the series with an original scene of her trying to escape captivity as a young slave, and near the end of this season, he reinforces the feeling that she’s trapped in a trauma that can’t be unlocked by a cheap way out.

We’re finally approaching the last episode, and after so much praise for the series, it’s also about time to address some issues around it. In our write-up for the first half of Jaadugar, we noted that designer and chief animator Yoshida had been critical both of the schedule and the preparedness of some staff members; it’s worth noting that he has been supportive of Saru’s young talent, so his complaints about whether people truly understood the job of a key animator feel more aimed at the countless subcontracted companies. The series remained in production well into its broadcast, and even when it finally wrapped up, Yoshida felt the need to point out he was exhausted, and this was the tightest schedule he’s ever had to deal with. So much so, that he replied to a viewer who hadn’t even directly reached out to him to double down on that stance. His renown has kept him relatively shielded from the madness of modern TV anime production, but Saru’s super busy, concurrent production model was more than enough stress for him.

To some degree, that type of burden always ends up affecting the quality of the show. By all means a high-quality anime on the whole, especially by current standards, Jaadugar has also been bumpy in spots. Certain episodes—#09 comes to mind—have uneven, less polished character art than the norm. At some point, the most ambitious sequences in the show become a coin flip about whether they’ll be fully realized or stumble a bit. Right before the incredible appearance of Toshiyuki Inoue on episode #06, an impressive rotation shot falls apart in the end; just pay attention to the way that Töregene’s eyes melt into position before it stops. During an otherwise excellent scene in episode #09, a grand sweeping shot becomes unintentionally choppy and rough for no fault of key animator Hiroki Naekawa. These noticeably (if you’re attentive to these details anyway) unpolished spots may not have arisen with a much more comfortable schedule, and an environment that didn’t force egregious levels of outsourcing like Saru does.

Out of all the recurring rough corners, the most notable of all is unsurprisingly the in-betweening. For the longest time, the industry’s lack of standards or even contempt for the job has gradually degraded what should be a fundamental step. These issues are so recurring across the landscape of anime that even viewers without extensive knowledge about production matters are now acquainted with terms like douga. And yet, even those who are more deeply in the know will often miss the nuance of what that entails.

The English word in-between makes you imagine the drawings that must be inserted in the gaps separating each sheet of key animation, meant to complete the movement in an appropriately smooth fashion. Although that’s part of the job, douga is an all-encompassing job; every drawing in a finished sequence has followed the in-betweening process, whether it was freshly drawn or traced from the original keys. In the former case, you’d be specifically looking at nakawari  (中割り), which holds the same literal meaning as the common English word.

This is worth pointing out now, not just because staff struggles should be highlighted just as much as their successes, but also to consider such challenges as the motivation behind interesting solutions. Over the last couple of episodes, Yoshida arranged two of the most glamorous cameos in the entire show. One of them was the return of Masashi Ando, fresh off his wonderful storyboards for episode #06. The two bonded through Studio Ghibli, just like they did with living legend Shinji Otsuka, who helps bring the penultimate episode to a close. It’s no surprise that Science Saru chose to share their sequences to promote the broadcast, and if you take a look at them, you may notice something: both scenes feature full key animation (全原画). This doesn’t mean that they’re full animation where each of the 24 frames is a unique drawing, but rather that these highly prestigious artists drew as many distinct poses as the scenes were meant to have, with no room for those pesky nakawari.

Anime’s chronic issues with in-betweening aren’t limited to shoddy drawings filling those gaps; they have a lot to do with tracing, with software, with the loss of authentic linework and kicking the can forward for already burdened compositing teams to falsify nuance and texture, and of course with the inescapability of scheduling and budget constraints for what is still seen as lesser work. It’s never not about labor! While skipping the need for nakawari doesn’t magically solve all problems, veteran artists who take pride in their work can at least bypass the common issue of complex movement intermittently melting into wobbly cuts. Otsuka and Ando enjoy this approach in the first place (especially the former), but it feels meaningful that they went the extra length even though they had little time at their disposal; in Ando’s case, that even demanded the help of Ruotien Ting to polish up the sequence, which fortunately turned out to be excellent.

In recent times, many older creators have lamented that because of the rise of certain tools and the general decrease of thorough training systems, younger animators have a restricted ability to convey things—not because of a particular flaw of their own, but because they aren’t used to drawing certain things. What notably began with the loss of artists capable of animating mechs has now spread to areas as fundamental as proper perspective. However,  speaking to Jaadugar‘s author during another conversation hosted by Souffle, Yoshida adds interesting nuance as a reputable veteran animator in his 50s. After all, he already paints his generation as one that didn’t get as much of an opportunity to draw animals as his predecessors and thus struggled with them, compared to the limitless ability of folks like Hayao Miyazaki. Yoshida explains that, when they had to work on Princess Mononoke, he basically had to learn by tracing older animators off the clock. A particularly interesting detail in this regard is that, when talking about the sequence with horses in Jaadugar‘s finale, he proudly said that if you want to draw these animals, it’s gotta be Masashi Ando. The punchline? They were born the same year, Ando simply had a bit of a headstart in the industry. That’s how fast things can change!

There is no better proof that Jaadugar’s team tried to save their best for last than the directorial lineup for the finale. On some level, it’s also pleasantly unsurprising; we’ve written at excruciating length about China’s love for Yamada, so of course he took another chance to storyboard and co-direct an episode for a project where she’s deeply involved. On the other hand, the surprise factor of featuring Ryousuke Nakamura as the director for the first half of the episode is unmatched. Beyond his skill and sensibilities—already newsworthy—this is simply a type of job he rarely accepts anymore. After the interesting yet bumpy experience that was Grimgar a decade ago, it has become exceedingly rare to see him and his partner Mieko Hosoi show up on anything but an opening, ending, or at most a short film. He reacted to this episode by wondering if it had been two decades since he last directed someone else’s storyboards (Grimgar aside, it was Kaiji in 2007), but 10 years without Nakamura episodes on TV already feels outrageous.

How did this duo fare, then? Before the obvious reveal that they did great, it’s worth noting that this is true of series composer and screenwriter Kanichi Katou as well. Jaadugar hasn’t been afraid to flesh out the script and alter the order of the events, and the finale is an excellent example of how much you can gain from what appear to be tiny changes. Despite not being shy about reiteration and increasing the dramatic volume, it has remained clinical when doing so. It hasn’t become a tedious show that constantly repeats things the viewer already knows, but in an arc that hinges on the bond between Sitara and Töregene, the anime underlining the former’s desperation to save the latter much more strongly feels like welcome emotional clarity. Just by switching the order of certain scenes, the TV show maximizes its momentum, and it even feels more aware of Sitara’s standing; you can feel that much in the changes regarding when and how she finds out about information relating to high-standing individuals.

That includes, for example, her surprise when hearing about Sorghaghtani’s decision. That is to say, her refusal to take the easy way out of the conflict that had been prepared for her, in the form of an arranged marriage. As it turns out, Sitara’s speech to her sworn enemy revitalized her, effectively establishing a new powerful party in the ongoing fight for control of the empire. Amusingly, that is also what Töregene will proceed to do in this very same episode, so Sitara ends up encouraging both her favorite and most hated person to make an identical choice.

Before that point, though, the interesting fingerprints of the directors are already all over the episode. Chinashi has been leaning more on heavy layering and masking in recent times, as seen in more comedic environments like his episode of Puniru. While that trend continues, Jaadugar #12 instead employs it to enhance the exposition and connect present and past. When it comes to the usage of these techniques, the most striking example is Töregene recalling how Boraqchin led her astray. Not only is the delivery sleek, but it culminates in a beautiful shot where both of them look past each other—exactly the opposite relationship she has with Sitara. After all, both this awaited meeting and the climax of the entire show are staged so that the two look at each other in the eyes.

Right before that beautiful closure to their journey, we’re treated to another stunning face-to-face between Sitara and Ögedei. The latter asks the protagonist to share her knowledge about the stars, and the storyboards themselves turn into pure character writing. Sitara’s view of the universe is delivered through aggrandizing, sleek storyboards, sustained by what she believes must be irrefutable science. It’s a proud, complex, and increasingly passionate speech that contrasts with the unassuming simplicity of Ögedei’s beliefs. We as the viewers know that Sitara is in fact wrong, but I believe that she feels like she might be as well. Sitara is a cocktail of contradictory emotions, with pride about knowledge linked to the people she loved, anger that she has constantly found herself thinking that there is much to learn about the Mongol empire, and fear that she might still know nothing herself; after all, this is the same episode where she admits to Töregene that she’s not all that wise. Yamada talks about Sitara as a person with earnest curiosity, who can’t help but feel attracted to the beauty and knowledge of her captors every now and then, but the beauty of Jaadugar is that she’s also burning with petty yet just hatred for them.

This could paint the picture of Ögedei as a humble, well-meaning ruler, but the series’ depiction of the Great Khan remains nuanced to the end. Sure, his attempt to make Sitara and Töregene sounds as benign as the dream to create a multicultural trade hub, but his body language makes it clear that he will do it through oppression; the world and these people, in the palm of his hand. His disarming power, expressed in a way that doesn’t turn him into the easy enemy that Sitara is always looking for, leaves her physically and emotionally exhausted. It’s no exaggeration to rank the ensuing sequence among the very best in the entire show, with Sitara’s increasingly brisker walking—key animated by the excellent talent that is Hiroki Uchiyama—and her explosive frustration, so small and human when surrounded by imperturbable nature.

Fortunately for her, Töregene arrives with an extended hand; one that quickly holds a flower, because the anime is happy to go all-in on the romantic framing between these two. Sitara and her have allowed their complicated situation and other people’s machinations to create a nearly irreparable rift between each other, so Töregene’s request to team up for good is introduced through uncomfortable, extreme Dutch angles. And yet, Sitara is happy to accept, so one step forward is all it takes to even the field and reinforce their partnership. We noted that episode #11’s theme was why they fight, and right before the end, China’s storyboards provide another beautiful example of the friends and foes that motivate these two. Their initial partnership was forged under the promise of becoming the storm, but the jada stone that was supposed to summon it was spent, co-opted by one of their enemies. And so, to defeat that witch, they must become one themselves too.

If that was the last we ever saw of Jaadugar, it would already be an excellent show. It goes without saying that it’s an incomplete story if you simply observe the events, but it ought to be equally obvious—at least to the type of person inclined to watch anime like this—that there is so much more to storytelling than that. Its characters have undergone journeys that stand on their own, even more so thanks to the refined delivery of this adaptation. While there are aspects where I feel Tomato Soup’s work is simply incomparable (I stand by the cultural importance of patterning that is much hazier in the anime), this team has used the benefit of hindsight, ample room to add connective tissue, and simply brilliant direction to put together a show I wholeheartedly recommend.

Am I saying this to calm down all the people who are rushing to ask for a sequel? Oh, hell no. Jaadugar’s ideas may be fascinating, but so is the more tangible story that is being told, so there’s plenty of reason to ask for it to continue. There’s no particular argument to refute people’s faith that it will happen either; speaking to Realsound, Gongora expressed his desire to continue the series until its very end, which contrasts with how timid staff members tend to be when asked about unannounced sequels. That said, I hope people can muster enough patience. We’re talking about a monthly manga that only just ended a maternity break, without having amassed enough material for a similarly sized season quite yet. While the author is enough of a fan of the studio to facilitate their work even if it involves sharing unpublished materials, we’ve also discussed at length how Saru schedules leave enough to be desired as is—Yoshida has made his feelings clear enough this time. If you can’t wait, a 2-3 year-long nap may be due.

Having written so much about its production, I also have to add that Jaadugar has been a fascinating little project that I believe we’ll be looking back at in the future. Yoshida and his guests may be reputable veterans, but it has also been an interesting showcase of up-and-coming talent. This includes Abel Gongora himself, whom I believe has a clearer identity as a director now that he has multiple projects under his belt. Above all else, I appreciate the edge he added to Sitara, which she may have lacked if this had been a Naoko Yamada-led effort. Not that I blame anyone for having desired one of those, but given that a certain something is already in the making, you’ve got something to look forward to in the future.
