issues.title: Never forget what matters with Dr David Urbansky, founder of Linkflare
issues.summary: FEATURED TOOL Welcome to this edition of our Tools for Thought series, where we interview founders on a mission to help us think better and work smarter. Dr David Urbansky is the founder of Linkflare, a universal bookmark manager that helps you save links, read distraction-free…
issues.author: Editorial Team
issues.content_html:
FEATURED TOOL

Welcome to this edition of our Tools for Thought series, where we interview founders on a mission to help us think better and work smarter. Dr David Urbansky is the founder of Linkflare, a universal bookmark manager that helps you save links, read distraction-free, and never forget the information that matters to you.

In this interview, we talked about why saving information is not the same as remembering it, how to turn bookmarks into useful knowledge, why spaced repetition belongs in a bookmarking tool, how automation can reduce the work of organizing information, why personal knowledge may matter even more in the age of AI, and much more. Enjoy the read!

Hi David, thank you for joining us. You believe that bookmarks should be more than a collection of saved links. Why does that matter?

I’m the kind of person who keeps lists of everything. I’ve been running my life on David Allen’s Getting Things Done for years, so I have to-do lists, someday-maybe lists, lists of things to remember. And it doesn’t stop at tasks: movies I want to watch, recipes I want to try, books, places we might visit one day. Capturing things is how I close open loops. Once something is written down, my head can let it go.

The problem was never the capturing, it was where everything ended up. The movies lived in watchlists on three different streaming platforms. The recipes sat in chat threads. Interesting quotes and facts went into a notebook or onto sticky notes, and book takeaways into OneNote, where I’ve kept my lists for twenty years now. Every app is happy to hold its own little list. None of them talk to each other, and none of them care whether you ever come back.

But coming back is the whole point. A bookmark is a small promise to your future self: I will read this, cook this, remember this. Most tools let you break that promise silently. I’d finish a book full of ideas, write down the takeaways, and six months later I couldn’t find the notes, let alone remember the ideas. Saving something feels productive in the moment, but saving is not remembering. That gap between what I collected and what I could actually find and use again bothered me for a very long time.

How did you come up with the idea for Linkflare?

My whole career has been about teaching machines to read the web. I did my PhD on web content extraction and assessment, and afterwards I built data APIs for developers. The biggest one, spoonacular, takes recipes and food content and turns them into structured information: ingredients, amounts, nutrition, cooking times. So for about fifteen years my job was helping companies turn messy web pages into clean data they could build products on.

Meanwhile, my own saved knowledge was a junk drawer. My bookmarks were plain URL strings. My reading backlog lived in Pocket. My lists were scattered across half a dozen apps. At some point the irony became hard to ignore: I was pointing extraction technology at the web all day for other people’s products, and never at the thing I personally cared about most, which is my own library.

Pocket shutting down was the final push. I had years of saved reading in there, and suddenly the platform underneath it was simply gone. That made something very clear to me: what we save is only as durable as the app we save it into. So I built Linkflare, which is essentially everything I know about understanding web content, pointed at your personal library. When you save a link, the system should understand what it is, pull out the parts that matter, and help you actually come back to it.

Most bookmarking tools are good at saving content. Linkflare seems much more focused on what happens after you save them. Can you tell us more about that?

Saving is the easy part. Every tool can store a URL. The question I find much more interesting is what all those saved things should turn into later.

Sometimes the answer is very practical. My fiancée and I save recipes all week, and on the weekend they become an actual meal plan instead of a pile of screenshots. Before a movie night we don’t scroll through streaming menus for half an hour, we open our shared watch list, sort by rating and pick something. And when friends are over, there’s even a little movie-night voting mode, so everyone gets a say. None of that works if a bookmark is just a dead string.

But the deeper answer is about memory. When I read an article and highlight the two paragraphs that actually matter, those highlights shouldn’t be buried in an archive. In Linkflare they can become knowledge cards, small pieces of knowledge in your own words, still connected to their source. And because knowledge fades when you never meet it again, spaced repetition is built in: the app resurfaces your cards for a short review right around the time you’d otherwise forget them. The reviewing happens in the same place as the collecting, with no extra app in between.

That’s the loop I care about. Save something in two seconds, actually read it, connect it to what you know, and remember it. Most tools stop after the first step.

People already have browser bookmarks, read-later apps, notes, and knowledge-management tools. What do you think is missing from that workflow?

Each of those tools holds one shard of the workflow. Browser bookmarks are just a title and a URL, no context, no memory. Read-later apps quietly fill up with things you’re never going to read. Notes apps hold pasted links nobody ever clicks again. And the knowledge-management tools are wonderful for your own thinking, but they’re an awkward home for the constant stream of things you find. The way I’d put it: Obsidian is where your own thoughts live. Linkflare is where the web’s knowledge lives, and gets remembered. They complement each other well.

What was missing for me personally was one trusted place with a loop built in. Take newsletters. I subscribe to more than I can read, Ness Labs included, and for years all those unread issues piling up in my inbox just made me feel guilty. My workaround was to save the article link to Pocket and archive the email, just to feel better. Now Linkflare subscribes to those feeds directly. New issues land in my link inbox next to everything else I’ve saved, I read them when I choose to, and my email inbox is for humans again.

Open tabs are the same story. If something looks interesting, I save it and close the tab with a clear conscience, because I know I’ll find it again.

Let’s talk about how Linkflare works in more detail. What does the experience look like for someone using it day to day?

My day starts in the inbox. Overnight, my feeds have delivered new articles, and instead of doomscrolling, I read a few of them. When I’m short on time, the built-in summaries help me get through more. I subscribe to Arnold Schwarzenegger’s Pump Club, for example, which is excellent but comes out every day, and that gets overwhelming fast. For those, the summary pulls out the most important points so I don’t always have to read the whole issue. Funnily enough, they clearly know it too: each issue now ends with an AI-generated summary of its own, and those are great.

During the day, saving is a reflex. I come across a paper or a blog post, click the browser extension, done. My fiancée sends me a recipe on TikTok, I share it to Linkflare, and it extracts the actual recipe out of the video: ingredients, steps, servings. There’s an oven-baked Big Mac wrap in my account right now that started as a TikTok video she sent me, and we’ve cooked it many times since. I hear about a film, save it from IMDb, and it lands in the watch list with its rating and where it’s streaming.

The important part is that Linkflare does the librarian work to save time. It recognizes what kind of thing you saved, an article, a recipe, a movie, a place, fills in the right metadata, and my rules do the filing. Videos, for example, go automatically into my inbox to watch later.

In the evening I read saved articles in the clean reader view, or I have one read aloud to me while I go for a walk. Whatever I highlight along the way is waiting for me afterwards, ready to become something more permanent.

One of the distinctive ideas in Linkflare is that different bookmarks become useful in different ways. How does that work?

A recipe and a movie need different things from a bookmarking tool. “I’ll cook this” needs different help than “I’ll watch this” or “I’ll read this”, so Linkflare treats them differently.

When you save something, it figures out what it is and enriches it. Recipes get ingredients, cooking times and nutrition information, even when the source is a video with no written recipe anywhere. Movies and shows get the director, the IMDb rating and where you can currently stream them. Books get the author and page count, places get a map, products get the current price and can alert you when it drops. Articles get a reading time, a distraction-free reader, and audio if you’d rather listen than read.

That metadata is exactly what makes a collection useful later. When we can’t decide what to watch, I sort our watch list by IMDb rating and we pick from the top. When I want to bake something ambitious on a weekend, I check the time first: there’s a sourdough bread in my account that takes 60 hours from start to finish. That’s exactly the kind of thing you’d never find again in a chat thread. And none of it costs you anything at save time: you press one button and the rest fills itself in.

You offer quite a bit of automation, from metadata and AI tagging to organization rules. How do you balance automation with letting people organize things their own way?

My rule is that automation prepares and the user decides. Linkflare fills in everything it can on its own: the type, the metadata, a preview image, tags if you turn on automatic tagging. But every field it writes is editable, so it never turns into a black box.

On top of that there’s automation you author yourself, which I like even better: rules. “Everything from YouTube goes to the inbox.” “Recipes go into Cooking.” You describe the rule once and the filing happens forever after. And when the built-in metadata isn’t enough, you can define your own structured fields, a number, a date, a text, whatever matches how you think, and filter and sort by them like everything else.

I tried hard not to impose my own organizational religion on anyone. Some people maintain a meticulous tree of collections, others throw everything into one big pool and rely on search and filters. Both work fine. The point is that organizing never becomes a second job. You already did the interesting part when you decided something was worth keeping.

Linkflare has spaced repetition built in, which most people associate with flashcard apps and language learning. Why bring memory practice into a bookmarking tool?

Because the forgetting curve doesn’t care where you learned something. Read a brilliant article on Monday, and by Friday most of it is gone. That’s just how memory works when you never revisit material.

That always struck me as a waste. We put real effort into finding and reading good things, and then let almost all of it evaporate. There are excellent flashcard apps, but hardly anyone sits down after reading an article to author flashcards about it. The friction is too high. So in practice, spaced repetition stays locked inside vocabulary drills and exam prep, while the knowledge we deliberately gather as adults gets nothing.

So we removed the friction. While you read in Linkflare, you highlight. Highlights and takeaways become knowledge cards, which you organize into topics. Any card you want to keep, you toggle into review, and the review queue does the rest: it brings each card back right around the time you’d otherwise forget it, at growing intervals. You can grade yourself, or have Linkflare generate a quiz question about the card and evaluate your answer.

Reviewing your own material also feels completely different from studying somebody else’s deck. You picked every single card, so every question is about something you once cared enough to save. A few minutes between two work sessions. It never feels like homework, but fun and thanks to some AI always different and fresh.

With search engines and AI assistants one keystroke away, some people would argue we don’t need to remember anything anymore. Why do you think internalizing knowledge still matters?

Knowledge you carry is the only knowledge you can think with. Connections don’t happen in a database, they happen in your head. You notice that an idea in an article contradicts something from a book you read last year, or that a concept from biology maps beautifully onto a problem at work. If neither of them is in your memory, no search engine will produce that spark for you.

There’s a social side too. Everyone can look facts up now, which is exactly why carrying knowledge has become rarer and more interesting. The most interesting person in the room isn’t the one who can google or ChatGPT fastest. It’s the person who can tell you the story behind the fact, connect it to what you just said, and pull in something surprising from a completely different field. That’s taking advantage of your curious mind.

I actually think AI assistants make remembering more valuable, not less. When answers are cheap, what sets people apart is judgment, taste, and the things they really know. The assistants are great at retrieving. The connecting and the doubting still happen in a human head, and they work with whatever you’ve actually retained.

Who exactly is Linkflare designed for?

Curious people and lifelong learners, first of all. People who read and watch and save a lot, and want it to make them smarter, which only works if you remember any of it later. They’re the ones who get the most out of highlights, knowledge cards, and the review queue.

And people who like order. If you recognize yourself in the mess I described earlier — movie lists on the streaming platforms, books in one app, recipes in chat threads, articles in a read-it-later tool, notes in a PKM system — Linkflare is one tidy home for all of those lists. No clutter, and everything stays findable.

And families. Some of the most-used collections in my own household are the shared ones.

What about you, how do you personally use Linkflare?

Everything I’ve described is from my real account, but here’s a bit more of it. The daily backbone is the inbox: newsletters and feeds land there, and I work through it in idle moments. Our watch list currently holds about sixty movies and shows, sorted by IMDb rating, which has ended more than one “what should we watch” discussion in under a minute. Recipes my fiancée and I save during the week turn into the weekend’s cooking. When we plan a trip, everything goes into a vacation collection, sights, restaurants, hotels, so the itinerary basically assembles itself.

The collection I cherish most is the one we share for our son: things we’d like to get him, places we want to take him. Either of us saves something in passing, and both of us see it.

On the knowledge side, I turn book takeaways and article highlights into knowledge cards. My review habit is nothing heroic: around ten cards a week, in the moments between work sessions when I would otherwise just check email. And lately, because Linkflare has an MCP server, I sometimes let Claude quiz me on my own cards in the middle of a work day. Being interrogated by my own library is still a slightly surreal experience.

And since we’re at Ness Labs: the highlight in the screenshot below is from one of yours, “The Omnipotence Dilemma”, a line about committing to your curiosity instead of chasing every thread at once — more or less the philosophy behind the whole product. Any highlight can be turned into a share card like that straight from the app.

Looking ahead, how do you see Linkflare and personal knowledge management evolving over the next few years?

There are two things I keep coming back to. The first: your library has to outlive any platform. Pocket’s shutdown was a warning shot for the whole industry. So your data stays exportable, and the business is funded by subscriptions rather than attention, which means I have no incentive to keep you scrolling. A tool for thought has to be on your side.

The second: your library should start working for you. Linkflare has an MCP server, which means AI assistants can, with your permission, search your bookmarks, save new ones, and quiz you on your knowledge cards. I find that direction far more interesting than generic chatbots, because this assistant knows what you’ve collected over the years, not just the internet at large. “What was that article about sleep I saved last year, and what did I highlight in it?” should simply have an answer.

Beyond that, I want the connections to get deeper. The tool should notice that something you save today relates to something you highlighted months ago, and tell you. I think the next years of personal knowledge management will be less about capturing more, because everyone has capture solved, and much more about resurfacing better — showing you the right memory at the moment you can use it, from a library you own.

Thank you so much for your time, David! Where can people learn more about Linkflare?

Everything starts on our website, and you can use it for free. I’m on X and on Bluesky as well, and I’d love to hear how you organize your corner of the web.

For Ness Labs readers we’ve set up something small: the code NESSLABS gets you 30 days of Linkflare Pro for free.

And if you only try one thing, make it a tiny experiment, in proper Ness Labs fashion: for one week, save everything interesting into the inbox instead of leaving tabs open, and spend five minutes a day reviewing what you captured. Watch what it does to your focus, and to how much you remember.

issues.title: Evidence-grounded AI writing with Jim Lau, founder of Flowing
issues.summary: FEATURED TOOL Welcome to this edition of our Tools for Thought series, where we interview founders on a mission to help us think better and work smarter. Jim Lau is the founder of Flowing, a desktop writing application for researchers and students who want AI assistance without…
issues.author: Editorial Team
issues.content_html:
FEATURED TOOL

Welcome to this edition of our Tools for Thought series, where we interview founders on a mission to help us think better and work smarter. Jim Lau is the founder of Flowing, a desktop writing application for researchers and students who want AI assistance without losing touch with their sources. It allows you to import your reference PDFs into a local library and use AI features that attach verifiable library snippets to every suggestion.

In this interview, we talked about how writing is a form of thinking and not just text production, how to use AI to strengthen human judgement, the importance of context and the challenge of resurfacing what we already know, how trust is based on traceability, and much more. Enjoy the read!

Hi Jim, thank you for joining us. You’re building Flowing around the idea that AI-assisted writing should stay grounded in the researcher’s own sources. Why do you think that matters?

Thank you for having me. I think the reason this matters comes down to a fundamental difference between writing and simply generating text.

Academic writing is not only about producing sentences that sound clear or convincing. It is a process of building a coherent argument where ideas, claims, evidence, and prior research connect with each other. A strong manuscript depends on how a research question is motivated, how previous studies support or challenge an argument, and how evidence connects with the conclusions.

Much of this coherence comes from the researcher’s years of reading, experiments, notes, and the specific body of literature they have built around a topic.

Researchers often do not struggle because information is unavailable. Over years of research, they build extensive research libraries containing hundreds or thousands of papers. The challenge is that valuable insights are often buried inside those PDFs, and reconnecting them with the writing process at the right moment can be difficult. A paper a researcher read months ago may contain exactly the idea or evidence they need, but finding that specific passage again while drafting can interrupt their train of thought.

For me, evidence-grounded AI writing means bringing a researcher’s own research library back into the moment of writing. The goal is to keep that knowledge present during writing — helping researchers reconnect with what they have learned while giving AI better context to work with.

How did you come up with the idea for Flowing?

Flowing evolved from my earlier exploration of how researchers interact with knowledge throughout their workflow.

Before Flowing, I built a research paper reader called Paperly. I initially focused on making references more accessible during reading, helping researchers move between papers and their cited sources without breaking their flow. Over time, I realized that reading was only the beginning of the challenge — the deeper question was how researchers could bring the knowledge they had accumulated back into the moments when they needed it most, especially during writing.

The emergence of generative AI brought a new dimension to this question. As researchers started experimenting with AI-assisted writing, it became clear that AI could provide valuable support during the writing process, but it also introduced new challenges around reliability and trust.

A chemistry professor I worked with experienced this while experimenting with AI-assisted writing for a manuscript. Although the generated text was often fluent and well-structured, he also encountered cases where some statements sounded convincing but did not accurately reflect the underlying research. This created a natural concern: how can researchers benefit from AI assistance while ensuring that their writing remains connected to reliable evidence and the actual context of their work?

That experience shifted my attention toward a different question: how could AI work with the literature and context researchers already rely on? Flowing grew from that direction.

A lot of the conversation around AI writing focuses on the model itself. You seem to believe context may be just as important. Can you tell us more about that?

I think the progress of AI models has been remarkable, and model quality will continue to matter. But when AI is working inside a specific manuscript, another question becomes important: what context does the model actually have access to?

We explored this through a comparison using a real chemistry research manuscript. We gave Flowing and ChatGPT the same manuscript, the same writing position, and the same instruction, and compared their continuation across four examples from different sections.

What we found was that both approaches could produce fluent academic writing, but the literature-grounded workflow was often better aligned with the manuscript’s existing terminology and reasoning. The difference came from having relevant research context available during the writing process.

I shared the full comparison, including the four examples and screenshots, here. What this suggested to me is that model capability and research-specific context are not competing ideas. They solve different parts of the problem.

Researchers already have search engines, reference managers, PDF readers, and AI chatbots. What do you think is missing from that workflow?

I think the interesting thing is that researchers already have many powerful tools. Search engines help them discover papers, reference managers help organize their libraries, PDF readers help them understand individual documents, and AI assistants can help with drafting and editing.

These tools are valuable on their own, but researchers often have to manually move between them throughout their workflow. A paper discovered through a search engine becomes a reference in a library, annotations remain inside a PDF reader, and writing happens somewhere else. The context built during the research process does not always follow naturally into the moment when researchers start writing.

This is the gap Flowing is trying to address. Rather than treating the research library as a separate archive, we want relevant knowledge to come back into the writing process when it is actually useful — without researchers repeatedly searching for the same passages or manually moving context between tools.

I also had an interesting exchange with Rob Cuthbert, Editor of SRHE News and Emeritus Professor of Higher Education Management. He mentioned that some of the workflow ideas behind Flowing resonated with his own thinking about academic writing. It was useful to hear a similar concern from someone who has spent a long time thinking about academic practice.

I don’t see Flowing as replacing the tools researchers already rely on. I see it as trying to make the knowledge accumulated across those tools much easier to carry into the actual process of thinking and writing.

Let’s talk about how Flowing works in more detail. What does the experience look like for someone writing a paper?

A typical workflow starts with importing the researcher’s existing papers into Flowing. From there, they can write directly in their manuscript while Flowing retrieves literature that is relevant to what they are currently working on.

For researchers who are just getting started, having a complete literature library is not a requirement. When relevant sources are missing, Flowing can analyze the current writing context and help identify highly related papers that researchers can choose to add to their library. Over time, the research library becomes richer and more closely aligned with the researcher’s ongoing work.

As researchers draft a paper, Flowing analyzes the current manuscript context and retrieves relevant information from the literature library to support different writing tasks. Instead of asking researchers to manually copy background information into an AI prompt, the relevant research context can be brought into the writing process when it becomes useful.

For example, when refining a paragraph, researchers can use Flowing’s polishing workflow to improve clarity and expression while keeping the terminology, concepts, and reasoning consistent with the underlying research context.

Similarly, when continuing a manuscript, Flowing can suggest possible next sentences or paragraphs based on both the existing manuscript and relevant literature context. The goal is to help researchers explore possible directions while staying connected to the knowledge behind their work.

Throughout this process, researchers remain in control of the final decisions. They can review suggestions, examine the supporting context, and decide what best fits their argument and research goals.

One of the distinctive features is the way Flowing surfaces evidence alongside the manuscript. How does that work?

One of the ideas behind Flowing is that evidence should be brought closer to the writing process itself. In many existing workflows, researchers have their papers organized in reference managers or folders, but the connection between those sources and the manuscript often requires manual searching. When a researcher is writing a specific paragraph, finding the exact passage that supports an idea can interrupt their flow.

Flowing addresses this by making snippets from the research library context-aware. Based on what the researcher is currently writing, Flowing surfaces relevant passages from their papers and presents them as Evidence Cards alongside the manuscript.

Each Evidence Card keeps the original source visible. Researchers can quickly review the relevant snippet, understand its context, and jump directly back to the original paper when they want to examine the full passage. This makes it easier to verify the connection between the writing and the underlying research.

Sometimes an Evidence Card also resurfaces something the researcher had forgotten — perhaps an explanation or perspective from a paper they read months earlier that suddenly becomes relevant again. I find that particularly interesting because the retrieved evidence is not only useful for AI; it can also help the researcher rediscover connections in their own reading.

AI can make writing faster, but writing is also part of how researchers think. How do you avoid automating too much of that process?

I think writing is not only a way to communicate research — it is also part of how researchers develop and refine their thinking. The goal of AI assistance should therefore not be to replace this process, but to support it.

AI can be valuable for reducing friction in writing, such as helping researchers refine expressions, explore possible structures, or continue developing an idea. However, the deeper parts of research writing — deciding what matters, how evidence should be interpreted, and where an argument should go — require the researcher’s own judgment.

This is why Flowing is designed around keeping researchers involved in the thinking process. Instead of generating a paper from scratch, Flowing brings relevant sources and context into the writing process, allowing researchers to evaluate ideas, explore possibilities, and make their own decisions.

In some ways, the role of AI is not only to create something new, but also to help researchers reconnect with and build upon the knowledge they have already accumulated.

I believe the best AI tools for research should make researchers more connected to their work, not less. AI can help with the process of writing, but the direction, interpretation, and intellectual ownership should remain with the researcher.

Who exactly is Flowing designed for?

Flowing is designed for researchers who are working with a growing body of literature and want to bring that knowledge more naturally into the writing process.

This includes PhD students, graduate researchers, academics, and anyone working on research-intensive writing projects where the connection between ideas, evidence, and previous literature is important.

The most common use cases are manuscript writing, literature reviews, research proposals, and other forms of academic writing where researchers need to maintain consistency with a large amount of existing knowledge.

Flowing is especially useful when researchers are not starting from a blank page, but are trying to turn years of reading and accumulated knowledge into a coherent piece of writing.

What about you, how do you personally use Flowing?

One moment that stood out to me happened while I was writing about agent-related research. Flowing surfaced a passage about context building from a well-known paper at exactly the point where it became relevant to what I was writing.

What I found interesting was that, if I am being realistic, I probably would not have searched for that term myself at that moment. It was relevant, but it was not the keyword I had in mind, and there is always a bit of human laziness involved when you are already focused on writing.

Seeing that passage appear at the right moment felt surprisingly helpful. It was almost like having a research assistant quietly place a useful piece of information beside me and say, “this might be relevant here.” That is one of the moments when I personally felt the value of this kind of workflow most clearly.

I also use my own research as a way to test Flowing carefully. I check whether continuation suggestions stay consistent with the original papers, and I built a separate agent that automatically collects and analyzes the Evidence Cards Flowing retrieves so I can evaluate their relevance and quality.

At the same time, I’m working with the chemistry professor I mentioned earlier to use Flowing for review-style writing, where we often need to connect ideas and evidence across many different papers.

Looking ahead, how do you see Flowing and AI-assisted research writing evolving over the next few years?

In the future, I hope research tools can turn scattered papers, evidence, references, and ideas into a connected, traceable knowledge network that is easier to think with.

Today, researchers often have to know what they are looking for before they can find it. You remember a concept, come up with a keyword, search for it, and then try to reconnect what you find with the problem in front of you. I would like that relationship with knowledge to become much more fluid. Relevant ideas should be within reach while you are reading or writing, even when you would not have thought to search for them explicitly.

Over time, I also hope this kind of system can support more associative exploration. A paragraph you are writing might connect to a concept in one paper, which in turn leads to a related method, disagreement, or perspective from another. These connections could help both researchers and AI move beyond simple retrieval and explore how different pieces of knowledge relate to one another, while always remaining traceable to the underlying evidence.

And this network should keep growing with the researcher. As new papers, notes, evidence, and ideas are added, the system should become better at reflecting the body of knowledge they have built over time, rather than treating every writing session as a new starting point.

For Flowing, that is the longer-term direction I find most exciting: making a researcher’s accumulated knowledge easier to reach and build on, so the writing process can also become a place where new connections emerge.

Thank you so much for your time, Jim! Where can people learn more about Flowing?

You can learn more about Flowing on our website. It includes an overview video, detailed documentation, and step-by-step tutorials to help you understand how Flowing works in different writing workflows. I also share more thoughts and experiments around evidence-grounded and context-aware AI writing on my Substack.

Thank you again for the opportunity to share the story behind Flowing. I truly appreciate the chance to discuss these ideas with the Ness Labs community, and I would be grateful to hear thoughts and feedback from researchers and anyone interested in exploring new ways of working with AI and knowledge.

issues.title: Jaadugar: A Witch In Mongolia Production Notes #01-06 – Historically Accurate Animation Meets Compelling Artifice
issues.summary: Jaadugar: A Witch in Mongolia is a one-of-a-kind effort in historical and cultural accuracy in TV anime, but also smart enough to introduce pointed, imaginative deceit to make for a more compelling story. Let’s delve into such a unique production! Chances are that you first…
issues.author: kViN
issues.content_html:
Jaadugar: A Witch in Mongolia is a one-of-a-kind effort in historical and cultural accuracy in TV anime, but also smart enough to introduce pointed, imaginative deceit to make for a more compelling story. Let’s delve into such a unique production!

Chances are that you first heard about Jaadugar: A Witch in Mongolia as framed through the lens of its historical accuracy, emphasized to a degree seldom seen in TV anime. There is no conversation about the series that doesn’t underline the presence of several cultural advisors, despite that approach greatly increasing the back-and-forths for approval; no collection of anecdotes that doesn’t mention how the desire to feature authentic speech led to hiring two Mongolian sumo wrestlers as voice actors; and just as importantly, no shortage of viewers happy to see their heritage in anime, in ways commercial works will rarely bother with. The team has proved their carefulness in the depiction of both Persian and Mongol societies, and beyond that, a genuine interest in learning about their customs and beliefs.

Its creators’ respect for the cultures depicted in the series isn’t just something they’ve been protecting inwards, but also a stance that the project has projected toward the audience. After all, one of the biggest promotional efforts leading up to the broadcast was a handful of interviews with its series directors during their location trip to Mongolia. While the brief introduction in Tus was sustained by remote research, both about 13th-century Persia and modern-day Iran, the production team actually made a trip to the location where the bulk of the story occurs. Accuracy and respect were always on their mind, and they want viewers to know that as well.

Chief director Naoko Yamada’s duties have changed ever since she became a freelance creator, but one aspect she’ll never compromise on is rooting stories in the physical realities of people. In an interview for Mantan (available translated over at Magical Stage), she noted that it doesn’t matter whether a narrative is fantastical or set in a different time period—she must find a way to ground them in people’s actual lives and environments. Despite not being permanently stationed at a physical studio anymore, she happily took the time to make this scouting trip to Mongolia. This particular pre-production stage has never been all that common, and the ready availability of visual materials only renders it unnecessary to the eyes of many, but the likes of Yamada will never leave it behind.

Alongside her was up-and-coming series director Abel Góngora, who has echoed similar feelings about the importance of keeping a tangible core built upon personal experiences. In his interview for Animate Times, shared in English by the Kyodo News portal, he emphasized all the aspects you simply must feel first-hand if you want to evoke them in animation; conceptual ones like people’s daily routines and their specific struggles, but also sensorial information like the smells, tastes, and the sheer impact of witnessing the vast steppe. In summary, all that you won’t get by simply reading books on the topic. Given his worry about honoring the cultures that this story revolves around, he found it particularly important to maintain realistic foundations, despite Jaadugar’s cartoony aesthetic.

Although we’ve focused on the leaders of the TV anime adaptation, it goes without saying that the deference to the cultures being portrayed is an attitude inherited from Tomato Soup’s original manga. Her detailed research involves reading up on the works of historians from various countries, visiting museums, as well as direct consultations about specific details. Although this process is fueled by her long-held interests in cultures like the Mongols, there is also her awareness as a foreign entity borrowing from other cultures to entertain a similarly disconnected audience; which is to say, that she wants to avoid making a mockery of the people she represents. For all her convictions, that’s easier said than done—speaking to Animate Times, she noted that the endless questioning by the anime team about the nuance of her intent made her realize a few chronological inaccuracies, as well as minute cultural aspects she’d never considered before. It’s only through combined efforts and respect that Jaadugar has become a beautiful crystallization of ancient Persia and Mongol.

The statements by everyone involved paint a picture of a series very dedicated to historical accuracy, and the results of their efforts demonstrate they’re not all talk. If you were to reduce Jaadugar to an objective retelling of history, though, you would be doing this series a disservice. This is not to say that a documentary-like stance is inherently less compelling, but dispassionate objectivity wouldn’t align with the directors’ sensibilities, and framing it as such would obscure very interesting aspects of this team’s mindset. It goes without saying that historical fiction isn’t factual—half the term tells you that—but striving for accuracy to this degree can make people forget that fundamental truth.

It’s in the ways one weaves reality with compelling lies that you learn the most about artists in this genre space. In that regard, a conversation between Yamada and Tomato Soup published by Souffle is perhaps the most revealing. The author reveals that writing historical works makes you seek as many factual records as possible, but paradoxically, an excess of information can become a hindrance as a storyteller. When it comes to somewhat modern history, the awareness that you’ll find countless detailed testimonies means you can’t take a single step without exhaustive research. Ultimately, you’re left with little room to create a compelling story of your own. On the other hand, looking back at medieval periods strikes a nice balance between the availability of information and the appeal of the unknown and uncontrasted. It’s in those gaps that Yamada believes the author has created some of Jaadugar’s most wonderful characters.

Given that appreciation, it’s no surprise that the team behind the anime was also prepared to escape from cold, objective facts whenever they thought it would benefit the story. Speaking to Indiewire, both series directors brought up one such example. Their cultural advisors rightfully pushed back against their desire to feature someone smoking in the background of the bustling Tus introduction, as that wouldn’t be true to the time period. While they understood that, Yamada argued that strolling through a bazaar in modern-day Iran would be synonymous with witnessing people smoking shisha on the ground. This idea was ultimately discarded, but it has become an example of their willingness to pull anachronistic tricks to reinforce the familiarity of the story for all viewers.

For a different type of concession to fantasy, Yoko Kuno‘s gorgeous opening features the type of surreally beautiful colors that wouldn’t normally fit the show’s more grounded palette.

In its own way, the anime’s distinct aesthetic is also the product of a delicate process of combining true-to-life concepts and tactical lies. Tomato Soup’s Osamu Tezuka-inspired artwork is deliberately flat and farcical, in a way that overly realistic renderings would erode the charm. How did they navigate that, then, as a team who desired to emphasize the authenticity as well? In an interview for WIRED alongside Góngora, Yamada talks about drawing inspiration from relevant cultural artifacts like Persian & Islamic miniatures and ancient Mongolian paintings, which directly anchor the show in its real setting. Conversely, Góngora points out other ingredients (like Toei Douga’s Wanpaku Ouji) when it came to putting together the earthen, muted, vintage colors that evoke a historical atmosphere. Be it through direct references or these tricks that help viewers make connections, the desire to create a world that feels real—even when it factually isn’t—remains the same.

One of the trickiest aspects to balance when bringing the setting to life was the world itself. Following the aforementioned guidelines, WIT color designer Narumi Konno and ex-KyoAni/ufotable art director Yuri Kabasawa have spearheaded an effort that succeeds at evoking the right time period and cultures. But what about the more physical aspect of those settings? Their starting point was Tomato Soup’s drawings, with their aforementioned flatness and visibly artificial space. Although you could tackle them in straightforward fashion, a team interested in showcasing how people live ought to place them in an environment where it feels like they could go on with their daily routine—something that demands a degree of three-dimensionality. Jaadugar’s answer, then, is to commit to neither fundamental understanding of space and instead go back and forth between flatness and believable spaciousness as it sees fit. This places a burden on individual episode directors to nail the balance, but we wouldn’t be here if they hadn’t done a great job with that.

That duality is also present in the character designs themselves, which does facilitate the back and forth. As seen in this IGN India piece, articulating the characters in a believable way was the biggest worry for Kazuki Endo as he sought a team to animate Jaadugar. As the TV Asahi producer explains, the simple-looking style may look like it makes the animation process easier… but that potential is also tied to the tremendous challenge of deriving fluid, compelling character acting out of such stylized forms. With designs featuring a higher level of detail and humanlike proportions, our brain will happily fill the gaps that TV animation inevitably has, allowing us to read basic character animation as actions we see in the real world. When you articulate Jaadugar’s clearly farcical designs, though, that bar for the suspension of disbelief raises exponentially. Endo was afraid that conventional studios wouldn’t be up for this challenge, so he took the proposal to Science Saru, as they were used to animating unorthodox designs. Fortunately for him, not only were they interested in the series, but also happened to be Tomato Soup’s dream studio.

Another highlight of Kuno’s opening is the chorus cuts. Albeit animated by Hiroki Uchiyama here, they’re conceptually reminiscent of Kuno’s student and independent work back in the day; defined by sepia tones and bewitching morphing, just like her old music videos used to be.

Who did they entrust with this tricky job, then? None other than Kenichi Yoshida, a Ghibli-trained titan best known for his exquisite designs on the likes of Eureka Seven, King Gainer, or G-Reco. His attitude made him immediately compatible with the job; and not only because he has been interested in the Mongol Empire since he was a child, though that certainly helps. Speaking to Mantan (again, translated at Magical Stage), Yamada emphasizes just how much research Yoshida does, even for the most minute choices as a character designer. Back during the release of Orbital Children, Mitsuo Iso went as far as calling Yoshida one of the few remaining true designers in anime. Which is to say, someone who won’t simply draw a few reference sheets, but carefully consider how every choice interacts with the narrative and other departments of the production process.

As Yoshida explained to Mantan, that meticulous mindset brought him to research items of clothing like turbans and hijab; not only how they’re constructed and the ways they’re worn in a vacuum, but also how that appearance might change depending on the current circumstances of the character—you certainly don’t dress yourself the same way in your everyday life and when you’re a war prisoner. Just like everyone else on the team, Yoshida combined these authentic ideas with the right amount of liberties to facilitate Jaadugar’s goals. This includes making its production somewhat easier too: we’ve mentioned how the producer at the origin of the project worried about articulating the stumpy designs in human-like fashion, and as Góngora reveals in his aforementioned Animate Times feature, Yoshida tweaked their proportions for that purpose. While it’s subtle enough you may not have noticed, the Jaadugar anime features slightly more elongated, taller human bodies, bringing them closer to the forms that animators find familiar.

After all, this process of taking liberties doesn’t simply amount to the occasional departure from factual history, but also to knowing when to distance yourself from the source material. Mind you, this doesn’t mean contradicting it, but rather confronting its ideas and reinforcing certain themes. Jaadugar is the story of Sitara’s rise as an increasingly powerful aide in the Mongol Empire; the very same that ravaged her home in Tus, killed many of her loved ones, and forcefully dragged her to foreign environments. Themes like revenge are built into that premise, but at the same time, we can’t forget that Sitara already was a slave in the household that took her in after her mother’s death.

In their research, the creators behind Jaadugar found that slavery has manifested itself in rather different forms across history. Ancient Persia may have been open to adopting individuals as a true member of a family, something that slight tweaks in the anime like the double premiere underline with more effectivity. And yet, there’s no denying she was part of an asymmetrical, restrictive dynamic that limited her personhood, hence why Góngora’s proposed theme of freedom feels particularly apt.

We see that emphasis on freedom before Mongol-shaped tragedy strikes. In fact, it’s one of the first things we witness, as Jaadugar #01 opens with an original scene where Sitara runs around Tus, trying to escape from her captors. First by the hand of Shuto Enomoto—the individual behind certain outstanding efforts at Saru—and later through the lively drawings of surprise guest Yuki Hayashi as she once again tries to flee, we experience that duality of space we talked about earlier. Jaadugar can switch from flat renderings that emphasize the symmetrical nature of the architecture to spacious, lived-in spaces with astonishing naturality. The first quest across this layered setting leads to Sitara watching flocks of birds take flight, signaling not just the beginning of the story but the desire for freedom that feels key to Góngora.

Given that we have a duality of series directors, it’s worth addressing the specificities of their roles, and why it was Góngora who storyboarded and directed (with the assistance of his close associate Takuya Fujikura) episode #01. In short, he was the one who first accepted the pitch to direct Jaadugar. At that point, Yamada had wrapped up The Colors Within, so the studio wanted to find a new project to continue borrowing her talents. When she heard that Góngora had gotten his hands on Jaadugar, a series that greatly appeals to her sensibilities, she proactively wormed her way into the project. Yamada took a supportive stance as the director who arrived ever so slightly later, deciding to foster Góngora’s imagination rather than restricting it with her own vision. As she jokingly summarizes, she took the position of Góngora’s personal cheerleader for Jaadugar.

Her assignment as chief director while Góngora stayed as the regular project leader translated into Yamada focusing more on structural, writing-related duties, while he commanded the operations in the trenches. We should mention, though, that this isn’t a perfectly clean binary of conceptual choices versus day-to-day audiovisual execution—nothing is ever that simple within a real production. The directors pointed out as much in the WIRED interview we referred to earlier, and the fact that we’ve started examining the series through a theme that Góngora chose demonstrates it as well.

Beyond the grand statements of purpose, Góngora’s storyboard for the first episode is also impressive in its subtler additions. Sitara’s first meeting with Muhammad is an important beat in the story, but at the same time, it’s also a fun interaction between two kids with a punchline in the form of him being flustered about her uncovered hair. While in the manga he’s talking about her headdress not covering her in full, the anime builds into that idea of the characters existing in a physical, real space, making her lose it altogether as she sneaks around.

Another excellent quality exhibited all across the first episode is the subtle three-dimensionality of the designs. This is an aspect that stood out as early as the promotional videos, and something the directors have since then effusively praised Yoshida for. Under his exclusive supervision, the premiere imbues all drawings with a sense of volume, but never betrays the simple silhouettes and flat appeal of Tomato Soup’s original work. It’s a fine line to thread, but he manages to make clearly farcical characters feel like they truly exist in a world, especially as the anime fleshes out everyone’s daily lives in Tus.

For as amazing as most aspects are, this introduction to the story also showcases the concessions the team had to make. Jaadugar is, maybe above all else, synonymous with patterns. Thematically, the intricate ornaments and lavish architecture convey the richness of the civilizations that are being portrayed. And just as importantly, the act of reading the series is akin to being hypnotized by the endlessly repeating shapes. The author’s simple style helps the drawings never become exhausting, but there’s something deeply mesmerizing about a world densely packed with culturally important shapes. While the anime is aware of how much this matters, the much hazier rendering of the world through Kabasawa’s art direction doesn’t have the same magnetic appeal. Similarly, and clearly related to the limitations of a production we’ll discuss later, clothes aren’t adorned in quite the same way.

Mind you, that is perfectly understandable. Introducing highly-detailed clothing into a project, especially when patterns are inescapable, greatly increases everyone’s workload. Although you can approach a challenge like that from multiple angles, none of them makes the downsides magically disappear. It goes without saying that excruciatingly drawing them by hand burdens the entire production line, from every step of the animation process to the departments that have to process their work, such as the painting team. This very season, we have a great example of that challenge in Sparks of Tomorrow, which partly roots the Meiji era aspect of the setting in everyone having their own—often multiple—distinct kimono with fully animated motifs. For as effective as that is in reinforcing the story’s identity, it has also made veterans at the studio note that it was an exhausting task even for a powerhouse like theirs, which effectively puts it outside the scope of TV anime.

To bypass that, many TV anime have traditionally opted for overlaying patterns that aren’t baked into the animation itself. Digital pipelines make this act trivial, but that doesn’t mean it becomes seamless with ease. Unless it’s perfectly fine-tuned anytime they’re on-screen, the separation between two clearly distinct layers in the clothes introduces a level of irreality to every single shot; that’s exactly what makes Gankutsuou one of the most fascinating anime ever made, but that level of swag might not be legal in the current era. Opting for a more believable angle instead, Jaadugar maintains these shapes in the character cels, simplifying them enough to make the animation process feasible.

One of the relative downsides of their concessions arrives alongside the Mongol invasion in episode #02. In a comic so dominated by these omnipresent patterns, their sacking of Tus is synonymous with the destruction of all shapes that defined the civilization that flourished there. Within an adaptation that is aware of this aspect but couldn’t afford to be equally thorough, the impact of that cultural annihilation isn’t quite as potent. Without getting too ahead of ourselves, this continues to be weaponized moving forward; Sitara understandably holds prejudices against her captors, but her view of them as savages is challenged in a fascinating way by the fact that she eventually witnesses Mongol clothing and interior patterns that are just as lavish as those seen in Tus. Again, the lesser prevalence in the anime reduces the meaningful impact of that reveal. To make up for that, though, the human component is arguably enhanced—after all, it’s finally time for Yamada to co-direct and storyboard an episode.

It’s no secret that, as a storyteller, Yamada always opts to frame narratives through character lenses. Jaadugar is a story about incomprehensibly large empires, about atrocities at such a scale that they physically impacted the planet. And yet, it’s specifically the story of Sitara and those who most closely surround her, which is the angle Yamada unsurprisingly chose to emphasize. Although the presentation of episode #02 is occasionally more grand than you’d expect from her (see the dramatic drops of blood when both her new family and their beloved books are taken away), the sense of intimacy when she’s at her lowest oozes Yamada’s touch. The clumsy but heartfelt attempt to console her, animated by Saru regular Eitetsu, is easily among the highlights of a very affecting episode.

Yamada’s means of conveying the heartbreak are particularly interesting, as she finds herself in an environment that encourages her to flex different stylistic muscles than usual. She has noted that her usual approach to frame animation as if it were shot through a camera lens wouldn’t fit the style of the series, and being more of a supportive presence than the leader she often is, she preferred not to stir the boat. Instead, the interiority of characters and their mood is projected by stylistic choices in realms other than the compositing. A particularly striking characteristic is the choices of color across episode #02; in contrast to the lively yet earthen Tus we’d seen so far, the palette after the destruction and when she becomes a war prisoner turns much more vivid than before. It’s a cruel, natural allure that reminds Sitara there is beauty in this world, even when she can no longer perceive it.

Perhaps the most obvious shift in Yamada’s toolset is the way Jaadugar portrays light. It’s worth prefacing this by saying that the production employs digital effects just like any other show, and it occasionally does so with exceptional grace. That said, it’s also a title where much of the expression of lighting falls upon cel layers, making it part of the drawings themselves. Yamada embraces this approach and grants it resonance; the final moments of a comrade’s fading life are defined by the sunset, one she wishes she could have experienced once more in very different circumstances.

The following episode, this time led by episode director and storyboarder Yujirou Abe, continues to use the show’s distinct lighting in pointed ways. Its introduction links it to the power of Genghis Khan, and even more clearly, those cel rays accompany the arrival of his mightiest son. Tolui is the youngest prince, yet he commands the strongest military forces, having recently been the leader behind Tus’ sacking. His dazzling arrival, in contrast to the more grounded depiction of the siblings awaiting him, underlines that he appears to be the empire’s crown jewel.

Sitara’s first exposure to the inner machinations of the empire gestures toward the incredible scope that the story gradually adopts, but #03 is by all means a breather after an intense double premiere. Spurred by history’s first LinkedIn user Shira, a fellow captive, Sitara adopts her master’s name Fatima and vows to recover the stolen book. She’ll pretend to lower her head and loan her talents to her captors, but all she desires is getting back at the empire that took everything from her. While she silences her rage, the show introduces someone who fruitlessly voices the exact same animosity. This person is Töregene, sixth wife of unassuming prince Ögedei, and her relationship with Sitara will end up being the most important bond in the entire show.

For now, however, this is indeed a more relaxed episode where the big narrative swing takes a backseat to certain themes. Above all else, it emphasizes the importance of cultural exchange, as well as how different groups of people have historically processed similar information in their own ways. Despite her hatred for the empire, Sitara is eager to learn their language and customs, which quickly become weapons to climb within their society. Conversely, the brutal Mongol also contain the likes of Tolui’s first wife Sorghaghtani, who understands that their rise to power is an opportunity to acquire the vast knowledge from all the territories they’ve conquered.

A recurring topic in Jaadugar, as we’ll see in future episodes, is the struggle against mortality. The inescapability of death and our stance regarding that universal truth are explored by various cultures in the series, with episode #03 featuring the visit of a supposedly immortal eastern sage. Speaking with an Uyghur individual, Sitara ends up sharing a story she once read, with the moral that one should wish for a healthy death rather than immortality. In response, the man reveals that the sage had told him that he wasn’t actually immortal, and that he shouldn’t be—both cultures had reached the same conclusion. This is all rendered in a particularly memorable way, as Sitara’s fable becomes a cut-out animation tale drawn by Ryoko Tanaka. Like many other neat aspects of the aesthetic, this draws direct influence from period-appropriate arc, but also introduces compelling lies to be more effective with a modern audience.

Abe’s storyboard further highlights the idea of convergent evolution of knowledge; people will face somewhat similar challenges regardless of their place of birth, so despite the formulation of the answers being different, you’ll be able to appreciate recognizable trains of thought during these cultural exchanges. As Sitara ponders how her captors keep track of time, she eventually realizes that clocks are built into their tents—using the same principle as the astrolabes she’s familiar with. While her hatred makes her object, the episode makes humanity’s commonalities very clear. How does Abe emphasize that, then? He builds upon the same principles that both cultures did. In more precise terms, his boards are full of overhead shots, as if he too was using light coming from above to formulate his solution.

As we reach the next episode, we witness Sitara steeling her resolve, but also more organic extensions of the source material. Timeskips are rather common across Jaadugar, and the anime will often spare some time to showcase life around the protagonist at that specific point in time. As she begins blending into Mongol, much of this additional material focuses on animals, which play a central role in their society. This choice also directly connects with the big swing that follows in the story: Genghis Khan, whom we’ve seen more as a symbol than a human being, has passed away. The almighty empire is suddenly trembling, and the anime’s portrayal of this shift is this episode’s most inspired choice. Drawing from the mythology around his ancestry, a painterly sequence animated by Bruno Carvalho depicts his passing as that of a majestic wolf. This is then followed by a falling star, incorporating the main motif of the series—one linked to all this shared knowledge, as well as the protagonist’s name.

The main culprit behind this rightfully ostentatious delivery is storyboarder and director Tomohisa Shimoyama, who tackles events that will change human history altogether and gives them extra oomph through grand, sweeping camerawork. While it’s occasionally a bit excessive, the reason this episode and the next one don’t land with quite as much elegance is that the rougher edges of the production begin to show. Jaadugar is far from the most troubled productions you’ll encounter on television, but Saru are a chronically busy studio. They were under a genius workaholic like founder Masaaki Yuasa, and they’ve remained that way even after multiple leadership changes.

As brilliant as their personnel often are, both the in-house folks and the key freelancers who keep assisting them, they lack the infrastructure to pump out high-quality work at the rate they attempt. Dandadan’s emergency split cours wasn’t an unexpected occurrence, and neither is the fact that Yoshida has been publicly critical of Jaadugar‘s schedule and his workload. Because his standards are high and he’s not used to the messiness of modern TV anime, the chief animator has gone as far as wondering if everyone actually understood what their job entails. Given that this is mismatch of expectations is related to the changes in roles like layouts, his words sparked industry-wide conversations, as well as wishes to work in more traditional and fundamentally sound projects.

Even in this less polished stretch, Jaadugar continues to pack a punch. The series subverts your expectations—unless you do know your history—by appointing the calm Ögedei as Genghis Khan’s successor, rather than the fiery Tolui. Then, it does so again by painting the latter as a perfectly supportive younger sibling, not a military-crazed attempt to usurp the throne. And yet, this stability may just be an illusion. Sitara is sent as a spy by Sorghaghtani, but in the process, she accidentally becomes entangled with Töregene. Ögedei’s sixth wife and first hater is struck by a particular expression: a calm, smiling hatred she has seen before. She goes out of her way to save the clumsy spy, during a tail end of the episode that noticeably raises the bar of quality.

As if to anticipate the arrival of one of the most dramatic, headstrong personalities in the show, Shinsaku Sasaki’s storyboard and Norikazu Ishigouoka’s processing feel much more intense than usual; vivid reds oozing with violence, tragic silhouettes, oppressive framing. It’s Töregene’s expression work that stands out as the highlight of the week, however. It was a specific smile that made her approach Sitara, so even in an episode that has to preserve energy, it makes sense that they went the extra length for this subtly stunning range of pain, numbness, and perhaps hope.

Although we pointed to some production roughness when explaining why some episodes don’t feel as polished as others, there’s also a dynamic as standard as what we just mentioned: prioritization. It’s no exaggeration to say that episode #06 is the most important episode since the premiere, a pivotal point deserving of a particularly focused effort. You could tell this was going to be the case even before the broadcast, with the announcement that the storyboard would be penned by Masashi Ando. If your knowledge of anime creators is limited to TV, that might not ring much of a bell. After all, Ando is a theatrical master, raised at Ghibli and once Satoshi Kon’s right-hand man. He rarely ever steps into TV anime projects, and if you’re wondering about the previous show lucky enough to feature him as a storyboarder, that would be none; his friend Yoshida can claim to be the first person to get Ando to agree to chart a full episode of television.

What is Ando like, then? We’ve written about him previously, in the context of the legendary studio he hails from but also in the way he once elevated a certain blockbuster director’s acting in ways he hasn’t seen before or since. Above all else, he’s a technically superlative animator who deeply values coherence and logic in animation. He’s not all the way bought into realistic motion as artists he’s close to like Hiroyuki Okiura are, but it’s clear that he wants animation to be sustained by consistent, though-out reasoning—be it on mechanical or emotional levels. As this episode edged closer, fans took it as an opportunity to bring up how that once caused his fallout with Hayao Miyazaki; a relationship thankfully fixed by now, as seen in The Boy and the Heron. Decades ago, though, the clash between his desire for coherence and Miyazaki’s more chaotic genius caused strife between the leading creatives behind Princess Mononoke and Spirited Away.

In more recent times, Ando’s most notable work is 2022’s The Deer King, which he ended up co-directing with Masayuki Miyaji while providing the designs, animation supervision, and part of the storyboard. It’s easy to draw links between that film and Jaadugar’s sixth episode, beginning with the fact that it may very well be payback to his pal; Yoshida helped him out as an animator in the movie, so it’s only fair that Ando contributes to a show where he’s leading the animation efforts. But beyond any causality, there are similarities between both works that make him feel especially fitting for this challenge. The Deer King may be completely fictional, but author Nahoko Uehashi majored in cultural anthropology and always imbues her fantasy with a historical feeling. After making a film about a story of hers, where different factions face an empire, featuring familiar cultural relationships with animals and even certain types of buildings, Ando was prepared as anyone to tackle a crucial episode of Jaadugar.

Töregene’s story begins 25 years in the past, as a member of the Naiman being offered as tribute to their allied people of the Merkits. She’s somewhat resigned to being effectively treated like an object, as her dolling up presents a good opportunity for Ando to show that thoroughness of his; the highly precise way her hair is braided may remind you that he felt compelled to draw reference sheets for that specific act in Your Name. As she’s shipped to what she believes to be a barbarian group, a specific cut inside a cart may be the first sign that someone is willing to tweak Jaadugar’s aesthetic rules. While even Naoko Yamada held back on her photographic instincts, episode #06 director Kotaro Matsunaga offers a more distinctly digital rendition of light—one of his sharpest weapons in the past. Be it in these subtle ways or during grander moments, lighting in this episode has a more modern spin to it. It doesn’t clash with the rest of the show, as it continues to build light on cel and BG layers in similarly nostalgic ways, but definitely comes across as more dazzling.

One such moment happens when she hears about local myths from her new family. While it’s hard to compete with Tomato Soup’s elegance, the anime’s striking choices of color, the way the river motifs are reflected in her expressions, and this newfound shininess sell the awe she feels. In the blink of an eye, Töregene goes from planning to escape to finding a place she belongs. Those with a keen eye may have noticed that, during the montage that conveys this change, we see her lying on the ground like she did in her birthplace, but more open to the world and closely accompanied.

Sadly, Töregene’s happiness is short-lived. As the Merkits move around at a worrying pace even for a nomadic group, the skirmishes they’ve been running away from catch up to them and she’s finally exposed to the truth. She was in fact given away to strengthen an alliance between different people to fight off Genghis Khan, but the Mongol menace can no longer be escaped. Her current husband consults the heavens about what they should do, in what may very well be the greatest scene in the entire show. His tribute dance manages to combine solemnity with raw emotion, really feeling like a desperate plea for her that is answered by a larger-than-life force.

Their response, though, doesn’t please Töregene. The Merkit leader foresees the defeat of their clan, but refusing to let that mean the death of their people, he appears to stage a more peaceful surrender. Their daughter Khulan will be offered as tribute to the Mongol empire, a familiar sad fate that Töregene hopelessly protests against. And yet, this heartbreak is only the beginning. Töregene witnesses the men in the tribe become slaves, and soon after that, their complete defeat after they secretly stage a rebellion fueled by hatred they only hid for long enough to protect some members of the clan. Her realization and haste as she finds out about their plan is brought to life by the legendary Toshiyuki Inoue, once again brought over to handle 2D horses that right about any other active animator would find too cumbersome to draw. However, it’s way too late. Töregene arrives when the forces led by Ödegei have already slaughtered everyone, under red skies that the Mongol prince believes to be the soul of the priest he’s had to slay.

Fascinated by her expression, Ögedei takes her as his wife. A short cut shows a horse crushing a bow, signifying the squashing of this rebellion of a puny archer tribe against the new lords of the steppes. Töregene can’t even be consoled by Khulan, who smiles coldly as she says that her foolish people had deserved it. It’s only now, after seeing Sitara down a similar expression, that Töregene can finally process how one could react that way. She may have lowered her head to remain alive, even had children with Ögedei, but she’s been waiting for the right person to stir the type of storm that can shake a whole empire. And now she has found her. As we’ll see in the following weeks, Jaadugar’s politics become increasingly more important, but the series’ interest in those remains rooted in personal circumstances like Sitara’s and Töregene’s. Nailing episode #06 was perhaps the most important challenge for this adaptation, and they’ve responded with one of the greatest episodes of 2026.
